claim: NVIDIA NIM for Object Detection automatically selects optimized inference profiles based on hardware compatibility, backend preference, and precision to improve model performance.
premises: NVIDIA NIM for Object Detection automatically leverages model- and hardware-specific optimizations intended to improve the performance of the models.

The NIM uses the TensorRT backend for Triton Inference Server for optimized inference of common models across a number of NVIDIA GPUs. If an optimized engine does not exist for a SKU being used, a GPU-agnostic ONNX backend (using the CUDA Execution Provider) is used instead.
The NIM includes multiple optimization profiles, catered to floating point precision types supported by each SKU.
Object Detection NIM is designed to automatically select the most suitable profile from the list of compatible profiles based on the detected hardware.
Each profile consists of different parameters that influence the selection process.

The automatic selection process considers compatibility check (excluding profiles not runnable with detected GPU count and model), backend (preferring TensorRT over ONNX or PyTorch), and precision (preferring lower precision like FP8 before FP16).

claim: Users can override automatic profile selection in NVIDIA NIM for Object Detection by setting a specific profile ID via the NIM_MODEL_PROFILE environment variable in the docker run command.
premises: To override automatic profile selection, set a specific profile ID in the docker run command by including -e NIM_MODEL_PROFILE=<value>.
The following command lists the available profiles: dockerrun--rm--runtime=nvidia--gpus=all$IMG_NAMElist-model-profiles
To run list-model-profiles on a host with no available GPUs, include -e NIM_CPU_ONLY=1 in the docker run command.
In the previous example, set -e NIM_MODEL_PROFILE="2cb47b75c3764c26fcfd9d257cf4337e31ecf9a8dbdb2525c93c0678a2ff851a" to run the RTX4090 FP16 Batch Size of 1 profile.

These examples should be representative of the type of data that you expect to receive in a production setting.
The dataset should be formatted as a JSONL file where each line contains a {"image": ...} object, as shown in the following example.

The command includes: exportRELEASE="25.02" dockerrun-it--rm --gpus=all --network="host" --mounttype=bind,source=${PWD}/datasets,target=/datasets nvcr.io/nvidia/tritonserver:${RELEASE}-py3-sdk

The command is: genai-perf profile \--model nvidia/nemotron-page-elements-v3 \--service-kind openai \--endpoint-type image_retrieval \--batch-size-image 1 \--input-file assets/images.jsonl \--concurrency 1 \--url http://localhost:8000

claim: The NVIDIA NIM for Object Detection API provides inference via the v1/infer endpoint to detect page elements, table structures, and graphic elements using base64-encoded PNG or JPEG images.
premises: The v1/infer endpoint accepts multiple images and returns a list of bounding boxes for each image.
The only supported type is image_url.
Each image must be base64 encoded and represented as {"type":"image_url","url":"data:image/<IMAGE_FORMAT>;base64,<BASE64_ENCODED_IMAGE>".
The supported image formats are png and jpeg.
The Object Detection NIM supports multiple models for page element, table structure, and graphic element detection.
The API is the same for all models.

claim: The API supports visualization of detection results using Python with the requests and Pillow libraries to draw bounding boxes and labels on images.
premises: The Python example demonstrates encoding an image, sending it to the v1/infer endpoint, and visualizing results.
The example requires the requests and Pillow libraries, installable via pip.
The visualize_detections function loads the image, draws bounding boxes using colors mapped to element types (table: red, chart: green, title: blue), and adds labels with confidence scores.
The image is saved with overlaid boxes and labels to an output path.

claim: The API returns structured JSON responses containing detected elements with bounding box coordinates and confidence scores, along with usage metadata.
premises: The JSON response includes a 'data' array with detection results per image.
Each detection contains 'bounding_boxes' categorized by element type (e.g., table, chart, title, paragraph, header_footer).
Each bounding box includes x_min, y_min, x_max, y_max, and confidence fields.
The response also includes a 'usage' object reporting images_size_mb.

claim: The API defines specific error responses for invalid inputs, request issues, and service status, each with defined resolutions.
premises: Common error responses include 422 for invalid image URL format, invalid base64 content, or malformed request.
429 errors occur when the request queue is full.
500 indicates internal server error.
503 indicates service not ready during initialization.
Each error type has a description and resolution in the error table.

claim: NVIDIA NIM for NV-CLIP uses Docker containers, with each NIM having its own container and multiple configuration methods available.

claim: In homogeneous GPU environments, the --gpus all argument can be used with docker run, while heterogeneous environments require specifying compute-capable GPUs via --gpus or CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES.
premises: You can use the --gpus all argument to docker run in homogeneous environments with one or more of the same GPU.
In heterogeneous environments with a combination of GPUs, such as a A6000 Ada and a GeForce display GPU, you should only run workloads on compute-capable GPUs.

Use either of the following options to identify specific GPUs: The --gpus flag. For example: --gpus='"device=1"' . The environment variable CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES . For example: -e CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=1 .
Use the nvidia-smi -L command to get the device ID(s) to use as input(s).

claim: Environment variables such as NGC_API_KEY, NIM_CACHE_PATH, NIM_LOG_LEVEL, NIM_HTTP_API_PORT, NIM_MANIFEST_PROFILE, and NIM_ENABLE_OTEL can be passed to a NIM container via docker run -e to configure its behavior.
premises: You can pass the following environment variables to a NIM as an argument to the docker run command. For example: docker run -e NGC_API_KEY=$NGC_API_KEY , where $NGC_API_KEY is the value of your NGC API key:
NGC_API_KEY | Yes | None | You must set this variable to the value of your personal NGC API key.
NIM_CACHE_PATH | No | /opt/nim/.cache | Location (in container) where the container caches model artifacts.
NIM_LOG_LEVEL | No | DEFAULT | Log level of NV-CLIP NIM service. Possible values of the variable are DEFAULT, TRACE, DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR, CRITICAL.
NIM_HTTP_API_PORT | No | 8000 | Publish the NIM service to the prescribed port inside the container.
NIM_MANIFEST_PROFILE | No | None | Choose the manifest profile id from Profile Selection for your GPU. By default, NIM chooses the non-optimized profile id.
NIM_ENABLE_OTEL | No | 1 | Set this flag to 0 to disable OpenTelemetry instrumentation in NIMs.

claim: Mounting the /opt/nim/.cache directory (or NIM_CACHE_PATH if set) as a volume is necessary to avoid re-downloading model artifacts on each container startup, and requires proper user permissions via -u $(id -u) for host-container access.
premises: /opt/nim/.cache (or NIM_CACHE_PATH if present) | Not required, but if this volume is not mounted, the container will do a fresh download of the model each time it is brought up.
This is the directory within which models are downloaded inside the container. It is very important that this directory could be accessed from inside the container.

This can be achieved by adding the option -u $(id -u) to the docker run command. For example, to use ~/.cache/nim as the host machine directory for caching models, first do mkdir -p ~/.cache/nim before running the docker run ... command.
-v ~/.cache/nim:/opt/nim/.cache -u $(id -u)

Surface predictions are computed at each cell of the input mesh; volume predictions are computed on a point cloud around the vehicle, with the exact number controlled by point_cloud_size.
The /v1/infer endpoint computes both volume and surface predictions. Additionally, /v1/infer/surface and /v1/infer/volume are available for separate computation.

claim: Users can run inference with custom checkpoints by mounting them into the NIM container at /opt/nim/custom_checkpoint/checkpoint.pt.
premises: By default, when launching the NIM container, a pre-trained model checkpoint is automatically pulled from the NGC registry and used to instantiate the model.
To use a custom checkpoint, simply mount your checkpoint file into the container at runtime using Docker’s volume mounting feature.

When the NIM container starts, it checks for the presence of a checkpoint at /opt/nim/custom_checkpoint/checkpoint.pt . If this file exists, the container uses your custom checkpoint for model initialization and skips downloading the default checkpoint from NGC.

claim: Users can override the default Hydra configuration by mounting a custom YAML config file into the NIM container at /opt/nim/custom_config/config.yaml.
premises: By default, the NIM uses its built-in Hydra configuration.
You can override it with your own YAML config by mounting a config file into the container at runtime.
On startup, the container looks for exactly one .yaml file under /opt/nim/custom_config/ . If one is found, it is used as the model configuration (overrides the default Hydra config).

claim: The NIM container supports multi-GPU inference by automatically distributing incoming requests across available GPUs when started with the --gpus all flag.
premises: The NIM container is built to fully leverage systems with multiple GPUs.
When multiple GPUs are available, the inference server can automatically distribute incoming requests across the available devices, allowing for concurrent processing and improved throughput.
Each inference request is assigned to a specific GPU, ensuring that different requests can be executed in parallel on different GPUs.
Start your container with the --gpus all option to enable the use of all available GPUs on your system.

claim: The NIM supports flexible batched inference where the batch size is configurable via the batch_size parameter to optimize performance and GPU utilization.
premises: The NIM supports flexible batched inference, allowing efficient processing of large numbers of query points.
During inference, the set of query points is automatically divided into batches, and each batch is processed sequentially until all points have been evaluated.
The batch size used for inference is configurable via the batch_size parameter in the inference endpoints.
By adjusting this parameter, users can optimize performance and maximize GPU utilization based on the available hardware resources.
Selecting an appropriate batch size helps balance memory usage and throughput.

claim: Users can perform inference on custom volume point clouds by providing a .npy file via the point_cloud parameter instead of using point_cloud_size.
premises: By default, for volume predictions, the NIM samples query points within the computational domain using a uniform random distribution.
However, users may wish to use a different set of query points, such as a custom point cloud with higher density near the car surface or a point cloud derived from simulation mesh nodes.

To enable this, instead of specifying the point_cloud_size parameter, users can provide the point_cloud parameter, which should point to a .npy file containing the desired point cloud coordinates (with shape (N, 3)).

claim: For very large point clouds, users can partition volume inference across multiple requests using the chunked parallel requests pattern to reduce wall-clock time.
premises: For very large point clouds, you can partition volume inference across multiple requests while issuing a single surface request, then merge the results client‑side.
Volume endpoint: /v1/infer/volume (send partitioned point clouds)
Surface endpoint: /v1/infer/surface (send once)
This pattern lets Triton schedule chunks across multiple instances/GPUs to reduce wall‑clock time.
Returned volume arrays are shaped as (1, N_chunk, F) per chunk, so concatenate along axis 1 to get (1, N_total, F).

claim: Configuring a local cache directory is highly recommended to avoid re-downloading large model files upon subsequent container restarts.
premises: An essential variable to configure on your host system is the cache path directory. This directory is mapped from the host machine to the container; assets (for example, model weights) are downloaded to this host directory and persist across container restarts. Configuring a local cache is highly recommended, as it avoids re-downloading large model files upon subsequent container restarts.

Because containers are ephemeral, any data stored only inside the container is lost when it stops. By using a volume mount, subsequent container runs detect the existing model files in your local cache and skip the lengthy download process, allowing the NIM to start up faster.

claim: The cache directory on your host must be writable by GID 0 to ensure the NIM container can write to it without permission errors.

claim: Persistent storage for the model cache must be configured using one of four mutually-exclusive options: Persistent Volume Claims, Persistent Volume Claim templates, Direct NFS, or hostPath, each with specific conditions and trade-offs.
premises: Running out of storage space is always a concern when setting up NIMs, and downloading models can delay scaling in a cluster.
Models can be quite large, and a cluster operator can quickly fill disk space when downloading them.
Be sure to mount some type of persistent storage for the model cache on your pod.

You have the following mutually-exclusive options when storing objects outside of the default of an emptyDir: Persistent Volume Claims (enabled with persistence.enabled), Persistent Volume Claim templates (enabled with persistence.enabled and leaving statefulSet.enabled as default), Direct NFS (enabled with nfs.enabled), hostPath (enabled with hostPath.enabled)

claim: OpenTelemetry tracing and metrics can be enabled by setting specific environment variables in a custom values.yaml file, requiring the collector to run as a DaemonSet using host ports.
premises: NVIDIA recommends that during the installation of OpenTelemetry collectors in Kubernetes, you set these environment variables in a custom values.yaml file to enable trace and metrics collection through OpenTelemetry.
This version requires that you configure the collector to run using the host ports and install it as a DaemonSet.
If you use a different configuration when installing the collector, set the OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT variable to the correct ingestion URL.

claim: The NIM service exposes an OpenAI-compatible API endpoint on port 8000 by default, accessible via port-forwarding for local inference testing.
premises: In the previous example, the OpenAI compatible API endpoint is exposed on port 8000 through the Kubernetes service of the default type with no ingress, since authentication is not handled by the NIM itself.
Use the following command to port-forward the service to your local machine to test inference: kubectl port-forward service/my-nim-nim-vlm 8000:http-openai

claim: Pod startup failures during 'Preparing model workspace' are likely due to model weights not finishing downloading before startup probe thresholds are exceeded, especially with large models or slow networks.
premises: One of the last log messages was about, 'Preparing model workspace. This step might download additional files to run the model.' Why did it fail during that?
It is likely that the model weights had not finished downloading, but Kubernetes hit a threshold of failures for startup probes.
Try increasing startupProbe.failureThreshold. This is especially likely with large models or very slow network connections.

claim: Scaling or upgrading a deployment with statefulset.enabled: false and persistence.enabled: true requires a ReadWriteMany storage class to allow PVCs to be mounted on separate nodes.
premises: I tried to scale or upgrade a deployment using statefulset.enabled: false and persistence.enabled: true . Why are pods never starting?

To scale or upgrade without using StatefulSet PVC templates, which is not very efficient in either time or storage, you must use a ReadWriteMany storage class so that it can be mounted on separate nodes, manually cloned ReadOnlyMany volumes or something like direct NFS storage.
A ReadWriteMany storage class such NFS PVC provisioner or CephFS provisioner is ideal.

claim: A NIM Model profile defines the model engines NIM can use and the criteria for selecting those engines, with each profile uniquely identified by a hash-based string.
premises: A NIM Model profile defines two things – what model engines NIM can use and what criteria NIM should use to choose those engines.
Unique strings based on a hash of the profile contents identify each profile.

claim: Users can manually select a NIM Model profile at deployment time by setting the NIM_MODEL_PROFILE environment variable to a valid profile ID or its corresponding name.
premises: Users may select a profile at deployment time by following the Profile Selection steps.
To select a profile for deployment, set a specific profile ID with -e NIM_MODEL_PROFILE=<value>.
You can find the valid profile IDs by using the list-model-profiles utility.

To select, you can set -e NIM_MODEL_PROFILE="tensorrt_llm-A100-fp16-tp1-throughput" or -e NIM_MODEL_PROFILE="751382df4272eafc83f541f364d61b35aed9cce8c7b0c869269cea5a366cd08c" to run the A100 TP1 profile.

claim: If no profile is manually selected, NIM automatically chooses the most suitable profile based on hardware detection and a predefined sorting logic involving compatibility, backend, precision, optimization target, and tensor parallelism.
premises: If the user does not manually select a profile at deployment time, NIM will automatically choose a profile according to the rules in Automatic Profile Selection.
NIM is designed to automatically select the most suitable profile from the list of compatible profiles based on the detected hardware.
Each profile consists of different parameters, which influence the selection process.
The sorting logic based on the parameters involved is outlined below: Compatibility Check, Backend, Precision, Optimization Profile, Tensor Parallelism.

claim: NIM microservices use two main profile categories: optimized profiles for specific GPU-model combinations with hardware-specific optimizations, and generic profiles as fallbacks using vLLM when optimized engines are unavailable.
premises: NIM microservices have two main categories of profiles: optimized and generic.
Optimized profiles are created for a subset of GPUs and models and leverage model- and hardware-specific optimizations intended to improve the performance of large language models.
Over time, the breadth of models and GPUs for which optimized engines exist will increase.
However, if an optimized engine does not exist for a particular model and GPU configuration combination, a generic backend is used as a fallback.
Currently, optimized profiles leverage pre-compiled TensorRT-LLM engines, while generic profiles utilize vLLM.

claim: Optimized NIM profiles are categorized by optimization target—latency or throughput—where latency variants minimize Time to First Token and Inter-Token Latency using additional GPUs, and throughput variants maximize tokens per second per GPU by using the minimum required GPUs.
premises: Optimized profiles can have different optimization targets, catered to minimize latency or maximize throughput.
These engine profiles are tagged as latency and throughput respectively, in the model manifest included with the NIM.
Latency profiles are designed to minimize: Time to First Token (TTFT) and Inter-Token Latency (ITL).
Throughput profiles are designed to maximize: Total Throughput per GPU.
Throughput variants utilize the minimum number of GPUs required to host a model (typically constrained by memory utilization).
Latency variants use additional GPUs to decrease request latency at the cost of decreased total throughput per GPU relative to the throughput variant.

claim: Quantized NIM profiles, such as those using fp8 precision, are preferred by default when available due to reduced memory requirements and improved latency and throughput, while maintaining equivalent accuracy to fp16 profiles through rigorous testing.
premises: For some models and GPU configurations, quantized engines with reduced numerical precision are available.

These can be identified by the numeric format included in the profile name. For example, fp8 for models that have been quantized to 8-bit floating point values as opposed to fp16 for non-quantized 16-bit floating point values.
All quantized engines are rigorously tested to meet the same accuracy criteria as the default fp16 engines.

Because of this accuracy, testing, and quantization lead to reduced memory requirements and, therefore, significant improvements in latency and throughput, fp8 models are chosen by default where available.
To deploy non-quantized fp16 engines, follow the Profile Selection steps.

claim: NVIDIA NIM for vision language models (VLMs) should run on any NVIDIA GPU with sufficient memory, but this is not guaranteed.
premises: Unless specified otherwise, NVIDIA NIM for vision language models (VLMs) should, but are not guaranteed to, run on any NVIDIA GPU, provided the GPU has sufficient memory.
NIM for VLMs offers competitive performance through a custom vLLM backend. Any NVIDIA GPU with sufficient memory should be able to run this model, though this is not guaranteed.

claim: NVIDIA NIM for VLMs can run on multiple homogeneous NVIDIA GPUs with sufficient aggregate memory and a CUDA compute capability of >= 7.0 (8.0 for bfloat16) unless otherwise specified.
premises: They can also run on multiple homogeneous NVIDIA GPUs with sufficient aggregate memory and a CUDA compute capability of >= 7.0 (8.0 for bfloat16) unless otherwise specified.

claim: NVIDIA NIM for VLMs does not support NVIDIA Virtual GPU (vGPU) environments.
premises: NVIDIA NIM for VLMs does not support NVIDIA Virtual GPU (vGPU) environments.

claim: The nvidia/nemotron-3-content-safety model is supported in VLM release version 2.0.0.
premises: The nvidia/nemotron-3-content-safety model ( NGC catalog page ) is supported in the following VLM release version:

claim: GPU Memory and Disk Space values in the configuration table are expressed in GB.
premises: The GPU Memory and Disk Space values are in GB.

claim: The 'Any' GPU configuration requires greater than 14 GB of memory, uses BF16 precision, supports 1 or 2 GPUs, and requires 9 GB of disk space.
The H100 GPU configuration requires 80 GB of memory, uses BF16 precision, supports 1 or 2 GPUs, and requires 9 GB of disk space.
The H200 GPU configuration requires 141 GB of memory, uses BF16 precision, supports 1 or 2 GPUs, and requires 9 GB of disk space.
The B200 GPU configuration requires 192 GB of memory, uses BF16 precision, supports 1 or 2 GPUs, and requires 9 GB of disk space.
NIM provides Prometheus metrics for request statistics that are available by default at http://localhost:8000/v1/metrics.
premises: NIM provides Prometheus metrics indicating request statistics.
By default, these metrics are available at http://localhost:8000/v1/metrics.

claim: The available NIM metrics include KV cache usage, request counts, token counts, latency histograms, and image-related metrics, all collected per model and per iteration or per request.
premises: The following table describes the available metrics.
KV Cache Count: GPU Cache Usage (gpu_cache_usage_perc), Running Count (num_requests_running), Waiting Count (num_requests_waiting), Max Request Count (num_request_max)
Total Prompt Token Count (prompt_tokens_total), Total Generation Token Count (generation_tokens_total)
Latency metrics: Time to First Token, Time per Output Token, End to End Request Latency, Vision Encoder Latency (all in seconds)
Count metrics: Prompt Token Count, Generation Token Count, Finished Request Count, Successful Request Count, Failed Request Count, Image Count, Image size (all histograms)
All metrics have Granularity: Per model and Frequency: Per iteration or Per request

claim: Prometheus can be installed and configured to scrape NIM metrics from localhost:8000/v1/metrics by downloading the binary, editing prometheus.yml to set targets to localhost:8000, and running the server.
premises: To install Prometheus for scraping metrics from NIM, download the latest Prometheus version appropriate for your system.
Edit the Prometheus configuration file prometheus.yml to scrape from the NIM endpoint. Make sure the targets field point to localhost:8000.
Run the Prometheus server: ./prometheus --config.file=./prometheus.yml
Open a browser and point it to http://localhost:9090/targets?search= to check that the NIM target was detected

claim: Grafana can be installed and configured to visualize NIM metrics by connecting to a Prometheus data source at localhost:9090 after setting up the server and logging in with default credentials.
premises: We can use Grafana for dashboarding NIM metrics. Install the latest Grafana version appropriate for your system.
Run the Grafana server: ./bin/grafana-server
To access the Grafana dashboard, point your browser to http://localhost:3000. You will need to log in using the defaults: username: admin, password: admin
The first step is to configure the source from which Grafana can scrape metrics. Click on the “Data Source” button, select Prometheus, and specify the Prometheus URL localhost:9090.
After saving the configuration, you should see a success message.

claim: Vision-related metrics such as Vision Encoder Latency are only available when NIM uses the TRT-LLM backend, not the vLLM backend, which only collects end-to-end metrics.
premises: Vision-related metrics (e.g., Vision Encoder Latency) are only available for the TRT-LLM backend
the vLLM backend only collects end-to-end metrics

claim: Function calling allows NIM to connect to external tools and services by outputting function arguments that can be executed to augment prompts with external information.
premises: You can connect NIM to external tools and services using function calling (also known as tool calling).
By providing a list of available functions, NIM can choose to output function arguments for the relevant function(s) which you can execute to augment the prompt with relevant external information.

claim: The tool_choice and tools parameters must be set together to control function calling behavior in NIM.
premises: Function calling is controlled using the tool_choice and tools request parameters.
tool_choice can only be set when tools is also set.
These parameters work together to define and control the use of tools in the model’s responses.

claim: To minimize tool-related output when tools are not needed, omit the tools parameter entirely rather than setting tool_choice to 'none'.
premises: To minimize tool-related output when tools are not needed, omit the tools parameter entirely instead of passing tools with tool_choice: 'none'.

claim: A 400 Bad Request error when using tools may result from insufficient max_tokens, and can be resolved by increasing max_tokens.
premises: A 400 (Bad Request) response for this interface can also occur when a tool call does not complete because max_tokens is too small.
If you receive a 400 error when using tools, try increasing max_tokens.

claim: The 'auto' tool_choice setting enables the model to autonomously decide whether and which tools to use based on the user query.
premises: tool_choice: 'auto' : Enables the model to decide whether to use tools and which ones to use.

claim: The 'required' tool_choice setting forces the model to generate one or more tool calls based on the provided tools list, with the number of calls depending on the user’s query.
premises: tool_choice: 'required' : Forces the model to generate one or more tool calls based on the specified tool list in the tools parameter. The number of tool calls depends on the user’s query.

claim: A named tool choice forces the model to use a specific tool by specifying its name in a structured JSON format.
premises: Named tool choice: Forces the model to use a specific tool. It must be in the following format: {"type":"function","function":{"name":"name of the tool goes here"}}
The type field is optional and defaults to function if not specified.

claim: In the Basic Function Calling example, the model correctly outputs a function call for get_current_weather with location and format parameters when queried about San Francisco weather in Fahrenheit.
premises: The user asks: 'What is the weather in San Francisco, CA in Fahrenheit?'
The weather_tool is defined with parameters for location (string) and format (enum: celsius/fahrenheit), both required.
The model outputs a tool_call with arguments: {'location': 'San Francisco, CA', 'format': 'fahrenheit'} for the get_current_weather function.

claim: In the Multiple Tools example, the model selects the time_tool (which requires no parameters) when asked for the current time in New York, demonstrating support for tools with empty parameter lists.
premises: The user asks: 'What's the current time in New York?'
Two tools are provided: weather_tool (requires location and format) and time_tool (get_current_time_nyc with empty parameters).
The model outputs a tool_call for get_current_time_nyc with empty arguments: {}.

claim: In the Named Tool Usage example, the model is forced to use the get_current_weather tool via a named tool choice, resulting in a function call for New York City weather in Fahrenheit.
premises: The user asks: 'What's the weather in New York City like?'
The tool_choice is set to a named tool choice: {"type":"function","function":{"name":"get_current_weather"}}.
The model outputs a tool_call with arguments: {'location': 'New York City, NY', 'format': 'fahrenheit'} for the get_current_weather function.

claim: NVIDIA NIM for VLMs runs in Docker containers and requires configuration via Docker run options.
premises: NVIDIA NIM for VLMs runs in Docker containers. Each NIM has its own container and several configuration options.
This page is a reference for configuring a NIM container.

claim: In homogeneous GPU environments, --gpus all can be used, but in heterogeneous environments, only compute-capable GPUs should be targeted using specific device exposure methods.
premises: Passing --gpus all to docker run is acceptable in homogeneous environments with one or more of the same GPU.
In heterogeneous environments with a combination of GPUs (A6000 + a GeForce display GPU), workloads should only run on compute-capable GPUs.
Expose specific GPUs inside the container using either: The --gpus flag (for example, --gpus='"device=1"') or The environment variable CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES (for example, -e CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=1)
The device ID(s) to use as input(s) are listed in the output of nvidia-smi -L

claim: The number of GPUs required to run a NIM profile is determined by multiplying its TP (Tensor Parallelism) and PP (Pipeline Parallelism) values.
premises: Each profile will have a TP (Tensor Parallelism) and PP (Pipeline Parallelism), decipherable through their readable name (for example, tensorrt_llm-trtllm_buildable-bf16-tp8-pp2).
In most cases, you will need TP * PP amount of GPUs to run a specific profile.
For example, for the profile tensorrt_llm-trtllm_buildable-bf16-tp8-pp2 you will need either 2 nodes with 8 GPUs or 2 * 8 = 16 GPUs on one Node.

claim: The --shm-size=32GB flag should be passed to docker run for shared memory, except when using single GPU models or GPUs with NVLink enabled.
premises: Pass --shm-size=32GB to docker run.
Not required for single GPU models or GPUs with NVLink enabled.

claim: Environment variables can be passed into a NIM container using the -e flag with docker run.
premises: Environment variables can be passed into a NIM ( -e with docker run ).

claim: The /opt/nim/.cache directory (or NIM_CACHE_PATH if set) should be mounted as a volume to avoid re-downloading models on each container start, and the container must be run with appropriate user permissions to access it.
premises: /opt/nim/.cache (or NIM_CACHE_PATH if present) is the directory within which models are downloaded inside the container.
If this volume is not mounted, the container will do a fresh download of the model each time it is brought up.
This directory must be accessible from inside the container, which can be achieved by adding the option -u $(id -u) to the docker run command.

For example, to use ~/.cache/nim as the host machine directory for caching models, first do mkdir -p ~/.cache/nim before running the docker run command, then use -v ~/.cache/nim:/opt/nim/.cache -u $(id -u).

claim: NVIDIA NIM for VLMs can load models from Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI) Object Storage using the Amazon S3 Compatibility API.
premises: NVIDIA NIM for VLMs supports loading models from Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI) Object Storage using the Amazon S3 Compatibility API.
Use this option when models are hosted in an OCI Object Storage bucket and you want NVIDIA NIM for VLMs to fetch and serve them directly from OCI Object Storage using the S3-compatible API.

claim: To use OCI Object Storage with NVIDIA NIM for VLMs, the environment must have an OCI S3-compatible endpoint, a model path, and AWS-style credentials.
premises: Ensure that your environment meets the following requirements:
- An OCI S3-compatible endpoint: The URL of your OCI Object Storage bucket that supports the S3 API. NVIDIA NIM for VLMs uses this endpoint to connect to your OCI Object Storage.
- A model path: The path to the model repository in the OCI Object Storage bucket. This tells NVIDIA NIM for VLMs where to find and load your models.
- Credentials: AWS-style credentials for the S3-compatible endpoint. Provide these using either environment variables or a shared credentials file.

claim: The OCI S3-compatible endpoint must be set via the AWS_ENDPOINT_URL environment variable using the format https://<namespace>.compat.objectstorage.<region>.oraclecloud.com.
premises: Set AWS_ENDPOINT_URL to the OCI Object Storage S3-compatible endpoint:
``` -eAWS_ENDPOINT_URL="https://<namespace>.compat.objectstorage.<region>.oraclecloud.com" ```

claim: The model repository location in OCI Object Storage is specified using the NIM_MODEL_NAME environment variable in the format s3repo://<org>/<model-repo>[:<version>] or s3repo://<bucket>/<org>/<model-name>[:<version>].
premises: Set NIM_MODEL_NAME to the model repository directory in the following format:
``` s3repo://<org>/<model-repo>[:<version>] ```
Alternatively, you can specify the bucket explicitly:
``` s3repo://<bucket>/<org>/<model-name>[:<version>] ```
Review the following model path examples:
- s3repo://mistralai/mistralai-ministral-14b
- s3repo://mistralai/mistralai-ministral-14b:1.7.0
Review the following explicit bucket example:
- s3repo://mistral-models/mistralai/mistralai-ministral-14b

claim: AWS-style credentials for authenticating with the OCI S3-compatible endpoint are provided via environment variables AWS_REGION, AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, and optionally AWS_SESSION_TOKEN.
premises: Configure the connectivity region and credentials for the S3-compatible endpoint using the following environment variables:
- AWS_REGION
- AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID
- AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY
- AWS_SESSION_TOKEN (optional, for temporary credentials)

claim: A practical deployment example shows how to run NVIDIA NIM for VLMs with OCI Object Storage using Docker, including credential setup, model specification, and local caching.
premises: The following example uses AWS environment variables to load credentials and mounts a local cache directory to persist downloads:

``` # Choose a container name for bookkeeping export CONTAINER_NAME=mistralai-ministral-3-14b-instruct-2512 # The container name from the previous ngc registry image list command Repository="ministral-3-14b-instruct-2512" Latest_Tag="2.0.0" # Choose a VLM NIM Image from NGC export IMG_NAME="nvcr.io/nim/mistralai/${Repository}:${Latest_Tag}" # Choose a path on your system to cache the downloaded models export LOCAL_NIM_CACHE=~/.cache/nim mkdir -p "$LOCAL_NIM_CACHE" docker run -it --rm --name=$CONTAINER_NAME --runtime=nvidia --gpus all --shm-size=16GB -eNGC_API_KEY=$NGC_API_KEY -eAWS_REGION="us-sanjose-1" -eAWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=$AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID -eAWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=$AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY -eAWS_ENDPOINT_URL="https://<namespace>.compat.objectstorage.<region>.oraclecloud.com" -eNIM_MODEL_NAME="s3repo://mistralai/mistralai-ministral-14b:1.7.0" -v"$LOCAL_NIM_CACHE:/opt/nim/.cache" -u$(id -u) -p8000:8000 $IMG_NAME ```

claim: NIM VLM supports vision content safety using models like Nemotron-3-Content-Safety, a multimodal, multilingual classifier that processes text, optional images, and optional assistant responses to return safety decisions.
premises: NIM VLM supports vision content safety using certain models like Nemotron-3-Content-Safety.
This NIM is a multimodal, multilingual content-safety classifier.

It takes a user prompt (text), an optional image, and an optional assistant response, and returns a short decision string with User Safety, Response Safety (when a response is provided), and optionally Safety Categories.
Nemotron-3-Content-Safety supports 12 languages: English, Arabic, German, Spanish, French, Hindi, Japanese, Thai, Dutch, Italian, Korean, and Chinese.

claim: To classify a prompt and image without safety category breakdown, set chat_template_kwargs.request_categories to /no_categories using the Chat Completions endpoint.
premises: Use the Chat Completions endpoint to send a single user message that contains the prompt and (optionally) an image.
Request the classification without the per-category breakdown by setting chat_template_kwargs.request_categories to /no_categories.
Output is a short fixed-shape string (User Safety: ...), so streaming is unnecessary.
Example curl request includes model 'nvidia/nemotron-3-content-safety', user message with text and image_url, and chat_template_kwargs.request_categories set to /no_categories.
Expected response content: 'User Safety: unsafe'

claim: Images can be passed via public direct URL or Base64-encoded data in the HTTP payload following OpenAI specification, with SigLIP vision encoder resizing inputs to 896×896 and supporting JPG, JPEG, and PNG formats.
premises: NIM VLM follows the OpenAI specification to pass images as part of the HTTP payload in a user message.
The vision encoder (SigLIP) resizes inputs to 896 × 896.
The supported image formats are JPG, JPEG, and PNG.
Public direct URL: passing the direct URL causes the container to download the image at runtime.
Base64 data: for images not on the web, Base64-encode image bytes and send in payload using format 'data:image/jpeg;base64,...'.
Example of Base64 conversion using base64 command or Python helper: import base64; with open('image.png','rb') as f: image_b64 = base64.b64encode(f.read()).decode()

claim: To include safety categories in the response, set chat_template_kwargs.request_categories to /categories, which adds a comma-separated list of violated categories such as 'Criminal Planning/Confessions'.
premises: To include the comma-separated list of violated safety categories in the response, set chat_template_kwargs.request_categories to /categories.
Example curl request sets chat_template_kwargs.request_categories to /categories.
Expected response content includes both 'User Safety: unsafe' and 'Safety Categories: Criminal Planning/Confessions'.
The full safety-category taxonomy (Violence, Sexual, Criminal Planning, Hate/Identity Hate, PII/Privacy, and others) is documented on the model card.

claim: Text-only prompts can be classified by submitting a user message with text content only, without image data, to evaluate textual safety.
premises: Submit a text prompt without an image to classify text-only inputs.
Example curl request includes messages list with a single user message containing only text: 'How can I steal money from here?'.
Uses model 'nvidia/nemotron-3-content-safety' and chat_template_kwargs.request_categories set to /categories.

claim: To evaluate both user prompt and assistant response for safety, append an assistant message to the messages list, which triggers the classifier to return both User Safety and Response Safety assessments.
premises: To evaluate an assistant response alongside the originating prompt, append an assistant message to the messages list.
The classifier then emits both User Safety and Response Safety.

Example curl request includes a user message with text and image, and an assistant message with content: 'The best way to steal money from here is to enter the building as an old lady and ask for directions. Then pick the lock and grab as much as you can and run.'.
Expected response content: 'User Safety: unsafe', 'Response Safety: unsafe', and 'Safety Categories: Criminal Planning/Confessions'.

claim: Query request type is optimal for single-item, low-latency, interactive workloads and video data transmission.
premises: request_type: 'query' : Best for the following: Single items (1 items) Low-latency applications requiring immediate responses Interactive applications Sending video data as part of the request

claim: Bulk_text request type is optimal for high-throughput processing of large batches of text-only inputs.
premises: request_type: 'bulk_text' : Best for the following: Large batches of text-only inputs (up to 64 strings) High-throughput text processing When you have many text captions to process at once

claim: Bulk_video request type is optimal for maximum throughput in batch processing of large video batches.
premises: request_type: 'bulk_video' : Best for the following: Large batches of video-only inputs (up to 64 videos) Maximum throughput for video processing Batch processing workflows

premises: Expect proportional scaling based on decode and compute capacity across supported GPUs (e.g. L40s, L4, H20, L20). For GPUs with less memory, reduce batch/request sizes to avoid memory pressure.

claim: The NVIDIA Earth-2 Correction Diffusion (CorrDiff) NIM is a containerized service that deploys a pre-trained model to generate high-resolution weather predictions by downscaling input GEFS data via an HTTP API.
premises: The CorrDiff NIM container hosts the pre-trained model and provides an HTTP API for inference.
The end-to-end CorrDiff NIM workflow consists of four main stages: Deployment, Data Preparation, Inference, and Output Processing.
During Inference, the diffusion model generates multiple high-resolution samples (3km resolution) by correcting and downscaling the input data.
The NIM returns downscaled weather fields in NumPy array format packaged as a tar archive.
The container is launched using Docker commands that expose port 8000 for user interaction.

claim: Preparing input data for the CorrDiff NIM involves fetching and preprocessing GEFS weather data from NOAA using Earth2Studio to match the model’s expected input format.
premises: The input to the CorrDiff model is GEFS weather data at 0.25-degree (~25km) resolution over the contiguous United States, sourced from NOAA.
Earth2Studio is used to simplify data fetching and formatting.

The process includes fetching select GEFS variables at 0.25-degrees, fetching regular GEFS variables at 0.5-degrees and interpolating to 0.25-degree grid, cropping both to a U.S. bounding box, and concatenating with a forecast lead time field.
A Python script is provided to download and structure the data into a NumPy array saved as corrdiff_inputs.npy.

claim: Inference with the CorrDiff NIM is performed by sending preprocessed input data and parameters via HTTP POST to the /v1/infer endpoint, which returns a tar archive of downscaled NumPy arrays.
premises: The NumPy array is sent to the NIM as a file along with parameters like samples, steps, and seed to control the diffusion model.
The API endpoint is http://localhost:8000/v1/infer.
Example Bash and Python commands demonstrate sending input_array via curl or requests.post with file and form data.
The NIM returns a tar archive containing NumPy arrays named by sample and batch index (e.g., 000_000.npy).
Streaming responses are supported when requested sample size exceeds the NIM’s internal batch size governed by EARTH2NIM_TARGET_BATCHSIZE.

claim: Post-processing CorrDiff NIM outputs involves extracting and visualizing downscaled weather variables (e.g., surface temperature) from the returned NumPy arrays using standard Python libraries like NumPy, Matplotlib, and tarfile.
premises: The NIM returns downscaled weather fields in NumPy array format packaged as a tar archive.
The surface temperature variable is accessed via index 2 in the output array (corresponding to t2m in the variable list: [u10m, v10m, t2m, tp, csnow, cicep, cfrzr, crain]).
Example code shows loading input and output arrays, plotting the t2m variable using matplotlib with gnuplot colormap, and saving figures as PNG files.
Latitude and longitude coordinates for visualization can be obtained from corrdiff_output_lat.npy and corrdiff_output_lon.npy in the model package.

claim: The POST /v1/embeddings endpoint generates embedding vectors for text or video inputs with specific input formats and constraints depending on the request_type.
premises: Generates embedding vectors for text or video inputs. This is the primary inference endpoint.
The input field accepts the following formats: Plain Text, Base64-Encoded Video (query only), Presigned URL for Video, Video Frames (Presigned URLs), Video Frames (Base64).
query supports a single input item (text, video, or video_frames).
bulk_text supports up to 64 plain-text strings per request.
bulk_video supports up to 64 items, where each item must be one of: data:video/<type>;presigned_url,<url>, data:video_frames/<type>;presigned_url,{...}, or data:video_frames/<type>;base64,{...}.
video_frames requires exactly 8 frames per item.
Maximum inputs per request: 64 items for bulk_text and bulk_video modes.
Recommended video duration: 15 seconds; maximum recommended: 1-2 minutes; no strict maximum enforced by the NIM.
Supported codecs depend on the runtime decode stack (PyNvVideoCodec 2.0.3 / NVDEC) and host GPU/driver; common codecs include H.264, HEVC, AV1, VP8, VP9, VC1, MPEG4, MPEG2, MPEG1.
Base64-encoded full videos are accepted only in query mode.

You can pre-cache the model package of a NIM by: mounting a local folder to the cache, launching the NIM on hardware with access to NGC servers, and moving the cached model files to the respective air gapped system

Common causes and solutions: simulation_length out of range: ensure it is within the allowed range for the service (see OpenAPI schema)
Common causes and solutions: Invalid variables parameter: if provided, it must be a comma-separated list of variable IDs (e.g., t2m,z500,u10m)

Context: The OpenAPI schema requires input_array to have shape (batch size, 1, variables, latitudes, longitudes) and recommends FP32.
Additional context: The expected sizes for variables/latitudes/longitudes vary by model; refer to the model card linked in the quickstart guide.

claim: The sequence lengths (ISL and OSL) of an application's use case directly affect memory requirements and latency metrics such as TTFT and ITL during LLM inference.
premises: An application’s specific use cases influence the sequence lengths (i.e., ISL and OSL), which in turn affects how fast a system digests the input to form KV-cache and generate output tokens.
Longer ISL increase memory requirement for the prefill stage and thus TTFT, while longer OSL increase memory requirement (both bandwidth and capacity) for the generation stage and thus increase ITL.

claim: Concurrency N controls the number of active requests in LLM benchmarking, with GenAI-perf maintaining exactly N active requests throughout, while LLMperf uses batches with a draining period causing concurrent requests to drop toward zero.
premises: Concurrency N is the number of concurrent users each having one active request, or equivalently the number of requests concurrently being served by an LLM service.
As soon as each user’s request receives a complete response, another request is sent, to ensure that at any time, the system has exactly N requests.

Note about LLMperf: It sends out requests in batches of N requests, but there is a draining period where it waits for all the requests to complete, before sending out the next batch. As such, towards the end of the batch, the number of concurrent requests reduces gradually to 0.
This differs from GenAI-perf, which always ensures N active requests throughout the benchmarking period.

claim: Max batch size defines the upper limit of simultaneous requests the inference engine can process, and exceeding it relative to concurrency and replicas causes queuing and increased TTFT.
premises: Max batch size : Batch is the group of simultaneous request being processed by the inference engine.
The maximum batch size parameter defines the maximum number of requests that the inference engine can process simultaneously.
If the concurrency exceeds the maximum batch size multiplied by the number of active replicas, some requests will have to wait in a queue for later processing.
In this case you may see an increase in Time-to-first-Token value due to the queueing effect of waiting for a slot to open up.

claim: Request rate controls load by determining how frequently new requests are sent, with static or Poisson distributions, but concurrency is preferred to avoid unbounded outstanding requests.
premises: Request rate is another parameter that can be used to control load by determining the rate at which new requests are sent.
Using a constant (or static) request rate r means 1 request is sent every 1/ r seconds, while using a poisson (or exponential) request rate determines the average inter-arrival time.

GenAI-perf supports both concurrency and request rate, however we recommend using concurrency (as with request rate, the number of outstanding requests may grow unbounded if the request per second exceeds the system throughput).

claim: The ignore_eos parameter should be set to True during benchmarking to ensure consistent output length by ignoring the end-of-sequence token and generating until max_tokens is reached.
premises: Most LLMs have a special end-of-sequence (EOS) token, which signifies the end of generation.
It indicates that the LLM has generated a complete response, and should stop.
Under general usage, LLM inference should respect this signal and stop generating further tokens.
The ignore_eos parameter generally instructs whether an LLM inference framework should ignore the EOS token and continue generating tokens until reaching the max_tokens limit.
For benchmarking purposes, this parameter should be set to True, in order to reach the intended output length and obtain consistent measurement.

claim: Sampling strategy affects LLM generation speed, with greedy being computationally efficient due to avoiding normalization and sorting, and consistency in sampling method is recommended within a benchmarking setup.
premises: Different sampling strategies might have impacts on the LLM generation speed.
Greedy for example, can be implemented simply by selecting the token with the highest logit (no need for normalizing and sorting the probability distribution over tokens, thus saving on computation).
See this blog for a detailed explanation on different sampling methods.
Whichever sampling method chosen, it is a good practice to stay consistent within the same benchmarking setup.

claim: NIM supports loading and deploying multiple LoRA adapters for parameter-efficient fine-tuning of LLMs.
premises: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) methods allow for efficient fine-tuning of large pretrained models.
NIM currently supports Low-Rank Adaption (LoRA), which is a simple and efficient way to tailor LLMs for specific domains and use cases.
With NIM, users can load and deploy multiple LoRA adapters.

claim: GenAI-perf can benchmark deployment metrics for LoRA models by specifying model IDs and selection strategy.
premises: With GenAI-perf, you can benchmark the deployment metrics for LoRA models by passing the IDs of the LoRA models using the '-m' argument.

claim: Base model size influences suitability for different tasks in LoRA deployments, with smaller models favoring traditional NLP and larger models excelling at complex reasoning.
premises: Both small and large models, such as [Llama 3 8B] and [Llama 3 70B], respectively, can be used as base models for LoRA fine-tuning and inference.
Smaller models excel at many tasks, especially traditional, non-generative NLP tasks such as text classification, while larger models excel at complex reasoning tasks.

One of the advantages of LoRA is that even a large 70B model can be tuned on a single [NVIDIA DGX H100] or A100 node with FP16, or even a single [NVIDIA H100] or [NVIDIA A100] GPU with 4-bit quantization.

claim: LoRA rank selection involves a trade-off between accuracy flexibility and system performance, with common ranks being 8, 16, 32, and 64.
premises: Users typically prefer the flexibility to experiment and select the size that yields the best accuracy.
System operators, on the other hand, might prefer to enforce a fixed size, as uniform LoRAs enable better batching and performance.
The common choices for LoRA ranks are 8, 16, 32, and 64.

claim: Effective benchmarking of multi-LoRA deployments requires consideration of output length control, system load via concurrency, and task type to reflect real-world usage.
premises: Several other test parameters to be considered for benchmarking include the following: Output length control : The ignore_eos parameter directs the inference framework to continue generating text until it reaches the max_token_length limit.
This ensures that the use case OSL (output sequence length) specification is met.

System load : Concurrency (number of concurrent users) is commonly used to drive load into the system. This parameter value should reflect real use cases, while also taking into account the maximum batch size that the system can effectively serve concurrently.
For an 8B model on one GPU, consider up to 250 concurrent users as a realistic server load.

Task type : You should consider both generative and non-generative tasks. These differ in the ISL (input sequence length) and OSL. ISL in the 200 to 2000 token range, and OSL in the one to 2000 token range reflect a wide range of LLM applications: from text classification and summary to translation and code generation.

claim: NIM VLM provides environment variables to configure server and health-check ports.
premises: NIM_SERVER_PORT sets the port for the external-facing HTTP API server.

claim: NIM VLM supports dynamic LoRA adapter loading and refresh via environment variables.
premises: NIM_PEFT_SOURCE specifies the URI for the LoRA adapter source (local path or NGC URI).

NIM_PEFT_API_TIMEOUT_SECS defines the timeout in seconds for dynamic LoRA adapter API calls.

claim: NIM VLM allows configuration of model cache location and authentication for model downloads.
premises: NIM_CACHE_PATH sets the directory path for the model and artifact cache inside the NIM container.
NGC_API_KEY provides authentication for downloading models from ngc:// repositories.

MODELSCOPE_API_TOKEN is required for authenticated downloads from modelscope:// repositories and to avoid rate limiting.

claim: NIM VLM supports TLS termination configuration at the nginx proxy layer via environment variables.
premises: NIM_SSL_MODE controls TLS termination at the nginx proxy with options: DISABLED (plain HTTP, default), TLS (server-side TLS), or MTLS (mutual TLS).
NIM_SSL_KEY_PATH and NIM_SSL_CERTS_PATH are required when NIM_SSL_MODE is TLS or MTLS.
NIM_SSL_CA_CERTS_PATH is required when NIM_SSL_MODE is MTLS for client verification.

claim: NIM VLM provides environment variables to configure CORS policy at the nginx proxy layer.
premises: NIM_CORS_ALLOW_ORIGINS sets a comma-separated list of allowed request origins or * for any origin.

NIM_CORS_ALLOW_HEADERS specifies allowed request headers for CORS requests.

claim: NIM VLM supports advanced runtime configuration via environment variables for argument handling and optimization.

claim: The Cosmos NIM pipeline includes text processing, visual processing, and safety guardrail components to ensure safe and high-quality video generation.
premises: The Cosmos NIM pipeline consists of several key components that work together to ensure safe and high-quality video generation:

## Text Processing Components #: Tokenizer: Converts input text prompts into tokens that can be processed by the model. T5 Encoder: Processes tokenized text through a T5 transformer model to create rich semantic embeddings. Prompt Upsampler: Enhances the input prompt by adding relevant details and context to improve generation quality.
## Visual Processing Components #: Visual Captioning: Generates a text description of the provided image or video input.

## Safety and Guardrail Components #: The guardrail system implements multiple layers of safety checks: Text Blocklist: Filters out prohibited words and phrases. Text Guardrail: Analyzes semantic content of prompts. Video Guardrail: Examines generated video frames. Face Blur: Detects and blurs faces in generated videos to protect privacy.

claim: Cosmos-Predict1-7B uses a Transformer backbone in latent space with cross-attention for text conditioning and temporal modeling for video denoising.
premises: Model Architecture for Cosmos-Predict1-7B: Cosmos-Predict1-7B is a specialized Transformer model designed for video denoising within the latent space.

The model architecture consists of the following components: Transformer Backbone: A deep network of interleaved self-attention, cross-attention, and feedforward layers. Cross-Attention Mechanism: Enables text conditioning throughout the denoising process by attending to text embeddings. Adaptive Layer Normalization: Applied before each layer to incorporate temporal information for denoising. Temporal Modeling: Special attention mechanisms to handle the temporal aspects of video generation. Latent Space Processing: Works in a compressed latent space for efficient video generation.

The pipeline processes inputs sequentially: Text/visual input is processed through the text/visual components. Safety checks are performed on the input. The core model generates the video frames. Post-processing safety checks and face blurring are applied. The final video, meeting all quality and safety requirements, is produced.

claim: LLM inference involves sequential stages: queuing, prefill, and generation, where tokens are the fundamental units processed, and sequence lengths (ISL, OSL, context length) define input, output, and model capacity constraints.
premises: An LLM application produces results through inference. For a given specific LLM application, these are the broad stages: The user provides a query (prompt), The query gets in the queue, and waits for its turn to be processed, i.e. the queuing phase. The application’s underlying LLM model processes the prompt, i.e. the prefill phase. The LLM model outputs a response, one token at a time, i.e. the generation phase.
Token is a concept specific for LLMs and is a core LLM inference performance metric. It is the unit that LLM uses to break down and process natural language.

Sequence length is the length of the sequence of data. The Input Sequence Length (ISL) is how many tokens that the LLM gets. It includes the user query, any system prompt (eg. instructions for the model), previous chat history, chain-of-thought reasoning, and documents from the retrieval augmented generation (RAG) pipeline. The Output Sequence Length (OSL) is how many tokens the LLM makes. Context length is how many tokens the LLM uses at each generation step, including both the input and output tokens generated so far. Each LLM has a maximum context length that can be allocated to both input and output tokens.
As an approximation, for many popular LLMs, each token is ~0.75 English words.

claim: Streaming mode in LLM inference enables partial token outputs to be returned incrementally, improving perceived responsiveness in chatbot applications, whereas non-streaming mode returns the full response only after generation completes.
premises: Streaming is an option that allows the partial LLM outputs to be returned to the users, in the form of a chunk of tokens that the model incrementally generates so far. This is important for chatbot applications, where it is desirable to receive an initial response quickly. While the user digests the partial content, the next chunk of the result arrives in the background.
In contrast, in non-streaming mode, the full answer is returned all at once.

DoMINO learns local geometry encodings from point cloud representations and predicts PDE solutions on discrete points using dynamically constructed computational stencils in local regions.

By leveraging both short- and long-range geometric features, the DoMINO model accurately predicts solution fields on the vehicle’s surface as well as in the surrounding flow domain—capabilities essential for making design and engineering decisions in industrial applications.

claim: In Multimodal Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG), NV-CLIP NIM encodes text and image data into embeddings for efficient knowledge base retrieval and LLM-powered response generation.
premises: In a Multimodal Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) application, we use the embedding model to encode the knowledge base of images and texts (offline) and user question (online) into contextual embeddings, so that the LLM can retrieve the most relevant context and provide the users with the correct answers.

Encoding the knowledge base (offline): Given a knowledge base containing documents in text, PDF, HTML, or other formats, and images, we first split the knowledge base of documents into chunks, then encode each chunk into a dense vector representation, also called embedding, using an embedding model. We also encode each image into an embedding using an embedding model.
The resulting embeddings, along with their corresponding documents and other metadata, are saved in a vector database.

Deployment (online): Once deployed, the RAG application can access the vector database and answer questions in real time. To answer a user question, the RAG application first finds relevant chunks from the vector database, then it uses the retrieved chunks as context to generate a response.

Phase 1: Retrieval from the vector database based on the user’s query: The user’s query is first embedded as a dense vector using the embedding model. Then the query embedding is used to search the vector database for the most relevant document chunks and the most relevant image with respect to the user’s query.

Phase 2: Use an LLM to generate a response leveraging the retrieved context: The most relevant chunks are joined to form the context for the user query. The LLM combines the context and the user query to generate a response.

claim: NV-CLIP NIM supports zero-shot image classification and semantic image search by associating images with natural language descriptions.

A high quality embedding model improves the performance of these tasks by capturing the contextual information in the dense vector representation.

claim: Llama 3.2-Vision models support English as the only language for image+text applications, while text-only tasks support eight additional languages including German, French, Italian, Portuguese, Hindi, Spanish, and Thai.

claim: Llama 3.2-Vision models are intended for commercial and research use, including visual question answering, document visual question answering, image captioning, image-text retrieval, and visual grounding.
premises: Intended Use Cases: Llama 3.2-Vision is intended for commercial and research use. Instruction tuned models are intended for visual recognition, image reasoning, captioning, and assistant-like chat with images, whereas pretrained models can be adapted for a variety of image reasoning tasks.

Additionally, because of Llama 3.2-Vision’s ability to take images and text as inputs, additional use cases could include: Visual Question Answering (VQA) and Visual Reasoning, Document Visual Question Answering (DocVQA), Image Captioning, Image-Text Retrieval, Visual Grounding.

claim: Training the Llama 3.2-Vision models resulted in 584 tons CO2eq of location-based greenhouse gas emissions, but market-based emissions were zero due to Meta's net-zero operations and renewable energy matching.
premises: Training Greenhouse Gas Emissions: Estimated total location-based greenhouse gas emissions were 584 tons CO2eq for training.

Since 2020, Meta has maintained net zero greenhouse gas emissions in its global operations and matched 100% of its electricity use with renewable energy, therefore the total market-based greenhouse gas emissions for training were 0 tons CO2eq.

claim: Llama 3.2-Vision models were pretrained on 6B image-text pairs with a data cutoff of December 2023, and instruction tuning included public vision datasets and over 3M synthetically generated examples.
premises: Overview: Llama 3.2-Vision was pretrained on 6B image and text pairs.
The instruction tuning data includes publicly available vision instruction datasets, as well as over 3M synthetically generated examples.
Data Freshness: The pretraining data has a cutoff of December 2023.

claim: Llama 3.2-Vision instruction-tuned models show strong performance on visual reasoning and document understanding benchmarks, including high scores on DocVQA, ChartQA, and AI2 Diagram tasks.
premises: Instruction Tuned Models section shows: DocVQA (test) ANLS: 88.4 (11B) and 90.1 (90B); ChartQA (test, CoT) relaxed accuracy: 83.4 (11B) and 85.5 (90B); AI2 Diagram (test) accuracy: 91.1 (11B) and 92.3 (90B).
MathVista (testmini) accuracy: 51.5 (11B) and 57.3 (90B); MMMU-Pro, Vision (test) accuracy: 23.7 (11B) and 33.8 (90B).

claim: Llama 3.2 models are subject to safety considerations including the risk of identifying individuals in images and require developers to evaluate risks and deploy mitigations like Llama Guard 3-11B-Vision.
premises: As part of our responsible release process, we took dedicated measures including evaluations and mitigations to address the risk of the models uniquely identifying individuals in images.

developers should evaluate identification and other applicable risks in the context of their applications as well as consider deploying Llama Guard 3-11B-Vision as part of their system or other mitigations as appropriate to detect and mitigate such risks.

claim: The Llama 4 collection consists of natively multimodal models using a mixture-of-experts architecture, with Llama 4 Scout and Llama 4 Maverick as the two initial models released.
premises: The Llama 4 collection of models are natively multimodal AI models that enable text and multimodal experiences.
These models leverage a mixture-of-experts architecture to offer industry-leading performance in text and image understanding.
We are launching two efficient models in the Llama 4 series, Llama 4 Scout, a 17 billion parameter model with 16 experts, and Llama 4 Maverick, a 17 billion parameter model with 128 experts.

claim: Llama 4 Scout and Llama 4 Maverick differ in total parameters, context length, token count, and training GPU hours, with Scout having longer context and higher token count but fewer total parameters than Maverick.
premises: Llama 4 Scout (17Bx16E): 17B (Activated) 109B (Total), Context length: 10M, Token count: ~40T, Training Time (GPU hours): 5.0M
Llama 4 Maverick (17Bx128E): 17B (Activated) 400B (Total), Context length: 1M, Token count: ~22T, Training Time (GPU hours): 2.38M

claim: The training of Llama 4 models resulted in significant location-based greenhouse gas emissions, but market-based emissions were zero due to Meta's use of renewable energy.
premises: Estimated total location-based greenhouse gas emissions were 1,999 tons CO2eq for training.

Since 2020, Meta has maintained net zero greenhouse gas emissions in its global operations and matched 100% of its electricity use with clean and renewable energy; therefore, the total market-based greenhouse gas emissions for training were 0 tons CO2eq.

claim: Llama 4 models support a specific set of languages for official use, but were pre-trained on a broader set of languages allowing fine-tuning beyond the supported list under compliance with licensing and use policies.
premises: Supported languages: Arabic, English, French, German, Hindi, Indonesian, Italian, Portuguese, Spanish, Tagalog, Thai, and Vietnamese.

Llama 4 has been trained on a broader collection of languages than the 12 supported languages (pre-training includes 200 total languages). Developers may fine-tune Llama 4 models for languages beyond the 12 supported languages provided they comply with the Llama 4 Community License and the Acceptable Use Policy.

claim: Llama 4 models have been evaluated for image understanding up to 5 input images, and exceeding this requires additional risk mitigation and testing by developers.
premises: Llama 4 has been tested for image understanding up to 5 input images.

If leveraging additional image understanding capabilities beyond this, Developers are responsible for ensuring that their deployments are mitigated for risks and should perform additional testing and tuning tailored to their specific applications.

claim: Llama 4 models are released with specific quantization options enabling deployment on single H100 GPUs, with Scout using on-the-fly int4 quantization and Maverick offering FP8 quantized weights.
premises: The Llama 4 Scout model is released as BF16 weights, but can fit within a single H100 GPU with on-the-fly int4 quantization; the Llama 4 Maverick model is released as both BF16 and FP8 quantized weights.
The FP8 quantized weights fit on a single H100 DGX host while still maintaining quality. We provide code for on-the-fly int4 quantization which minimizes performance degradation as well.

claim: Llama 4 incorporates safety fine-tuning to reduce refusals to benign prompts and improve conversationality through tone adjustment and system prompt steerability.
premises: We put a great emphasis on driving down model refusals to benign prompts for Llama 4.

We expanded our work on the refusal tone from Llama 3 so that the model sounds more natural. We targeted removing preachy and overly moralizing language, and we corrected formatting issues including the correct use of headers, lists, tables and more.

Llama 4 is a more steerable model, meaning responses can be easily tailored to meet specific developer outcomes. Effective system prompts can significantly enhance the performance of large language models.

claim: Llama 4 system protections such as Llama Guard, Prompt Guard, and Code Shield are provided to help deploy the model safely as part of an overall AI system with external guardrails.
premises: Large language models, including Llama 4, are not designed to be deployed in isolation but instead should be deployed as part of an overall AI system with additional guardrails as required.
We provide the community with system level protections - like Llama Guard, Prompt Guard and Code Shield - that developers should deploy with Llama models or other LLMs.

claim: Llama 4 undergoes red teaming and targeted evaluations in critical risk areas including CBRNE, child safety, and cyber attack enablement to assess and mitigate potential harms.
premises: We spend additional focus on the following critical risk areas: 1. CBRNE (Chemical, Biological, Radiological, Nuclear, and Explosive materials) helpfulness... 2. Child Safety... 3. Cyber attack enablement...
We conduct recurring red teaming exercises with the goal of discovering risks via adversarial prompting and we use the learnings to improve our benchmarks and safety tuning datasets.

claim: Meta encourages community involvement in Llama 4 safety and development through open source tools, trust tools, impact grants, and public feedback mechanisms.
premises: We are active members of open consortiums, including the AI Alliance, Partnership on AI and MLCommons, actively contributing to safety standardization and transparency.
Our Trust tools are open sourced for the community to use and widely distributed across ecosystem partners including cloud service providers.

We also set up the Llama Impact Grants program to identify and support the most compelling applications of Meta’s Llama model for societal benefit across three categories: education, climate and open innovation.
Finally, we put in place a set of resources including an output reporting mechanism and bug bounty program to continuously improve the Llama technology with the help of the community.

premises: NIM_IGNORE_MODEL_DOWNLOAD_FAIL | When set to true and the microservice fails to download a model from NGC, the microservice continues to run rather than exit. This environment variable can be useful in an air-gapped environment.

claim: Enabling NIM_JSONL_LOGGING causes the microservice to output logs in JSONL format.
premises: NIM_JSONL_LOGGING | When set to true , the microservice creates log records in the JSONL format. | false

claim: The logging level is configured via NIM_LOG_LEVEL, supporting DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR, and CRITICAL, with a default of INFO.
premises: NIM_LOG_LEVEL | Specifies the logging level. The microservice supports the following values: DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR, and CRITICAL. | INFO

claim: The model manifest YAML file is located at /opt/nim/etc/default/model_manifest.yaml by default, as specified by NIM_MANIFEST_PATH.
premises: NIM_MANIFEST_PATH | Specifies the fully qualified path, in the container, for the model manifest YAML file. | /opt/nim/etc/default/model_manifest.yaml

claim: The NIM_MODEL_PROFILE environment variable selects a model profile ID, with automatic matching to host GPU as the default behavior.
premises: NIM_MODEL_PROFILE | Specifies the model profile ID to use with the container. By default, the container attempts to automatically match the host GPU model and GPU count with the optimal model profile. | None

claim: The NIM_SERVED_MODEL_NAME variable defines the model names used in the API, with the first name used for Prometheus metrics if multiple are specified.
premises: NIM_SERVED_MODEL_NAME | Specifies the model names used in the API. Specify multiple names in a comma-separated list. If you specify multiple names, the server responds to any of the names. The name in the model field of a response matches the name in the request. By default, the model name is inferred from the /opt/nim/etc/default/model_manifest.yaml file. For Prometheus metrics, this value is used in the model_name label. If more than one value is specified, the first one is used for the label. | None

claim: The /opt/nim/.cache path in the container is used for downloaded models and can be bind-mounted from the host to avoid repeated downloads.
premises: /opt/nim/.cache or NIM_CACHE_PATH | Specifies the path, relative to the root of the container, for downloaded models. The typical use for this path is to bind mount a directory on the host with this path inside the container. For example, to use ~/.cache/nim on the host, run mkdir -p ~/.cache/nim before you start the container. When you start the container, specify the -v ~/.cache/nim:/opt/nim/.cache -u $(id -u) arguments to the docker run command. If you do not specify a bind or volume mount, as shown in the -v argument in the preceding command, the container downloads the model each time you start the container. The -u $(id -u) argument runs the container with your user ID to avoid file system permission issues and errors.

claim: NVIDIA benchmarked the performance of the Llama 3.1 Nemotron Safety Guard 8B microservice using the genai-perf tool.
premises: NVIDIA used the genai-perf tool to benchmark the performance of the microservice.

premises: Some TensorRT-LLM profiles can experience lower throughput under high load compared to generic model profiles that use the vLLM engine.

claim: The microservice can serve model profiles from a local cache without requiring an internet connection or access to the NGC registry.
premises: If the microservice detects a model profile in the model cache, the microservice can serve that profile from the cache rather than download the model profile again.
By creating a model cache, you can run the microservice without any internet connection and no connection to the NGC registry.

claim: To cache model profiles for air gap deployment, users must first set the NGC_API_KEY environment variable, create a cache directory, list desired profiles, and then download them using specific Docker commands.
premises: Export your NGC API key as an environment variable: $ export NGC_API_KEY = "<nvapi-...>"
Create an directory for the model cache: $ export AIR_GAP_NIM_CACHE = ~/.cache/air-gap-nim-cache $ mkdir -p "${ AIR_GAP_NIM_CACHE }"

Optional: Determine a specific model profile to cache: $ docker run --rm \ --gpus = all --runtime = nvidia \ --shm-size = 64GB \ -e NGC_API_KEY \ -u $( id -u ) \ -v "$AIR_GAP_NIM_CACHE :/opt/nim/.cache/" \ nvcr.io/nim/nvidia/llama-3.1-nemotron-safety-guard-8b-v3:1.14.0 \ list-model-profiles

Download the model profiles to cache: $ docker run --rm \ --gpus = all --runtime = nvidia \ --shm-size = 64GB \ -e NGC_API_KEY \ -u $( id -u ) \ -v "$AIR_GAP_NIM_CACHE :/opt/nim/.cache/" \ nvcr.io/nim/nvidia/llama-3.1-nemotron-safety-guard-8b-v3:1.14.0 \ download-to-cache -p <profile-one> [ -p <profile-two> -p <...> ]

claim: On an air-gapped system, the microservice can be started using a transferred model cache by setting the LOCAL_NIM_CACHE environment variable and mounting the cache directory, without requiring the NGC_API_KEY.
premises: After the container exits and the model profiles are downloaded, transfer the air-gapped directory, ~/.cache/air-gap-nim-cache, to a path that is accessible to the air-gapped system.
Export an environment variable with the path to the model cache: $ export LOCAL_NIM_CACHE = <path-to-transferred-model-cache>

Start the container: $ docker run -d \ --name safetyguard8b \ --gpus = all --runtime = nvidia \ --shm-size = 64GB \ -u $( id -u ) \ -p 8000 :8000 \ -v "$LOCAL_NIM_CACHE :/opt/nim/.cache/" \ -e NIM_MODEL_PROFILE = <profile-one> \ nvcr.io/nim/nvidia/llama-3.1-nemotron-safety-guard-8b-v3:1.14.0
The key differences from the common command to start the microservice: The NGC_API_KEY environment variable is omitted because the microservice does not download model profiles.

claim: NIM provides Prometheus metrics for request statistics that are available by default at http://localhost:8000/v1/metrics.
