claim: Model profiles are optimized configurations for NVIDIA NIM microservices, each identified by a unique 64-character hexadecimal profile ID, stored in the model manifest file at /opt/nim/etc/default/model_manifest.yaml, and support automatic selection based on GPU model and count or manual specification.
premises: The models for NVIDIA NIM microservices use model engines that are tuned for specific NVIDIA GPU models, number of GPUs, precision, and so on.
NVIDIA produces model engines for several popular combinations and these are referred to as model profiles.
Each model profile is identified by a unique 64-character string of hexadecimal digits that is referred to as a profile ID.
The NIM microservices support automatic profile selection by determining the GPU model and count on the node and attempting to match the optimal model profile.
Alternatively, NIM microservices support running a specified model profile, but this requires that you review the profiles and know the profile ID.
The available model profiles are stored in a file in the NIM container file system.
The file is referred to as the model manifest file and the default path is /opt/nim/etc/default/model_manifest.yaml in the container.

claim: Release v1.0.0 is the first release of NVIDIA NemoGuard JailbreakDetect NIM and introduces the /v1/classify endpoint for detecting jailbreak attempts.
premises: This is the first release of NVIDIA NemoGuard JailbreakDetect NIM.
The /v1/classify endpoint accepts an end-user request in the input field of a JSON payload.
The microservice responds with a JSON payload that includes two fields.
The jailbreak field is a Boolean value and indicates whether the end-user request appears to be a jailbreak attempt.
The score field is a floating-point value between 1 and -1 that indicates the classification and model confidence.

Nemotron Safety Guard NIM shares some underlying technology with NVIDIA NIM for LLMs.

claim: To access NVIDIA NIM for Image OCR container images and model assets, you must generate an API key from NVIDIA NGC and select specific services during creation.
premises: To access the NIM container images and model assets on NGC, you must generate a personal API key.
To create your key, go to https://org.ngc.nvidia.com/setup/api-keys.
When you create your key, for Services Included, select the following: NGC Catalog, Private Registry (if you are an Early Access participant).

claim: To use the NGC API key conveniently in terminal commands, export it as an environment variable named NGC_API_KEY and persist it in shell configuration files.
premises: To conveniently use your API key in the commands in the following sections, you can export your key as an environment variable named NGC_API_KEY.

Run one of the following commands to make your key available when you start a new terminal session: # If using bashecho"export NGC_API_KEY=<value>">>~/.bashrc, # If using zshecho"export NGC_API_KEY=<value>">>~/.zshrc

claim: To authenticate with NGC and pull NIM container images, use the docker login command with $oauthtoken as username and NGC_API_KEY as password.
premises: Before you can pull the NIM container image from NGC, first authenticate to NGC by using the following command: echo"$NGC_API_KEY"|dockerloginnvcr.io--username'$oauthtoken'--password-stdin
Use $oauthtoken as the username and NGC_API_KEY as the password.
The $oauthtoken username is a special name that indicates that you will authenticate with an API key and not a user name and password.

claim: Before pulling certain NIM container images, you must accept the license terms on the NGC Catalog for the specific model.
premises: Some NIM models require that you accept the license terms on NGC before you can pull the container image and model assets.
To accept the license terms, browse to the model or container page on the NGC Catalog, read and then click Accept Terms.
For example, accept terms for the following container: nemotron-ocr-v1

claim: The nemotron-ocr-v1 NIM container can be launched via Docker with specific flags to enable GPU access, API key provisioning, cache mounting, and port forwarding.
premises: The following command launches a Docker container for the nemotron-ocr-v1 model.
exportNIM_MODEL_NAME=nvidia/nemotron-ocr-v1
exportCONTAINER_NAME=$(basename$NIM_MODEL_NAME)
exportIMG_NAME="nvcr.io/nim/nvidia/$CONTAINER_NAME:1.3.0"
exportLOCAL_NIM_CACHE=~/.cache/nim
mkdir-p"$LOCAL_NIM_CACHE"
dockerrun-it--rm--name=$CONTAINER_NAME\--runtime=nvidia\--gpusall\--shm-size=16GB\-eNGC_API_KEY\-v"$LOCAL_NIM_CACHE:/opt/nim/.cache"\-u$(id-u)\-p8000:8000\$IMG_NAME

claim: To verify the NIM service is ready to accept inference requests, query the health endpoint at http://localhost:8000/v1/health/ready and expect a JSON response with 'ready': true.
premises: After you launch the NIM, it might take a few seconds for the service to be ready to accept requests.
To verify that the service is ready, run the following code: curl-X'GET''http://localhost:8000/v1/health/ready'
If the service is ready, you should see a response similar to the following: {"ready":true,}

claim: To run inference on the NIM service, send a POST request to /v1/infer with a JSON payload containing a base64-encoded image and merge_levels set to ['word'].
premises: After the service is ready, use code similar to the following to run inference.
API_ENDPOINT="http://localhost:8000"
IMAGE_SOURCE="https://assets.ngc.nvidia.com/products/api-catalog/nemo-retriever/image-ocr/example-1.png"
if[[ $IMAGE_SOURCE==http* ]];then BASE64_IMAGE=$(curl-s${IMAGE_SOURCE}|base64-w0);else BASE64_IMAGE=$(base64-w0${IMAGE_SOURCE})fi
JSON_PAYLOAD='{"input": [{"type": "image_url","url": "data:image/jpeg;base64,'${BASE64_IMAGE}'"}],"merge_levels": ["word"]}'
echo"${JSON_PAYLOAD}"|\curl-XPOST"${API_ENDPOINT}/v1/infer"\-H'accept: application/json'\-H'Content-Type: application/json'\-d@-

claim: The NIM can be configured to deploy across multiple GPUs using the --gpus flag in docker run, with options to specify all GPUs, a number of GPUs, or specific GPU devices.
premises: The NIM deploys a single model across however many GPUs that you specify and are visible inside the docker container.
If you do not specify the number of GPUs, the NIM defaults to one GPU.
When using multiple GPUs, Triton distributes inference requests across the GPUs to keep them equally utilized.
Use the docker run --gpus command-line argument to specify the number of GPUs that are available for deployment.
- Example using all GPUs: docker run --gpus all ...
- Example using two GPUs: docker run --gpus 2 ...
- Example using specific GPUs: docker run --gpus '"device=1,2"' ...

claim: Multiple NIM containers can run on the same GPU by specifying identical GPU device IDs in their respective --gpus arguments.
premises: You can deploy Image OCR NIM (NeMo Retriever OCR) alongside another NIM (for example, llama3-8b-instruct) on the same GPU (for example, A100 80GB, A100 40GB, or H100 80GB).
Use the docker run --gpus command-line argument to specify the same GPU as shown in the following code.
dockerrun--gpus'"device=1"'...$IMG_NAME
dockerrun--gpus'"device=1"'...$LLM_IMG_NAME

claim: To pre-fetch NIM model assets for air-gapped use, first list available model profiles, then download the selected profile to cache, and finally serve the model from cache in an isolated network.
premises: If model assets must be pre-fetched, such as in an air-gapped system, you can download the assets to the NIM cache without starting the server.
To download assets first run list-model-profiles to determine the desired profile, and then run download-to-cache with that profile.
exportNIM_MODEL_NAME=nvidia/nemotron-ocr-v1
exportCONTAINER_NAME=$(basename$NIM_MODEL_NAME)
exportIMG_NAME="nvcr.io/nim/nvidia/$CONTAINER_NAME:1.3.0"
exportLOCAL_NIM_CACHE=~/.cache/nim
mkdir-p"$LOCAL_NIM_CACHE"
dockerrun-it--rm--name=$CONTAINER_NAME\-eNIM_CPU_ONLY=1\-u$(id-u)\$IMG_NAMElist-model-profiles
exportNIM_MODEL_PROFILE=<selectedprofile>
dockerrun-it--rm--name=$CONTAINER_NAME\--gpusall\--shm-size=16GB\-eNGC_API_KEY\-eNIM_CPU_ONLY=1\-v"$LOCAL_NIM_CACHE:/opt/nim/.cache"\-u$(id-u)\$IMG_NAMEdownload-to-cache--profiles$NIM_MODEL_PROFILE

dockerrun-it--rm--name=$CONTAINER_NAME\--runtime=nvidia\--gpus=all\--shm-size=16GB\--network=none\-v$LOCAL_NIM_CACHE:/mnt/nim-cache:ro\-u$(id-u)\-\eNIM_CACHE_PATH=/mnt/nim-cache\-eNGC_API_KEY\-p8000:8000\$IMG_NAME

claim: To stop and remove the NIM Docker container, use docker stop followed by docker rm unless the --rm flag was used during startup.
premises: To stop the Docker container, run the following code: dockerstop$CONTAINER_NAME
To remove the Docker container, run the following code. If you included the --rm flag when you started the container, you don’t need this step: dockerrm$CONTAINER_NAME

claim: The NVIDIA NIM for Image OCR (NeMo Retriever OCR) runs as a Docker container and can be configured using command-line arguments, environment variables, and volume mounts.
premises: NVIDIA NIM for Image OCR (NeMo Retriever OCR) uses docker containers under the hood.
Each NIM is its own Docker container and there are several ways to configure it.
The remainder of this documentation describes the ways to configure a NIM container.

claim: GPU access for the NIM container is managed via the NVIDIA Container Toolkit using either the --gpus flag or the NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES environment variable.
premises: The NIM container is GPU-accelerated and uses NVIDIA Container Toolkit for access to GPUs on the host.
You can specify the --gpus all command-line argument to the docker run command if the host has one or more of the same GPU model.

Expose specific GPUs to the container by using either of the following methods: Specify the --gpus argument, such as --gpus="device=1"; Set the NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES environment variable, such as -e NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=1.
Run the nvidia-smi -L command to list the device IDs to specify in the argument or environment variable.

claim: Low PID limits can cause the NIM container to stall, crash, or fail after serving few requests, and can be resolved by increasing the PID limit at container, node, or OS level.
premises: In certain deployment or container runtime environments, default process and thread limits (PID limits) can interfere with NIM startup.

If the PID limit is too low, you might see symptoms such as: NIM starts up partially, but fails to reach ready state, and then stalls; NIM starts up partially, but fails to reach ready state, and then crashes; NIM serves a small number of requests, and then fails.
To verify that PID limits are impacting the NIM container, you can remove or adjust the PID limit at the container, node, and operating system level.
Removing the PID limit and then checking for success is a useful diagnostic step.
To increase the PID limit in a docker run command, set --pids-limit=-1.
To increase the PID limit in a podman run command, set --pids-limit=-1.
To increase the PID limit in Kubernetes, set the PodPidsLimit on the kubelet on each node.
To increase the PID limit at the operating system level, see your OS-specific documentation.

claim: Increasing shared memory via the --shm-size flag may be necessary for the NIM container due to tokenization scaling with CPU cores in Triton’s Python backend.
premises: Tokenization uses Triton’s Python backend capabilities that scales with the number of CPU cores available.
You may need to increase the available shared memory given to the microservice container.
Example providing 1g of shared memory: docker run ... --shm-size=1g ...

claim: Triton Ensemble Models in the NIM can be tuned via environment variables to improve stability under high concurrency and resource constraints.
premises: The NVIDIA NIM for Image OCR (NeMo Retriever OCR) enables you to configure the underlying Triton Ensemble Models by using environment variables.
For most use cases, the default values for these variables are sufficient.
However, for highly concurrent workloads in resource-constrained environments, you can tune the values of the following environment variables to improve the stability of the NIM.
NIM_TRITON_IDLE_BYTES_LIMIT: The threshold for idle VRAM memory (bytes) after which the Torch CUDA cache is emptied and all inter-process communication (IPC) files are closed. Default: 1GB
NIM_TRITON_FLUSH_INTERVAL: This option determines after how many requests the NIM_TRITON_IDLE_BYTES_LIMIT is checked. Default: 1 (After every request)

NIM_TRITON_RATE_LIMIT: If set, this option configures Triton to rate limit the execution count throughout the ensemble model pipeline to the provided integer value. GPU-bound model inference is given priority, while other components (pre-processors, post-processors, etc.) are given lower priority. Default: None

claim: Bind mounting a host directory to /opt/nim/.cache in the NIM container avoids repeated model downloads and prevents permission issues when using -u $(id -u).
premises: The following table identifies the paths that are used in the container.
Container Path: /opt/nim/.cache or NIM_CACHE_PATH

Description: Specifies the path, relative to the root of the container, for downloaded models. The typical use for this path is to bind mount a directory on the host with this path inside the container.
For example, to use ~/.cache/nim on the host, run mkdir -p ~/.cache/nim before you start the container.
When you start the container, specify the -v ~/.cache/nim:/opt/nim/.cache -u $(id -u) arguments to the docker run command.
If you do not specify a bind or volume mount, as shown in the -v argument in the preceding command, the container downloads the model each time you start the container.
The -u $(id -u) argument runs the container with your user ID to avoid file system permission issues and errors.

claim: NVIDIA NIM for Image OCR supports exporting metrics and traces in OpenTelemetry-compatible format and exposes Prometheus metrics via the microservice and Triton Inference Server.
premises: NVIDIA NIM for Image OCR (NeMo Retriever OCR) supports exporting metrics and traces in an OpenTelemetry-compatible format.
Additionally, the microservice and its underlying NVIDIA Triton Inference Server expose metrics through Prometheus endpoints.

claim: Specific environment variables control OpenTelemetry instrumentation and export behavior for the NIM microservice.
premises: NIM_ENABLE_OTEL set to 1 enables OpenTelemetry instrumentation in NIMs.
OTEL_SERVICE_NAME specifies the service name in exported metrics.
OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT specifies the OTLP HTTP receiver endpoint (gRPC not supported).
OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER=otlp exports metrics to the OTLP endpoint in OTLP format (default: container log).
OTEL_TRACES_EXPORTER=otlp exports traces to the OTLP endpoint in OTLP format (default: container log).

claim: Prometheus-formatted metrics from the NIM microservice and Triton Inference Server are accessible via specific endpoints.
premises: The NIM microservice exposes metrics in Prometheus format at <nim-host>:8000/v1/metrics.
The Triton Inference Server exposes metrics in Prometheus format at <nim-host>:8002/metrics.

claim: An OpenTelemetry Collector configuration can receive metrics and traces from NIM and Triton and export them to backends like Zipkin, OTLP, or debug output.
premises: Two receivers are defined: an OTLP receiver for metrics and traces from NIM, and a Prometheus receiver for Triton metrics.
Three exporters are defined: Zipkin, OTLP (to downstream backends like Datadog), and debug (for console output).
Traces are received exclusively by the OTLP receiver and exported by Zipkin and debug exporters.
Metrics are received by both OTLP and Prometheus receivers and exported by OTLP and debug exporters.

claim: NVIDIA NIM for Image OCR (NeMo Retriever OCR) automatically leverages model- and hardware-specific optimizations to improve model performance.
premises: NVIDIA NIM for Image OCR (NeMo Retriever OCR) automatically leverages model- and hardware-specific optimizations intended to improve the performance of the models.
The NIM uses the TensorRT backend for Triton Inference Server for optimized inference of common models across a number of NVIDIA GPUs.
If an optimized engine does not exist for a SKU being used, a GPU-agnostic ONNX backend (using the CUDA Execution Provider) is used instead.
The NIM includes multiple optimization profiles, catered to floating point precision types supported by each SKU.

claim: Image OCR NIM (NeMo Retriever OCR) automatically selects the most suitable profile based on detected hardware, preferring TensorRT backend and lower precision profiles.
premises: Image OCR NIM (NeMo Retriever OCR) is designed to automatically select the most suitable profile from the list of compatible profiles based on the detected hardware.
Each profile consists of different parameters that influence the selection process.

The automatic selection process considers compatibility check (excluding profiles not runnable with detected GPU configuration), backend (preferring TensorRT over ONNX or PyTorch), and precision (preferring lower precision like FP8 before FP16).
The model profile is logged at startup, as shown in the example log entry.

claim: Users can override automatic profile selection by specifying a profile ID via the NIM_MODEL_PROFILE environment variable in the docker run command.
premises: To override automatic profile selection, set a specific profile ID in the docker run command by including -e NIM_MODEL_PROFILE=<value>.
The command 'docker run --rm --runtime=nvidia --gpus all $IMG_NAME list-model-profiles' lists the available profiles.
To run list-model-profiles on a host with no available GPUs, include -e NIM_CPU_ONLY=1 in the docker run command.
An example output shows compatible profiles with details like precision, backend, GPU type, and batch size.
In the example, setting -e NIM_MODEL_PROFILE="2cb47b75c3764c26fcfd9d257cf4337e31ecf9a8dbdb2525c93c0678a2ff851a" runs the RTX4090 FP16 Batch Size of 1 profile.

claim: The genai-perf tool can be used to benchmark the performance of NVIDIA NIM for Image OCR (NeMo Retriever OCR).
premises: To benchmark the performance of NVIDIA NIM for Image OCR (NeMo Retriever OCR), you can use the genai-perf tool.
genai-perf is pre-installed in the Triton Server SDK container.
For the remainder of this section, we will use genai-perf==0.0.11 that comes packaged with the Triton Server SDK 25.02.

claim: High benchmarking concurrencies may cause NVIDIA NIM for Image OCR (NeMo Retriever OCR) to fail to respond to genai-perf requests in a timely fashion, resulting in timeout errors.
premises: In some cases the server might return {"error":"Triton inference request timed out: "}.
This can occur because at high benchmarking concurrencies NVIDIA NIM for Image OCR (NeMo Retriever OCR) fails to respond to genai-perf requests in a timely fashion.

claim: NVIDIA NIM for Image OCR (NeMo Retriever OCR) can be deployed on Kubernetes using Helm.
premises: You can deploy NVIDIA NIM for Image OCR (NeMo Retriever OCR) on Kubernetes by using Helm.
The Helm chart simplifies NIM deployment on Kubernetes.
The chart supports deployment with a variety of possible cluster, GPU, and storage configurations.

claim: Helm charts provide benefits for managing the deployment and lifecycle of NIM microservices.
premises: The benefits of Helm Charts are as follows:
- Help manage the deployment and lifecycle of the microservice.
- Use a centralized distribution mechanism for charts.
- The charts are hosted on NVIDIA NGC.
- Enable you to customize the deployment when you specify a custom values file.

claim: Deploying the NIM requires setting up environment variables and secrets for NGC authentication.
premises: This helm chart requires that you have a secret with your NGC API key configured for downloading private images, and one with your NGC API key (below named ngc-api).
These instructions will assume that you have your NGC_API_KEY exported in the environment.
exportNGC_API_KEY="<YOUR NGC API KEY>"

claim: The Helm chart can be fetched from NVIDIA NGC using a specific helm fetch command.
premises: You can fetch the helm chart from NGC by executing the following command:
helmfetchhttps://helm.ngc.nvidia.com/nim/nvidia/charts/nvidia-nim-nemotron-ocr-v1-1.3.0.tgz--username='$oauthtoken'--password=$NGC_API_KEY

claim: A dedicated Kubernetes namespace should be created for deployment.
premises: You can choose to deploy to whichever namespace is appropriate, but for documentation purposes we will deploy to a namespace named nemotron-ocr-v1-nim.
kubectlcreatenamespacenemotron-ocr-v1-nim

claim: Two types of secrets must be created for the NIM to function: an image pull secret and a generic API key secret.
premises: - Add an image pull secret for downloading the container image from NVIDIA NGC. kubectl create secret -n nemotron-ocr-v1-nim docker-registry ngc-secret \ --docker-server = nvcr.io \ --docker-username = '$oauthtoken' \ --docker-password = " ${ NGC_API_KEY } "
- Add a generic secret that the container uses for downloading models from NVIDIA NGC. kubectl create -n nemotron-ocr-v1-nim secret generic ngc-api --from-literal = NGC_API_KEY = ${ NGC_API_KEY }

claim: The Helm chart supports configurable storage options including persistent volumes and hostPath for model storage.
premises: This NIM downloads models at startup.
By default, models are stored in an emptyDir volume, which means they are re-downloaded each time the pod restarts.
For production use, we recommend that you use persistent storage to avoid repeated downloads.
This chart supports two general categories:
- Persistent Volume Claims (enabled by persistence.enabled )
- hostPath (enabled by hostPath.enabled )
By default, persistence.enabled is set to false and the chart uses an emptyDir volume for model storage.

claim: Persistent storage can be configured using either a dynamically provisioned PVC or an existing claim, or via hostPath on the node.
premises: When you set persistence.enabled=true , the chart creates a PersistentVolumeClaim that uses the cluster’s default storage class, or the class specified by persistence.storageClass .
If you want to store the models on an existing PersistentVolumeClaim , specify that value in persistence.existingClaim :
--setpersistence.enabled=true\--setpersistence.existingClaim=my-existing-pvc
To use a local directory on the node instead of a PVC:
--sethostPath.enabled=true\--sethostPath.path=/path/to/local/model-store

claim: The Helm chart can be deployed with or without persistent storage using specific helm upgrade--install commands.
premises: Use the following command to create a deployment with persistent storage.
helmupgrade--install\--namespacenemotron-ocr-v1-nim\image-ocr\--setpersistence.enabled=true\--setpersistence.storageClass="local-nfs"\nvidia-nim-nemotron-ocr-v1-1.3.0.tgz
Use the following command to deploy without persistent storage (models are stored in emptyDir and are re-downloaded on pod restart).
helmupgrade--install\--namespacenemotron-ocr-v1-nim\image-ocr\nvidia-nim-nemotron-ocr-v1-1.3.0.tgz

claim: The model version can be customized during deployment using the image.tag parameter.
premises: You can also change the version of the model in use by adding the following after --namespace .
--setimage.tag=1.3.0\

claim: After deployment, pod status should be checked to confirm successful deployment and readiness.
premises: After deploying check the pods to ensure that it is running, initial image pull and model download can take upwards of 15 minutes.
kubectlgetpods-nnemotron-ocr-v1-nim
The pod should eventually end up in the running state.
NAMEREADYSTATUSRESTARTSAGE\nnvidia-nim-nemotron-ocr-v1-01/1Running08m44s

claim: Events should be checked to detect deployment failures.
premises: Check events for failures:
kubectlgetevents-nnemotron-ocr-v1-nim

claim: Minikube users should enable persistent storage with the standard storage class for optimal behavior.
premises: Minikube will create a hostPath based PV and PVC by default with this chart.
We recommend that you add the following to your helm commands.
--setpersistence.enabled=true\--setpersistence.storageClass=standard

claim: The deployed NIM service can be accessed locally via port-forwarding on port 8000 for inference testing.
premises: In the previous example the API endpoint is exposed on port 8000 through the Kubernetes service of the default type with no ingress, since authentication is not handled by the NIM itself.
Use the following command to port-forward the service to your local machine to test inference.
kubectlport-forward-nnemotron-ocr-v1-nimservice/image-ocr-nvidia-nim-nemotron-ocr-v18000:8000

claim: Inference can be tested using a Python script that processes PNG images and sends them to the OCR API endpoint.
premises: Create a directory data/structured-imgs and copy in some .png formatted images so that data looks like so:
$mkdir-pdata/structured-imgs
$lsdata/structured-imgs\nsample1.pngsample2.pngsample3.pngsample4.png
Send an inference request by running the following commands and Python 3.11 script.

# Create a virtual env (venv) for this test to isolate the dependenciespython3-mvenvnemotron_ocr_venvsourcenemotron_ocr_venv/bin/activate# Install pillow and requests libraries into your python 3 environmentpip3installrequestspillow

# nemotron_ocr_inference_test.pyimportbase64importjsonimporttimefromioimportBytesIOfrompathlibimportPathimportrequestsfromPILimportImageimages=[]image_paths=list(Path("data/structured-imgs").glob("*.png"))forimage_pathinimage_paths:image=Image.open(image_path)buffered=BytesIO()image.save(buffered,format="PNG")base64_image=base64.b64encode(buffered.getvalue()).decode("utf-8")image_url=f"data:image/png;base64,{base64_image}"image={"type":"image_url","url":image_url}images.append(image)payload={"input":images}start=time.time()print(json.dumps(requests.post("http://localhost:8000/v1/infer",json=payload).json()))print(f"{len(image_paths)}images completed in{time.time()-start}seconds")
# Run inference on the .png files in the /data/structured-imgs directorypython3nemotron_ocr_inference_test.py

claim: Container logs can be viewed by first identifying the pod name and then retrieving its logs.
premises: Use the following command to view the container log messages.
# Step 1: Find the actual pod namekubectlgetpods-nnemotron-ocr-v1-nim
# Step 2: Use the actual pod name from step 1kubectllogs-f-nnemotron-ocr-v1-nim<pod-name-from-step-1>

claim: The v1/infer endpoint accepts multiple images and returns text detections with bounding boxes and confidence scores.
premises: The v1/infer endpoint accepts multiple images and returns a list of text detections with associated bounding boxes and confidence scores from each image.
OCR NIM output provides confidence scores and float [0, 1] bounding boxes associated with each text detection, and total processed images size (in MB)

claim: Image inputs must be base64-encoded data URLs with PNG or JPEG format and follow the structure data:image/<format>;base64,<encoded_data>.
premises: The only supported type is image_url.
Each image must be base64 encoded, and should be represented in the following JSON format. The supported image formats are png and jpeg.
{"type":"image_url","url":"data:image/<IMAGE_FORMAT>;base64,<BASE64_ENCODED_IMAGE>"}
Invalid image URL format: The image URL doesn’t follow the required data URL format. Ensure all URLs follow the pattern: data:<image-media-type>;base64,<base64-image-data>

claim: The merge_levels parameter controls how text detections are merged per image, supporting word, sentence, or paragraph levels with paragraph as default.
premises: Inference requests also support the optional merge_levels entry. The merge_levels entry is an array of strings (expected to be the same length as input) that specifies the level at which to merge the text detections per-image. The supported levels are word, sentence, and paragraph. The default value is paragraph.
For example, to specify word-level merging for the above example: {"input":[{"type":"image_url","url":"data:image/png;base64,<BASE64_ENCODED_IMAGE>"}, ...],"merge_levels":["word","word","word"]}

claim: The API returns structured JSON responses containing text predictions, bounding box coordinates, and usage metrics like total image size in MB.
premises: OCR NIM output provides confidence scores and float [0, 1] bounding boxes associated with each text detection, and total processed images size (in MB):

claim: Health check endpoints /v1/health/live and /v1/health/ready can be used to verify service availability before inference.
premises: Service Health: Use the health check endpoints (/v1/health/live and /v1/health/ready) to verify the service is operational before sending inference requests.
cURL Request: Use the following command to query the health endpoints.
Response: {"ready":true} and {"live":true}

claim: Common API errors include 422 for invalid image URL or base64, 429 for rate limiting, and 500/503 for server or initialization issues, each with specific resolutions.
premises: 422 (Unprocessable Entity) | Invalid image URL format | The image URL doesn’t follow the required data URL format | Ensure all URLs follow the pattern: data:<image-media-type>;base64,<base64-image-data>
422 (Unprocessable Entity) | Invalid base64 content | The base64-encoded data in the URL is invalid | Verify that your base64 encoding process is correct and that the image data is not corrupted
422 (Unprocessable Entity) | Malformed request | The JSON payload structure is incorrect | Verify that your request format matches the API specification

429 (Too Many Requests) | Request queue full | The number of concurrent requests exceeds the configured queue size | Reduce the request rate, or increase the queue size by using NIM_TRITON_MAX_QUEUE_SIZE
500 (Internal Server Error) | Server error | An unexpected error occurred during processing | Check server logs for details and report the issue if persistent
503 (Service Unavailable) | Service not ready | The service is still initializing or loading models | Check health endpoints and wait for the service to complete initialization

claim: Troubleshooting tips include verifying image format (PNG/JPEG), resizing large images, using correct MIME types in base64 encoding, adjusting timeouts, and implementing backoff for 429 errors.
premises: - Invalid Image Format: The API supports PNG and JPEG formats. Ensure your images are in one of these formats before encoding.
- Image Size Limits: Very large images may cause processing issues. Consider resizing large images before sending them to the API.
- Base64 Encoding: When encoding images, ensure you’re using the correct MIME type in the data URL: For JPEG: data:image/jpeg;base64,... For PNG: data:image/png;base64,...
- Request Timeout: If requests are timing out, the model may be processing a large batch or complex images. Consider adjusting timeout settings in your client application.
- Rate Limiting: If you’re receiving 429 errors, implement backoff strategies in your client application to handle rate limiting gracefully.

claim: NVIDIA NIM for Image OCR (NeMo Retriever OCR) uses specific environment variables to configure container behavior, including model serving, telemetry, Triton inference settings, and repository access.
premises: The documentation describes environment variables for NVIDIA NIM for Image OCR (NeMo Retriever OCR)
Environment variables are set using the -e command-line argument to the docker run command

claim: NVIDIA NeMo Retriever Reranking NIM provides easy access to state-of-the-art reranking models for enterprise semantic search applications.
premises: The NVIDIA NeMo Retriever Reranking API provides easy access to state-of-the-art models that are foundational building blocks for enterprise semantic search applications, delivering accurate answers quickly at scale.
Developers can use these APIs to create robust copilots, chatbots, and AI assistants from start to finish.
NeMo Retriever Reranking models are built on the NVIDIA software platform, incorporating CUDA, TensorRT, and Triton to offer out-of-the-box GPU acceleration.

claim: NeMo Retriever Reranking NIM reorders citations by query match quality and is a key step in retrieval pipelines involving multiple datastores.
premises: NVIDIA NeMo Retriever Reranking NIM (Reranking NIM) reorders citations by how well they match a query.
This is a key step in the retrieval process, especially when the retrieval pipeline involves citations from different datastores that each have their own algorithms for measuring similarity.

claim: NeMo Retriever Reranking NIM is packaged as a Docker container accelerated by NVIDIA Triton Inference Server and exposes an OpenAI-compatible API.
premises: Each NeMo Retriever Reranking NIM packages a reranking model, such as NV-RerankQA-Mistral4B-v3, into a Docker container image.
All Reranking NIM Docker containers are accelerated with NVIDIA TritonTM Inference Server and expose an API compatible with OpenAI’s API standard.
The Reranking NIM offers a fine-tuned, ready-to-use reranker based on Mistral 7B, with a reduced size of 3.5B parameters by using only half of the weights.

claim: NeMo Retriever Reranking NIM includes enterprise-ready features such as high performance, scalable deployment, flexible integration, and enterprise-grade security.
premises: The Reranking NIM comes with enterprise-ready features, such as a high-performance inference server, flexible integration, and enterprise-grade security.
High Performance – The Reranking NIM is optimized for high-performance deep learning inference with NVIDIA TensorRT TM and NVIDIA Triton TM Inference Server.
Scalable Deployment – The Reranking NIM seamlessly scales from a few users to millions.

Flexible Integration – The Reranking NIM can be easily incorporated into existing data pipelines and applications. Developers are provided with an OpenAI-compatible API in addition to custom NVIDIA extensions.
Enterprise-Grade Security – The Reranking NIM comes with security features such as the use of safetensors, continuous patching of CVEs, and constant monitoring with our internal penetration tests.

claim: Reranking improves recall@5 in both single and hybrid datastore retrieval pipelines, with measurable gains across multiple benchmarks.
premises: The above table shows that reranking improves recall not only when combining data sources, but also when only using a single datastore.
For those experiments, the datastores have a top_k of 100. Ave recall@5 is an average of scores across FiQA, HotpotQA, BEIR, NQ, and TechQA.

| Pipeline | Avg recall@5 |
| --- | --- |
| Dense | 0.5699 |
| Dense + Reranking | 0.7070 |
| Dense + Sparse | 0.5856 |
| Dense + Sparse + Reranking | 0.7137 |

claim: Using NeMo Retriever Reranking NIM involves a trade-off in increased latency and computational cost for improved retrieval accuracy.
premises: In exchange for that improvement, the trade-off is increased cost and latency.
On an H100, reranking 500 passages will cost ~1,750ms.

The remainder of this section describes the various ways to configure a NIM container.

claim: The NIM container requires GPU access via the NVIDIA Container Toolkit and allows specific GPU selection using --gpus or NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES.
premises: The NIM container is GPU-accelerated and uses NVIDIA Container Toolkit for access to GPUs on the host.
You can specify the --gpus all command-line argument to the docker run command if the host has one or more of the same GPU model.
If the host has a combination of GPUs, such as an A6000 and a GeForce display GPU, run the container on compute-capable GPUs only.

Expose specific GPUs to the container by using either of the following methods: Specify the --gpus argument, such as --gpus="device=1"; Set the NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES environment variable, such as -e NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=1.
Run the nvidia-smi -L command to list the device IDs to specify in the argument or environment variable.

claim: Low PID limits can cause NIM container startup failures, and increasing the PID limit via --pids-limit=-1 resolves these issues in Docker, Podman, Kubernetes, or at the OS level.
premises: In certain deployment or container runtime environments, default process and thread limits (PID limits) can interfere with NIM startup.

If the PID limit is too low, you might see symptoms such as: NIM starts up partially, but fails to reach ready state, and then stalls; NIM starts up partially, but fails to reach ready state, and then crashes; NIM serves a small number of requests, and then fails.
To verify that PID limits are impacting the NIM container, you can remove or adjust the PID limit at the container, node, and operating system level.
Removing the PID limit and then checking for success is a useful diagnostic step.
To increase the PID limit in a docker run command, set --pids-limit=-1.
To increase the PID limit in a podman run command, set --pids-limit=-1.
To increase the PID limit in Kubernetes, set the PodPidsLimit on the kubelet on each node.
To increase the PID limit at the operating system level, see your OS-specific documentation.

claim: Increasing shared memory via --shm-size=1g may be necessary for the NIM container due to tokenization scaling with CPU cores in Triton’s Python backend.
premises: Tokenization uses Triton’s Python backend capabilities that scales with the number of CPU cores available.
You may need to increase the available shared memory given to the microservice container.
Example providing 1g of shared memory: dockerrun...--shm-size=1g...

claim: Triton Ensemble Models in NVIDIA NIM for Object Detection can be tuned via environment variables to improve stability under high concurrency and resource constraints.
premises: The NVIDIA NIM for Object Detection enables you to configure the underlying Triton Ensemble Models by using environment variables.
For most use cases, the default values for these variables are sufficient.
However, for highly concurrent workloads in resource-constrained environments, you can tune the values of the following environment variables to improve the stability of the NIM.
NIM_TRITON_IDLE_BYTES_LIMIT: The threshold for idle VRAM memory (bytes) after which the Torch CUDA cache is emptied and all inter-process communication (IPC) files are closed. Default Value: 1GB
NIM_TRITON_FLUSH_INTERVAL: This option determines after how many requests the NIM_TRITON_IDLE_BYTES_LIMIT is checked. Default Value: 1 (After every request)

NIM_TRITON_RATE_LIMIT: If set, this option configures Triton to rate limit the execution count throughout the ensemble model pipeline to the provided integer value. GPU-bound model inference is given priority, while other components of the ensemble model pipeline (pre-processors, post-processors, etc.) are given lower priority. Default Value: None

claim: The NIM container uses specific paths like /opt/nim/.cache for model storage, which can be bind-mounted to host directories to avoid repeated downloads and permission issues.
premises: The following table identifies the paths that are used in the container.
/opt/nim/.cache or NIM_CACHE_PATH: Specifies the path, relative to the root of the container, for downloaded models.
The typical use for this path is to bind mount a directory on the host with this path inside the container.
For example, to use ~/.cache/nim on the host, run mkdir -p ~/.cache/nim before you start the container.
When you start the container, specify the -v ~/.cache/nim:/opt/nim/.cache -u $(id -u) arguments to the docker run command.
If you do not specify a bind or volume mount, the container downloads the model each time you start the container.
The -u $(id -u) argument runs the container with your user ID to avoid file system permission issues and errors.

claim: NVIDIA NIM for Object Detection supports exporting metrics and traces in an OpenTelemetry-compatible format and exposes Prometheus metrics from both the microservice and Triton Inference Server.

claim: OpenTelemetry metrics and traces from the NIM microservice can be configured using specific environment variables including NIM_ENABLE_OTEL, OTEL_SERVICE_NAME, OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT, OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER, and OTEL_TRACES_EXPORTER.
premises: The following environment variables are related to exporting OpenTelemetry metrics and traces from the NIM microservice.
NIM_ENABLE_OTEL: Set to 1 to enable OpenTelemetry instrumentation in NIMs. Default value: None
OTEL_SERVICE_NAME: Specifies the name of the service to use in the exported metrics.
OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT: Specifies the endpoint of an OTLP HTTP receiver. Currently, gRPC is not supported.
OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER="otlp": Specifies to export metrics to the specified OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT in OTLP format. By default, metrics are printed to the container log.
OTEL_TRACES_EXPORTER="otlp": Specifies to export traces to the specified OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT in OTLP format. By default, traces are printed to the container log.

claim: Metrics from both the NIM microservice and Triton Inference Server are accessible via Prometheus endpoints at <nim-host>:8000/v1/metrics and <nim-host>:8002/metrics respectively.
premises: The NIM microservice and Triton Inference Server also expose metrics in Prometheus format.
You can access these metrics through the NIM microservice API at <nim-host>:8000/v1/metrics, and the Triton metrics endpoint at <nim-host>:8002/metrics, respectively.

claim: An OpenTelemetry Collector can be configured with OTLP and Prometheus receivers to collect metrics and traces from NIM and Triton, and export them via Zipkin, OTLP, and debug exporters.
premises: Two receivers are defined: an OTLP receiver that receives both metrics and trace data from the NIM microservice, and a Prometheus receiver that scrapes Triton Inference Server metrics.

Three exporters are defined: a Zipkin exporter to a running Zipkin instance, an OTLP exporter to a downstream collector or backend such as Datadog, and a debug exporter that prints received data to the console (helpful for testing and development).
Traces are received exclusively by the OTLP receiver and exported by both the Zipkin and debug exporters.
Metrics are received by the OTLP and Prometheus receivers.
The metrics are exported by the OTLP and debug exporters.

claim: Prometheus can be installed and configured to scrape metrics from the NIM Triton endpoint at localhost:8002 to monitor NIM metrics.
premises: To install Prometheus for scraping metrics from NIM, download the latest Prometheus version appropriate for your system.

claim: Grafana can be used to create dashboards for NIM metrics by configuring Prometheus as a data source at localhost:9090 after installing and running the Grafana server.
premises: We can use Grafana for creating dashboards for NIM metrics. Install the latest Grafana version appropriate for your system.
Run the Grafana server: cd grafana-v11.0.0/ && ./bin/grafana-server
To access the Grafana dashboard point your browser to http://localhost:3000. You need to login by using the following default credentials: username: admin, password: admin

The first step is to configure the source for Grafana. Click Data Source, select Prometheus, and then specify the Prometheus URL localhost:9090. Save the configuration and you should see a success message.
Now you are ready to create a dashboard with metrics from NIM.

These restrictions can be customized through environment variables, allowing for flexibility in different deployment scenarios.

The supported environment variables include ALLOWED_MIME_TYPES, DOMAIN_WHITELIST, DOMAIN_BLACKLIST, IMAGE_CONNECTION_TIMEOUT, IMAGE_READ_TIMEOUT, IGNORE_SSL_ERRORS, MAX_IMAGE_SIZE, DOWNLOAD_CHUNK_SIZE, IMAGE_URI_HTTPS_ONLY, IMAGE_URI_ALLOW_REDIRECTS, and SUPPORTED_IMAGE_EXT.

claim: VISTA-3D is a research-focused foundation model for medical image segmentation, not intended for direct clinical diagnosis without validation.
premises: VISTA-3D (Versatile Imaging SegmenTation and Annotation) is an interactive foundation model developed for precise segmentation and annotation of human anatomies in medical imaging.
It’s primarily used for comprehensive body exploration, detailed sectional views, and interactive point-prompt segmentation in medical research and analysis.

VISTA-3D is primarily a research tool. While it can assist in creating accurate ground-truth data for medical imaging analysis, it should not be used directly for clinical diagnosis without proper validation and regulatory approval.

claim: To use a fine-tuned VISTA-3D model in VISTA-3D NIM, the model bundle must be mounted to /opt/bundle and the NIM_MANIFEST_PROFILE environment variable must be set to the specific profile ID for user-provided bundles.
premises: Once you have the fine-tuned VISTA-3D bundle at your local storage, you simply need to mount it to /opt/bundle and set the correct model manifest profile for it by setting NIM_MANIFEST_PROFILE environment variable.
Here is the list of available profiles: 43d0baebee73b7bdc2f9c7edf5c726b2323b4f7283eab92fab893d451592656d : utilizes the user provided VISTA-3D bundle (fine-tuned model) at /opt/bundle.

claim: If the VISTA-3D model fails to load in NIM, it is likely due to an incorrect mount path for the fine-tuned bundle or missing bundle files in the mounted directory.
premises: Model not loading: Ensure that the path to the fine-tuned bundle is correct and that the bundle is properly mounted to /opt/bundle.
You may see this error if the bundle is not mounted under /opt/bundle: nimlib.exceptions.ManifestDownloadError: ... InvalidRepoID: pathdoesnotexist:/opt/bundle
and this one if the local directory (which is mounted to /opt/bundle) does not contain the necessary bundle files: nimlib.exceptions.ManifestDownloadError: ... Objectnotfound

claim: Using an incorrect NIM_MANIFEST_PROFILE value may result in automatic profile selection instead of the intended user-provided model, so the correct profile ID must be explicitly set and verified in logs.
premises: Incorrect Profile: Verify that the NIM_MANIFEST_PROFILE environment variable is set to the correct profile ID. The profile ID needs to be one of the above-mentioned IDs. Otherwise, you may end up with some automatic profile selection.

claim: The inference request payload requires an image URL and may optionally include prompts and a local working directory for saving results.
premises: The inference request payload is defined as follows:

- "image" : This field requires a valid URL that points to a 3D medical image in either NIfTI or NRRD format. The URL should be accessible and correctly formatted to ensure the image can be retrieved for processing.
- "Prompts" : This optional field allows users to provide specific prompts for running interactive annotation.
- "local_working_dir" : This optional field allows users to provide a mounted volume for saving inference results.

claim: The prompts field in the inference request payload supports class labels and point coordinates for interactive annotation.
premises: - "Prompts" : This optional field allows users to provide specific prompts for running interactive annotation. The prompts are given in the form of a dictionary with two possible keys: "classes" : A list of label names or indices that serve as class prompts. This list can contain strings (e.g., ["spleen", "liver"]) or integers (e.g., [3, 1]). "points" : A dictionary where the keys are label names or indices, and the values are lists of tuples representing user click points. Each tuple contains three integers corresponding to the coordinates (x, y, z) of a point.

claim: The local_working_dir field maps a host-mounted volume to a container path for saving inference results.
premises: - "local_working_dir" : This optional field allows users to provide a mounted volume for saving inference results. If the directory is /path/on/host/results/ , then in the inference request payload, local_working_dir should be /path/in/container/results/ .

{"image":"https://assets.ngc.nvidia.com/products/api-catalog/vista3d/example-1.nii.gz","prompts":{"classes":["spleen"],"points":{"spleen":[[123,212,151],[123,212,152]]}},"local_working_dir":"/path/in/container/results/"}

claim: The NIM container supports configuration via environment variables passed as -e arguments to docker run, including required and optional settings for API keys, cache paths, ports, and logging levels.
premises: The following table describes the environment variables that can be passed into a NIM, as a -e argument added to a docker run command:
NGC_API_KEY | Yes | None | You must set this variable to the value of your personal NGC API key.
NIM_CACHE_PATH | No | /opt/nim/.cache | Location (in container) where the container caches model artifacts.
NIM_HTTP_TRITON_PORT | No | 8080 | Set the HTTP API port for the triton backend server.

NIM_LOG_LEVEL | No | INFO | Logging threshold for the container image. Accepts strings representing any of the following values (decreasing severity, case-insensitive): CRITICAL, ERROR, WARNING, WARN, INFO, DEBUG.
NIM_HTTP_API_PORT | No | 8000 | Publish the NIM HTTP API port to the prescribed port inside the container.

claim: The /opt/nim/.cache directory (or NIM_CACHE_PATH if set) inside the container can be mounted to a local host path using a volume bind mount to persist model caches and avoid re-downloading models on each container startup.
premises: The following table describes the paths inside the container into which local paths can be mounted.
/opt/nim/.cache (or NIM_CACHE_PATH if present) | Not required, but if this volume is not mounted, the container will do a fresh download of the model each time it is brought up.

This is the directory within which models are downloaded inside the container. It is very important that this directory could be accessed from inside the container. This can be achieved by adding the option -u $(id -u) to the docker run command.

For example, to use ~/.cache/nim as the host machine directory for caching models, first do mkdir -p ~/.cache/nim before running the docker run ... command. | -v ~/.cache/nim:/opt/nim/.cache -u $(id -u)

claim: To run the Hive AI Generated Image Detection NIM container, users must export NGC_API_KEY, NIM_REPOSITORY_OVERRIDE, AWS_REGION, AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, and AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY as environment variables.
premises: Export your personal API key and model credentials as environment variables: export NGC_API_KEY = "..." export NIM_REPOSITORY_OVERRIDE = "s3://..." export AWS_REGION = "..." export AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID = "..." export AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY = "..."

Start the NIM container with one of the Multimodal Safety models: Hive’s AI Generated Image Detection docker run -it --rm --name = nim-server \ --runtime = nvidia \ --gpus = '"device=0"' \ -e NIM_REPOSITORY_OVERRIDE \ -e AWS_REGION \ -e AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID \ -e AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY \ -e NIM_HTTP_API_PORT = 8003 \ -p 8003 :8003 \ -p 8002 :8002 \ nvcr.io/nim/hive/ai-generated-image-detection:1.0.0

claim: The Hive AI Generated Image Detection model returns a probability score for is_ai_generated and normalized scores for possible_sources that sum to 1.0.
premises: Expected output: is_ai_generated represents probability value between 0 and 1.0 indicating the likelihood that the input image was generated by a Generative AI model. possible_sources provides further details as to the image’s source, with support for the most popular AI art generators currently in use. If the model cannot identify a source, it will return none as a possible source. All possible source scores are normalized to sum to 1.0, with each score ranging from 0 to 1.0.

claim: The Hive Deepfake Image Detection model returns bounding box data with vertices, bbox_confidence, and is_deepfake for each detected face, and optionally includes a base64-encoded image with overlaid bounding boxes if return_image is true.
premises: Expected output: Each detected face in the input image is represented a bounding box with: bbox_confidence - a confidence value between 0 and 1.0 indicating the model’s confidence in the detection of the face. vertices - an array of coordinates representing the geometric description of the detected bounding box with the top-left and the bottom-right corners coordinates. is_deepfake - a probability value between 0 and 1.0 indicating the likelihood that the detected face is a deepfake. image - a base64-encoded string representing the input image with overlaid bounding boxes indicating the detected faces. This field is only included in the response if the return_image parameter is set to true in the payload.

claim: To cache models locally and avoid re-downloading, users must set LOCAL_NIM_CACHE, create the directory, set permissions, and mount it to /opt/nim/.cache/ in the container.
premises: The first time you start the container, the microservice downloads the model from NGC. You can avoid this download step on future runs by caching the model locally.

Hive’s AI Generated Image Detection export LOCAL_NIM_CACHE = ~/.cache/nim_sdxl
mkdir -p " $LOCAL_NIM_CACHE "
chmod 777 $LOCAL_NIM_CACHE
docker run -it --rm --name = nim-server \
--runtime = nvidia \
--gpus = '"device=0"' \
-e NIM_REPOSITORY_OVERRIDE \
-e AWS_REGION \
-e AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID \
-e AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY \
-e NIM_HTTP_API_PORT = 8003 \
-p 8003 :8003 \
-p 8002 :8002 \
-v " $LOCAL_NIM_CACHE :/opt/nim/.cache/" \
nvcr.io/nim/hive/ai-generated-image-detection:1.0.0

When you use a model cache, if you change the model profile in NIM_MODEL_PROFILE, then delete the contents of the cache directory on the host before you start the container. Deleting the directory contents ensure that the microservice loads only the specified model profile.

claim: The NIM container can be started with specific runtime flags to enable GPU access, port forwarding, and container naming.
premises: --runtime=nvidia | Ensure NVIDIA drivers are accessible in the container.
--gpus '"device=0"' | Expose NVIDIA GPU 0 inside the container. If you are running on a host with multiple GPUs, you need to specify which GPU to use.

-p 8003:8003 | Forward the port where the NIM HTTP server is published inside the container to access from the host system. The left-hand side of : is the host system ip:port (8003 here), while the right-hand side is the container port where the NIM HTTP server is published.
--name=<container-name | Give a name to the NIM container. Use any preferred value.
--rm | Delete the container after it stops (see Docker docs ).
-it | --interactive + --tty (see Docker docs )

claim: Environment variables configure key aspects of the NIM container, including API ports, logging, model paths, and Triton Inference Server behavior.
premises: The following table identifies the environment variables that are used in the container.
Set environment variables with the -e command-line argument to the docker run command.
NIM_GRPC_API_PORT specifies the network port number, in the container, for gRPC access to the microservice. Default Value: 50051
NIM_HTTP_API_PORT specifies the network port number, in the container, for HTTP access to the microservice. Default Value: 8003
NIM_LOG_LEVEL specifies the logging level. Supported values: DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR, CRITICAL. Default Value: INFO
NIM_CACHE_PATH specifies the fully qualified path, in the container, for downloaded models. Default Value: /opt/nim/.cache
NIM_IGNORE_MODEL_DOWNLOAD_FAIL, when set to true, allows the microservice to continue running if model download from NGC fails, useful in air-gapped environments. Default Value: false
NIM_LOGGING_JSONL, when set to true, creates log records in JSONL format. Default Value: false
NIM_TRITON_LOG_VERBOSE, when set to 1, starts NVIDIA Triton Inference Server with verbose logging. Default Value: 0
NIM_TRITON_REQUEST_TIMEOUT specifies timeout in microseconds for Triton Inference Server; default 0 indicates no timeout. Default Value: 0
NIM_TRITON_GRPC_PORT specifies the gRPC port number for NVIDIA Triton Inference Server. Default Value: 8001
NIM_HTTP_TRITON_PORT specifies the network port number, in the container, for NVIDIA Triton Inference Server. Default Value: 8080
NIM_HTTP_MAX_WORKERS specifies the number of worker threads for HTTP requests. Default Value: 1
NIM_MANIFEST_PATH specifies the fully qualified path, in the container, for the model manifest YAML file. Default Value: /opt/nim/etc/default/model_manifest.yaml
NIM_MODEL_PROFILE specifies the model profile ID to use; by default, the container attempts to automatically match host GPU model and count with optimal profile. Default Value: None

NIM_SERVED_MODEL_NAME specifies model names used in the API; multiple names can be comma-separated; server responds to any; response model name is first in list; default inferred from model_manifest.yaml. Default Value: None
NIM_API_KEY is required for NGC access; no default value. Description: Set this variable to the value of your personal NGC API key.

claim: Bind mounting host directories to container paths like /opt/nim/.cache avoids repeated model downloads and prevents permission issues.
premises: The following table identifies the paths that are used in the container.

/opt/nim/.cache or NIM_CACHE_PATH specifies the path, relative to the root of the container, for downloaded models. The typical use for this path is to bind mount a directory on the host with this path inside the container.
For example, to use ~/.cache/nim on the host, run mkdir -p ~/.cache/nim before you start the container.
When you start the container, specify the -v ~/.cache/nim:/opt/nim/.cache -u $(id -u) arguments to the docker run command.
If you do not specify a bind or volume mount, the container downloads the model each time you start the container.
The -u $(id -u) argument runs the container with your user ID to avoid file system permission issues and errors.

Set environment variables with the -e command-line argument to the docker run command.
NGC_API_KEY: Set this variable to the value of your personal NGC API key.

NIM_ENABLE_KV_CACHE_REUSE: Specifies to enable key-value caching when set to True, the default value. Caching can improve performance when more than 90% of the initial prompt is identical across multiple requests.

NIM_LOG_LEVEL: Specifies the logging level. The microservice supports the following values: DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR, and CRITICAL.

NIM_MODEL_PROFILE: Specifies the model profile ID to use with the container. By default, the container attempts to automatically match the host GPU model and GPU count with the optimal model profile.
NIM_SERVED_MODEL_NAME: Specifies the model names used in the API. Specify multiple names in a comma-separated list.

claim: The microservice can serve models in an air-gapped system by using a pre-cached model profile from a local directory without requiring internet access or connection to the NGC registry.
premises: The microservice supports serving models in an air gap system – also known as air wall, air-gapping, or disconnected network.
If the microservice detects a model profile in the model cache, the microservice can serve that profile from the cache rather than download the model profile again.
By creating a model cache, you can run the microservice without any internet connection and no connection to the NGC registry.

claim: To prepare for air-gapped deployment, model profiles must be cached on a machine with internet access using the NGC API key and specific Docker commands to list and download profiles into a designated cache directory.
premises: On a machine with internet access and connectivity to the NGC registry, perform the following steps to cache model profiles:
Export your NGC API key as an environment variable: $ export NGC_API_KEY = "<nvapi-...>"
Create a directory for the model cache: $ export AIR_GAP_NIM_CACHE = ~/.cache/air-gap-nim-cache $ mkdir -p "${AIR_GAP_NIM_CACHE}"
Optional: Determine a specific model profile to cache: [docker run command with list-model-profiles]
Download the model profiles to cache: [docker run command with download-to-cache -p <profile-one> ...]
For more information about the commands, refer to Utilities for NVIDIA NIM for LLMs in the NIM for LLMs documentation.

claim: To run the microservice on an air-gapped system, transfer the cached model directory and start the container with the LOCAL_NIM_CACHE environment variable pointing to the transferred cache, omitting the NGC_API_KEY since no download occurs.
premises: After the container exits and the model profiles are downloaded, transfer the air-gapped directory, ~/.cache/air-gap-nim-cache, to a path that is accessible to the air-gapped system.
Perform the following steps on the air-gapped system to start the microservice and use model cache:
Export an environment variable with the path to the model cache: $ export LOCAL_NIM_CACHE = <path-to-transferred-model-cache>
Start the container: [docker run command with -v "$LOCAL_NIM_CACHE:/opt/nim/.cache/" and -e NIM_MODEL_PROFILE=<profile-one>]
The key differences from the common command to start the microservice: The NGC_API_KEY environment variable is omitted because the microservice does not download model profiles.
Optional: The NIM_MODEL_PROFILE variable specifies the model profile to run.

claim: Llama 3.1 NemoGuard 8B TopicControl NIM and its underlying NVIDIA Triton Inference Server support exporting metrics and traces in OpenTelemetry-compatible format and expose Prometheus metrics endpoints for observability.
premises: Llama 3.1 NemoGuard 8B TopicControl NIM supports exporting metrics and traces in an OpenTelemetry-compatible format.
Additionally, the microservice and its underlying NVIDIA Triton Inference Server expose metrics through Prometheus endpoints.

claim: Environment variables such as NIM_ENABLE_OTEL, OTEL_SERVICE_NAME, OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT, OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER, and OTEL_TRACES_EXPORTER control OpenTelemetry instrumentation and export behavior in the NIM microservice.
premises: NIM_ENABLE_OTEL: Set to 1 to enable OpenTelemetry instrumentation in NIMs. Default value: None
OTEL_SERVICE_NAME: Specifies the name of the service to use in the exported metrics.
OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT: Specifies the endpoint of an OTLP HTTP receiver. Currently, gRPC is not supported.
OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER="otlp": Specifies to export metrics to the specified OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT in OTLP format. By default, metrics are printed to the container log.
OTEL_TRACES_EXPORTER="otlp": Specifies to export traces to the specified OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT in OTLP format. By default, traces are printed to the container log.

claim: Metrics from both the NIM microservice and Triton Inference Server are accessible via Prometheus endpoints at <nim-host>:8000/v1/metrics and <nim-host>:8002/metrics respectively.
premises: The NIM microservice and Triton Inference Server also expose metrics in Prometheus format.
You can access these metrics through the NIM microservice API at <nim-host>:8000/v1/metrics, and the Triton metrics endpoint at <nim-host>:8002/metrics, respectively.

claim: An OpenTelemetry Collector configuration with OTLP and Prometheus receivers, and Zipkin, OTLP, and debug exporters enables collection and export of metrics and traces from the NIM microservice and Triton Inference Server.
premises: Two receivers are defined: an OTLP receiver that receives both metrics and trace data from the NIM microservice, and a Prometheus receiver that scrapes Triton Inference Server metrics.

Three exporters are defined: a Zipkin exporter to a running Zipkin instance, an OTLP exporter to a downstream collector or backend (e.g., Datadog), and a debug exporter that prints received data to the console (helpful for testing and development).
Traces are received exclusively by the OTLP receiver and exported by both the Zipkin and debug exporters.
Metrics are received by the OTLP and Prometheus receivers and exported by the OTLP and debug exporters.

claim: Model profiles are used by NVIDIA NIM microservices to tune model engines for specific GPU configurations and are identified by unique 64-character hexadecimal profile IDs.
premises: The models for NVIDIA NIM microservices use model engines that are tuned for specific NVIDIA GPU models, number of GPUs, precision, and so on.
NVIDIA produces model engines for several popular combinations and these are referred to as model profiles.

claim: The logging level for the NIM can be controlled using the NIM_LOG_LEVEL environment variable.
premises: The logging level for the NIM can be controlled using the environment variable NIM_LOG_LEVEL.
This variable allows you to specify the level of logging detail you want to see in the container’s logs.

claim: Different logging levels provide varying degrees of detail, with DEBUG logging all inputs and outputs and higher levels reducing log verbosity.
premises: DEBUG : This level will log all inputs and outputs for each endpoint of the server.
INFO : This level will log important events and information about the server’s operation.
WARNING : This level will log warnings about potential issues or errors.
ERROR : This level will log errors that occur during the server’s operation.
CRITICAL : This level will log critical errors that prevent the server from functioning properly.

claim: The default logging level for the NIM is INFO if NIM_LOG_LEVEL is not set.
premises: If no value is provided for NIM_LOG_LEVEL , the default logging level will be INFO .
This means that logs of level INFO and higher are recorded.

claim: Best practice recommends setting the logging level to INFO or WARNING unless detailed debugging is needed.
premises: When setting the logging level, you should consider the trade-off between logging detail and log size.
If you set the logging level to DEBUG , you may generate very large logs that can be difficult to manage.
However, if you set the logging level to a higher level (such as INFO or WARNING ), you may miss important debugging information.
It is generally recommended to set the logging level to INFO or WARNING unless you have a specific need for more detailed logging.

NIM Telemetry offer the following capabilities: Enhances performance and reliability ; Improves compatibility across deployments ; Accelerates troubleshooting and bug resolution ; Informs smarter optimizations and future releases ; Protects user privacy and data security ; Fully optional and configurable .

SAIR (Structurally Augmented IC50 Repository), is the largest public dataset of protein–ligand 3D structures paired with binding potency measurements.

SAIR, produced by SandboxAQ , contains over one million protein–ligand complexes (1,048,857 unique pairs) and a total of 5.2 million 3D structures, curated from the ChEMBL and BindingDB databases and cofolded using the Boltz-1x model.

claim: Release 2.2.0 introduces telemetry control capabilities that enhance performance, reliability, compatibility, and troubleshooting while protecting user privacy.
premises: Telemetry control : NIM Telemetry helps NVIDIA deliver a faster, more reliable experience with greater compatibility across a wide range of environments, while maintaining strict privacy protections and giving users full control.

Benefits: Enhances performance and reliability : Provides an anonymous system and NIM-level insights that help NVIDIA identify bottlenecks, tune performance across hardware configurations, and improve runtime stability.
Improves compatibility across deployments : Helps detect and resolve version, driver, and environment compatibility issues early, reducing friction across diverse infrastructure setups.
Accelerates troubleshooting and bug resolution : Allows NVIDIA to diagnose errors and regressions faster, leading to quicker support response times and higher overall availability.

Informs smarter optimizations and future releases : Real-world, aggregated telemetry data helps guide the optimization of NIM runtimes, model packaging, and deployment workflows, ensuring updates target the scenarios that matter most to users.
Protects user privacy and data security : Collects only minimal, anonymous metadata, such as hardware type and NIM version. No user data, input sequences, or prediction results are collected.
Fully optional and configurable : Telemetry collection is disabled by default. You can toggle telemetry at any time using environment variables.
Configuration: Set NIM_TELEMETRY_MODE=0 to disable telemetry (default) Set NIM_TELEMETRY_MODE=1 to enable telemetry

claim: Accuracy benchmarking for RFdiffusion verifies that the NIM container reproduces sequences generated by the public GitHub version under fixed random number conditions.
premises: Accuracy benchmarking for RFdiffusion involves generating long sequences under fixed scaffolding input.
Given a fixed scaffolding input, there are hundreds of possible configurations at the same length.
We currently only test whether sequences generated under fixed random number conditions in the NIM container match those generated by the public version on GitHub.
The sequences generated by the GitHub version have undergone manual verification beforehand.
This test assesses NIM’s ability to faithfully reproduce these sequences.

claim: RFdiffusion NIM performance is measured as average generated amino acids per second per step, normalized by sequence length and diffusion steps, enabling time estimation for protein structure generation.
premises: The run time of RFdiffusion depends on number of atoms, number and length of chains, and how many chains need to be generated.
To represent overall performance, we measure RFdiffusion’s main performance characteristic as the average number of generated amino acids per second.
We calculate this by normalizing performance results (in milliseconds) by the length of the generated sequence (number of amino acids) and the number of diffusion steps.
This provides an intuitive performance metric; for instance, generation time for a protein binder can be estimated by multiplying the metric by protein length and number of steps.

claim: The NIM includes a benchmarking script that measures both accuracy and performance, is packaged in the Docker image, and requires a local cache directory to avoid re-downloading test data.

claim: Running NIM containers can be stopped using docker stop with the container name, and removed with docker rm if not intended for restart.
