Use docker kill if stop is not responsive. Then, follow it with docker rm $CONTAINER_NAME if you do not intend to restart this container as-is (using docker start $CONTAINER_NAME) in which case you will need to follow the Launch NIM steps again to start a new container for your NIM.
If you did not start a container with --name, look at the output of docker ps to get a container ID for the image you used.

claim: NVIDIA NIM for Cosmos WFM provides configurable sampling parameters to control video generation behavior.
premises: NVIDIA NIM for Cosmos WFM (World Foundation Models) exposes a suite of sampling parameters for fine-grained control over the generation behavior of the model.
Below is a complete reference on how to configure the sampling parameters of an inference request.

claim: The guidance_scale parameter controls the trade-off between prompt adherence and diversity in generated outputs.
premises: Higher guidance values increase the weight of the prompt, resulting in sharper, more detailed, and highly aligned samples, but may reduce diversity and introduce artifacts.
Lower guidance values produce more diverse samples closer to the learned distribution of the model, but may reduce alignment with the prompt.
Adjusting this value allows you to fine-tune the trade-off between creativity and prompt adherence in the generated outputs.

claim: Control parameters like edge, depth, vis, and seg allow conditional video generation using structural inputs from source video.
premises: At least one control type must be provided

Edge detection control parameters. Contains: control (optional; b64 encoded or URL - if omitted, auto-generated from source video), mask (b64 encoded or URL to the mask for edge control), control_weight (0.0-1.0, default 1.0), preset_edge_threshold (one of: very_low, low, medium, high, very_high; default: medium).

Depth estimation control parameters. Contains: control (optional; b64 encoded or URL - if omitted, auto-generated from source video), mask (b64 encoded or URL to the mask for depth control), control_weight (0.0-1.0, default 1.0).

Visual/blur control parameters. Contains: control (optional; b64 encoded or URL - if omitted, auto-generated from source video), mask (b64 encoded or URL to the mask for visual control), control_weight (0.0-1.0, default 1.0), preset_blur_strength (one of: very_low, low, medium, high, very_high; default: medium).

Segmentation control parameters. Contains: control (optional; b64 encoded or URL - if omitted, auto-generated from source video), mask (b64 encoded or URL to the mask for segmentation control), control_weight (0.0-1.0, default 1.0), control_prompt (text prompt for on-the-fly segmentation using SAM2+GroundingDINO; describes what objects to segment, e.g., ‘car building tree’; if not provided, uses first 128 words of main prompt as fallback; only used when control is not provided).

claim: The control_weight parameter adjusts the influence of control inputs, with values over 1.0 sum being scaled down proportionally.
premises: The control_weight parameter (0.0-1.0) controls the strength of each control input’s influence on the generated video.
Higher values (closer to 1.0) enforce stricter adherence to the control structure, ideal for precision applications like autonomous driving.
Lower values (closer to 0.0) allow more creative freedom and deviation from the control input, suitable for artistic applications.

When multiple controls are combined (e.g., edge=1.0, depth=0.5, seg=0.8), weights exceeding a sum of 1.0 are automatically scaled down proportionally to maintain balanced influence while preserving their relative ratios.

claim: Control inputs can be auto-generated from source video or explicitly provided, but omitting the control field (not setting to null) triggers auto-generation.
premises: To have the NIM auto-generate control inputs from the source video, omit the control field entirely —do not set it to null or an empty string, as this will cause errors.
Auto-generation (control extracted from input video): {"edge":{"control_weight":1.0}}
Explicit control (provide your own control video): {"edge":{"control_weight":1.0,"control":"https://example.com/edge_video.mp4"}}

claim: Base64-encoded videos are recommended over URLs to avoid timeout errors during inference.
premises: If you encounter timeout errors when providing video URLs (especially for larger files), use base64-encoded videos instead.
URL downloads have an internal timeout, and large files may not download in time on the first request.
Base64-encoded videos bypass this limitation.

claim: Video input must have between 93 and 480 frames for the video-to-video inference task.
premises: Input video must have between 93 and 480 frames (num_frames = duration * frame_rate).

claim: In homogeneous GPU environments, passing --gpus all to docker run is acceptable.
premises: Passing --gpus all to docker run is acceptable in homogeneous environments with one or more of the same GPU.

claim: In heterogeneous GPU environments, only compute-capable GPUs should be used, and specific GPUs must be exposed via --gpus or CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES.
premises: In heterogeneous environments with a combination of GPUs, workloads should only run on compute-capable GPUs.
Expose specific GPUs inside the container using one of the following: The --gpus flag (e.g. --gpus='"device=1"') or The environment variable CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES (e.g. -e CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=1)
The device ID(s) to use as input(s) are listed in the output of nvidia-smi -L

claim: Passing --ipc=host to docker run is required for multi-GPU setups not using NVLink, but unnecessary on SXM systems or single-GPU profiles.
premises: Passing --ipc=host to docker run is required when not using NVLink for multi-GPU setups.
It is unnecessary on SXM systems or when using profiles with only 1 GPU.

claim: The NIM container supports configurable environment variables for controlling model caching, HTTP server behavior, logging, model download, and specialized features like video encoding and checkpoint paths.
premises: NIM_CACHE_PATH: Path in the container where models are downloaded and stored. This is the location where you may want to mount a persistent cache
NIM_HTTP_API_PORT: Server port used by the Uvicorn HTTP server running the FastAPI
NIM_LOG_LEVEL: Logging threshold for the container image. Accepts strings representing any of the following values (decreasing severity, case-insensitive): CRITICAL, ERROR, WARNING, INFO, DEBUG
NIM_DISABLE_MODEL_DOWNLOAD: Disable model download on container startup
NIM_IGNORE_MODEL_DOWNLOAD_FAIL: If this value is set to 1, model download failures will be ignored so that the container keeps running
NIM_VIDEO_SAVE_QUALITY: Determines the ffmpeg compression quality when encoding the video. Accepted values are between 1 and 9. The compression quality does not affect the diffusion process itself
NIM_ENABLE_WARMUP: Set to 1 to enable warmup for various components
NIM_PERF_PROFILE: Set the performance profile to use for the NIM. Accepted values are latency and throughput
NIM_EDGE_CHECKPOINT, NIM_VIS_CHECKPOINT, NIM_DEPTH_CHECKPOINT, NIM_SEG_CHECKPOINT: Path to the finetuned checkpoint to use for edge, vis, depth, and seg control in the NIM

claim: The /opt/nim/.cache directory (or NIM_CACHE_PATH if set) is used for storing downloaded models and can be mounted from the host to avoid repeated downloads.
premises: /opt/nim/.cache (or NIM_CACHE_PATH if present): This volume is not required, but if it is not mounted, the container will do a fresh download of the model each time it is brought up.
Models are downloaded to this directory inside the container.
For example, to use ~/.cache/nim as the host machine directory for caching models, first execute mkdir -p ~/.cache/nim before running the docker run ... command.

claim: The NIM_ALLOW_URL_INPUT parameter is only applicable to the cosmos-predict1-7b-video2world NIM and controls whether visual input URLs can be passed to the container.
premises: NIM_ALLOW_URL_INPUT: This parameter is only applicable to the cosmos-predict1-7b-video2world NIM. Set to 1 to allow passing URLs of the visual input to the NIM. Set to 0 to disable passing URLs to the NIM.

claim: Cosmos-Predict1-7B models are pre-trained generative models for Physical AI available in Text2World and Video2World variants.
premises: Cosmos-Predict1-7B models are pre-trained, generative models designed for Physical AI.

They are available in two variants: Cosmos-Predict1-7B-Text2World (text-to-video from textual descriptions) and Cosmos-Predict1-7B-Video2World (video from images or other videos with optional text input).

claim: Predict 1 configurations require NVIDIA GPUs with Ampere architecture or later and are optimized using TensorRT and TensorRT-LLM for specific GPU models.
premises: Predict 1 requires NVIDIA GPUs with Ampere architecture or later.

The following configurations are optimized using NVIDIA TensorRT (TRT) and NVIDIA TensorRT-LLM (TRT-LLM) for specific GPU models: H200 (141GB, FP8, 1-8 GPUs), H100 SXM (80GB, FP8, 1-8 GPUs), H100 NVL (94GB, FP8, 1-8 GPUs), H100 PCIe (80GB, FP8, 1-8 GPUs).

claim: Latency profiles in NIM use context-parallel distribution to reduce inference time nearly linearly with GPU count, with CP=8 for 8 GPUs, CP=4 for 4-7 GPUs, CP=2 for 2-3 GPUs, and CP=1 for 1 GPU.
premises: Latency profiles use a parallelized diffusion component with context-parallel (CP) distribution across exposed GPUs, reducing inference time nearly linearly with GPU count.
Four configurations are available: CP=8 (8 GPUs), CP=4 (4-7 GPUs), CP=2 (2-3 GPUs), CP=1 (1 GPU).
Performance example: With an H100 SXM GPU, generating 121 frames takes ~5 minutes with CP1 but ~1 minute with CP8.

claim: Throughput profiles use quantized and TRT-accelerated diffusion components replicated across GPUs to enable concurrent requests and increase throughput nearly linearly with GPU count, but may produce visual artifacts.
premises: Throughput profiles use quantized and TRT-accelerated diffusion components replicated across GPUs, enabling concurrent requests and increasing overall system throughput nearly linearly with GPU count.

TRT-accelerated profiles run diffusion with lower precisions. Throughput is increased up to double that of the latency profile (with 8x H100 SXM), but they may produce visual artifacts not observed with the latency profile.
Throughput profiles are only available on H200, H100 SXM, H100 PCIe, and H100 NVL GPUs.

claim: Cosmos-Transfer2.5-2B is a lighter, more efficient model than Transfer1-7B, supporting latency and throughput profiles with context parallelism or model replication across GPUs.
premises: Cosmos-Transfer2.5-2B is a lighter and more efficient model compared to Transfer1-7B.

It supports two profile types: Latency profiles (use context parallelism to distribute work across GPUs, processing requests sequentially with reduced inference time) and Throughput profiles (replicate the model across GPUs, enabling parallel request processing for higher overall throughput).

claim: Output videos from NIM are encoded in .mp4 container using VP9 codec, while input video support for Cosmos-Predict1-7B-Video2World depends on GPU type and includes a subset of codecs like VP9, VP8, VC1, MPEG-1, MPEG-2, H.264, H.265, and AV1.
premises: Output videos encoded in the b64_video output field always use the .mp4 container and VP9 codec.
For Cosmos-Predict1-7B-Video2World, any video container supported by ffmpeg native demuxers is supported.
Depending on GPU type, supported codecs will be a subset of: VP9, VP8, VC1, MPEG-1, MPEG-2, H.264, H.265 (HEVC), AV1.
Refer to the Video Decode GPU Support Matrix (NVDEC) for details concerning your platform.

claim: AlphaFold2-Multimer NIM provides three main endpoints for protein structure prediction: predict-structure-from-sequences, predict-msa-from-sequences, and predict-structure-from-msa.
premises: AlphaFold2-Multimer NIM provides the following endpoints: protein-structure/alphafold2/multimer/predict-structure-from-sequences, protein-structure/alphafold2/multimer/predict-MSA-from-sequences, protein-structure/alphafold2/multimer/predict-structure-from-MSA
Below, we outline the three endpoints of the API.
The predict-structure-from-sequences endpoint provides a full end-to-end structural prediction pipeline.
The predict-msa-from-sequences endpoint generates Multiple Sequence Alignments (MSAs) and templates used for structural prediction.
The predict-structure-from-msa endpoint takes the results of the predict-msa-from-sequences endpoint and runs structural prediction.

claim: The predict-structure-from-sequences endpoint requires at least 1 and up to 6 amino acid sequences and supports tunable parameters including databases, algorithm, e_value, bit_score, iterations, and relax_prediction.
premises: It requires at least 1 and up to 6 amino acid sequences, though there are many tunable parameters:
- sequences : An array of valid amino acid sequences.
- databases : A list containing any of uniref90 , mgnify , and small_bfd .
- algorithm : The algorithm used for Multiple Sequence Alignment. Currently, only jackhmmer is supported.
- e_value : The sequence e-value for filtering sequences in the MSA.
- bit_score : The sequence bit-score to use for filtering before MSA.
- iterations : The number of MSA iterations to perform.
- relax_prediction : Set to True to run structural relaxation after prediction. This is set to True by default

claim: The predict-msa-from-sequences endpoint generates MSAs and templates for use in structural prediction and is useful for batching CPU-intensive MSA runs across different nodes.
premises: The predict-msa-from-sequences endpoint generates Multiple Sequence Alignments (MSAs) and templates used for structural prediction.
This is useful if you want to batch prediction on different (CPU-intensive) nodes.
It takes the following parameters: sequences, databases, algorithm, e_value, bit_score, iterations
- sequences : An array of valid amino acid sequences.
- databases : A list containing any of uniref90 , mgnify , and small_bfd .
- algorithm : The algorithm used for Multiple Sequence Alignment. Currently, only jackhmmer is supported.
- e_value : The sequence e-value for filtering sequences in the MSA.
- bit_score : The sequence bit-score to use for filtering before MSA.
- iterations : The number of MSA iterations to perform.

claim: The predict-structure-from-msa endpoint requires pre-computed MSA alignments and templates as input and performs structural prediction, with a recommendation to use Python requests over cURL due to input escaping complexities.
premises: The predict-structure-from-msa endpoint takes the results of the predict-msa-from-sequences endpoint and runs structural prediction.

Note : We do not recommend running the msa-to-structure prediction using CURL. This is because the inputs have characters that require careful escaping in bash . For the best user experience, we recommend interacting with this endpoint via the Python requests module.
The predict-structure-from-msa endpoint takes the following arguments: sequences, alignments, templates, relax_prediction
- sequences : An array of valid amino acid sequences.
- alignments : The MSA results from predict-msa-from-sequences .
- templates : Templates from the structural database search.
- relax_prediction : Set to True to run structural prediction after prediction. This is set to True by default

claim: The structural prediction process in AlphaFold2-Multimer scales quadratically with sequence length, making long sequences computationally intensive and potentially requiring several hours to predict.
premises: The structural prediction module scales quadratically with sequence length.
Long sequences can take several hours to predict.

claim: The AlphaFold2-Multimer NIM has been tuned for performance, but MSA and structure prediction remain computationally expensive and performance varies based on system configuration and input characteristics.
premises: The AlphaFold2-Multimer NIM has been tuned to improve performance.
However, the Multiple Sequence Alignment (MSA) and structure prediction processes are still computationally expensive.

Performance will also vary significantly depending on: Which NVIDIA GPUs are attached and available to the NIM; How many CPU cores are available to the NIM; The speed of the Solid State Drive (SSD) available to the NIM; The parameters used to configure the NIM at runtime; The number and composition of amino acid sequences provided to the NIM.

claim: Recommended system requirements for optimal AlphaFold2-Multimer NIM performance include at least 1x NVIDIA A100 GPU, 1TB NVMe Gen 4 SSD (>3,500MB/s), 24+ physical CPU cores, and 200 Mbps+ internet download speed.
premises: At least 1x NVIDIA A100 GPU.
At least 1 Terabyte (1000 Gigabytes) of SSD storage (preferably NVMe Gen 4 with a speed of >3,500MB/s).
At least 24 CPU cores (physical cores).
An internet connection with a download speed of at least 200 Mbps.

claim: Performance expectations vary by hardware configuration: A100 with ≥64 CPU cores and ≥180GB RAM enables sequences up to 3,000 amino acids to succeed (though may take several hours), A100 with ≥32 CPU cores and ≥128GB RAM offers good performance with limited MSA, L40S with same CPU/RAM gives reduced structural prediction speed but similar MSA, and minimum CUDA GPU with ≥32GB VRAM, ≥12 CPU cores, ≥64GB RAM only supports short sequences (<600 aa) with poor experience.
premises: A100 and ≥ 64 CPU cores and ≥ 180GB of RAM (Best): Sequences up to 3,000 amino acids should succeed, but NIM may take several hours to run. Fastest MSA configuration.

A100 and ≥ 32 CPU cores and ≥ 128GB of RAM (Good): Similar speed to the 'Best' configuration, but with more limited MSA performance. Use fewer runners per MSA and fewer cores per MSA (refer to the Sequence to MSA section).
L40S and ≥ 32 CPU cores and ≥ 128GB of RAM (Good): Reduced structural prediction speed compared to A100. Similar MSA performance compared to using the same number of cores with A100 GPU.

NVIDIA CUDA GPU with ≥ 32GB of VRAM and ≥ 12 CPU cores and ≥ 64GB of RAM (Minimum, Poor Experience): Short sequences will run on this configuration, but sequences longer than 600 amino acids may fail in either MSA or structural prediction. MSA will be very slow, and the number of MSA runners should be set to 1 (refer to the Sequence to MSA section).

claim: MSA performance depends on disk speed and CPU cores, can be tuned via NIM_PARALLEL_THREADS_PER_MSA and NIM_PARALLEL_MSA_RUNNERS environment variables, and runtime scales linearly with sequence length and number of input sequences but can grow significantly for sequences with many database hits.
premises: MSA performance is largely dependent on disk speed and CPU cores. Make sure your NIM cache is on a fast SSD, and that you have allocated at least 24 cores to the NIM.
Increase the threads used per MSA process. This can be done using the NIM_PARALLEL_THREADS_PER_MSA environment variable.
Increase the number of concurrent MSA processes. This can be done using the NIM_PARALLEL_MSA_RUNNERS environment variable.

MSA runtime for short sequences can vary dramatically, but generally runtime scales linearly with sequence length and the number of input sequences to align. For sequences with many 'hits' (alignments) in the database (i.e. sequences with motifs observed in many other proteins), the MSA runtime can grow significantly regardless of sequence length.

In general, expect MSA to take anywhere between one minute and six hours per query. Note that these are approximate runtime estimates, and that performance will further vary significantly between machines and input queries.

claim: Structure prediction performance is primarily GPU-dependent, grows exponentially with sequence length (doubling length at least quadruples time), and typically takes between four minutes and 24 hours, with actual performance varying by hardware and input.
premises: Structure prediction performance is mostly dependent on GPU capability. If you find structure prediction to be a bottleneck, consider utilizing a more powerful GPU (for example, switching from A30 to A100).

The time required for structure prediction grows exponentially with sequence length. As a rule of thumb, a sequence that is twice as long will take at least four times as long during the structural prediction phase.

In general, expect the structural prediction component to take anywhere between four minutes and 24 hours. Note that these are approximate runtime estimates, and that performance will further vary significantly between machines and input queries.

claim: The predict-structure-from-sequence endpoint performs end-to-end structural prediction from an amino acid sequence and requires a sequence input with optional tunable parameters including databases, algorithm, e_value, bit_score, iterations, and relax_prediction.
premises: The predict-structure-from-sequence provides a full end-to-end structural prediction pipeline. It requires nothing but an input amino acid sequence, though there are many tunable parameters: sequence, databases, algorithm, e_value, bit_score, iterations, relax_prediction
sequence : A valid amino acid sequence. Refer to the table of amino acid codes if you are unsure if your sequence is valid.

databases : A list containing any of “uniref90”, “mgnify”, and “small_bfd”. These databases contain sequences used to generate a Multiple Sequence Alignment that is used as input to the structural prediction neural network in AlphaFold2. In general, passing all three will provide the most accurate structural prediction at the cost of requiring the longest runtime.

algorithm : The algorithm used for Multiple Sequence Alignment. The available options are jackhmmer and mmseqs2 . mmseqs2 provides significantly improved performance (especially for long sequences), whereas the AlphaFold2 model was trained using the outputs of JackHMMer.

e_value : The sequence e-value for filtering sequences in the MSA. Smaller is stricter; fewer sequences will be included, however, this will also reduce the sensitivity of the MSA. The default value is in general a good choice. This value ranges from 0 to 1.
bit_score : The sequence bit-score to use for filtering before MSA. If passed, this is used in place of e-value for filtering. A good starting place is around 200. This value is greater than zero.
iterations : The number of MSA iterations to perform. In general, the default iterations=1 is sufficient and takes the least amount of time.
relax_prediction : Set to True to run structural relaxation after prediction. This is set to True by default and helps fix clashes in the predicted structure.

claim: The predict-msa-from-sequence endpoint generates Multiple Sequence Alignments and templates for use in structural prediction and is useful for batching MSA inference across nodes.
premises: The predict-msa-from-sequence endpoint generates the Multiple Sequence Alignments and templates used for structural prediction.
This is useful if you want to batch prediction on different nodes.

sequence : A valid amino acid sequence. Refer to the table of amino acid codes if you are unsure if your sequence is valid.

These databases contain sequences used to generate a Multiple Sequence Alignment that is used as input to the structural prediction neural network in AlphaFold2. In general, passing all three will provide the most accurate structural prediction at the cost of requiring the longest runtime. If you must pick only one, uniref90 is considered the best choice, though it is still recommended to run with all three.

algorithm : The algorithm used for Multiple Sequence Alignment. The available options are jackhmmer and mmseqs2 . mmseqs2 provides significantly improved performance (especially for long sequences), whereas the AlphaFold2 model was trained using the outputs of JackHMMer.

e_value : The sequence e-value for filtering sequences in the MSA. Smaller is stricter; fewer sequences will be included, however, this will also reduce the sensitivity of the MSA. The default value is in general a good choice. This value ranges from 0 to 1.
bit_score : The sequence bit-score to use for filtering before MSA. If passed, this is used in place of e-value for filtering. A good starting place is around 200. This value is greater than zero.
iterations : The number of MSA iterations to perform. In general, the default iterations=1 is sufficient and takes the least amount of time.

claim: The predict-structure-from-msa endpoint performs structural prediction using precomputed MSA and templates, and is recommended to be accessed via Python requests due to bash escaping complexities with input data.

premises: Structure prediction performance is mostly dependent on GPU capability. If you find structure prediction to be a bottleneck, consider utilizing a more powerful GPU (for example, switching from A30 to A100).

The time required for structure prediction grows exponentially with sequence length. As a rule of thumb, a sequence that is twice as long will take at least four times as long during the structural prediction phase.
In general, expect the structural prediction component to take between four minutes and 24 hours.

claim: The AlphaFold2 NIM allows customization of the NIM cache location both on the host file system and inside the container.
premises: The location of the NIM cache can be changed on both the local file system and within the NIM.

To change the location of the cache inside the container, you must mount the new destination path and provide the new path in the NIM_CACHE_PATH environment variable.

claim: The AlphaFold2 NIM can be configured to use an alternative port for HTTP or gRPC requests by modifying the -p option and setting the NIM_HTTP_API_PORT environment variable.
premises: If you have other HTTP or gRPC servers running, you may need to make the 8000 port available by using another port for your NIM.

An example shows setting the NIM to run on port 7979 using -p7979:7979 and -eNIM_HTTP_API_PORT=7979.

claim: The AlphaFold2 NIM supports tuning of MSA parallelism via two environment variables: NIM_PARALLEL_MSA_RUNNERS and NIM_PARALLEL_THREADS_PER_MSA, with constraints based on CPU core count.
premises: There are two layers of tunable parallelism for MSA: NIM_PARALLEL_MSA_RUNNERS controls coarse-grained parallelism, and NIM_PARALLEL_THREADS_PER_MSA controls threads per MSA process.
The product of NIM_PARALLEL_MSA_RUNNERS and NIM_PARALLEL_THREADS_PER_MSA should be <= the number of CPU cores available to the NIM.
Default values are NIM_PARALLEL_MSA_RUNNERS=3 and NIM_PARALLEL_THREADS_PER_MSA=8, which work well for most machines.
On a 32-core machine, setting NIM_PARALLEL_MSA_RUNNERS=3 and NIM_PARALLEL_THREADS_PER_MSA=10 fits the workload to the machine.

claim: The Boltz2 NIM container requires curl, jq, and the Python requests module to run the provided examples for inference and response processing.

jq is used to process and reformat responses from the NIM so they are easier to read.
The Python requests module facilitates HTTP requests made in many of the examples for this NIM.

claim: The Boltz2 NIM container can be started with GPU support using either the legacy --runtime=nvidia flag or the recommended --gpus flag for Docker 19.03+.
premises: For Docker 19.03+, you can use the --gpus flag instead, which works without additional configuration.

Example commands show usage of --gpus all and --gpus '"device=0"' to specify GPU usage.
The preceding command starts the container with the default profile, using all available system GPUs.

claim: Model caching can be enabled by setting the LOCAL_NIM_CACHE environment variable and mounting it as a volume to avoid re-downloading models on subsequent runs.
premises: Create a NIM Cache. If one already exists, you may use the existing one. export LOCAL_NIM_CACHE = ~/.cache/nim
mkdir -p ${ LOCAL_NIM_CACHE } chmod 777 ${ LOCAL_NIM_CACHE }
The first time you start the container, the microservice downloads the model from NGC. You can avoid this download step on future runs by caching the model locally.
Run the container with the cache directory as a volume mount: -v $LOCAL_NIM_CACHE:/opt/nim/.cache

claim: To run the Boltz2 NIM on a Slurm-based HPC cluster, Enroot must be used to import and run the NGC container after setting up NGC authentication credentials.

Important: NGC_API_KEY: You must export your NGC API key before running the Slurm script so that Enroot can pull the image from NGC.

Create the credentials file so Enroot can pull images from NGC. Replace YOUR_NGC_API_KEY with your NGC API key: echo 'machine nvcr.io login $oauthtoken password YOUR_NGC_API_KEY' > ~/.config/enroot/.credentials
Enroot: Version 3.4.1 or newer is supported.
On the login node, verify Enroot is installed: enrootversion && whichenroot

claim: The Boltz-2 NIM container can be deployed using Docker with specific environment variables and volume mounts for API access on port 8000.
premises: Run the NIM container: export LOCAL_NIM_CACHE=~/.cache/nim export NGC_API_KEY=<YourNGCAPIKey> docker run --rm --name boltz2 --runtime=nvidia --shm-size=16G -e NGC_API_KEY -v$LOCAL_NIM_CACHE:/opt/nim/.cache -p8000:8000 nvcr.io/nim/mit/boltz2:1.7.0
Verify the NIM is ready by checking the health endpoint: curl -X GET 'http://localhost:8000/v1/health/ready' -H 'accept: application/json'

claim: The Boltz-2 NIM API supports protein structure prediction via POST requests to /biology/mit/boltz2/predict with configurable input parameters including polymers, ligands, constraints, and prediction settings.
premises:
Endpoint path: /biology/mit/boltz2/predict
Request type: post

Input parameters include: polymers (required, list of Polymer objects with id, molecule_type, sequence, etc.), ligands (optional list), constraints (optional list of Pocket or Bond), recycling_steps (int, default 3), sampling_steps (int, default 50), diffusion_samples (int, default 1), step_scale (float, default 1.638), output_format (string, default 'mmcif')
Outputs include: structures (list of Structure), confidence_scores (list of float), affinities (dictionary when predict_affinity is true), metrics (dictionary)

claim: The Boltz-2 NIM provides a health check endpoint at /v1/health/ready to verify service readiness, returning HTTP 200 when the microservice is ready to accept requests.
premises:
Endpoint path: /v1/health/ready
Input parameters: None.
Outputs: The output of the endpoint is a JSON response with a value that indicates the readiness of the microservice. When the NIM is ready, it returns the response 200.
Example: curl -s -w "\nStatus code: %{http_code}\n" -H "Content-Type: application/json" $URL returns status code 200 when ready

claim: The Boltz-2 NIM automatically selects the most suitable profile for the detected hardware by default, attempting to use TensorRT-LLM and TF32 for maximum performance, and falling back to PyTorch with a warning if TensorRT-LLM is not supported.
premises: The Boltz-2 NIM is designed to automatically select the most suitable profile for the detected hardware from the list of available profiles.
By default, the NIM will attempt to use TensorRT-LLM and NVIDIA TensorFloat32 (TF32) for inference for maximum performance.
If the attached GPU does not support TensorRT-LLM, the NIM will automatically fall back to PyTorch and issue a warning.

claim: Users can manually override the automatic profile selection by setting the NIM_MODEL_PROFILE environment variable at startup to ensure reproducibility or force a specific performance characteristic.
premises: While the NIM automatically selects a profile, you can manually override this selection to use a specific model configuration.
This can be useful for ensuring reproducibility or forcing a particular performance characteristic.
Use the NIM_MODEL_PROFILE environment variable at startup to specify the desired profile.

claim: Fine-grained control over acceleration features is possible through environment variables that enable or disable TensorRT and TF32 for specific modules like pairformer, affinity, and diffusion.
premises: For fine-grained control over performance, you can enable or disable specific acceleration features using the following environment variables.
NIM_BOLTZ_STRUCTURE_OPTIMIZED_BACKEND sets the backend for the pairformer module with default 'trt' and fallback to 'torch'.
NIM_BOLTZ_AFFINITY_OPTIMIZED_BACKEND sets the backend for the affinity module with default 'trt' and fallback to 'torch'.
NIM_BOLTZ_ENABLE_DIFFUSION_TF32 enables or disables TF32 for the diffusion model, with default '1' (enabled) for performance boost on Ampere and newer GPUs.

claim: Deploying the Boltz-2 NIM on multi-GPU systems requires proportional increases in CPU cores and system RAM, with a recommendation of 12 additional CPU cores and 32 GB RAM per additional GPU.
premises: The Boltz-2 NIM is designed to run with one or more NVIDIA GPUs.
When increasing the number of GPUs allocated to the NIM, it is recommended to also increase the allocated number of CPU cores and RAM.
As a rule of thumb, for each additional GPU allocated, you should also allocate another additional 12 CPU cores and 32 GB of additional system RAM.

claim: Startup-time input limits for polymer chains, ligands, and polymer length can be customized via environment variables to prevent excessive resource usage and out-of-memory errors.
premises: The Boltz-2 NIM can be configured at startup time using environment variables to control input limits and resource usage.
These settings help prevent excessively large requests that could impact performance or cause out-of-memory errors.
NIM_MAX_POLYMER_INPUTS sets the maximum number of polymer chains (default: 12).
NIM_MAX_LIGAND_INPUTS sets the maximum number of ligands (default: 20).
NIM_MAX_POLYMER_LENGTH sets the maximum allowed length for individual polymer sequences (default: 4096).

claim: Performance optimization parameters such as recycling steps, sampling steps, diffusion samples, and step scale allow trade-offs between prediction quality and computational cost, with defaults suitable for most production workloads.
premises: The Boltz-2 NIM provides several parameters that can be tuned to optimize performance for your specific use case.
Recycling steps (range: 1-10, default: 3) control iterative refinement; higher values improve accuracy but increase computation time.
Sampling steps (range: 10-1,000, default: 50) control diffusion sampling; more steps improve quality but increase runtime.
Diffusion samples (range: 1-25, default: 1) control independent structure predictions; more samples increase diversity but multiply computational cost.
Step scale (range: 0.5-5.0, default: 1.638) affects sampling temperature; lower values increase diversity, higher values may improve convergence.

These parameters offer a tradeoff between prediction quality and computational cost. For production workloads, consider starting with default values and adjusting based on specific quality and latency requirements.

claim: Binding affinity prediction requires additional parameters and significantly more computational resources than structure prediction, including higher sampling steps, affinity-specific sampling, and molecular weight correction for certain ligands.
premises: When performing binding affinity prediction with ligands, additional parameters control the quality and performance of the affinity calculation.
Affinity sampling steps (range: 10-1,000, default: 200) control diffusion sampling for affinity and are typically higher than structural sampling steps.
Affinity diffusion samples (range: 1-10, default: 5) control independent affinity predictions averaged for reliability.
Molecular weight correction (affinity_mw_correction, default: False) can improve accuracy for certain ligands.
Binding affinity prediction requires significantly more computational resources than structure prediction alone.
The affinity-specific parameters typically use higher values than their structural counterparts to ensure accurate binding energy estimates.

claim: Working with ligands and binding affinity prediction introduces unique performance characteristics including increased GPU memory usage, 2-4x runtime increase, reduced concurrent request capacity, and a limit of one ligand affinity prediction per request despite supporting up to 20 ligands per request.
premises: Working with ligands and binding affinity prediction has unique performance characteristics:
- Memory scaling: Protein-ligand complexes require additional GPU memory compared to protein-only predictions
- Runtime impact: Binding affinity prediction can increase total runtime by 2-4x compared to structure-only prediction
- Concurrent requests: Due to higher memory usage, fewer concurrent requests may be possible when using binding affinity prediction
- Ligand count limits: The NIM supports up to 20 ligands per request, but binding affinity can only be predicted for one ligand at a time

claim: Repeated queries against the Boltz-2 NIM can be executed serially using a loop to process multiple sequences, with each request being blocking and limited to one per submitter at a time.
premises: In computational biology and drug discovery, it is common to need to analyze hundreds, thousands, or even millions of protein sequences to find candidates with the desired properties.
Repeated queries against the NIM can be submitted as subsequent requests.
For example, requests from a list of sequences can be submitted using a for loop.
Each request is blocking, which means a maximum of one request from a single submitter will run at a time when calling the NIM in this manner.

claim: The Boltz-2 NIM uses Docker containers, each with its own container, and can be configured in several ways.
premises: The Boltz-2 NIM uses Docker containers.
Each NIM has its own Docker container and there are several ways to configure it.
The section below describes how to configure a NIM container.

claim: In environments with multiple GPUs, specific GPUs can be exposed inside the container using the --gpus flag or the NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES environment variable.
premises: In environments with a combination of GPUs, you can only expose specific GPUs inside the container using either:
- The --gpus flag. For example, docker run --gpus='"device=1"' ...
- The environment variable NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES. For example, to expose only Device 1, pass -e NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=1. To expose GPU IDs 1 and 4, pass -e NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=1,4.

claim: The Boltz-2 NIM container image is available on NVIDIA Container Registry as nvcr.io/nim/mit/boltz2:<version>, with example usage showing nvcr.io/nim/mit/boltz2:1.7.0.
premises: The Boltz-2 NIM container image on NVIDIA Container Registry is nvcr.io/nim/mit/boltz2:<version> (NGC org nim, team mit).
Examples on this page use the substituted form nvcr.io/nim/mit/boltz2:1.7.0, which resolves to that path.

claim: Environment variables such as NGC_API_KEY, NIM_CACHE_PATH, NIM_HTTP_API_PORT, and others can be passed to the Boltz-2 NIM container via -e flags in docker run to configure behavior including API authentication, caching, port exposure, logging, and telemetry.
premises: The following table describes the environment variables that can be passed into a NIM as a -e argument added to a docker run command:
| ENV | Required? | Default | Notes |
| NGC_API_KEY | Yes | None | You must set this variable to the value of your personal NGC API key. |
| NIM_CACHE_PATH | No | /opt/nim/.cache | Location (in container) where the container caches model artifacts. |
| NIM_HTTP_API_PORT | No | 8000 | Publish the NIM service to the prescribed port inside the container... |
| NIM_LOG | No | INFO | Controls NIM service logging... |
| NIM_LOG_LEVEL | No | INFO | Alternative NIM logging level control... |
| TLLM_LOG_LEVEL | No | INFO | Controls TensorRT-LLM backend logging... |
| MODEL_PATH | No | Unset | This variable enables a hard override of the NIM’s model path... |
| NIM_BOLTZ_ENABLE_DIFFUSION_TF32 | No | 1 | Integer: 1 enables TF32 for diffusion inference (default); 0 disables it... |
| NIM_BOLTZ_STRUCTURE_OPTIMIZED_BACKEND | No | trt | Controls the backend used for the pairformer... |
| NIM_DEFAULT_RANDOM_SEED | No | 42 | Controls the random seed used for torch / trt inference. |
| NIM_TELEMETRY_MODE | No | 0 | String 0 disables telemetry (default)... |
| NIM_TELEMETRY_ENABLE_ON_RTX | No | false | String true allows telemetry on RTX GPUs when NIM_TELEMETRY_MODE is not 0... |

claim: NIM Telemetry collects minimal host and NIM information to improve performance, reliability, and compatibility, is disabled by default on RTX GPUs, and can be enabled via NIM_TELEMETRY_MODE and NIM_TELEMETRY_ENABLE_ON_RTX.
premises: NIM Telemetry collects minimal host and NIM information to help improve performance, reliability, and compatibility across deployments. Collection is disabled by default on RTX GPUs and can be enabled explicitly when you opt in.
## NIM_TELEMETRY_MODE #
Controls telemetry collection mode.
- 0 — Disables telemetry.
- 1 — Enables baseline collection (hardware and NIM information).
Default: 0
## NIM_TELEMETRY_ENABLE_ON_RTX #
Set to true to allow telemetry collection on RTX GPUs. This setting applies only when NIM_TELEMETRY_MODE is not 0 (for example, when baseline collection is enabled on the deployment).
Default: false

claim: The /opt/nim/.cache directory (or NIM_CACHE_PATH if set) inside the container should be mounted as a volume to persist model artifacts and avoid re-downloading on each container startup.
premises: The following table describes the paths inside the container into which local paths can be mounted:
| Container path | Required | Notes | Docker argument example |

| /opt/nim/.cache (or NIM_CACHE_PATH if present) | Not required, but if this volume is not mounted, the container will do a fresh download of the model each time it is brought up. | This is the directory within which models are downloaded inside the container. It is very important that this directory can be accessed from inside the container. This can be achieved by setting the permissions of the local directory to read-write-execute (777). For example, to use ~/.cache/nim as the host machine directory for caching models, first do mkdir -p ~/.cache/nim, then chmod 777 ~/.cache/nim before running the docker run command. | -v ~/.cache/nim:/opt/nim/.cache |

claim: The Boltz-2 NIM supports logging configuration via environment variables NIM_LOG, NIM_LOG_LEVEL, and TLLM_LOG_LEVEL, which can be set to DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR, CRITICAL, or VERBOSE (for TLLM_LOG_LEVEL) to control verbosity for debugging or production use.
premises: The Boltz-2 NIM provides logging environment variables to control verbosity for different components. You can configure these when starting the container to adjust the level of detail in logs for debugging or production use.
## Example: Running with Logging Configuration #
The following example shows how to run the NIM with standard logging configuration:
export LOCAL_NIM_CACHE=~/.cache/nim
export NGC_API_KEY=<YourNGCAPIKey>
docker run --rm --name boltz2 --runtime=nvidia \
\--shm-size=16G \
\-e NGC_API_KEY \
\-e NIM_LOG=INFO \
\-e NIM_LOG_LEVEL=INFO \
\-e TLLM_LOG_LEVEL=INFO \
\-v$LOCAL_NIM_CACHE:/opt/nim/.cache \
nvcr.io/nim/mit/boltz2:1.7.0
## Example: Debug Logging for Troubleshooting #
To enable verbose logging for troubleshooting issues, set the log levels to their most detailed settings:
export LOCAL_NIM_CACHE=~/.cache/nim
export NGC_API_KEY=<YourNGCAPIKey>
docker run --rm --name boltz2 --runtime=nvidia \
\--shm-size=16G \
\-e NGC_API_KEY \
\-e NIM_LOG=DEBUG \
\-e NIM_LOG_LEVEL=DEBUG \
\-e TLLM_LOG_LEVEL=VERBOSE \
\-v$LOCAL_NIM_CACHE:/opt/nim/.cache \
nvcr.io/nim/mit/boltz2:1.7.0

claim: The Boltz-2 NIM's accuracy should match the reference implementation when using equivalent parameters and inputs.
premises: The Boltz-2 NIM is based on the state-of-the-art Boltz-2 architecture for biomolecular structure prediction.
The NIM’s accuracy should match that of the reference implementation when using equivalent parameters and inputs.

claim: TensorRT backend consistently outperforms the OSS backend for both structure and binding affinity prediction on H100 GPUs across all benchmark cases.

claim: To resolve simulation instability producing NaN energies or mid-trajectory crashes, reduce the timestep, validate input coordinates, adjust NPT settings, and verify PBC mode configuration.
premises: If simulations produce NaN energies or crash mid-trajectory, do the following:
- Reduce the timestep: The default dt of 1.0 fs might be too large. 'config': { 'dt': 0.5 }
- Check input coordinates: Ensure that coordinates are physically reasonable. Overlapping atoms or extreme distortions cause numerical instability.
- Adjust NPT settings: Reduce barostat_diag_max and barostat_shear_max to use more conservative cell moves.
- Verify PBC mode: Periodic structures require ALCHEMI_NIM_PBC=true (the default) and a valid cell in the request. For isolated molecules, set ALCHEMI_NIM_PBC=false.

For inorganic solids (periodic systems), start the container with ALCHEMI_NIM_PBC=true, which is the default.
For isolated molecules, start the container with ALCHEMI_NIM_PBC=false.
To run both workloads, launch separate containers for periodic and non-periodic workloads.
A PBC mode mismatch is reported in the container logs or returned as an error response from the API.

claim: To resolve model loading failure when using an externally mounted model, verify the volume mount path matches ALCHEMI_NIM_MODEL_PATH, check file permissions for readability, and avoid read-only mounts if write access is needed for caching.

- If using a read-only volume mount (:ro) for custom models causes crashes, mount the directory as read-write (omit :ro). The NIM might require write access to the cache.

claim: The debug exporter supports three verbosity levels: basic, normal, and detailed, with basic as the default.
premises: The following settings are optional: - `verbosity` (default = `basic`): the verbosity of the debug exporter: `basic`, `normal` or `detailed`.

## Verbosity levels
The following subsections describe the output from the exporter depending on the configured verbosity level - `basic`, `normal` and `detailed`. The default verbosity level is `basic`.

claim: When `useinternallogger` is true (default), the exporter uses the collector's internal logger and is affected by the collector's logging configuration; when false, it uses `outputpaths` and setting `outputpaths` when `useinternallogger` is true results in a configuration error.
premises: - `useinternallogger` (default = `true`): uses the collector's internal logger for output. See below for description.

- `outputpaths` (default = `["stdout"]`): a list of file paths to write output to. This option can only be used when `useinternallogger` is `false`. Special strings "stdout" and "stderr" are interpreted as standard output and standard error respectively. All other values are treated as file paths. Setting `outputpaths` when `useinternallogger` is `true` results in a configuration error.

When `useinternallogger` is set to `true` (the default), the exporter uses the collector's [internal logger][internal_telemetry] for output. This comes with the following consequences:
- The output from the exporter may be annotated by additional output from the collector's logger.
- The output from the exporter is affected by the collector's [logging configuration][internallogsconfig] specified in `service::telemetry::logs`.

When `useinternallogger` is set to `false`, the exporter does not use the collector's internal logger. Changing the values in `service::telemetry::logs` has no effect on the exporter's output. The exporter's output is sent to the paths specified in `outputpaths` (default: `["stdout"]`). You can configure `outputpaths` to send output to `stderr`, a file, or multiple destinations.

claim: The debug exporter supports sampling configuration via `sampling_initial` and `sampling_thereafter`, where the default value of `1` for `sampling_thereafter` disables sampling, and values higher than `1` enable sampling.
premises: - `sampling_initial` (default = `2`): number of messages initially logged each second.

- `sampling_thereafter` (default = `1`): sampling rate after the initial messages are logged (every Mth message is logged). The default value of `1` means that sampling is disabled. To enable sampling, change `sampling_thereafter` to a value higher than `1`. Refer to Zap docs for more details on how sampling parameters impact number of messages.

NIM LLM brings state-of-the-art LLM serving to enterprise and developer workflows with validated containers, curated weights, and direct alignment with upstream inference engines.

claim: NIM LLM offers three distinct offerings—NIM Day 0, NIM Turbo, and NIM Certified—to balance publication speed, peak performance, and enterprise lifecycle guarantees.
premises: NIM LLM is available under three NIM offerings so you can choose the right balance of publication speed, peak performance, and enterprise lifecycle guarantees:
- NIM Day 0: Fast access to newly released models with functional validation on a smaller set of NVIDIA GPUs.
- NIM Turbo: Validated best-in-class inference performance for top models.

- NIM Certified: Enterprise production packaging with broader compatibility, documented refresh cadence, CVE patching, OSRB compliance, security updates, FedRAMP ready branches for government use cases, and NVIDIA AI Enterprise support.

claim: NIM LLM provides key benefits including faster feature access, uncompromised performance, and reduced operational burden by aligning with upstream engines and eliminating abstraction layers.
premises: NIM LLM aligns with upstream engines and eliminates heavy downstream abstraction layers to provide the following benefits:
- Faster Feature Access: You receive updates in weeks rather than months, ensuring rapid access to the latest upstream engine optimizations, new CUDA versions, and hardware support.
- Uncompromised Performance: You get direct access to raw vLLM capabilities without the latency of abstraction layers.
- Reduced Operational Burden: You can use pre-validated configurations to eliminate the trial and error of tuning complex LLM deployments.

claim: NIM LLM enables reliable deployment of generative AI across industries for use cases such as chatbots, content generation, sentiment analysis, and language translation.
premises: NIM LLM enables organizations to reliably deploy generative AI capabilities across a wide range of applications at scale, including the following:
- Chatbots and Virtual Assistants: Build bots with human-like language understanding and responsiveness.
- Content Generation and Summarization: Generate high-quality content or distill lengthy articles into concise summaries with ease.
- Sentiment Analysis: Understand user sentiments in real time, driving better business decisions.
- Language Translation: Remove language barriers with efficient and accurate translation services.

claim: NIM Certified provides enterprise-ready packaging with stability, security, and compliance features for long-lived production deployments.
premises: For long-lived production deployments, NIM Certified adds the packaging and architectural guardrails that enterprise environments require.
While open-source inference engines change rapidly, NIM Certified provides the stability and support required for production enterprise environments.
Key packaging features include: Curated Model Weights and Quantization; Enterprise Support and Security; FedRAMP Compliance; Health and Observability.

claim: NIM LLM version 2.0 adopts a one container, one backend architecture using vLLM exclusively for predictable behavior and direct upstream access.
premises: The NIM LLM container is designed for deployment simplicity, startup reliability, and inference performance parity with upstream engines.

Unlike the 1.x architecture that bundled multiple backends into a single container, NIM LLM version 2.0 embraces a one container, one backend philosophy for predictable behavior and direct access to upstream features.
- Inference Engine (vLLM): The core engine that executes model inference and provides native OpenAI-compatible API endpoints.

claim: NIM LLM supports both model-specific and model-free containers to accommodate different deployment needs, including early access to new models and secure enterprise environments.
premises: NIM LLM supports two distinct deployment modalities to cater to different operational needs: Model-Specific NIMs and Model-Free NIMs.
Model-Specific NIMs include a model-specific manifest, curated model weights, validated quantization profiles, and optimal runtime configurations tailored specifically for the target model.

A model-free NIM is a flexible container that serves a model you configure dynamically at runtime, generating its model manifest at runtime and supporting remote repositories (NGC, Hugging Face, Amazon S3, Google Cloud Storage) and local directories.

You can use model-free NIMs when: you need early support for a newly released model architecture that vLLM supports; you deploy custom-trained or heavily fine-tuned models; or you want to reduce container approvals in secure enterprise environments by validating a single container for multiple models.

claim: Migrating from NIM LLM 1.x to 2.0 involves shifting to single backend containers, transparent model behavior, and direct upstream alignment.
premises: Moving from NIM 1.x to 2.0 involves a shift in how containers are structured and how model differences are handled.

Key architectural changes include: Single Backend Containers (replacing multi-backend with dedicated vLLM), Transparent Model Behavior (tool-calling and differences no longer hidden), and Upstream Alignment (enterprise shims streamlined, features driven directly upstream).

claim: NIM LLM is built on vLLM through an active upstream partnership that ensures mutual benefits for NVIDIA and the open source community.
premises: NIM LLM is built on vLLM, an open source, high-throughput inference engine for large language models.
NVIDIA actively collaborates with the vLLM community, contributing optimizations upstream and integrating community-driven innovations into NIM LLM.
NVIDIA is committed to sustaining this upstream partnership and ensuring its contributions strengthen vLLM for the entire community.
This collaboration ensures NIM LLM users benefit from the latest advances in LLM serving technology while the broader open source ecosystem gains access to hardware-level improvements.

claim: To start using the MSA Search NIM, users must first complete prerequisites including compatible hardware and software, an NGC account and API key, Docker authentication with NGC, and Python 3 with the requests module.
premises: Before you begin, ensure you have completed the setup described in the Prerequisites and Support Matrix, including: Compatible hardware and software, NGC account and API key, Docker authentication with NGC, Python 3 with the requests module (for running examples)

claim: Starting the NIM container requires setting the NGC_API_KEY environment variable, creating a local cache directory with specific permissions, and running a Docker command that mounts the cache and exposes port 8000.
premises: Ensure you have logged in to Docker and set your NGC_API_KEY environment variable as described in the Prerequisites.
Create a local cache directory for the NIM.

export LOCAL_NIM_CACHE=~/.cache/nim
mkdir -p "$LOCAL_NIM_CACHE"
sudo chmod 0777 -R "$LOCAL_NIM_CACHE"
Start the NIM container: docker run -it --rm --runtime=nvidia --gpus all -e NGC_API_KEY -v "$LOCAL_NIM_CACHE:/opt/nim/.cache" -p 8000:8000 nvcr.io/nim/colabfold/msa-search:2

claim: The MSA Search NIM service can be confirmed as ready by sending a curl request to the health check endpoint at http://localhost:8000/v1/health/ready.
premises: Confirm the service is ready to respond to inference requests: curl http://localhost:8000/v1/health/ready

claim: The MSA Search NIM can perform standard multiple sequence alignment on protein sequences using either a Python client or curl to send requests to the /biology/colabfold/msa-search/predict endpoint.
premises: The following examples demonstrate how to use the MSA Search NIM to perform multiple sequence alignment on protein sequences.
Save the following Python example to a file named nim_client.py: [code showing POST to /biology/colabfold/msa-search/predict]
You can also use curl to send requests directly: [curl command to /biology/colabfold/msa-search/predict]

claim: The MSA Search NIM supports paired MSA search for protein complexes by finding homologous sequences for each chain and pairing them by species to preserve co-evolutionary signals for accurate structure prediction.
premises: The MSA Search NIM also supports paired MSA search for protein complexes (multimers).
Paired search finds homologous sequences for each chain and pairs them by species, preserving co-evolutionary signals essential for accurate complex structure prediction.
The response contains alignments_by_chain with paired alignments for each chain (for example, “A”, “B”), where each chain has the same number of sequences paired by species.

claim: The MSA Search NIM supports structural template search by querying PDB databases to find proteins with similar structures and retrieving corresponding mmCIF structure files.
premises: The MSA Search NIM supports structural template search for finding homologous protein structures.
Template search queries PDB databases to find proteins with similar structures and retrieves the corresponding mmCIF structure files.

The response includes: search_hits : Template hits in M8 format organized by database, structures : Retrieved mmCIF structure files for the top hits, alignments : MSA alignments (same as standard MSA search)

claim: The port for the OpenFold3 NIM can be changed by setting the -p option and the NIM_HTTP_API_PORT environment variable.
premises: The -p option sets the port for the NIM.
Set the NIM_HTTP_API_PORT environment variable to the new port.
The following is an example of setting the NIM to run on port 6626: ... -eNIM_HTTP_API_PORT=6626 -p6626:6626 ...

claim: The backend optimization for the OpenFold3 NIM can be overridden by setting the NIM_OPTIMIZED_BACKEND environment variable.
premises: By default, the NIM will run in TensorRT mode for supported GPUs.
You can override the default backend optimization by setting the NIM_OPTIMIZED_BACKEND environment variable.
The following backend options are available: trt (default), torch, torch_baseline

claim: The template chain selection threshold in OpenFold3 NIM is controlled by the CIF_DIRECT_MIN_SCORE environment variable, which validates template chain similarity using sequence_identity × query_coverage.
premises: You can control the minimum score threshold using the CIF_DIRECT_MIN_SCORE environment variable.
Score Calculation: score = sequence_identity × query_coverage
Default Value: 0.1 (10% identity × coverage)
Configuration Example: ... -eCIF_DIRECT_MIN_SCORE=0.2 ...
- CIF_DIRECT_MIN_SCORE=0.2 sets the minimum score threshold to 0.2.

claim: Task-specific profiles in MSA Search NIM reduce storage requirements and startup time by downloading only necessary databases for specific use cases.
premises: The MSA Search NIM includes task-specific profiles that download only the databases required for specific use cases.
This reduces storage requirements and startup time.

claim: The PDB70-only profile (hash: 3087b7ea46d601200c1f90c9246a7aa344e487056286497515900b0924d7853a) is a minimal profile suitable for quick testing and requires approximately 100 MB of storage.
premises: The example below uses the PDB70-only profile (databases:pdb70, roughly ~100 MB on disk)—a small quick-start choice.
Profile hashes may change between NIM releases. Always use list-model-profiles to get the current hashes for your version.

claim: Profiles containing Uniref30 require approximately 500 GB of storage and are used for paired MSA search in protein complexes.
premises: Profiles that include Uniref30 (for example the databases:uniref30 hash) require on the order of ~500 GB.
databases:uniref30 | Uniref30 | Paired MSA search for protein complexes. Uniref30 is the only database used for species-based sequence pairing. | ~500 GB

claim: Custom databases can be used with MSA Search NIM by mounting them into the container and setting the NIM_MODEL_NAME environment variable, which completely replaces default databases.
premises: You can use custom or manually downloaded MMSeqs2 databases with the MSA Search NIM by mounting them into the container and configuring the NIM_MODEL_NAME environment variable.

Custom databases completely replace the default databases. When you set NIM_MODEL_NAME, the NIM will only use databases found in that directory – it will not mix custom databases with the default model profile databases.

claim: The NIM automatically discovers sequence databases by scanning for **/*.idx files and PDB structure archives via **/pdb*.zip at startup, with database names derived from parent directory names.
premises: The NIM automatically discovers databases at startup using glob patterns: Sequence databases: The NIM scans for **/*.idx files (MMSeqs2 index files). Each .idx file found registers a searchable database. The database name is derived from the parent directory name (for example, pdb70_220313/pdb70_220313.idx registers as pdb70_220313).
PDB structure archive: For structural template search, the NIM looks for a **/pdb*.zip file containing mmCIF structure files. This archive is used to retrieve 3D structures for template hits.

claim: Databases downloaded from NGC are already pre-indexed and ready for GPU Server use, requiring no additional indexing.
premises: Databases downloaded from NGC are already pre-indexed and ready for GPU Server use.
No additional indexing is required for these databases.

claim: Indexing is required when using custom MMseqs2 databases created from FASTA sequences or third-party databases not downloaded from NGC.
premises: Indexing is only required when:
- You have created a custom MMseqs2 database from FASTA sequences
- You are using third-party databases not downloaded from NGC

claim: The NIM container provides GPU-accelerated MMseqs2 tools, and a helper function simplifies running MMseqs2 commands with proper Docker and GPU configuration.
premises: The NIM container includes MMseqs2 with GPU support.

Define a helper function to simplify running MMseqs2 commands: mmseqs_run(){dockerrun-u$(id-u):$(id-g)--rm--runtime=nvidia--gpusall--entrypointmmseqs\-v"$PWD":/work-w/worknvcr.io/nim/colabfold/msa-search:2"$@"}
You can run any MMseqs2 command with that helper function.

claim: Re-indexing a downloaded database like PDB70 involves removing existing index files and recreating them using MMseqs2 with specific GPU-compatible parameters.
premises: This example demonstrates the indexing process by downloading the PDB70 database, removing its index files, and re-creating them.
mmseqs_runcreateindexpdb70_220313tmp--remove-tmp-files1--split1--index-subset2rm-rftmp
The key parameters for GPU Server indexing are: --split 1 : Single split for GPU memory, --index-subset 2 : Create GPU-compatible index subset

claim: The MMseqs2 User Guide and command-specific help are available for additional reference on indexing and other operations.
premises: For comprehensive MMseqs2 documentation, run: mmseqs_run--help
Or for help on a specific command: mmseqs_runcreateindex--help
For additional information, refer to the MMseqs2 User Guide.

claim: Starting with version 2.0.0, MSA NIM configuration for optimal performance has been drastically simplified, with the GPU Server enabled by default and pre-indexed ColabFold databases, eliminating the need for manual database preparation and complex configuration tuning.
premises: Starting with version 2.0.0, MSA NIM configuration for optimal performance has been drastically simplified.
The GPU Server is now enabled by default with pre-indexed ColabFold databases.
This eliminates the need for manual database preparation and complex configuration tuning.
For most users, the default settings will provide excellent performance out of the box.

claim: With version 2.0.0, the MSA Search NIM no longer manages GPU allocation internally across multiple GPUs in a node and is designed to work with external load-balancers and orchestration platforms for scaling based on demand.
premises: With version 2.0.0, the MSA Search NIM no longer internally manages GPU allocation across multiple GPUs in a node.
Instead, the NIM is designed to work with external load-balancers and orchestration platforms that can scale NIM instances up and down based on demand.
Examples include NVIDIA Cloud Functions and popular container orchestration solutions and similar platforms that support scalable, distributed deployments of containerized applications.

claim: The recommended approach for scaling MSA Search NIM in production is to allocate the minimum number of GPUs per instance and rely on horizontal scaling through orchestration to achieve better resource utilization, dynamic scaling, improved fault tolerance, and simplified deployment and maintenance.
premises: The recommended approach is to allocate the minimum number of GPUs to each individual NIM instance and rely on horizontal scaling through orchestration.

This allows for: Better resource utilization across your infrastructure, Dynamic scaling based on actual workload demands, Improved fault tolerance through instance redundancy, Simplified deployment and maintenance.

claim: The accuracy of MSA Search NIM is measured by comparing search results against expected alignments and evaluating sequence identity.
premises: MSA Search NIM performs multiple sequence alignment by searching protein sequence databases for similar sequences to a query and aligning them to establish similar regions.
The accuracy of the NIM is measured by comparing the search results against expected alignments and evaluating the sequence identity of the returned matches.

claim: ColabFold search demonstrates higher sequence identity in uniref30_2302 due to its cascaded search approach building iterative profiles for higher sensitivity.
premises: ColabFold search (cascaded): Implements cascaded search of generated profiles for higher sensitivity
The ColabFold search type demonstrates higher sequence identity percentages in uniref30_2302 due to its cascaded search approach, which builds iterative profiles to find more sensitive matches.

claim: Paired MSA search accuracy is evaluated on 2-chain protein complexes using mean sequence identity per chain and identity correlation as pairing quality metrics.
premises: Paired MSA search accuracy is evaluated on 2-chain protein complexes.
The table below shows mean sequence identity per chain and pairing quality metrics:
- Chain Identity : Mean sequence identity of alignments found in uniref30_2302 for each chain (with NIM_GLOBAL_MAX_MSA_DEPTH set to 500).
- Identity Correlation : Pearson correlation between chain A and chain B sequence identities across paired rows.

claim: Increasing the fraction of unknown residue X in query sequences leads to decreased MSA depth and mean sequence identity, with short sequences being more sensitive to X residues than long ones.
premises: MSA Search NIM accepts the unknown residue X in query sequences.
Depth and identity decrease monotonically as the fraction of X residues increases.
Short sequences are more sensitive to unknown residues. At 50% X, the 52 aa protein (7WJ0_A) collapses to near-zero depth because too few real residues remain for a meaningful search.
The 759 aa protein (7QE1_A) retains most of its depth at 50% X since enough informative residues remain.

claim: Search speed improves with higher fractions of unknown residue X, especially for longer sequences, due to reduced workload in downstream alignment and filtering.
premises: Search speed improves with more unknown residues, especially for longer sequences.
The 759 aa protein sees a ~30% speedup at 90% X because fewer hits survive prefiltering, reducing work in downstream alignment and filtering stages.
Short sequences show a modest ~10% speedup since their baseline search time is already small.

claim: AlphaFold2 search type performs faster than ColabFold search type due to its single-pass search strategy per database, while ColabFold requires multiple iterations for its cascaded approach.
premises: AlphaFold2 search (iterative): Performs single-pass searches per database
ColabFold search (cascaded): Implements cascaded search of generated profiles for higher sensitivity

The AlphaFold2 search type performs faster than ColabFold due to its single-pass search strategy per database, while ColabFold implements a more sensitive cascaded search approach that requires multiple search iterations.

claim: Paired MSA search performance depends on the number of chains, sequence lengths, and pairing strategy, with performance not directly comparable to monomer searches due to different databases and scaling characteristics.
premises: Paired MSA search for protein complexes uses the ColabFold cascaded search approach with additional species-based pairing.
Performance depends on: Number of chains, Sequence lengths, Pairing strategy
Paired MSA search performance is not directly comparable to monomer searches due to different databases being used and varying scaling characteristics.

claim: Structural template search performance varies with the number of template hits and structures retrieved, with many hits potentially slowing performance due to structure retrieval overhead.
premises: Structural template search combines ColabFold cascaded MSA search with template database queries and structure retrieval.
Performance depends on the number of structures retrieved.
Template search performance varies with the number of template hits found and structures retrieved. Queries with many template hits may be slower due to structure retrieval overhead.

claim: The MSA Search NIM exposes Prometheus metrics at the /v1/metrics endpoint for monitoring service health, performance, and usage patterns.
premises: The MSA Search NIM exposes Prometheus metrics at the /v1/metrics endpoint.
These metrics can be used for monitoring service health, performance, and usage patterns.

claim: NIM Telemetry enhances performance, reliability, compatibility, troubleshooting, and optimization while protecting user privacy and being fully optional and configurable.
premises: NIM Telemetry helps NVIDIA deliver a faster, more reliable experience with greater compatibility across a wide range of environments, while maintaining strict privacy protections and giving users full control.

Benefits include: enhancing performance and reliability, improving compatibility across deployments, accelerating troubleshooting and bug resolution, informing smarter optimizations and future releases, protecting user privacy and data security, and being fully optional and configurable.

claim: Telemetry collection in MSA Search NIM is controlled by environment variables NIM_TELEMETRY_MODE and NIM_TELEMETRY_ENABLE_LOGGING.
premises: Telemetry collection is disabled by default.
You can toggle telemetry at any time using environment variables.
NIM_TELEMETRY_MODE controls telemetry collection: set to 0 to disable (default), set to 1 to enable.
NIM_TELEMETRY_ENABLE_LOGGING enables logging for telemetry operations and is only applicable when NIM_TELEMETRY_MODE=1.

claim: Users can refer to NVIDIA’s Privacy Policy and NIM Telemetry Settings for more information about data privacy, what is collected, and how to configure telemetry.
premises: For more information about data privacy, what is collected, and how to configure telemetry, refer to:
- NVIDIA’s Privacy Policy
- NIM Telemetry Settings

claim: Release 2.4.0 extends GPU support by adding NVIDIA GH200 superchips, RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Workstation Edition, and NVIDIA H200.
premises: This release extends GPU support with the addition of NVIDIA GH200 superchips and the RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Workstation Edition, and adds support for NVIDIA H200.

NVIDIA GH200 144GB : Added support for GH200 with 144GB memory

premises: This release extends GPU support with the addition of the GB10 architecture and updates cuEquivariance for enhanced performance.
GB10 DGX Spark support : Added support for GB10 DGX Spark SKUs with sequence lengths up to 1536 residues
cuEquivariance integration : Updated to cuEquivariance 0.8.1 for GB10 support

claim: Release 2.2.0 extends GPU support by adding the GB200 architecture with TensorRT-BioNeMo support for sequence lengths up to 2048 residues.
premises: This release extends GPU support with the addition of the GB200 architecture.
GB200 support : Added TensorRT-BioNeMo support for GB200 SKUs with sequence lengths up to 2048 residues

claim: Release 2.1.0 focuses on security improvements, performance enhancements for newer GPU architectures, extended sequence length support, and introduces telemetry control.
premises: This release focuses on security improvements, performance enhancements for newer GPU architectures, and extended sequence length support.
Security : Addressed all CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) issues
cuEquivariance integration : Updated to cuEquivariance 0.7.0 for improved equivariant operations
Enhanced B200 support : Enabled trimul kernel optimization for B200 SKUs in PyTorch backend
Extended sequence length : Support for longer sequences up to 2048 residues on A100, H100, and B200 GPUs with TensorRT-BioNeMo

Telemetry control : NIM Telemetry helps NVIDIA deliver a faster, more reliable experience with greater compatibility across a wide range of environments, while maintaining strict privacy protections and giving users full control.

claim: Release 2.0.0 removes HHR-based template processing in favor of explicit mmCIF template support and adds TensorRT integration for new GPU architectures.
premises: This release removes HHR-based template processing in favor of explicit mmCIF template support and adds TensorRT integration for new GPU architectures.
Enhanced GPU support : TensorRT-BioNeMo integration for L40S, B200, and RTX 6000 Ada Generation

Removed : Removed the following functionalities: The downloading and decompressing of a bundled database of structure files at NIM startup; The web API accepting input fields containing HHR content; The input data processing code that uses the HHR content to select template structures from the de-compressed database of structure files
Simplified : Template workflow now uses only mmCIF format using explicit_templates, where users can submit one or multiple mmCIF strings as part of their structure prediction requests.
Reduced footprint : Smaller container size and faster startup without bundled databases

claim: Release 1.2.0 introduces support for user-supplied mmCIF input features for structure prediction.
premises: This release introduces support for user-supplied mmCIF input features.
Users can now submit one or multiple mmCIF strings as part of their structure prediction requests.
The structure prediction network can utilize these user-supplied mmCIF inputs for enhanced flexibility and custom workflows.
This feature enables new use cases where users provide their own structural templates or data in mmCIF format.

claim: Release 1.1.0 introduces significant performance improvements through TensorRT (TRT) optimization.
premises: This release introduces significant performance improvements through TensorRT (TRT) optimization.
Enhanced inference performance using TensorRT optimization
Improved model execution speed
Optimized memory usage during inference

premises: This is the first release of NVIDIA NIM for OpenFold2.

claim: The Enroot credentials file must be created at ~/.config/enroot/.credentials with specific permissions and content to allow image pulls from NGC.

cat~/.config/enroot/.credentials

premises: The NIM cache allows you to download models and store previously-downloaded models so that you don’t need to download them again later when you run the NIM again.
The NIM cache must be readable and writable by the NIM, so in addition to creating the directory, the permissions on this directory need to be set to globally readable writable.
The NIM cache directory can be set up as follows: mkdir-p~/.cache/nim and chmod-R777~/.cache/nim

claim: To access the OpenFold2 API after launching the container on a Slurm node, you must create an SSH tunnel to the compute node where the container is running.

claim: The NGC CLI tool must be version 3.41.1 or newer to be compatible with the documented setup process.

claim: The OpenFold2 NIM provides an endpoint for structure prediction from MSA and templates.

claim: The endpoint should be interacted with using the Python requests module, not curl, due to input escaping complexities in bash.

claim: The sequence field is required, while input_id is optional but recommended for tracking and correlating requests.
premises: The field sequence is required.

claim: The filter-step parameters control post-alignment quality filtering, including sequence identity, score, diversity, and redundancy thresholds, with separate settings for profile and follow-up database steps.
premises: These control quality filtering applied after the align step. Separate variables are provided for the profile (first-database) and follow-up (subsequent database) filter steps.
NIM_MMSEQS_PROFILE_FILTER_QID | 0 | Minimum sequence identity with query (0–1) in the profile filter step. Set to 0 to disable.
NIM_MMSEQS_PROFILE_FILTER_QSC | 0.0 | Minimum score per aligned residue with query sequence in the profile filter step.
NIM_MMSEQS_PROFILE_FILTER_DIFF | 0 | Diversity filter: keep at least this many sequences in each MSA block of length 50 in the profile filter step. Set to 0 to disable diversity filtering.

NIM_MMSEQS_PROFILE_FILTER_MIN_ENABLE | 100 | Only apply filtering when the MSA has more than this many sequences in the profile filter step. Set to 0 to always filter.

NIM_MMSEQS_FOLLOWUP_FILTER_MAX_SEQ_ID | 1.0 | Maximum pairwise sequence identity (0–1) for redundancy reduction in the follow-up filter step. Set to 1.0 to disable.
NIM_MMSEQS_FOLLOWUP_FILTER_MIN_ENABLE | 100 | Only apply filtering when the MSA has more than this many sequences in the follow-up filter step. Set to 0 to always filter.
