claim: Template-guided structure prediction in OpenFold3 NIM uses CIF format protein structures to improve prediction accuracy through automatic chain extraction, sequence alignment, scoring, and selection.
premises: OpenFold3 NIM supports template-guided structure prediction using pre-existing protein structures in CIF format.
The system parses each CIF file and extracts all protein chains along with their amino acid sequences.
Each template chain is aligned to your query sequence using sequence alignment algorithms.
Each template chain is scored using the formula: score = sequence_identity × coverage.

For each CIF file: if a chain_id is specified, that specific chain is validated against the minimum score threshold; if no chain_id is specified, the chain with the highest score is automatically selected; all chains must have scores above the minimum threshold (default: 0.1, configurable via CIF_DIRECT_MIN_SCORE); if no chain meets the threshold, the template is excluded.
Selected templates are used during the diffusion process to guide the model toward structures similar to the provided templates.

claim: Best practices for template selection in OpenFold3 NIM include using templates with high sequence identity (>40%), good coverage of the query sequence, high-resolution experimental structures, and providing 1-4 diverse templates when available.
premises: Templates are most effective when: you have structures of homologous proteins (>30% sequence identity), experimental structures are available for similar protein sequences, you want to constrain predictions to a specific conformation, and high-accuracy predictions from other tools are available.

For best results: High sequence identity: Use templates with >40% identity to your query; Good coverage: Templates should cover most of your query sequence; Structure quality: Prefer high-resolution experimental structures; Multiple templates: Provide 1-4 diverse templates when available.

claim: When using multi-chain CIF files, OpenFold3 NIM automatically selects the best matching chain by default but allows manual chain specification via chain_id, with each file contributing at most one chain and multiple CIF files enabling templates from multiple chains.
premises: When using CIF files containing multiple chains: By default, the system automatically selects the best matching chain based on sequence similarity; You can optionally specify which chain to use via the chain_id field in the template; Each template file contributes at most one chain; Provide multiple CIF files if you want templates from multiple chains.

claim: Template files in OpenFold3 NIM must be in CIF format, contain valid protein structure coordinates with properly annotated standard amino acid residues and chain identifiers, and are limited to protein molecules only—DNA, RNA, and ligand templates are not supported.
premises: Templates must be in CIF format (.cif files); PDB format is not currently supported.
Template files must contain valid protein structure coordinates.
Standard amino acid residues should be properly annotated.
Chain identifiers should be present in the CIF file.
Templates are only supported for protein molecules.
DNA, RNA, and ligand templates are not currently supported.
Each protein molecule can have multiple templates.

claim: The minimum score threshold for chain selection in OpenFold3 NIM's template processing is controlled by the CIF_DIRECT_MIN_SCORE environment variable, which defaults to 0.1 and can be configured to adjust template selection behavior.
premises: The template processing behavior can be customized using environment variables.
CIF_DIRECT_MIN_SCORE controls the minimum score threshold for chain selection (default: 0.1).
Refer to Template Configuration Options for details.

Run the NIM container with the following command: docker run --rm -it --name molmim --runtime=nvidia -e CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 -e NGC_CLI_API_KEY -p 8000:8000 nvcr.io/nim/nvidia/molmim:1.0.0
This command starts the NIM container and exposes port 8000 for the user to interact with the NIM.

claim: The health check endpoint must return {"status":"ready"} before proceeding with inference.

You can use the following command to query the health check: curl -X 'GET' 'http://localhost:8000/v1/health/ready' -H 'accept: application/json'

claim: Inference can be run to generate embeddings from a SMILES string and save the output to output.json.
premises: Run inference to get the embeddings of a molecule from its SMILES string representation and save the output to output.json using the following command.
curl -X 'POST' 'http://localhost:8000/embedding' -H 'accept: application/json' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"sequences": ["CC(Cc1ccc(cc1)C(C(=O)O)C)C"]}' > output.json

claim: The output.json file can be viewed using cat or formatted with jq for improved readability.
premises: View the outputs. You can use the cat tool print the outputs to the command line as with the following command: cat output.json
However, we recommend installing jq, a command-line tool that can format JSON for improved readability.
You can use jq to visualize the output from the file: jq output.json

or you can pipe the output directly to jq as in the following command: curl -X 'POST' 'http://localhost:8000/embedding' -H 'accept: application/json' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"sequences": ["CC(Cc1ccc(cc1)C(C(=O)O)C)C"]}' | jq

claim: Model checkpoint caching can be implemented to avoid re-downloading the MolMIM weights on subsequent container runs.
premises: On initial startup, the container will download the MolMIM checkpoint from NGC
You can skip this download step on future runs by caching the model weights locally using a cache directory
Example: create cache directory with export LOCAL_NIM_CACHE=~/.cache/nim and mkdir -p "$LOCAL_NIM_CACHE", then run container with -v "$LOCAL_NIM_CACHE:/home/nvs/.cache/nim"

claim: Benchmarking the accuracy and performance of the MolMIM NIM involves measuring reconstruction accuracy and decoding time via POST requests to the /hidden and /decode endpoints.
premises: Accuracy can be measured by evaluating the reconstruction accuracy, which is the ability of the model to accurately generate the original input SMILES string from its encoded representation.
Performance can be measured by the time it takes for the model to generate the output starting from the input, which is known as the decoding time.

The script sends a POST request to the model’s /hidden endpoint to encode the input SMILES string, and then sends another POST request to the /decode endpoint to decode the encoded representation back into a SMILES string.
The script measures the time it takes for each of these steps and checks if the generated SMILES string matches the original input.

claim: The logging level of the MolMIM NIM can be controlled using the NIM_LOG_LEVEL environment variable, with DEBUG logging all inputs and outputs and CRITICAL as the default level.

The following logging levels are available: DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR, CRITICAL.
DEBUG : This level logs all inputs and outputs for each endpoint of the server.
If no value is provided for NIM_LOG_LEVEL, the default logging level will be CRITICAL.
To set the logging level, you can pass the NIM_LOG_LEVEL environment variable when starting the NIM. For example: docker run -e NIM_LOG_LEVEL=DEBUG

claim: The /embedding endpoint retrieves embeddings from MolMIM for input molecules provided as SMILES strings.
premises: /embedding - Retrieve the embeddings from MolMIM for a given input molecule.
Request Body: sequences : array of strings (SMILES strings)
Response: embeddings : array of arrays of floating point numbers (embeddings)

claim: The /hidden endpoint retrieves the hidden state representation (latent code) from MolMIM for input molecules provided as SMILES strings.
premises: /hidden - Retrieve the hidden state from MolMIM for a given input molecule (shown as the “latent code” in Figure 1 of the MolMIM manuscript ).
Request Body: sequences : array of strings (SMILES strings)
Response: hiddens : array of arrays of arrays of floating point numbers (hidden states) mask : array of arrays of booleans (mask)

claim: The /decode endpoint decodes a hidden state representation into a SMILES string sequence using previously generated hidden state data.
premises: /decode - Decode a hidden state representation into a SMILES string sequence.
Request Body: hiddens : array of arrays of arrays of floating point numbers (hidden states) mask : array of arrays of booleans (mask)
Response: generated : array of strings (SMILES strings)
Note: For each of the /decode commands below, you will need the saved output from the previous calls to the /hidden endpoint.

claim: The /sampling endpoint samples the latent space around a seed molecule to generate new molecule samples in an unguided fashion within a scaled radius.
premises: /sampling - Sample the latent space within a given scaled radius from a seed molecule. This method generates new molecule samples from the given input in an unguided fashion.

Request Body: sequences : array of strings (SMILES strings) beam_size : integer (beam width, between 1 and 10, default: 1) num_molecules : integer (number of molecules, between 1 and 10, default: 1) scaled_radius : floating point number (scaled radius, between 0 and 2, default: 0.7)
Response: generated : array of arrays of strings (SMILES strings)

claim: The /generate endpoint creates novel molecules, optionally optimizing for a property like QED or plogP using CMA-ES-guided sampling or random sampling.
premises: /generate - Generate novel molecules (optionally while optimizing against a certain property). This method generates new optimized molecules if CMA-ES-guided sampling is enabled.

Request Body: smi : string (SMILES string) algorithm : string (algorithm to use, either “CMA-ES” or “none”, default: “CMA-ES”) iterations : integer (number of iterations, between 1 and 1000, default: 10) min_similarity : floating point number (minimum similarity, between 0 and 0.7, default: 0.7) minimize : boolean (whether to minimize the property, default: false) num_molecules : integer (number of molecules, between 1 and 100, default: 10) particles : integer (number of particles, between 2 and 1000, default: 30) property_name : string (property to optimize, either “QED” or “plogP”, default: “QED”) scaled_radius : floating point number (scaled radius, between 0 and 2, default: 1.0)
Response: generated : array of strings (SMILES strings)

The /generate endpoint provides two alternate options: - CMA-ES - a black-box optimization algorithm that can guide MolMIM sampling to optimize for a specific property; in this case, either QED or plogP. - Random sampling - functions similarly to the /sampling endpoint, but with less flexibility for the sampling parameters.

Required parameters for each algorithm type: - For the “CMA-ES” algorithm: smi num_molecules property_name minimize min_similarity particles iterations - For random sampling (“none”) algorithm: smi num_molecules particles scaled_radius

claim: PST (Prompt Segmentation Threshold) manages memory usage for long prompts by splitting generation into three phases: large forward pass up to threshold, token-by-token processing of excess tokens, and regular generation with sampling after full input processing.

The response is captured in output.json and includes a success status and generated molecules with scores

claim: Users can run molecular generation inference using Python by sending a POST request to the GenMol NIM API with the requests library, handling JSON input and output, and raising for HTTP errors.
premises: The Python script imports json and requests

Headers include Accept: application/json
The JSON payload contains the same SAFE template and parameters as the curl example: smiles, num_molecules=5, temperature=1.0, noise=1.0, scoring='QED'

claim: The input to GenMol NIM is a SAFE text sequence that may include masked fragment placeholders for controlled molecular generation, supporting de novo, motif extension, scaffold decoration, or linker design based on template completeness.
premises: The input is a SAFE text sequence with masked fragments as a template for molecular generation
SAFE extends SMILES with explicit fragment and attachment-point structure
The masked fragment placeholder uses the form [*{min_len-max_len}] to specify token generation bounds
If an empty template is provided, the model performs de novo generation
If a partial SAFE or SMILES template is provided, the model performs conditioned generation such as motif extension, scaffold decoration, or linker design

claim: NIM forwards tracing headers (X-Request-Id and traceparent) from clients to the inference backend on inference endpoints but not on management or health endpoints.
premises: NIM supports request correlation and distributed tracing through standard HTTP headers
The proxy layer forwards tracing headers from clients to the inference backend on the following inference endpoints: /v1/chat/completions, /v1/completions, /v1/embeddings, /v1/responses
Tracing headers are not forwarded on management or health endpoints

claim: The X-Request-Id header is forwarded by NIM to the backend and used as the internal request ID for logging, enabling correlation across services.
premises: Include an X-Request-Id header in your request to tag it with a correlation identifier
NIM forwards this value to the backend, where the backend adopts it as the internal request ID

When correlating logs across services, the X-Request-Id value appears in backend log entries associated with that request because it is used as the request identifier throughout the inference pipeline

claim: The traceparent header is forwarded by NIM to the backend to propagate W3C Trace Context, but OpenTelemetry spans are only generated if tracing is enabled via OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TRACES_ENDPOINT.
premises: NIM forwards the W3C Trace Context traceparent header to the inference backend
If your application uses OpenTelemetry or another W3C-compatible tracing system, include the traceparent header to propagate trace context through NIM
When OpenTelemetry tracing is enabled on the backend, this allows inference spans to appear in your existing distributed traces

The proxy layer always forwards the traceparent header to the backend. However, the backend only creates OpenTelemetry spans from it when tracing is enabled through the OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TRACES_ENDPOINT environment variable. Without this configuration, the backend logs a warning and discards the trace context

claim: The container can cache models locally to avoid downloading them on subsequent runs by mounting a cache directory.
premises: When the container starts for the first time, it downloads the required models from NGC.
To avoid downloading the models on subsequent runs, you can cache them locally by using a cache directory.
Create the cache directory on the host machine, set LOCAL_NIM_CACHE, and mount it to /opt/nim/.cache in the container.

claim: SSL can be enabled in Eye-Contact NIM to secure communication using mutual TLS or TLS authentication by providing certificate and key files.
premises: Eye-Contact NIM provides an SSL mode to ensure secure communication between clients and the server by encrypting data in transit.
To enable SSL, you need to provide the path to the SSL certificate and key files in the container.
NIM_SSL_MODE can be set to 'mtls', 'tls', or 'disabled'; if set to 'mtls', the container uses mutual TLS authentication; if set to 'tls', it uses TLS authentication.
The container must mount the SSL certificate and key files and set NIM_SSL_CERT_PATH and NIM_SSL_KEY_PATH accordingly.
The SSL certificate and key files must be readable by the user running the container on the host machine.

claim: The server supports multiple concurrent inputs per GPU, and total concurrency scales with the number of GPUs and the MAXINE_MAX_CONCURRENCY_PER_GPU setting.
premises: To run the server in multi-input concurrent mode, set the environment variable MAXINE_MAX_CONCURRENCY_PER_GPU to an integer greater than 1 in the server container.
The server will then accept as many concurrent inputs per GPU as specified by the MAXINE_MAX_CONCURRENCY_PER_GPU variable.

Since Triton distributes the workload equally across all GPUs, if there are NUM_GPUS GPUs, the total number of concurrent inputs supported by the server will be NUM_GPUS * MAXINE_MAX_CONCURRENCY_PER_GPU.

claim: GPU hardware limitations on NVENC/NVDEC sessions can restrict the number of concurrent video inputs the Eye Contact NIM can process.
premises: The Eye Contact NIM uses NVENC/NVDEC hardware acceleration for video encoding and decoding.
GPUs without NVENC/NVDEC hardware support are not supported, including A100, H100, and B100 products.
Some GPUs support only a limited number of concurrent NVENC sessions, which means NIM can only process that same number of concurrent inputs on those GPUs.
If incoming requests to the NIM exceed the GPU’s maximum concurrent encode/decode limit, the processing fails.

claim: The --lossless flag enables lossless video encoding, overriding bitrate settings to maximize quality at the cost of larger file sizes.
premises: The following parameters are available to configure the functionality of the NIM.
- lossless - Enables lossless video encoding. This setting overrides any bitrate configuration to ensure maximum quality output, though it results in larger file sizes.
pythoneye-contact.py--lossless

claim: The --bitrate argument sets the target video encoding bitrate in bits per second, with higher values improving quality but increasing file size.
premises: - bitrate - Sets the target bitrate for video encoding in bits per second (bps). Higher bitrates result in better video quality but larger file sizes. The default is 20,000,000 bps (20 Mbps).
For example, setting --bitrate 5000000 targets 5 Mbps encoding.
pythoneye-contact.py--bitrate5000000

claim: The --idr-interval argument controls the frequency of IDR frames, affecting seeking precision and file size trade-offs.
premises: - idr-interval - Sets the interval between IDR (Instantaneous Decoding Refresh) frames in the encoded video. IDR frames are special I-frames that clear all reference buffers, allowing the video to be decoded from that point without needing previous frames.

A lower interval (e.g. 8 frames) provides better seeking/editing capabilities but increases file size, while a higher interval (e.g. 30 frames) reduces file size but may make seeking less precise. The default is 8 frames.
pythoneye-contact.py--idr-interval10

claim: Custom encoding parameters can be passed as a JSON string to fine-tune the NVENC encoder, but incorrect values may cause encoding failures or poor quality.
premises: - Custom encoding - Allows passing custom encoding parameters as a JSON string. This provides fine-grained control over the encoding process.
pythoneye-contact.py--custom-encoding-params'{"idrinterval": "20", "maxbitrate": "3000000'}'
Note: Custom encoding parameters are for expert users who need fine-grained control over video encoding. Incorrect values may cause encoding failures or poor quality output.

claim: The temporal flag controls temporal filtering for landmark computation in eye contact, with default behavior enabled when set to true.
premises: - temporal - (UINT32) Flag to control temporal filtering (default 0xffffffff ). When set to true, the landmark computation for eye contact is temporally optimized.

claim: The detect_closure flag toggles eye closure and occlusion detection, which can be disabled to maintain gaze estimation during occlusion.
premises: - detect_closure - (UINT32) Flag to toggle detection of eye closure and occlusion. If turned off, blink and occlusion detection turns off. claim: The NVIDIA Eye Contact NIM provides two processing modes: streaming and transactional, differing in data storage, processing start, timing, and output delivery.
premises: The NVIDIA Eye Contact NIM provides two modes for processing input files: streaming and transactional.
| Aspect | Streaming Mode | Transactional Mode |
| Data Storage | Only frames being processed are temporarily copied in memory. | Entire video and audio files are temporarily copied on disk. |
| Processing Start | NIM starts processing as soon as data chunk for first frame arrives. | NIM waits to receive entire files before starting. |
| Processing Timing | Continuous processing without waiting for complete input. | Processing begins after all data is received. |
| Output Delivery | Output frames are generated and returned immediately. | Complete output video is returned to client after inference is finished for whole video. |

claim: Streaming mode is the recommended way to use the NVIDIA Eye Contact NIM, offering low latency, resource efficiency, and scalability for large files, with automatic server-side detection of streamable inputs.
premises: Streaming mode is the recommended way to use the NVIDIA Eye Contact NIM.
It allows inference to begin without receiving the whole video from the client.
It processes video frames incrementally, and inference begins as soon as the first frame of information is available.
The output frames are streamed back to the client immediately after inference.
This mode delivers the lowest latency and best resource efficiency, and it scales well to large files.
The Eye Contact NIM server automatically detects streamable videos and uses the streaming inference path internally.
You do not need to enable any server-side setting or pass any flag to the NIM to get streaming behavior.
Simply provide a streamable video as input.

Use streaming mode for these use cases: Best overall performance. The NIM is optimized for this path. Streamable video inputs. Applications that benefit from receiving output as it is generated, without waiting for the entire file to be uploaded. Large video files that benefit from incremental processing and reduced disk I/O.
Streaming mode works with streamable videos in which metadata is positioned at the beginning of the file. Videos that are not streamable can be easily converted to a streamable format.
To make any video streamable, use FFmpeg with the following command: ffmpeg -i sample_video.mp4 -movflags+faststart sample_streamable.mp4

To run the NVIDIA Eye Contact NIM in streaming mode, go to the scripts directory and pass the streamable video as input: python eye-contact.py --target <server_ip:port> --input ../assets/sample_streamable.mp4 --output <output_filepath>

Note: The --streaming flag in the sample client is optional and does not change the inference behavior on the server. It only enables streaming-mode logging on the client side. The server automatically detects streamable inputs and uses the streaming inference path internally regardless of whether the flag is passed.

claim: Transactional mode is used when the input video is not streamable, requiring the entire file to be received before processing begins, and is suitable for non-streamable files, small videos, or applications that can wait for full processing.
premises: In transactional mode, the NIM receives the entire video file before processing can begin.
The server automatically falls back to this mode when the input video is not streamable.

Transactional mode applies to the following use cases: Videos that are not optimized for streaming (such as non-streamable MP4 files in which metadata is located at the end of the file, requiring the entire file to be downloaded before playback can begin). Processing of small video files for which streaming overhead is unnecessary. Applications that can wait for complete processing before receiving output.

To run the NVIDIA Eye Contact NIM with a non-streamable input, pass the file as input. The server detects that the video is not streamable and processes it in transactional mode automatically: python eye-contact.py --target <server_ip:port> --input <non-streamable_input_filepath> --output <output_filepath>
Tip: For best performance, convert your videos to a streamable format and use streaming mode. See the FFmpeg command earlier on this page.

Note: The first inference is not indicative of the model’s actual performance because it includes the time taken by the Triton Inference Server to load the models in addition to the time required to process the inference request.

claim: To integrate NeMo Guardrails microservice with NemoGuard Jailbreak Detect, users must configure Docker containers for both services and set required environment variables.

claim: A Guardrails configuration for jailbreak detection must be added via a POST request to the Guardrails microservice, specifying the jailbreak detection model and its connection details.
premises: A POST request is sent to ${GUARDRAILS_BASE_URL}/v1/guardrail/configs with headers Accept: application/json and Content-Type: application/json.
The request body includes a configuration named 'demo-jailbreak-detection' in the 'default' namespace with a description and data containing prompts, models, and rails.
The models array specifies a main model of type 'nim' with model 'meta/llama-3.3-70b-instruct' and parameters.base_url set to 'https://integrate.api.nvidia.com/v1'.
The rails.input.flows includes 'jailbreak detection model'.
The rails.config.jailbreak_detection specifies nim_base_url as 'http://jailbreak_detect:8000/' and nim_server_endpoint as 'v1/classify'.
Field engine specifies nim.
Field parameters.base_url specifies the IP address and port of the NVIDIA NemoGuard JailbreakDetect NIM host.
The rails definition specifies the NemoGuard NIM as the model.

claim: When a weakly-designed jailbreak request is submitted, the system classifies it as safe and allows the LLM to generate a response that includes a hypothetical bank robbery plan.
premises: A POST request is sent to ${GUARDRAILS_BASE_URL}/v1/guardrail/chat/completions with headers Accept: application/json and Content-Type: application/json.

The request body includes a model 'meta/llama-3.3-70b-instruct', a user message containing a weakly-designed jailbreak prompt pretending to be STAN and asking for a bank robbery plan, guardrails config_id set to 'demo-jailbreak-detection', and stream: false, top_p: 1.
The classification model classifies the prompt as safe and does not consider it a serious risk.
The request is sent to the LLM, which generates a completion describing a five-step hypothetical bank robbery plan while emphasizing it is not intended to be taken literally and prioritizing safety.
The response includes guardrails_data with config_ids containing 'demo-jailbreak-detection'.

claim: When a more challenging jailbreak request simulating DAN Mode is submitted, the system classifies it as a risky jailbreak attempt and NeMo Guardrails responds with a refusal message.
premises: A text file payload.json is created with a user message attempting to simulate DAN Mode, including detailed instructions to generate uncensored content, ignore policies, and adopt a persona that can generate offensive or harmful content.
The request includes model 'meta/llama-3.3-70b-instruct', guardrails config_id set to 'demo-jailbreak-detection', stream: false, and top_p: 1.
The request is sent via curl to ${GUARDRAILS_BASE_URL}/v1/guardrail/chat/completions with appropriate headers and the payload.json file as data.
The classification model classifies the request as a risky jailbreak attempt.
NeMo Guardrails instructs the system to reject the input based on this classification.
NeMo Guardrails responds with a refusal message containing content 'I'm sorry, I can't respond to that.' and empty usage statistics.
The response includes guardrails_data with config_ids containing 'demo-jailbreak-detection'.

claim: Starting the JailbreakDetect container requires logging into NVIDIA NGC, pulling the nemoguard-jailbreakdetect image, creating a cache directory with appropriate permissions, and running the container with GPU support, shared memory, environment variable, and volume mount.
premises: Log in to NVIDIA NGC so you can pull the container. Export your NGC API key as an environment variable: $ export NGC_API_KEY = "<nvapi-...>" Log in to the registry: $ docker login nvcr.io --username '$oauthtoken' --password-stdin <<< $NGC_API_KEY
Download the container: $ docker pull nvcr.io/nim/nvidia/nemoguard-jailbreak-detect:1.10.1
Create a model cache directory on the host machine: $ export LOCAL_NIM_CACHE = ~/.cache/nemoguard-jailbreakdetect $ mkdir -p "${ LOCAL_NIM_CACHE }" $ chmod 777 "${ LOCAL_NIM_CACHE }"

Run the container with the cache directory as a volume mount: $ docker run -d \ --name nemoguard-jailbreakdetect \ --gpus = all --runtime = nvidia \ --shm-size = 64GB \ -e NGC_API_KEY \ -v "${ LOCAL_NIM_CACHE }":/opt/nim/.cache/ \ -p 8000:8000 \ nvcr.io/nim/nvidia/nemoguard-jailbreak-detect:1.10.1

claim: The classify endpoint returns a JSON object with a 'jailbreak' Boolean indicating whether the input is a jailbreak attempt and a 'score' float between -1 and 1 representing confidence, where positive scores indicate jailbreak and negative scores indicate safe input.
premises: The classify endpoint returns a JSON payload with two fields:
| Field Name | Description |
| jailbreak | A Boolean value and indicates whether the end-user request appears to be a jailbreak attempt. |
| score | A floating-point value between 1 and -1 that indicates the model confidence. Positive values are associated with requests classified as a jailbreak and negative values with safe input. |
Example safe input request output: { "jailbreak" : false , "score" : -0.9935975138523108 }
Example unsafe input request output: { "jailbreak" : true , "score" : 0.9533652216609169 }
The unsafe classification prompt is based on a test from the garak project.

claim: MAISI Nim supports multi-GPU configurations to enhance performance and speed up image processing.
premises: If the num_output_samples parameter is set to N and there are N visible GPUs, then N images will be processed in parallel, with each GPU handling one image.
If the num_output_samples parameter is larger than the number of GPUs (M), then M images will be processed in parallel and the remaining images will be queued and processed as GPUs become available.
The number of GPUs available on your system must be correctly configured and visible; you can set CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES when running a Docker container to specify which GPUs should be used.
Example: using `--gpus "all" -eCUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0,1` exposes GPUs 0 and 1 to the container.

If you use `--gpus "device=2,3"` instead of `--gpus "all"`, the GPUs are renumbered inside the container (host GPU 2 → container GPU 0, host GPU 3 → container GPU 1), so you should still set `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0,1` to correctly map the GPUs.

claim: To write generated images and masks to blob storage, the pre_signed_url parameter must be specified in the request.
premises: The pre_signed_url parameter is a pre-signed URL that allows you to securely upload files to a blob storage service, such as AWS S3, without requiring direct access to your storage credentials.
This URL is generated with specific permissions and an expiration time, ensuring that the upload can only occur within a defined time frame and with the specified permissions.

claim: A pre-signed URL for uploading an object to an S3 bucket can be generated using the boto3 library in Python.
premises: Different cloud providers have different ways to produce pre-signed URLs; AWS S3 is used as an example.
boto3 is pre-installed in AWS CloudShell and credentials are automatically configured; for local environments, AWS credentials must be properly configured.

Example code: create an S3 client, define bucket name, object key, expiration time, call `generate_presigned_url('put_object', Params={'Bucket':bucket_name,'Key':object_key}, ExpiresIn=expiration)`, and print the resulting URL.

claim: After obtaining a valid pre-signed URL, it can be specified as the pre_signed_url field in the request payload to the MAISI Nim inference endpoint.
premises: The request payload includes fields such as num_output_samples, body_region, anatomy_list, output_size, spacing, image_output_ext, label_output_ext, and pre_signed_url.
The request is posted to `http://localhost:8000/v1/maisi/run` using `requests.post`.
On a successful response (status_code 200), a success message is printed; otherwise, the status code and response body are printed.

claim: To write generated images and masks to a local mounted directory, specify the local_working_dir parameter in the request payload after mounting the directory in the container.
premises: The local directory must be mounted when running the NIM container using `-v /path/on/host:/path/in/container`.
Ensure the directory has correct permissions (e.g., `sudo chmod -R 777`).
If the host directory is `/path/on/host/results/`, then in the inference request payload `local_working_dir` should be set to `/path/in/container/results/`.

claim: A custom timeout for image generation can be set via the GENERATE_IMAGE_TIMEOUT environment variable when running the container.

claim: The microservice can serve models in an air-gapped environment by using a cached model profile, allowing operation without internet or NGC registry connection.
premises: The microservice supports serving models in an air gap system (also known as air wall, air-gapping, or disconnected network).
If the microservice detects a model profile in the model cache, it can serve that profile from the cache rather than download the model profile again.
By creating a model cache, you can run the microservice without any internet connection and no connection to the NGC registry.

claim: To cache model profiles for air-gapped use, you must export the NGC API key, create a cache directory, optionally list desired model profiles, and then download them using specific Docker commands.
premises: On a machine with internet access and connectivity to the NGC registry, perform the following steps to cache model profiles:
Export your NGC API key as an environment variable: $ export NGC_API_KEY = "<nvapi-...>"
Create an directory for the model cache: $ export AIR_GAP_NIM_CACHE = ~/.cache/air-gap-nim-cache $ mkdir -p "${ AIR_GAP_NIM_CACHE }"

Optional: Determine a specific model profile to cache: docker run --rm --gpus=all --runtime=nvidia --shm-size=64GB -e NGC_API_KEY -u $(id -u) -v "${AIR_GAP_NIM_CACHE}:/opt/nim/.cache/" nvcr.io/nim/nvidia/nemoguard-jailbreak-detect:1.10.1 list-model-profiles

Download the model profiles to cache: docker run --rm --gpus=all --runtime=nvidia --shm-size=64GB -e NGC_API_KEY -u $(id -u) -v "${AIR_GAP_NIM_CACHE}:/opt/nim/.cache/" nvcr.io/nim/nvidia/nemoguard-jailbreak-detect:1.10.1 download-to-cache -p <profile-one> [ -p <profile-two> -p <...> ]

claim: To run the microservice on an air-gapped system, transfer the cached directory, set LOCAL_NIM_CACHE to its path, and start the container without NGC_API_KEY, optionally specifying NIM_MODEL_PROFILE.
premises: After the container exits and the model profiles are downloaded, transfer the air-gapped directory, ~/.cache/air-gap-nim-cache, to a path accessible to the air-gapped system.
Perform the following steps on the air-gapped system to start the microservice and use model cache:
Export an environment variable with the path to the model cache: $ export LOCAL_NIM_CACHE = <path-to-transferred-model-cache>

Start the container: docker run -d --name nemoguard-jailbreakdetect --gpus=all --runtime=nvidia --shm-size=64GB -u $(id -u) -p 8000:8000 -v "${LOCAL_NIM_CACHE}:/opt/nim/.cache/" -e NIM_MODEL_PROFILE=<profile-one> nvcr.io/nim/nvidia/nemoguard-jailbreak-detect:1.10.1

The key differences from the common command to start the microservice: The NGC_API_KEY environment variable is omitted because the microservice does not download model profiles. Optional: The NIM_MODEL_PROFILE variable specifies the model profile to run.

claim: NIM LLM is a production-ready solution for running large language models using NVIDIA inference microservices.
premises: NVIDIA NIM for Large Language Models (NIM LLM) is a production-ready way to run large language models with NVIDIA inference microservices (NIMs).
NIM LLM brings state-of-the-art LLM serving to enterprise and developer workflows with validated containers, curated weights, and direct alignment with upstream inference engines.

claim: NIM LLM offers three distinct offerings—NIM Day 0, NIM Turbo, and NIM Certified—to balance publication speed, peak performance, and enterprise lifecycle guarantees.
premises: NIM LLM is available under three NIM offerings so you can choose the right balance of publication speed, peak performance, and enterprise lifecycle guarantees:
- NIM Day 0: Fast access to newly released models with functional validation on a smaller set of NVIDIA GPUs.
- NIM Turbo: Validated best-in-class inference performance for top models.

- NIM Certified: Enterprise production packaging with broader compatibility, documented refresh cadence, CVE patching, OSRB compliance, security updates, FedRAMP ready branches for government use cases, and NVIDIA AI Enterprise support.

claim: NIM LLM provides key benefits including faster feature access, uncompromised performance, and reduced operational burden by aligning with upstream engines and eliminating abstraction layers.
premises: NIM LLM aligns with upstream engines and eliminates heavy downstream abstraction layers to provide the following benefits:
- Faster Feature Access: You receive updates in weeks rather than months, ensuring rapid access to the latest upstream engine optimizations, new CUDA versions, and hardware support.
- Uncompromised Performance: You get direct access to raw vLLM capabilities without the latency of abstraction layers.
- Reduced Operational Burden: You can use pre-validated configurations to eliminate the trial and error of tuning complex LLM deployments.

claim: NIM LLM enables deployment of generative AI across diverse use cases such as chatbots, content generation, sentiment analysis, and language translation.
premises: NIM LLM enables organizations to reliably deploy generative AI capabilities across a wide range of applications at scale, including the following:
- Chatbots and Virtual Assistants: Build bots with human-like language understanding and responsiveness.
- Content Generation and Summarization: Generate high-quality content or distill lengthy articles into concise summaries with ease.
- Sentiment Analysis: Understand user sentiments in real time, driving better business decisions.
- Language Translation: Remove language barriers with efficient and accurate translation services.

claim: NIM Certified provides enterprise-ready packaging with stability, security, and compliance features for long-lived production deployments.
premises: For long-lived production deployments, NIM Certified adds the packaging and architectural guardrails that enterprise environments require.
While open-source inference engines change rapidly, NIM Certified provides the stability and support required for production enterprise environments.

Key packaging features include: Curated Model Weights and Quantization; Enterprise Support and Security (continuous CVE patching, security updates, OSRB compliance); FedRAMP Compliance; Health and Observability (built-in management APIs for readiness, liveness, and model metadata integrating with Kubernetes and enterprise platforms).

claim: The NIM LLM 2.0 architecture uses a one container, one backend design with three primary components: nim-llm, nimlib, and the vLLM inference engine.
premises: The NIM LLM container is designed for deployment simplicity, startup reliability, and inference performance parity with upstream engines.
The architecture is organized into three primary components:

- nim-llm (Orchestration Layer): The entry point that orchestrates the startup sequence, manages configuration priorities such as CLI flags, environment variables, and runtime configs, and injects enterprise features like custom middleware and Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) adapters.

- nimlib (Profile and Model Management): Handles model licensing, hardware-aware profile selection, model downloading, and NIM-specific management API endpoints (for example, health and readiness checks).
- Inference Engine (vLLM): The core engine that executes model inference and provides native OpenAI-compatible API endpoints.

Unlike the 1.x architecture that bundled multiple backends into a single container, NIM LLM version 2.0 embraces a one container, one backend philosophy for predictable behavior and direct access to upstream features.

claim: NIM LLM supports both model-specific and model-free containers to meet varying operational needs, from easy deployment of standard models to flexible serving of custom or emerging models.
premises: NIM LLM supports two distinct deployment modalities to cater to different operational needs:

Model-Specific NIMs: These containers include a model-specific manifest, curated model weights, validated quantization profiles, and optimal runtime configurations tailored specifically for the target model. This is the fastest path to production for supported models.
Use model-specific NIMs when: You deploy standard, widely-used models (for example, Llama 3); You want an easy deployment experience with validated configurations and curated weights.

Model-Free NIMs: A model-free NIM is a flexible container that serves a model you configure dynamically at runtime. Rather than relying on a pre-packaged manifest, a model-free NIM generates its model manifest at runtime, supporting remote repositories (NGC, Hugging Face, Amazon S3, and Google Cloud Storage) and local directories.

You can use model-free NIMs when: You need early support for a newly released model architecture that vLLM supports, but an official model-specific NIM is not yet available; You deploy custom-trained or heavily fine-tuned models stored in your own infrastructure (for example, private S3 buckets or local storage); You want to reduce container approvals in secure enterprise environments. By validating and approving a single model-free NIM container, your security and OSRB teams can enable the deployment of multiple different models without requiring a new security pass for each specific model.

claim: Migrating from NIM LLM 1.x to 2.0 involves adopting single backend containers, transparent model behavior, and upstream alignment by removing downstream forks.
premises: Moving from NIM 1.x to 2.0 involves a shift in how containers are structured and how model differences are handled. Key architectural changes include:
- Single Backend Containers: The multi-backend container (vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, and others) is replaced by a dedicated vLLM container.
- Transparent Model Behavior: Tool-calling behaviors and model differences are no longer hidden or emulated. They are exposed transparently, aligning with standard community practices.
- Upstream Alignment: Enterprise shims have been streamlined. Features are now driven directly upstream rather than maintained as downstream forks.

claim: NIM LLM is built on vLLM and benefits from NVIDIA's upstream collaboration, ensuring users receive latest LLM serving advances while strengthening the open source ecosystem.
premises: NIM LLM is built on vLLM, an open source, high-throughput inference engine for large language models.
NVIDIA actively collaborates with the vLLM community, contributing optimizations upstream and integrating community-driven innovations into NIM LLM.
NVIDIA is committed to sustaining this upstream partnership and to ensuring that its contributions strengthen vLLM for the entire community.
This collaboration ensures that NIM LLM users benefit from the latest advances in LLM serving technology while the broader open source ecosystem gains access to hardware-level improvements.

claim: LoRA lets you serve a base model plus one or more fine-tuned adapters without retraining or rebuilding the full model.

claim: NIM LLM supports two LoRA serving modes: static LoRA and dynamic LoRA.
premises: NIM LLM supports two LoRA serving modes:
- Static LoRA : Adapters are discovered from a directory at startup.
- Dynamic LoRA : Adapters can be loaded and unloaded while the server is running.

claim: In static LoRA mode, the NIM container discovers adapters in NIM_PEFT_SOURCE during startup and loads valid adapters; changes after startup require a container restart to apply.
premises: After you complete the required LoRA setup, NIM LLM uses static LoRA when NIM_PEFT_REFRESH_INTERVAL is not set.
In static LoRA mode, the NIM container discovers adapters in NIM_PEFT_SOURCE during startup and loads valid adapters.
If you add, remove, or update adapters after startup, restart the NIM container to apply those changes.

claim: Dynamic LoRA allows adapters to be loaded and unloaded while the server is running, using directory monitoring or runtime API calls.
premises: Use dynamic LoRA when you need to add or remove adapters without restarting the deployment.
You can manage adapters through directory monitoring, runtime API calls, or both.

claim: Before configuring static or dynamic LoRA, you must mount a directory containing adapters, set NIM_PEFT_SOURCE to that directory, optionally pass native vLLM LoRA flags, and select a LoRA-capable profile.
premises: Mount a directory (containing LoRA adapters) to the container.
Set NIM_PEFT_SOURCE to that directory.
Optionally, pass native vLLM LoRA flags.
When available for your model, select a -feat_lora profile so the deployment uses LoRA-compatible runtime settings.
Example: exportNIM_MODEL_PROFILE=vllm-fp16-tp1-pp1-feat_lora
If you are not sure which profiles are available in your deployment, query the model and profile metadata from your environment. Then choose the LoRA-capable profile.

claim: Under NIM_PEFT_SOURCE, each adapter must reside in its own subdirectory containing adapter_config.json and either adapter_model.safetensors or adapter_model.bin.
premises: Expected adapter layout under NIM_PEFT_SOURCE :
/opt/nim/loras/
├── adapter_a/
│   ├── adapter_config.json
│   └── adapter_model.safetensors   # or adapter_model.bin
└── adapter_b/
├── adapter_config.json
└── adapter_model.bin
Only valid, readable adapter directories are loaded.

claim: NIM LLM passes the following LoRA-related flags to vLLM: --enable-lora, --max-loras, --max-cpu-loras, --max-lora-rank.
premises: NIM passes the following LoRA-related flags to vLLM:

premises: After you complete the shared LoRA setup, set NIM_PEFT_REFRESH_INTERVAL (polling interval in seconds) to enable dynamic LoRA through directory monitoring.
When NIM_PEFT_SOURCE and NIM_PEFT_REFRESH_INTERVAL are set, NIM starts the LoRA watcher and enables runtime LoRA updates for vLLM.

claim: You can manually load or unload LoRA adapters at runtime using the vLLM endpoints POST /v1/load_lora_adapter and POST /v1/unload_lora_adapter.

claim: To manage adapters via the directory watcher, copy a new adapter folder into NIM_PEFT_SOURCE to load, or remove an adapter folder from NIM_PEFT_SOURCE to unload, then wait one refresh interval for /v1/models to reflect the change.
premises: To manage adapters through the directory watcher, use the following actions:
- Load : copy a new adapter folder into NIM_PEFT_SOURCE .
- Unload : remove an adapter folder from NIM_PEFT_SOURCE .
- Wait one refresh interval for /v1/models to reflect changes.

claim: If you use both the directory watcher and the manual API together, an adapter that the API removes but that remains present in the directory can be reloaded by the watcher during the next scan.
premises: If you use both the watcher and the manual API together, an adapter that the API removes but that is still present in the directory can be reloaded by the watcher during the next scan.

claim: You can serve multiple LoRA adapters at the same time, subject to GPU memory limits, by discovering adapter IDs via /v1/models and specifying the adapter ID in the model field of inference requests.
premises: You can serve multiple adapters at the same time, subject to GPU memory limits.
Use /v1/models to discover available adapter IDs, then send the adapter ID in the request model field.

claim: The provided code example demonstrates a minimal local workflow for serving a fine-tuned Llama model with LoRA, covering environment variable setup, adapter directory preparation, static or dynamic LoRA container launch, model verification via /v1/models, and sending an inference request targeting a loaded adapter.
premises: Set up the environment variables and create the LoRA adapter directory.

Start the model by using one of the following options: Use static LoRA loading. docker run -it --rm --gpus all \ -v " $LOCAL_NIM_CACHE :/opt/nim/.cache" \ -v " $PWD /loras:/opt/nim/loras" \ -p 8000 :8000 \ -e NGC_API_KEY \ -e NIM_MODEL_PROFILE \ -e CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES \ -e NIM_PEFT_SOURCE = /opt/nim/loras \ <nim-llm-image> Use dynamic LoRA loading with the watcher enabled. docker run -it --rm --gpus all \ -v " $LOCAL_NIM_CACHE :/opt/nim/.cache" \ -v " $PWD /loras:/opt/nim/loras" \ -p 8000 :8000 \ -e NGC_API_KEY \ -e NIM_MODEL_PROFILE \ -e CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES \ -e NIM_PEFT_SOURCE = /opt/nim/loras \ -e NIM_PEFT_REFRESH_INTERVAL = 10 \ <nim-llm-image>
Verify that the models loaded. curl -s localhost:8000/v1/models | jq

Send an inference request to an adapter. curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "model": "my_lora_adapter", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hello!"}], "max_tokens": 64 }' | jq

premises: Verify that you have supported hardware and software. For details, refer to the support matrix.
If you are running on an RTX AI PC or Workstation, install WSL2. For instructions, refer to NIM on WSL2 documentation.
Create an account on NVIDIA NGC and generate an API key to access the NIM container images and model assets on NGC.
Note: Deploying on Kubernetes is not supported for WSL.

claim: Generating a personal API key on NGC with the NGC Catalog and Private Registry (if an Early Access participant) selected is required to access NIM container images and model assets.
premises: To access the NIM container images and model assets on NGC, you must generate a personal API key.
To create your key, go to https://org.ngc.nvidia.com/setup/api-keys.
When you create your key, for Services Included, select the following: NGC Catalog, Private Registry (if you are an Early Access participant).
You can include more services if you are going to use this key for other purposes.

claim: Exporting the NGC API key as an environment variable (e.g., NGC_API_KEY) or storing it securely enables its use in subsequent commands.
premises: To conveniently use your API key in the commands in the following sections, you can export your key as an environment variable named NGC_API_KEY.
For example, run the following code in your terminal: export NGC_API_KEY=<yourAPIkeyvalue>.

Run one of the following commands to make your key available when you start a new terminal session: (for bash) echo "export NGC_API_KEY=<value>">>~/.bashrc; (for zsh) echo "export NGC_API_KEY=<value>">>~/.zshrc.
Note: Other, more secure options include saving your API key value in a file (retrieve it by using cat $NGC_API_KEY_FILE), or saving your key in a password manager.

claim: To pull the NIM container image from NGC, authenticate using docker login with username '$oauthtoken' and password equal to the NGC_API_KEY environment variable.
premises: Before you can pull the NIM container image from NGC, first authenticate to NGC by using the following command: echo "$NGC_API_KEY"|docker login nvcr.io --username '$oauthtoken' --password-stdin.
Use $oauthtoken as the username and NGC_API_KEY as the password.
The $oauthtoken username is a special name that indicates that you will authenticate with an API key and not a user name and password.

claim: Accepting the license terms on NGC for a NIM model is required before pulling its container image and model assets.
premises: Some NIM models require that you accept the license terms on NGC before you can pull the container image and model assets.
To accept the license terms, browse to the model or container page on the NGC Catalog, read and then click Accept Terms.

claim: The provided docker run command launches a NIM container for the llama-nemotron-rerank-1b-v2 model with the necessary runtime, GPU access, environment variables, cache mount, user mapping, and port forwarding.
premises: The following command launches a Docker container for the llama-nemotron-rerank-1b-v2 model.

export NIM_MODEL_NAME=nvidia/llama-nemotron-rerank-1b-v2; export CONTAINER_NAME=$(basename$NIM_MODEL_NAME); export IMG_NAME="nvcr.io/nim/nvidia/$CONTAINER_NAME:1.11.0"; export LOCAL_NIM_CACHE=~/.cache/nim; mkdir -p "$LOCAL_NIM_CACHE".
docker run -it --rm --name=$CONTAINER_NAME --runtime=nvidia --gpus all --shm-size=16GB -e NGC_API_KEY -v "$LOCAL_NIM_CACHE:/opt/nim/.cache" -u$(id -u) -p8000:8000 $IMG_NAME

Flag descriptions: --runtime=nvidia ensures NVIDIA drivers are accessible; --gpus all exposes all NVIDIA GPUs; --shm-size=16GB allocates host memory for multi-GPU communication; -e NGC_API_KEY provides the container with the token to download models; -v mounts the cache directory; -u$(id -u) avoids permission mismatches; -p 8000:8000 forwards the host port to the container.

claim: The NIM can be deployed across multiple GPUs as specified by the docker run --gpus argument, with Triton distributing inference requests equally; if no GPU count is given, it defaults to one GPU, and Multi-instance GPU (MIG) mode is not supported.
premises: The NIM deploys a single model across however many GPUs that you specify and are visible inside the docker container.
If you do not specify the number of GPUs, the NIM defaults to one GPU.
When using multiple GPUs, Triton distributes inference requests across the GPUs to keep them equally utilized.
Use the docker run --gpus command-line argument to specify the number of GPUs that are available for deployment.
- Example using all GPUs: docker run --gpus all ...
- Example using two GPUs: docker run --gpus 2 ...
- Example using specific GPUs: docker run --gpus '"device=1,2"' ...
GPU clusters with GPUs in Multi-instance GPU mode (MIG), are currently not supported.

claim: Model assets can be downloaded to the NIM cache without starting the server by first listing model profiles and then downloading the selected profile, which is useful for air-gapped systems.
premises: If model assets must be pre-fetched, such as in an air-gapped system, you can download the assets to the NIM cache without starting the server.
To download assets first run list-model-profiles to determine the desired profile, and then run download-to-cache with that profile.

The commands involve setting environment variables for container name, image, cache path, and running the container with appropriate flags (e.g., --gpus all, -e NGC_API_KEY, -e NIM_CPU_ONLY=1, -v cache mount).

By default, the download-to-cache command downloads the most appropriate model assets for the detected GPU; to override this behavior and download a specific model, set the NIM_MODEL_PROFILE environment variable when launching the container.
Use the list-model-profiles command available within the NIM container to list all profiles.

premises: To stop the Docker container, run the following code: docker stop $CONTAINER_NAME.
To remove the Docker container, run the following code. If you included the --rm flag when you started the container, you don’t need this step: docker rm $CONTAINER_NAME.

claim: The NVIDIA NeMo Retriever Reranking NIM runs as a Docker container and can be configured in multiple ways.
premises: NVIDIA NeMo Retriever Reranking NIM use docker containers under the hood.
Each NIM is its own Docker container and there are several ways to configure it.
The remainder of this section describes the various ways to configure a NIM container.

claim: The NIM container requires GPU access via the NVIDIA Container Toolkit and allows specification of GPUs using --gpus or NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES.
premises: The NIM container is GPU-accelerated and uses NVIDIA Container Toolkit for access to GPUs on the host.
You can specify the --gpus all command-line argument to the docker run command if the host has one or more of the same GPU model.
If the host has a combination of GPUs, such as an A6000 and a GeForce display GPU, run the container on compute-capable GPUs only.

Expose specific GPUs to the container by using either of the following methods: Specify the --gpus argument, such as --gpus="device=1"; Set the NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES environment variable, such as -e NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=1.
Run the nvidia-smi -L command to list the device IDs to specify in the argument or environment variable.

claim: The memory footprint of the NIM container varies by model backend, with ONNX profiles allocating memory dynamically and TensorRT profiles pre-allocating based on maximum input shapes.
premises: The memory footprint of the NVIDIA NeMo Retriever Reranking NIM depends on the model backend and loaded profiles.
For ONNX model profiles, memory is allocated dynamically according to the requests.
For TensorRT model profiles, all optimization profiles are loaded at startup and memory is pre-allocated based on the maximum input shapes.
Triton dynamically selects the optimal profile at runtime based on actual input shapes.
Refer to the support matrix for the approximate memory footprint by compute capability.

claim: Low PID limits in container runtime environments can cause the NIM container to fail during startup or after serving limited requests, and can be resolved by increasing the PID limit.
premises: In certain deployment or container runtime environments, default process and thread limits (PID limits) can interfere with NIM startup.
These set limits are set by Docker, Podman, Kubernetes, or the operating system.

If the PID limit is too low, you might see symptoms such as: NIM starts up partially, but fails to reach ready state, and then stalls; NIM starts up partially, but fails to reach ready state, and then crashes; NIM serves a small number of requests, and then fails.
To verify that PID limits are impacting the NIM container, you can remove or adjust the PID limit at the container, node, and operating system level.
Removing the PID limit and then checking for success is a useful diagnostic step.
To increase the PID limit in a docker run command, set --pids-limit=-1.
To increase the PID limit in a podman run command, set --pids-limit=-1.
To increase the PID limit in Kubernetes, set the PodPidsLimit on the kubelet on each node.
To increase the PID limit at the operating system level, see your OS-specific documentation.

claim: Increasing shared memory via the --shm-size flag may be necessary for the NIM container due to tokenization scaling with CPU cores using Triton’s Python backend.
premises: Tokenization uses Triton’s Python backend capabilities that scales with the number of CPU cores available.
You may need to increase the available shared memory given to the microservice container.
Example providing 1g of shared memory: dockerrun...--shm-size=1g...

claim: The NIM container uses specific paths for model caching, and binding host directories to /opt/nim/.cache avoids repeated model downloads and permission issues.
premises: The following table identifies the paths that are used in the container.
Container Path: /opt/nim/.cache or NIM_CACHE_PATH
Description: Specifies the path, relative to the root of the container, for downloaded models.
The typical use for this path is to bind mount a directory on the host with this path inside the container.
For example, to use ~/.cache/nim on the host, run mkdir -p ~/.cache/nim before you start the container.
When you start the container, specify the -v ~/.cache/nim:/opt/nim/.cache -u $(id -u) arguments to the docker run command.
If you do not specify a bind or volume mount, as shown in the -v argument in the preceding command, the container downloads the model each time you start the container.
The -u $(id -u) argument runs the container with your user ID to avoid file system permission issues and errors.

claim: NVIDIA NeMo Retriever Reranking NIM can be deployed on Kubernetes using Helm.
premises: You can deploy NVIDIA NeMo Retriever Reranking NIM on Kubernetes by using Helm.
The Helm chart simplifies NIM deployment on Kubernetes.
The chart supports deployment with a variety of possible cluster, GPU, and storage configurations.

claim: Persistent storage is recommended for production deployment to avoid repeated model downloads.
premises: By default, models are stored in an emptyDir volume, which means they are re-downloaded each time the pod restarts.
For production use, we recommend that you use persistent storage to avoid repeated downloads.
This chart supports two general categories: Persistent Volume Claims (enabled by persistence.enabled) and hostPath (enabled by hostPath.enabled).

These will likely have the same key in it, but they will have different formats (dockerconfig.json vs opaque).
Use the following procedure to create the secrets for this chart: [kubectl create secret docker-registry ngc-secret] and [kubectl create secret generic ngc-api].

claim: To generate rankings with NVIDIA NeMo Retriever Reranking NIM, you send a POST request to the /v1/ranking endpoint specifying model, query, passages, and optional truncate parameter.
premises: To generate rankings, use the following code.

curl -X'POST' 'http://localhost:8000/v1/ranking' -H'accept: application/json' -H'Content-Type: application/json' -d'{"model": "nvidia/llama-nemotron-rerank-1b-v2","query": {"text": "which way should i go?"},"passages": [{"text": "two roads diverged in a yellow wood, and sorry i could not travel both and be one traveler, long i stood and looked down one as far as i could to where it bent in the undergrowth;"},{"text": "then took the other, as just as fair, and having perhaps the better claim because it was grassy and wanted wear, though as for that the passing there had worn them really about the same,"},{"text": "and both that morning equally lay in leaves no step had trodden black. oh, i marked the first for another day! yet knowing how way leads on to way i doubted if i should ever come back."},{"text": "i shall be telling this with a sigh somewhere ages and ages hence: two roads diverged in a wood, and i, i took the one less traveled by, and that has made all the difference."}],"truncate": "END"}'

claim: The NeMo Retriever Reranking API relies solely on the query and passage texts for reranking, ignoring any external scores, and its behavior depends on the truncate parameter (NONE or END).
premises: A request to the NeMo Retriever Reranking API includes a query , a list of passages , and an optional truncate parameter (either NONE or END , defaulting to NONE ).
It then reranks the passages based on relevance.
While many datastores return scores for passages , those scores are not used by the Reranking API.
Only the text of the query and candidate passages are used, and are ranked according to the model’s understanding of the content.

If truncate is NONE , the container returns an error for inputs whose tokenized representation exceeds the token limit for the underlying model. If truncate is END , all tokens beyond the token limit are ignored.

claim: The API enforces a model-specific token limit; if truncate is END, excess tokens are discarded, which can render the service useless when the query consumes the entire limit.
premises: The NeMo Retriever Reranking API allows over 9,000 characters of text to be passed in for query and passages , however this far higher than current model limits.
The token limit is a function of the underlying model.
For NV-Rerank-QA-Mistral-4B , the total token limit is 503 including the query.
So if your query is 200 tokens and a passage is 400 tokens, the rightmost 97 tokens will get truncated.
Note that this means if your query is 503 tokens and truncate is END , the entire passage will be truncated, rendering the reranking service useless.

claim: A single reranking request can include up to 512 passages.
premises: You can pass up to 512 passages in a single reranking call.

claim: The API returns rankings sorted by descending logit, where each entry’s index indicates the original passage position and logit is the model’s raw score for that query‑passage pair.
premises: The results from a reranking request will include a list of objects with index and logit keys.
They will be sorted descending by logit value.
logit is the raw, unnormalized predictions that a model generates for each query / passage pair.
The index references the index of the passage being referred to in the request.

So if the request list included passages ["bears", "house", "grass"] and the indexes in the response are 1,2,0 then the response is saying that the sorted passages order is ["house", "grass", "bears"].

premises: The following environment variables are related to exporting OpenTelemetry metrics and traces from the NIM microservice.
NIM_ENABLE_OTEL: Set to 1 to enable OpenTelemetry instrumentation in NIMs. Default value: None
OTEL_SERVICE_NAME: Specifies the name of the service to use in the exported metrics.
OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT: Specifies the endpoint of an OTLP HTTP receiver.
OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER="otlp": Specifies to export metrics to the specified OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT in OTLP format.

claim: An OpenTelemetry Collector can be configured with OTLP and Prometheus receivers to receive metrics and traces, and export them via Zipkin, OTLP, and debug exporters.

Three exporters are defined: - A Zipkin exporter to a running Zipkin instance. - An OTLP exporter to a downstream collector or backend, such as Datadog. - A debug exporter that prints received data to the console.
Traces are received exclusively by the OTLP receiver and exported by both the Zipkin and debug exporters.
Metrics are received by the OTLP and Prometheus receivers. The metrics are exported by the OTLP and debug exporters.

claim: Following the provided procedure (download, set NGC_API_KEY, launch NIM, start observability stack, open Grafana, add Prometheus datasource, import dashboard) enables observation of metrics and traces in Grafana.

premises: This page documents all environment variables supported by NIM LLM.
Set variables using -e flags when you run the container.
The following variables control log format and verbosity.
The following variables control model selection, model loading, and related runtime behavior.
The following variables control server and health-check ports.

The following variables provide credentials for authenticated model downloads.

NIM uses TLS in two distinct directions. Inbound TLS secures client connections to the NIM inference API (nginx layer). Outbound TLS secures connections the container makes from itself when downloading model artifacts from NGC, Hugging Face, or a corporate registry such as JFrog Artifactory.
These variables configure Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) policy at the nginx proxy layer.
