premises: Create a dedicated Kubernetes namespace for NIM. A namespace is a logical partition within a cluster. It isolates resources such as pods, services, secrets, and so on from other workloads. Creating a dedicated namespace for NIM keeps resources organized and helps avoid naming conflicts with other applications in the cluster.

claim: Two secrets are required for NIM deployment: an image pull secret for NGC container registry access and a generic secret containing the NGC API key for model downloads.
premises: Create an image pull secret for NGC container registry access: export NGC_API_KEY = ${ YOUR_NGC_API_KEY } kubectl create secret -n nim-service docker-registry ngc-secret \ --docker-server = nvcr.io \ --docker-username = '$oauthtoken' \ --docker-password = ${ NGC_API_KEY }
Create a secret with the NGC API key for model downloads: kubectl create secret -n nim-service generic ngc-api-secret \ --from-literal = NGC_API_KEY = ${ NGC_API_KEY }

claim: A NIMCache custom resource must be created and reach Ready status before deploying a NIMService to ensure model artifacts are pre-downloaded and available.
premises: Create a NIMCache custom resource to pre-download model artifacts to persistent storage
Monitor the caching progress: kubectl get nimcache -n nim-service -w
Wait until the NIMCache status shows Ready before proceeding.
Confirm the NIMCache is in Ready state before deploying the NIMService. The NIM pod mounts the cache PVC at /model-store and will fail if the model artifacts are not present.

claim: The NIMService custom resource deploys the NIM service with configurable image, pull policy, secrets, storage reference, GPU resources, and service exposure.
premises: After the cache is ready, create a NIMService custom resource to deploy the NIM service.

kubectl create -n nim-service -f - <<'EOF'apiVersion:apps.nvidia.com/v1alpha1kind:NIMServicemetadata:name:meta-llama3-8b-instructspec:image:repository:<NIM_LLM_MODEL_SPECIFIC_IMAGE>tag:"2.0.4"pullPolicy:IfNotPresentpullSecrets:-ngc-secretauthSecret:ngc-api-secretstorage:nimCache:name:meta-llama3-8b-instructprofile:''resources:limits:nvidia.com/gpu:1expose:service:type:ClusterIPport:8000EOF

claim: After deploying NIMService, the deployment can be verified by checking resource status, pod status, and testing inference via port forwarding and API calls.
premises: Check the NIMService status: kubectl get nimservice -n nim-service
Check that the pod is running: kubectl get pods -n nim-service
After the NIMService is ready, test inference with port forwarding: kubectl port-forward -n nim-service svc/meta-llama3-8b-instruct 8000 :8000
Query the /v1/models endpoint to discover the model name to use in inference requests: curl -s http://localhost:8000/v1/models

Send a chat completion request using the model name returned by /v1/models : curl -s http://localhost:8000/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "model": "meta/llama-3.1-8b-instruct", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hello!"}], "max_tokens": 64 }'

claim: Additional NIM or vLLM configuration can be passed to the NIM pod using the NIMService env field, such as vLLM arguments via NIM_PASSTHROUGH_ARGS, model profiles via spec.storage.nimCache.profile, and log level via NIM_LOG_LEVEL.
premises: The NIM Operator sets environment variables on the NIM pod. To pass additional NIM or vLLM configuration, use the NIMService env field.
Pass additional vLLM arguments (for example, prefix caching) through NIM_PASSTHROUGH_ARGS :\nspec:env:-name:NIM_PASSTHROUGH_ARGSvalue:"--enable-prefix-caching--max-num-batched-tokens8192"
Select a specific model profile by setting spec.storage.nimCache.profile :\nspec:storage:nimCache:name:meta-llama3-8b-instructprofile:'vllm-fp8-tp1-pp1'
The operator sets NIM_JSONL_LOGGING=1 and NIM_LOG_LEVEL=INFO by default. Override the log level:\nspec:env:-name:NIM_LOG_LEVELvalue:"DEBUG"

claim: NIM LLM exposes vLLM’s native Prometheus metrics at /v1/metrics for use in autoscaling, alerting, and capacity planning.
premises: NIM LLM exposes vLLM’s native Prometheus metrics at /v1/metrics . Use these metrics for autoscaling, alerting, and capacity planning in operator deployments.

claim: The NIMService supports creating a Prometheus ServiceMonitor for automatic metric scraping, with the metrics endpoint path hardcoded to /v1/metrics.
premises: The NIMService supports creating a Prometheus ServiceMonitor for automatic metric scraping. The operator hardcodes the metrics endpoint path to /v1/metrics :\nspec:metrics:enabled:trueserviceMonitor:additionalLabels:{}

claim: The NIM Operator supports horizontal pod autoscaling (HPA) based on custom Prometheus metrics like vllm:num_requests_waiting, as standard CPU/memory metrics are not useful for scaling NIM.
premises: The NIM Operator supports horizontal pod autoscaling (HPA) based on custom Prometheus metrics. Standard CPU and memory metrics are not useful for scaling NIM. Use inference-specific metrics instead.

The following example shows HPA configuration in a NIMService spec:\nspec:scale:enabled:truehpa:minReplicas:1maxReplicas:4metrics:-type:Podspods:metric:name:vllm:num_requests_waitingtarget:type:AverageValueaverageValue:"10"
This requires the Prometheus Adapter to be installed and configured to expose vLLM metrics as Kubernetes custom metrics.

claim: If a NIMCache is stuck in Pending or NotReady state, troubleshooting should include checking storage class, PVC status, job logs for artifact download, NGC API key validity, and cache status conditions.
premises: If NIMCache remains in Pending or NotReady , use the following checks to isolate the issue:
- Verify the storage class is available and can provision volumes: kubectl get storageclass
- Check the PVC status: kubectl get pvc -n nim-service

- The NIMCache controller creates a Kubernetes Job named <nimcache-name>-job to download model artifacts. Check the job status and its pod logs: kubectl get jobs -n nim-service\n- kubectl logs -n nim-service -l job-name = meta-llama3-8b-instruct-job
- Ensure the NGC API key secret is correct and the image pull secret has access to the NIM container image.
- Check the NIMCache status conditions for details: kubectl describe nimcache -n nim-service meta-llama3-8b-instruct

claim: If a NIMService pod fails to start, troubleshooting should include checking pod events and logs, GPU availability, NIMCache readiness, and model profile validity.
premises: If the NIMService pod fails to start, use the following checks to isolate the issue:
- Check pod events: kubectl describe pod -n nim-service -l app = meta-llama3-8b-instruct
- Check pod logs: kubectl logs -n nim-service -l app = meta-llama3-8b-instruct
- Verify GPU resources are available: kubectl get nodes -o json | jq '.items[].status.allocatable[\"nvidia.com/gpu\"]'
- Confirm the NIMCache is in Ready state before deploying the NIMService. The NIM pod mounts the cache PVC at /model-store and will fail if the model artifacts are not present.
- If you use a specific model profile through spec.storage.nimCache.profile , verify that the profile name matches one available in the cached model manifest.

claim: Health probe failures in NIMService can be addressed by adjusting the startup probe threshold for slow-loading models or verifying service port alignment with the NIM container's port.
premises: The nginx proxy in the NIM container serves the health endpoints. /v1/health/live responds immediately, even during model loading, while /v1/health/ready only returns 200 after the model is fully loaded. By default, both endpoints use the NIM service port ( NIM_SERVER_PORT , which defaults to 8000). If NIM_HEALTH_PORT is set, the health endpoints move to that dedicated port instead.

The operator configures a startup probe on /v1/health/ready with a default failureThreshold of 120 and a periodSeconds of 10, giving the model up to 20 minutes to load before the pod is killed. If readiness or startup probes are failing:

- For large models that take longer to load, increase the startup probe failure threshold in the NIMService spec: spec : startupProbe : enabled : true probe : httpGet : path : /v1/health/ready port : 8000 initialDelaySeconds : 30 periodSeconds : 10 failureThreshold : 240
- Check that spec.expose.service.port matches the port used by the NIM container (default 8000). The operator sets NIM_SERVER_PORT automatically from this value.

claim: If NIMService or NIMCache resources are not being reconciled, the NIM Operator pod's health should be verified by checking its status and logs.
premises: If the NIMService or NIMCache resources are not being reconciled, verify the operator itself is healthy:\nkubectlgetpods-nnim-operator\nkubectllogs-nnim-operator-lapp.kubernetes.io/name=k8s-nim-operator

claim: Azure supports two deployment paths for NIM LLM: AKS for self-managed Kubernetes deployment and Microsoft Foundry for managed deployment using Azure ML Managed Online Endpoints.
premises: Azure supports two deployment paths: AKS (Azure Kubernetes Service) and Microsoft Foundry.
AKS is a self-managed Kubernetes deployment using the NIM LLM Helm chart, providing full control over infrastructure including GPU node pools and persistent storage.
Microsoft Foundry is a managed deployment using Azure ML Managed Online Endpoints, simplifying infrastructure management with built-in health checks.

claim: Deploying NIM LLM on AKS requires creating an AKS cluster with GPU nodes, installing the NVIDIA GPU Operator, creating Kubernetes secrets for NGC and Hugging Face access, and deploying via Helm chart.
premises: To deploy NIM LLM on Azure AKS, create an AKS cluster with GPU nodes using Azure CLI commands including resource group creation, cluster creation, and GPU node pool addition with --gpu-driver none.
Install the NVIDIA GPU Operator by adding the NVIDIA Helm repository, updating Helm repo index, and installing nvidia/gpu-operator.
Create Kubernetes secrets including namespace, NGC image pull secret, NGC API key secret, and optionally Hugging Face token secret for gated models.
Deploy NIM LLM using Helm by fetching the chart from NGC, viewing default values, and installing with a custom values file.
Verify deployment by getting the service endpoint, checking health endpoint, and sending an inference request via curl.

claim: Deploying NIM LLM on Microsoft Foundry requires setting up Azure ML workspace, installing Azure AI ML Python SDK, and deploying as a managed online endpoint using the Python SDK with environment configuration and traffic routing.
premises: Prerequisites for Microsoft Foundry deployment include Azure CLI, Azure ML extension, Azure Machine Learning workspace, NGC API key, and Azure AI ML Python SDK.

Deploy with Python SDK by creating ML client, defining ManagedOnlineEndpoint and ManagedOnlineDeployment, configuring environment with ACR image and inference routes (liveness, readiness, scoring), setting instance type, environment variables (NGC_API_KEY, NIM_MODEL_PROFILE), request settings, and probe settings.
Route traffic to the deployment by setting traffic allocation to 100% for the nim deployment.
Retrieve endpoint URL and primary key for inference requests.
Verify deployment by sending an inference request using httpx with Bearer token authentication and JSON payload.

claim: NIM supports deployment on Google Cloud Platform (GCP) through two main approaches: Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) for self-managed Kubernetes with Helm charts and Vertex AI for fully managed ML platform.
premises: NIM supports deployment on Google Cloud Platform (GCP) through two approaches: Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) : Self-managed Kubernetes deployment using Helm charts with complete control over infrastructure, GPU node pools, and persistent storage. Vertex AI : Fully managed ML platform with built-in load balancing, auto-scaling, and automatic authentication.

claim: Deploying NIM LLM on GKE requires setting up a GPU-enabled cluster, configuring authentication and environment variables, creating secrets for model access, and deploying via Helm with specific values files depending on the model source.
premises: To deploy NIM LLM on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE), create a GKE cluster with GPU-enabled node pools and prepare your Google Cloud environment for NIM LLM workloads.
Prerequisites include a GCP project with permissions, sufficient GPU quota, and required tools (Google Cloud SDK, kubectl, Helm 3, gke-gcloud-auth-plugin).
Initial setup involves authenticating with gcloud auth login, setting project, enabling required APIs (container, compute, storage, artifactregistry), and setting environment variables.

Steps include creating a VPC network, GKE cluster, GPU node pool (with specific GPU types like NVIDIA L4, A100, H100), getting cluster credentials, verifying GPU availability, creating secrets (NGC registry secret, ngc-api secret, optional Hugging Face token), creating Helm values files (model-specific or model-free with GCS storage), installing the Helm release, monitoring deployment, configuring network access via firewall rule, testing the deployment, and cleanup procedures.

claim: Deploying NIM on Vertex AI requires pushing the NIM image to Artifact Registry, storing models in GCS, registering the model in Vertex AI, and deploying to an endpoint with specific GPU and driver version requirements.
premises: Vertex AI is a fully managed ML platform that eliminates the need for infrastructure management and provides built-in load balancing, auto-scaling, and authentication through Application Default Credentials (ADC).
Key constraints: container images must be sourced from Artifact Registry only, model storage must be in GCS using gs:// protocol, and authentication uses ADC automatically.
Prerequisites include a GCP project with permissions for Vertex AI, Artifact Registry, and GCS, sufficient GPU quota, and required tools (Google Cloud SDK, Docker, optional google-cloud-aiplatform).

Initial setup involves authenticating, setting project, enabling required APIs (aiplatform, artifactregistry, storage, compute), setting environment variables, creating GCS bucket and granting Vertex AI service account access, creating Artifact Registry repository and granting read access, configuring Docker authentication.

Steps include pulling NIM image from NGC, re-tagging and pushing to Artifact Registry, uploading model to GCS, registering model in Vertex AI with appropriate environment variables (NIM_REPOSITORY_OVERRIDE for percent-encoded GCS keys or NIM_MODEL_PATH for standard directory structure), creating endpoint, and deploying model with machine type g2-standard-8 and accelerator type nvidia-l4,count=1, potentially overriding minimum GPU driver version to 580.65.06 or later due to CUDA 13.0+ requirement.
Testing is done via Vertex AI REST API using rawPredict endpoint with bearer token authentication.
Cleanup involves undeploying model, deleting endpoint, deleting model from registry, deleting Artifact Registry image, and optionally deleting infrastructure (repository and GCS bucket).

claim: Deploying NIM LLM on Amazon EKS requires setting up a Kubernetes cluster with GPU nodes, installing necessary operators and drivers, and then deploying the NIM Helm chart.
premises: This guide walks through deploying NIM LLM on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) with GPU-accelerated nodes.
The deployment process includes creating an EKS control plane and adding a GPU-capable managed node group.
The deployment process includes installing the NVIDIA GPU Operator and the Amazon EBS CSI Driver after the node group is available.
The deployment process includes creating the namespace, secrets, storage, and installing the Helm chart to deploy NIM after the cluster is ready.

claim: Deploying NIM LLM on Amazon SageMaker involves building and pushing a container image to ECR, creating a SageMaker model with appropriate environment variables, and setting up an endpoint for real-time inference.
premises: This guide covers deploying NIM LLM on Amazon SageMaker using managed real-time inference endpoints.
The guide includes steps to build and push the NIM image to an ECR repository in your account.

The guide includes steps to create a SageMaker model that references the ECR image and sets runtime environment variables for model storage and serving (such as NIM_MODEL_PATH, NIM_REPOSITORY_OVERRIDE, or NIM_SERVED_MODEL_NAME).
The guide includes steps to create an endpoint configuration and endpoint, and to verify the deployment by checking the endpoint status and running an inference request.

claim: NIM LLM downloads model artifacts at container startup using a manifest-driven approach that specifies which files to download and from which sources.
premises: NIM LLM downloads model artifacts at container startup using a manifest-driven approach
The model manifest describes which files to download and where to download them from
Supported model sources are NGC (ngc://), Hugging Face (hf://), Amazon S3 (s3://), Google Cloud Storage (gs://), ModelScope (modelscope://), and Local Storage (local://)

claim: To use NGC as a model source for NIM, one must use the ngc:// URI format, authenticate via API key environment variables, and follow the download steps setting NGC_API_KEY and NIM_MODEL_PROFILE before running the download-to-cache command.
premises: NGC uses API key authentication
NIM checks NGC_CLI_API_KEY (priority 1) and NGC_API_KEY (priority 2) environment variables
Both Personal API Keys (starting with nvapi-) and Legacy API Keys are supported
URI format for NGC models is ngc://{org}/{team}/{model}:{version}?file={filename}
Downloading from NGC: set NGC_API_KEY and NIM_MODEL_PROFILE, then run docker run ... download-to-cache --profile $NIM_MODEL_PROFILE
Downloading behind a corporate proxy: also set HTTPS_PROXY (and optionally NO_PROXY, SSL_CERT_FILE, REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE)

claim: Hugging Face models are accessed via hf:// URIs, authenticated with HF_TOKEN, and can be customized via HF_HOME and HF_ENDPOINT environment variables, with download steps involving setting HF_TOKEN and NIM_MODEL_PROFILE and running the download-to-cache command.
premises: URI format for Hugging Face models is hf://{org}/{model}:{revision}?file={filename}
Hugging Face uses a bearer token for authentication via the HF_TOKEN environment variable (API token for private or gated models, recommended even for public models to avoid rate limiting)

Additional environment variables: HF_HOME (default ~/.cache/huggingface; when both HF_HOME and NIM_CACHE_PATH are set, HF_HOME must equal $NIM_CACHE_PATH/huggingface/hub) and HF_ENDPOINT (default https://huggingface.co; base URL of the Hugging Face Hub API, can redirect to a private Enterprise Hub, mirror, or local proxy)
Hugging Face-compatible proxies are supported by setting HF_ENDPOINT to e.g., http://localhost:8090 for an Olah proxy
Downloading from Hugging Face: set HF_TOKEN and NIM_MODEL_PROFILE, then run docker run ... download-to-cache --profile $NIM_MODEL_PROFILE

claim: Amazon S3 (and S3-compatible) storage is accessed via s3:// URIs, authenticated using the AWS credential provider chain, with optional S3-compatible settings (AWS_ENDPOINT_URL, addressing style variables), and models can be downloaded directly or via NGC mirroring and NIM_REPOSITORY_OVERRIDE.
premises: URI format for Amazon S3 objects is s3://{bucket}/{key}

Authentication uses the standard AWS credential provider chain discovering credentials in order: environment variables (AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY) priority 1, AWS credentials file (~/.aws/credentials) priority 2, IAM instance profile priority 3, ECS container credentials priority 4

S3-compatible storage: set AWS_ENDPOINT_URL to redirect to a provider (e.g., MinIO); variables AWS_S3_ADDRESSING_STYLE (virtual/path, default virtual) and AWS_S3_USE_PATH_STYLE (True/False, default False) control addressing style; required for services such as MinIO and Ceph; NIM automatically detects Oracle OCI Object Storage endpoints and enables path-style addressing
Mirroring NGC models to S3: set NGC_API_KEY, then run docker mirror s3 command with manifest and bucket
Downloading from S3: set AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, AWS_REGION, and NIM_MODEL_PROFILE, then run docker download-to-cache
Redirecting NGC downloads to S3: set NIM_REPOSITORY_OVERRIDE to an s3:// bucket, provide AWS credentials, and run the container with those environment variables
Note: when using NIM_REPOSITORY_OVERRIDE with S3, model assets must be stored with percent-encoded keys; use the mirror s3 command for correct encoding

claim: Google Cloud Storage is accessed via gs:// URIs, authenticated using Google Application Default Credentials (ADC), with mirroring and downloading steps similar to S3, and NGC downloads can be redirected to GCS via NIM_REPOSITORY_OVERRIDE.
premises: URI format for Google Cloud Storage objects is gs://{bucket}/{key}

Authentication: GCS uses Google’s Application Default Credentials (ADC) discovering credentials from: GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS environment variable (path to a service account key file), Vertex AI managed environment credentials, Google Compute Engine metadata service, Cloud Run environment, and gcloud CLI user credentials
Example: export GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS="/path/to/sa.json"
Mirroring NGC models to GCS: set NGC_API_KEY and GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS, then run docker mirror gcs command with manifest and bucket
Downloading from GCS: set GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS and NIM_MODEL_PROFILE, then run docker download-to-cache with volume mount for credentials

Redirecting NGC downloads to GCS: set GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS and NIM_REPOSITORY_OVERRIDE="gs://my-models-bucket", then start the container with those environment variables and credential volume mount

claim: ModelScope models are accessed via modelscope:// URIs, authenticated with MODELSCOPE_API_TOKEN, configurable via MODELSCOPE_ENDPOINT and MODELSCOPE_CACHE, and downloaded using the download-to-cache command.
premises: URI format for ModelScope models is modelscope://{org}/{model}:{revision}?file={filename}
Note: ModelScope uses master as the default branch, unlike Hugging Face which uses main
Authentication: environment variable MODELSCOPE_API_TOKEN (API token for private models, recommended even for public models to avoid rate limiting)
ModelScope-compatible proxies: set MODELSCOPE_ENDPOINT="http://your-modelscope-proxy:port"
Additional environment variable: MODELSCOPE_CACHE default $NIM_CACHE_PATH/modelscope/hub; must be consistent with NIM_CACHE_PATH when both are set
Downloading from ModelScope: set MODELSCOPE_API_TOKEN and NIM_MODEL_PROFILE, then run docker run ... download-to-cache --profile $NIM_MODEL_PROFILE

claim: Local storage enables NIM to access existing filesystem models via local:// URIs, creating symlinks for zero extra disk usage and near-instant setup, with workflows for preparing a local model store, using a local model, and running air-gapped deployments.
premises: URI format for local filesystem paths is local://{absolute_path}
Examples: local:///mnt/models/llama-3.1-8b (model directory) and local:///mnt/models/llama-3.1-8b?file=config.json (specific file)
Note: Only the local:// URI scheme is supported for local filesystem access; alternatives such as file:// or bare paths are not supported

How It Works: Unlike remote sources, Local Storage does not download files; it creates symlinks in the workspace pointing directly to the source files → zero additional disk usage, near-instant setup (milliseconds), and source files must remain accessible for the duration of the NIM deployment

Preparing a Local Model Store: the create-model-store command downloads a model from a remote source (e.g., NGC) and creates a properly formatted local model store; example includes setting NGC_API_KEY, NIM_MODEL_PROFILE, mounting cache and store directories, and running create-model-store
Using a Local Model: set NIM_MODEL_PROFILE, mount the local model directory read-only and the cache, then run download-to-cache
Air-Gapped Deployment: similar to using a local model but with --network none to isolate the container; example mounts /opt/models/llama-3.1-8b read-only

claim: NIM provides global configuration options including cache path (NIM_CACHE_PATH), repository override (NIM_REPOSITORY_OVERRIDE) for redirecting downloads to alternative storage, a distinction between NIM_REPOSITORY_OVERRIDE and NIM_MODEL_PATH for different use cases, a switch to disable model download (NIM_DISABLE_MODEL_DOWNLOAD), and proxy environment variable support for corporate firewalls with optional TLS certificate handling.
premises: Cache Path: variable NIM_CACHE_PATH default /opt/nim/.cache; directory used for model assets in the container; must be a valid, writable path

Repository Override: NIM_REPOSITORY_OVERRIDE redirects model downloads from the default NGC source to an alternative storage location at runtime; supported protocols as override targets are ngc:// (NGC-compatible proxy servers), s3:// (AWS S3 and S3-compatible storage), gs:// (Google Cloud Storage), http://, https:// (HTTP/HTTPS servers); note: it does NOT support model registries (hf://, modelscope://) as override targets; to use Hugging Face or ModelScope models, specify the corresponding URIs directly in the model manifest

NIM_REPOSITORY_OVERRIDE vs NIM_MODEL_PATH: table comparing Purpose (Mirror NGC models to your own storage vs Serve custom/fine-tuned models directly), Manifest (Uses built-in NGC manifest vs No manifest required), Upload format (Percent-encoded flat keys vs Standard directory structure), Checksum verification (Yes from NGC manifest vs No), Use case (Air-gapped deployments, NGC mirrors vs Custom models, fine-tuned weights); guidance: use NIM_REPOSITORY_OVERRIDE to serve an NGC model from your own S3/GCS bucket (air-gapped, latency, cost); use NIM_MODEL_PATH to serve a custom or fine-tuned model directly from cloud storage
Disabling Model Download: variable NIM_DISABLE_MODEL_DOWNLOAD default False; disables model download on container startup; useful for multi-node scenarios where only one node needs to download

Proxy Support: NIM honors standard proxy environment variables HTTPS_PROXY, HTTP_PROXY, NO_PROXY; if a corporate proxy performs TLS inspection (re-signing HTTPS traffic with a private CA), a combined CA bundle must be mounted and SSL_CERT_FILE and REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE set; example docker run command shows mounts and env vars for this scenario

claim: NIM provides CLI commands download-to-cache, create-model-store, and mirror to manage model profiles, create local model stores, and mirror NGC models to object storage, each with specific arguments and usage patterns.
premises: download-to-cache: downloads model profiles to the NIM cache; usage: download-to-cache [-h] [--all] [--profiles [PROFILES ...]] [--lora] [--model-uri MODEL_URI] [--manifest-file MANIFEST_FILE] [--model-cache-path MODEL_CACHE_PATH] [--use-cache] [--verify-checksums]; arguments: --all (download all profiles), --profiles [PROFILES ...] (specific profiles), --lora (default LoRA profile, cannot combine with --profiles or --all), --model-uri MODEL_URI (model URI to download, supported schemes: ngc://, hf://, s3://, gs://, modelscope://, local://), --manifest-file MANIFEST_FILE (manifest file path), --model-cache-path MODEL_CACHE_PATH (directory path of model cache), --use-cache (check for cached assets before downloading), --verify-checksums (verify downloaded files match manifest checksums, enabled by default)

create-model-store: creates a properly formatted model store directory from a cached model profile; usage: create-model-store [-h] --profile PROFILE --model-store MODEL_STORE [--model-cache-path MODEL_CACHE_PATH] [--use-cache]; arguments: --profile PROFILE (required profile hash), --model-store MODEL_STORE (required directory path where the model profile is extracted and copied to), --model-cache-path MODEL_CACHE_PATH (directory path of model cache), --use-cache (check for cached assets before downloading)

mirror: mirrors model profiles from NGC to a destination object storage bucket; usage: mirror {s3,gcs} [-h] -b BUCKET [--profiles [PROFILES ...]] [--manifest-file MANIFEST_FILE] [--model-cache-path MODEL_CACHE_PATH]; arguments: s3 or gcs (destination storage type, required), -b BUCKET / --bucket BUCKET (destination bucket name, required), --profiles [PROFILES ...] (profiles to mirror, default profile if omitted), --manifest-file MANIFEST_FILE (manifest file path), --model-cache-path MODEL_CACHE_PATH (directory path of model cache)

claim: LoRA enables serving a base model with one or more fine-tuned adapters without retraining or rebuilding the full model.
premises: LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) lets you serve a base model plus one or more fine-tuned adapters without retraining or rebuilding the full model.

claim: NIM LLM provides two LoRA serving modes: static LoRA and dynamic LoRA.
premises: NIM LLM supports two LoRA serving modes:
- Static LoRA : Adapters are discovered from a directory at startup.
- Dynamic LoRA : Adapters can be loaded and unloaded while the server is running.

claim: Shared LoRA setup requires mounting an adapter directory, setting NIM_PEFT_SOURCE to that directory, optionally passing vLLM LoRA flags, and selecting a LoRA-capable profile.
premises: Before you configure static LoRA or dynamic LoRA, complete the shared setup in this section. These settings tell NIM LLM where to find adapters and ensure that the deployment uses a LoRA-capable profile.

Complete the following setup for both static LoRA and dynamic LoRA: - Mount a directory (containing LoRA adapters) to the container. - Set NIM_PEFT_SOURCE to that directory. - Optionally, pass native vLLM LoRA flags.
When available for your model, select a -feat_lora profile so the deployment uses LoRA-compatible runtime settings.

claim: In static LoRA mode, NIM LLM loads adapters from NIM_PEFT_SOURCE at startup and requires a container restart to reflect adapter changes.
premises: After you complete the required LoRA setup, NIM LLM uses static LoRA when NIM_PEFT_REFRESH_INTERVAL is not set.
In static LoRA mode, the NIM container discovers adapters in NIM_PEFT_SOURCE during startup and loads valid adapters.
If you add, remove, or update adapters after startup, restart the NIM container to apply those changes.

claim: Dynamic LoRA enables runtime adapter addition/removal without restarting via directory monitoring (NIM_PEFT_REFRESH_INTERVAL) or manual API endpoints.
premises: Use dynamic LoRA when you need to add or remove adapters without restarting the deployment. You can manage adapters through directory monitoring, runtime API calls, or both.
After you complete the shared LoRA setup, set NIM_PEFT_REFRESH_INTERVAL (polling interval in seconds) to enable dynamic LoRA through directory monitoring.
When NIM_PEFT_SOURCE and NIM_PEFT_REFRESH_INTERVAL are set, NIM starts the LoRA watcher and enables runtime LoRA updates for vLLM.
You can also use vLLM runtime endpoints for manual control: - POST /v1/load_lora_adapter - POST /v1/unload_lora_adapter

claim: Adapter load and unload actions can be performed via the directory watcher (copying/removing adapter folders) or the manual API (POST endpoints), and using both mechanisms together may cause the watcher to reload an adapter that the API removed but left in the directory.
premises: To manage adapters through the directory watcher, use the following actions: - Load : copy a new adapter folder into NIM_PEFT_SOURCE . - Unload : remove an adapter folder from NIM_PEFT_SOURCE . - Wait one refresh interval for /v1/models to reflect changes.
To manage adapters through the manual API, use the following actions: - Load with POST /v1/load_lora_adapter . - Unload with POST /v1/unload_lora_adapter .
If you use both the watcher and the manual API together, an adapter that the API removes but that is still present in the directory can be reloaded by the watcher during the next scan.

claim: Multiple adapters can be served simultaneously subject to GPU memory limits, and their IDs can be discovered via /v1/models and specified in the request model field.
premises: You can serve multiple adapters at the same time, subject to GPU memory limits.
Use /v1/models to discover available adapter IDs, then send the adapter ID in the request model field.

claim: The provided code example demonstrates a complete workflow for serving a fine-tuned Llama model with LoRA, including environment setup, adapter directory preparation, static or dynamic container startup, model verification, and an inference request targeting a loaded adapter.
premises: The following example shows a minimal local workflow for serving a fine-tuned Llama model with LoRA. It includes shared setup, static and dynamic startup commands, model discovery, and an inference request that targets a loaded adapter.

To serve a fine-tuned Llama model with LoRA, complete the following steps: - Set up the environment variables and create the LoRA adapter directory. ... - Start the model by using one of the following options: Use static LoRA loading. ... Use dynamic LoRA loading with the watcher enabled. ... - Verify that the models loaded. curl -s localhost:8000/v1/models | jq - Send an inference request to an adapter. curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/v1/chat/completions ...

claim: Before deploying NIM LLM on OCI OKE, you must install OCI CLI, kubectl, Helm, obtain an NGC API key, ensure GPU quota, and have a configured VCN with subnets, internet gateway, route table, and security lists.
premises: Install the following tools before proceeding: - OCI CLI - kubectl - Helm
You also need an NGC API key with access to NIM LLM container images and Helm charts.

Your OCI tenancy must have GPU quota available in the target region. Verify quota in the OCI Console under Limits, Quotas and Usage and ensure the compartment has a configured VCN, subnets, internet gateway, route table, and security lists.

claim: To run NIM LLM workloads, create an OKE cluster with GPU-capable worker nodes, set required environment variables, configure a public API endpoint, choose appropriate GPU shape, set boot volume size to at least 500 GB, and configure kubectl access.
premises: Set environment variables used throughout this guide: export CLUSTER_OCID="${YOUR_CLUSTER_OCID}" export NAMESPACE="nim-llm" export NIM_LLM_CHART_VERSION="${YOUR_CHART_VERSION}" export OCI_REGION="${YOUR_OCI_REGION}" export RELEASE_NAME="my-nim"

Create an OKE cluster with a GPU-capable node pool using the OCI Console: - Navigate to Developer Services > Kubernetes Clusters (OKE) > Create cluster and select Quick create . - Configure a public API endpoint and choose a GPU shape appropriate for your model. - Under Advanced options , set the boot volume size to at least 500 GB . The OCI default (approximately 47 GB, presenting as approximately 35 GB inside the OS) is exhausted by NIM LLM container images and the model cache during a single deployment.
After the cluster is created, configure kubectl access: ociclusterc... (command shown in text)
Verify connectivity by running: kubectl get nodes

claim: After creating the OKE cluster, you must expand the on-disk filesystem inside the OS to match the boot volume size to avoid DiskPressure and pod eviction during deployment.
premises: OKE does not automatically grow the on-disk filesystem inside the OS, even when the boot volume itself is sized correctly at the node-pool level. Expand the file system before deployment. Without this step, the node hits DiskPressure during deployment, and pods are evicted.
Check first: kubectl describe nodes | grep ephemeral-storage | head-1
If ephemeral-storage reads as approximately 35 GB (about 37206272Ki ), grow the filesystem in-place using a privileged pod (no SSH access required): ... (commands shown)
Re-run the kubectl describe nodes check to confirm ephemeral-storage now matches the boot volume size.

claim: Install the NVIDIA GPU Operator on OKE nodes to manage GPU device plugin, container toolkit, and runtime class, disabling the bundled driver and clearing the NoSchedule taint to allow GPU visibility and workload sharing.
premises: The NVIDIA GPU Operator manages the GPU device plugin, container toolkit, and runtime class on OKE nodes. OKE GPU node images ship with the NVIDIA driver pre-installed, so the operator is deployed with the bundled driver disabled:
helm repo add nvidia https://helm.ngc.nvidia.com/nvidia
helm repo update
helm install --wait gpu-operator nvidia/gpu-operator --namespace gpu-operator --create-namespace --set driver.enabled=false --set toolkit.enabled=true

OKE GPU node pools occasionally attach a nvidia.com/gpu:NoSchedule taint to the node. The chart tolerates the taint, but clearing it lets non-GPU workloads share the node: kubectl taint nodes --all nvidia.com/gpu:NoSchedule-2>/dev/null||true

Verify the operator is running and GPUs are visible to the cluster: kubectl get pods -n gpu-operator; kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{": "}{.status.allocatable.nvidia\.com/gpu}{" GPU(s)\\n"}{end}'
If a node advertises fewer GPUs than its shape provides, restart the device plugin: kubectl rollout restart -n gpu-operator daemonset/nvidia-device-plugin-daemonset

claim: Create two Kubernetes secrets in the deployment namespace—ngc-secret (docker-registry) for pulling images from nvcr.io and ngc-api (generic) for providing the NGC_API_KEY—to allow the NIM LLM pod to authenticate and pull required container images.
premises: The Helm chart requires two secrets in the deployment namespace. Missing either one causes the pod to fail with CreateContainerConfigError after scheduling:
- ngc-secret (type docker-registry ) is used by the kubelet to pull images from nvcr.io .
- ngc-api (type generic ) is mounted as the NGC_API_KEY environment variable so the pod can authenticate to NGC for the model download.

export IMAGE_PULL_SECRET="ngc-secret" export NGC_API_KEY="${YOUR_NGC_API_KEY}" kubectl create namespace $NAMESPACE kubectl create secret docker-registry $IMAGE_PULL_SECRET --namespace $NAMESPACE --docker-server=nvcr.io --docker-username='$oauthtoken' --docker-password="$NGC_API_KEY" kubectl create secret generic ngc-api --namespace $NAMESPACE --from-literal=NGC_API_KEY="$NGC_API_KEY"
Confirm both secrets exist and ngc-api is non-empty: kubectl get secret -n $NAMESPACE; kubectl get secret ngc-api -n $NAMESPACE -o jsonpath='{.data.NGC_API_KEY}' | base64 -d | wc -c

claim: Ensure persistent storage for NIM LLM model caching by using the default OCI Block Volume storage class (oci-bv) or optionally creating an Ultra High Performance Block Volume storage class (oci-bv-uhp) and referencing it via persistence.storageClass.
premises: NIM LLM requires persistent storage to cache the downloaded model across pod restarts. The Helm chart provisions a PVC automatically when you set persistence.enabled=true on helm install (covered in the next section). The PVC uses the cluster’s default storage class, which is oci-bv on OKE for OCI Block Volume.
For faster cold starts on large models, optionally create an Ultra High Performance Block Volume storage class and reference it with persistence.storageClass :

apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: StorageClass
metadata:
  name: oci-bv-uhp
provisioner: blockvolume.csi.oraclecloud.com
parameters:
  vpusPerGB: "30"
volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer
allowVolumeExpansion: true
reclaimPolicy: Delete

claim: Deploy the NIM LLM Helm chart with appropriate configuration—specifying the container image repository and tag, GPU resource limits, persistence enabled and size, NIM_MAX_MODEL_LEN, and optionally the ultra performance storage class—to successfully run the model on OKE.
premises: Fetch the Helm chart from NGC: helm fetch https://helm.ngc.nvidia.com/nim/charts/nim-llm-${NIM_LLM_CHART_VERSION}.tgz
Optional: View the default chart values to understand available configuration options. helm show values nim-llm-${NIM_LLM_CHART_VERSION}.tgz

Install the chart with inline --set flags. The following example uses nvcr.io/nim/meta/llama-3.1-8b-instruct on a single GPU. Adjust the image, GPU count, and persistence.size to match your model. helm install $RELEASE_NAME nim-llm-${NIM_LLM_CHART_VERSION}.tgz \
  --namespace $NAMESPACE \
  --set image.repository = nvcr.io/nim/meta/llama-3.1-8b-instruct \
  --set image.tag = " $NIM_LLM_CHART_VERSION " \
  --set 'resources.limits.nvidia\.com/gpu=1' \
  --set persistence.enabled = true \
  --set persistence.size = 80Gi \
  --set-string 'env[0].name=NIM_MAX_MODEL_LEN' --set-string 'env[0].value=32768'

Note The chart’s default persistence.size of 50Gi does not provide enough headroom for the model weights and the container image cache. Use 80Gi as a safe minimum for approximately 10 GB to 16 GB model weights, and increase the size proportionally for larger models. NIM_MAX_MODEL_LEN caps the KV-cache allocation to fit the available VRAM. Adjust per your shape’s GPU memory.

Note If you created the optional oci-bv-uhp storage class in the previous section, add --set persistence.storageClass=oci-bv-uhp to the command above to provision the PVC on Ultra High Performance block storage. Omit this flag to use the cluster default ( oci-bv ).

claim: After deployment, verify that the NIM LLM pod is running, GPU is bound, correct versions are reported, and the service can serve inference requests both inside and outside the cluster.
premises: Watch the pod come up: kubectl get pods -n $NAMESPACE -w First-time startup includes image pull, model download from NGC, and engine initialization. Expect five to ten minutes on the oci-bv-uhp storage class and 15 to 25 minutes on default oci-bv .

Confirm the chart and NIM LLM versions, and that the GPU is bound to the pod: helm list -n $NAMESPACE export POD = $( kubectl -n $NAMESPACE get pod -l app.kubernetes.io/instance = $RELEASE_NAME -o jsonpath = '{.items[0].metadata.name}' ) kubectl exec -n $NAMESPACE $POD -- nvidia-smi -L
kubectl logs -n $NAMESPACE $POD | grep 'NIM Version'
List the served model and send a test inference request from inside the pod: kubectl exec -n $NAMESPACE $POD -- curl -sS http://localhost:8000/v1/models | python3 -m json.tool

kubectl exec -n $NAMESPACE $POD -- curl -sS http://localhost:8000/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"model":"<MODEL_NAME>","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Hello!"}],"max_tokens":128}' Replace <MODEL_NAME> with the value advertised by /v1/models .

To call the service from outside the cluster, use kubectl port-forward : kubectl port-forward -n $NAMESPACE svc/ $RELEASE_NAME -nim-llm 8000 :8000 # In another terminal: curl http://localhost:8000/v1/health/ready

claim: To clean up all resources created by the guide, uninstall the Helm release, delete the Kubernetes secrets, delete the namespace, delete the OKE cluster, and manually remove any remaining OCI Block Volumes or Load Balancers to avoid ongoing charges.
premises: # Remove the Helm release helm uninstall $RELEASE_NAME --namespace $NAMESPACE
# Delete Kubernetes secrets kubectl delete secret ngc-api $IMAGE_PULL_SECRET --namespace $NAMESPACE
# Delete the namespace (also deletes the chart-managed PVC) kubectl delete namespace $NAMESPACE
# Delete the OKE cluster (also removes managed node pools) oci ce cluster delete --cluster-id ${CLUSTER_OCID} --region ${OCI_REGION} --force

Note
Deleting the cluster does not automatically remove associated OCI Block Volumes or Load Balancers. Delete these manually from the OCI Console to avoid ongoing charges.

claim: NIM LLM allows users to specify parser and chat template files via CLI arguments using bare filenames, which it automatically resolves to absolute paths inside the container.
premises: NIM LLM supports vLLM CLI arguments that take file paths — --reasoning-parser-plugin, --tool-parser-plugin, and --chat-template.
NIM automatically resolves these paths so you can reference plugin files by bare filename without knowing the container’s internal directory layout.

claim: Built-in reasoning parsers can be used by name without providing a plugin file, and an authoritative list is available in the vLLM reasoning parser registry.
premises: Pass any of these names to --reasoning-parser (no --reasoning-parser-plugin needed): deepseek_r1, deepseek_v3, ernie45, glm45, granite, holo2, hunyuan_a13b, kimi_k2, minimax_m2, minimax_m2_append_think, mistral, nemotron_v3, olmo3, openai_gptoss, qwen3, seed_oss, step3, step3p5.
For the authoritative list, refer to the vLLM reasoning parser registry.

claim: Built-in tool-call parsers can be used by name without a plugin file, with an authoritative list in the vLLM tool-call parser registry.
premises: Pass any of these names to --tool-call-parser (no --tool-parser-plugin needed): deepseek_v3, deepseek_v31, ernie45, glm45, glm47, granite, granite-20b-fc, granite4, hermes, hunyuan_a13b, internlm, jamba, kimi_k2, llama3_json, llama4_json, llama4_pythonic, longcat, minimax, minimax_m2, mistral, olmo3, openai, phi4_mini_json, pythonic, qwen3_coder, qwen3_xml, seed_oss, step3, step3p5, xlam.
For the authoritative list, refer to the vLLM tool-call parser registry.

claim: Custom parser or chat template files can be supplied via three mechanisms: placing in the model checkpoint directory (auto-discovered), volume-mounting at an absolute path, or using the NIM_PASSTHROUGH_ARGS environment variable.
premises: When you do need a custom parser or chat template, NIM LLM accepts the file in three ways.
Option 1: Place the file in the model checkpoint directory (auto-discovered).
Option 2: Volume-mount at an absolute path.
Option 3: Use NIM_PASSTHROUGH_ARGS (Kubernetes / Helm).

claim: NIM LLM resolves file-path arguments following a specific precedence order: URL-shaped values pass through; built-in names pass through; literal path; bare filename in checkpoint directory; otherwise error.
premises: For each file-path argument, NIM LLM applies the following rules in order:
- URL-shaped values (containing ://, e.g., https://... , s3://... ) pass through to vLLM unchanged. NIM LLM does not attempt remote resolution.
- Built-in names (no file extension and no path separator, e.g., tool_chat_template_mistral) pass through to vLLM unchanged.
- Literal path exists (absolute or relative to the working directory) — used as-is, converted to an absolute path.
- Bare filename in checkpoint dir — if <checkpoint_dir>/<filename> exists, used and logged.
- Not found anywhere — NIM LLM exits with a non-zero code and a clear error listing all searched locations.

claim: If the same filename exists in both the working directory and the checkpoint directory, the literal path (working directory) is chosen and a warning is logged; to use the checkpoint version, specify an absolute path.
premises: Conflict: Same Filename in Both the Working Directory and Checkpoint # If the same filename exists at both the literal path (typically /opt/nim/) and the checkpoint directory, the literal path wins and a warning is logged.
This can happen when a derived Dockerfile copies a file into /opt/nim/, or when a Kubernetes ConfigMap is mounted at the working directory.
To force a specific file, pass an absolute path.

claim: When a plugin file is not found in any searched location, NIM LLM reports an error listing the locations searched and provides remediation steps.
premises: Error: “Plugin file for … not found” # If you see an error like the following, the plugin file does not exist at any searched location:
ERROR: Plugin file for --reasoning-parser-plugin not found: 'my_parser.py'.
Searched locations:
- /opt/nim/my_parser.py
- /tmp/nim_abc123/my_parser.py
To provide a custom plugin, either:
1. Place the file in the model checkpoint directory
2. Volume-mount it and use an absolute path
3. Use a built-in parser name (no file extension needed)

claim: Built-in parser names are internal vLLM identifiers that may differ from model card names; e.g., Nemotron-3 Nano model card references nano_v3 parser but NIM LLM provides built-in nemotron_v3 parser.
premises: Built-in parser names are vLLM internal identifiers — they may differ from the names shown on a model card.
For example, the model card for Nemotron-3 Nano references a nano_v3 parser shipped as an external .py file, but NIM LLM ships a built-in nemotron_v3 parser that works without any plugin file.
When in doubt, try the built-in name first.

claim: Custom logits processors in NIM LLM extend vLLM's native logits processor API and can be enabled via CLI flag with volume mounting.
premises: NIM LLM supports custom logits processing by passing through to vLLM’s native logits processor API
You can write your own processor, mount it into the container as a volume, and enable it with a single CLI flag

To run a custom logits processor, place your processor script in a local directory, volume-mount that directory into the container, and pass the processor’s module path to NIM by using the --logits-processors CLI argument

claim: Custom logits processors must implement five specific methods: validate_params, __init__, apply, is_argmax_invariant, and update_state.
premises: Custom processors extend vllm.v1.sample.logits_processor.LogitsProcessor and implement the following five methods

The following table lists the methods and their purposes: validate_params (class method, validates per-request parameters), __init__ (runs during server startup), apply (called every engine step), is_argmax_invariant (returns True if processor never changes which token has highest logit), update_state (called every engine step with BatchUpdate)
The BanTokenProcessor example implements all five methods as defined in the interface

claim: Clients can enable custom logits processors per request by passing parameters via vllm_xargs in the request payload.
premises: Custom logits processors operate at the batch level, but clients can enable specific logits processors per request by passing custom arguments using vllm_xargs
Requests opt in by sending {"vllm_xargs": {"ban_token_id": <int>}}; requests that do not send this parameter are unaffected
The curl example demonstrates passing vllm_xargs with ban_token_id: 42 in the JSON body to /v1/completions endpoint

claim: Air-gap deployment allows running a NIM without internet connectivity by transferring pre-staged model assets from a network-connected machine to an isolated system.
premises: Air-gap deployment lets you run a NIM without an internet connection, for example, with no connection to remote model registries such as NGC or Hugging Face Hub.
This guide describes how to prepare, transfer, and run NIM LLM in an air-gapped environment.
Air-gap deployment follows a two-phase workflow: network-connected phase (download model assets with internet access) and air-gapped phase (run NIM container with no outbound network access).
Transfer the model assets between these phases using any allowed channel, such as an archive copy, scp, rsync, or physical media.
In the air-gapped phase, do not set NGC_API_KEY or HF_TOKEN. The NIM must load all model assets from local storage only.

claim: Model-specific NIM requires pre-staging model assets via download-to-cache and optionally create-model-store during the network-connected phase for use in air-gapped deployment.
premises: For model-specific NIM, the NIM container ships with a model manifest that defines the model and one or more profiles.
Use a model-specific container image for this workflow, such as ${NIM_LLM_MODEL_SPECIFIC_IMAGE}:2.0.4.
Model weights are not shipped inside the container. At startup, NIM loads the model from cache if present, or downloads it when the system has network and credentials.
For air-gap, you must pre-stage the model using download-to-cache (and optionally create-model-store) during the connected phase, then transfer the cache or model store to the air-gapped system.

claim: Model-free NIM with a local path enables air-gapped deployment without any download steps if the model directory is already present on the isolated system.
premises: For model-free NIM, the model is configured at runtime by the user using NIM_MODEL_PATH or the positional vLLM model CLI argument. The container does not ship a fixed model manifest.
Use the model-free container image for this workflow, such as ${NIM_LLM_MODEL_FREE_IMAGE}:2.0.4.

When NIM_MODEL_PATH points to a local path (e.g., /mnt/models/my-llama), NIM serves directly from that path. No download occurs, so if the model directory is already present on the air-gapped system, you do not need to use download-to-cache or create-model-store.

When using a model-free NIM with a local model path, no download occurs at startup. If the model directory is already on the air-gapped system, you can run without download-to-cache or create-model-store and without any API keys.

claim: Model-free NIM with a remote URI requires network access only on the first deployment to generate and cache a runtime manifest, after which it can run in strict air-gap mode using a persistent volume claim (PVC).
premises: When NIM_MODEL_PATH is a remote URI (e.g., ngc://org/team/model:tag), NIM generates a runtime manifest on the first deployment and automatically persists it inside NIM_CACHE_PATH.
On subsequent restarts — including in strict air-gap environments — NIM finds the cached manifest in the same cache volume and skips regeneration, making no outbound network or authentication calls.
No extra environment variables are required; mounting the same PVC at NIM_CACHE_PATH is sufficient.

Prerequisites: The NIM cache from the first (network-connected) deployment must be on a persistent volume (PVC) that is re-mounted between deployments. Both model assets and the manifest are stored there.
If the cache volume is not mounted or was not populated by a prior network-connected deployment, NIM will attempt to regenerate the manifest and fail in a strict air-gap environment.

claim: During the network-connected phase behind a proxy or TLS-inspecting proxy, HTTP_PROXY, HTTPS_PROXY, and SSL_CERT_FILE must be configured to enable successful model downloads, but these settings are not required in the air-gapped phase.
premises: If the network-connected phase runs behind a corporate or outbound proxy, you must configure the standard proxy environment variables so that downloads are routed correctly.

When running the network-connected phase behind a proxy, you may need to specify environment variables to direct HTTP and HTTPS traffic through your organization’s proxy servers. The following variables are commonly used: HTTP_PROXY, HTTPS_PROXY, NO_PROXY.
Note: In the air-gapped phase, there is no outbound traffic so proxy variables are not needed.

When outbound HTTPS traffic goes through a TLS-inspecting proxy, or when downloading from a corporate registry whose TLS certificate is signed by an internal CA, you must inject the corporate CA certificate so that TLS verification succeeds. Set SSL_CERT_FILE to point to a combined CA bundle inside the container.
Warning: Setting SSL_CERT_FILE replaces the container’s default trust store. Always create a combined bundle that includes the default CAs and your corporate CA.
Note: CA certificate injection is only relevant during the network-connected phase. After the deployment is fully air-gapped, there is no outbound HTTPS traffic and no CA configuration is needed.

claim: NIM LLM supports OpenAI-compatible tool calling through vLLM's tool calling engine, enabling integration with MCP servers and client libraries using the OpenAI tools format.
premises: NIM LLM supports OpenAI-compatible tool calling through vLLM’s tool calling engine
Tool calling lets models invoke external functions by returning structured tool calls instead of text responses
This enables integration with Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers and any client library that uses the OpenAI tools format

claim: Enabling tool calling in NIM LLM requires both --enable-auto-tool-choice and --tool-call-parser arguments to be set together, either via CLI or NIM_PASSTHROUGH_ARGS in environments like Kubernetes.
premises: Tool calling requires two vLLM engine arguments: --enable-auto-tool-choice and a --tool-call-parser that matches your model
Pass these as CLI arguments to nim-serve
In environments where CLI arguments are not available, such as Kubernetes, use NIM_PASSTHROUGH_ARGS
Both --enable-auto-tool-choice and --tool-call-parser are required together

claim: The /v1/chat/completions endpoint with the tools parameter is used to send tool definitions and receive tool calls once tool calling is enabled in NIM LLM.
premises: Once enabled, use the /v1/chat/completions endpoint with the tools parameter to send tool definitions and receive tool calls
For request/response format, examples, and the tool result loop, refer to the vLLM tool calling documentation

claim: NIM LLM does not connect directly to MCP servers; instead, the client application must manage MCP server connections, convert tool definitions to OpenAI tools format, and handle tool execution and result routing.
premises: NIM LLM does not connect to MCP servers directly
To use MCP tools, your client application connects to MCP servers, converts tool definitions to the OpenAI tools format, and sends them in the tools array of a Chat Completions request
The model returns tool calls in the response, and your application executes them against the MCP server and returns results to the model

claim: vLLM accepts MCP tool schemas converted to OpenAI format even if they include extra fields like strict or additionalProperties, which are not part of the core function definition schema.
premises: MCP tool schemas converted to OpenAI format may include extra fields such as strict or additionalProperties that are not part of the core function definition schema
vLLM accepts these fields without error

claim: For agentic applications with LangChain and LangGraph, create_react_agent from langgraph.prebuilt must be used to implement the full tool-calling loop with NIM LLM, as using langchain.agents.create_agent with ProviderStrategy bypasses tool execution and causes the model to only describe tool calls.
premises: When building agentic applications with LangChain and LangGraph, use create_react_agent from langgraph.prebuilt to implement tool calling with NIM LLM
This agent correctly executes the full tool-calling loop: generating a tool call, executing the tool, feeding the result back to the model, and producing a final response

Do not use langchain.agents.create_agent with ProviderStrategy for tool calling. This pattern bypasses the tool execution loop, causing the model to describe intended tool calls instead of executing them

claim: To use NIM LLM with LangChain and LangGraph, install langchain-nvidia-ai-endpoints, langgraph, and langchain-core packages, then construct an agent using ChatNVIDIA and create_react_agent with a defined tool.
premises: Install the required packages: pip install langchain-nvidia-ai-endpoints langgraph langchain-core

Create an agent with create_react_agent and invoke it: from langchain_nvidia_ai_endpoints import ChatNVIDIA; from langgraph.prebuilt import create_react_agent; llm = ChatNVIDIA(base_url="http://localhost:8000/v1", model="your-model-name"); agent = create_react_agent(model=llm, tools=[your_tool]); response = agent.invoke({"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Your query"}])

claim: If the model returns text instead of a tool call, verify that --enable-auto-tool-choice is set, --tool-call-parser is correct for the model, and the tools array is included in the request.
premises: If the model returns text instead of a tool call, do the following:
- Verify that --enable-auto-tool-choice is set.
- Verify that --tool-call-parser is set to the correct parser for your model.
- Check that the tools array is included in the request.

claim: Seeing the error "auto" tool choice requires --enable-auto-tool-choice and --tool-call-parser to be set indicates that both arguments must be provided when launching the container, regardless of deployment method.
premises: If you see "auto" tool choice requires --enable-auto-tool-choice and --tool-call-parser to be set
both arguments must be provided when launching the container

claim: At startup, NIM validates CUDA driver initialization via torch.cuda.init(), and if this fails, it results in a RuntimeError indicating a potential driver mismatch.
premises: At startup, NIM validates that the CUDA driver can initialize via torch.cuda.init()
If this check fails, startup will fail with a RuntimeError: CUDA driver failed to initialize: <error message>

claim: Error 803 indicates the container is loading a bundled CUDA compat driver that does not match the host's kernel driver, which is the most common cause of CUDA driver initialization failure.
premises: Common error messages include: 'Error 803: system has unsupported display driver / cuda driver combination'
The container is loading a bundled CUDA compat driver that does not match the host’s kernel driver. This is the most common cause.

claim: Error 802 indicates the NVIDIA kernel driver is not loaded or the fabric manager is not running, which is required on NVSwitch systems like DGX A100/H100.
premises: Common error messages include: 'Error 802: system not yet initialized'
The NVIDIA kernel driver is not loaded or fabric manager is not running (required on NVSwitch systems like DGX A100/H100).

claim: The NIM container image includes CUDA compat libraries that can interfere with host driver loading if the NVIDIA Container Toolkit fails to bind-mount the host's userspace CUDA driver.
premises: The NIM container image ships CUDA compat libraries at /usr/local/cuda-*/compat/
At runtime, the NVIDIA Container Toolkit should bind-mount the host’s userspace CUDA driver into the container, overriding the bundled compat libraries
If this mechanism fails, the container loads the bundled compat driver, which may not match the host’s kernel driver

claim: Common reasons for failure to mount the host driver include missing or misconfigured NVIDIA Container Toolkit, incorrect container runtime settings, CDI mode misconfiguration, and LD_LIBRARY_PATH prioritizing compat libraries.
premises: Common reasons the host driver is not mounted:
- NVIDIA Container Toolkit is not installed or not configured
- The container runtime is not set to nvidia ( --runtime=nvidia or equivalent)
- CDI mode is enabled but not properly configured
- The LD_LIBRARY_PATH inside the container prioritizes compat libraries over the host driver

claim: Resolution steps include verifying the NVIDIA Container Toolkit installation, using the NVIDIA runtime, checking the loaded libcuda.so path, and ensuring nvidia-fabricmanager runs with matching version on NVSwitch systems for Error 802.
premises: - Verify the NVIDIA Container Toolkit is installed and configured: nvidia-ctk --version
- Ensure the container uses the NVIDIA runtime: docker run --runtime = nvidia --gpus all ...
- Check which libcuda.so is loaded inside the container: [command] The path should point to the host driver (e.g., /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libcuda.so.1), not to /usr/local/cuda-*/compat/

- For Error 802 on NVSwitch systems, ensure nvidia-fabricmanager is running and its version matches the driver: nvidia-smi # check driver version, nv-fabricmanager --version # must match, sudo systemctl start nvidia-fabricmanager

Total GPUs = 16

PP = 1
Node A: 8 GPUs, Node B: 8 GPUs

env:-name:OUTLINES_CACHE_DIRvalue:/custom/path/outlines

Create the image pull secret: kubectl create secret docker-registry ngc-secret \ --docker-server = nvcr.io \ --docker-username = '$oauthtoken' \ --docker-password = " ${ NGC_API_KEY } "
Create the NGC API key secret: kubectl create secret generic nvidia-nim-secrets \ --from-literal = NGC_API_KEY = " ${ NGC_API_KEY } "
Create values.yaml with a minimal configuration: [yaml block showing image, model, persistence, resources, imagePullSecrets]
Install the release: helm install my-nim nim-llm/ -f values.yaml

claim: Enabling LoRA adapters with Helm requires creating a PVC for LoRA storage, populating it with adapter artifacts under /loras/, updating values.yaml to set NIM_PEFT_SOURCE to /loras and mount the PVC, then upgrading the Helm release.
premises: Create a dedicated PVC for the LoRA adapters: [yaml block for nvidia-nim-lora-pvc.yaml]
kubectl apply -f nvidia-nim-lora-pvc.yaml

Add LoRA adapters to the PVC under /loras . For each adapter, create one directory that contains the adapter artifacts: /loras/\ -   adapter_name/\ -     adapter_config.json\ -     adapter_model.safetensors   # or adapter_model.bin

Update values.yaml :\ env :\ - name : NIM_PEFT_SOURCE\ value : /loras\ extraVolumes :\ lora-adapter :\ persistentVolumeClaim :\ claimName : nvidia-nim-lora-pvc\ extraVolumeMounts :\ lora-adapter :\ mountPath : /loras
Apply the updated values: helm upgrade my-nim nim-llm/ -f values.yaml

claim: The containerSecurityContext Helm value sets the container-level security context for the NIM container, supports the capabilities field (unlike podSecurityContext), and is applied in both single-node and multi-node (LeaderWorkerSet) deployments.
premises: The containerSecurityContext Helm value sets the Kubernetes container-level security context for the NIM container.
It is applied in both single-node and multi-node (LeaderWorkerSet) deployments.
Unlike podSecurityContext , the container-level security context supports the capabilities field, which is required for certain multi-node configurations.

claim: For multi-node deployments with multiNode.enabled=true, the LeaderWorkerSet CRD and controller must be pre-installed, and the system requires Kubernetes v1.26 or later, as LeaderWorkerSet has this version requirement.
premises: When you set multiNode.enabled=true , the chart creates LeaderWorkerSet resources.
Install the LeaderWorkerSet CRD and controller before installing the NIM Helm chart.
LeaderWorkerSet requires Kubernetes v1.26 or later.

claim: In GB200 and GB300 NVL72 systems, the NIM container must have SYS_PTRACE and IPC_LOCK Linux capabilities set via containerSecurityContext.capabilities.add to enable CUDA IPC, IMEX channel operations, and GPUDirect RDMA memory pinning across nodes.
premises: GB200 and GB300 NVL72 systems use IMEX (Inter-Memory Exchange) channels for cross-node NVLink communication.
The containers must have the following Linux capabilities:
containerSecurityContext:capabilities:add:-SYS_PTRACE-IPC_LOCK
- SYS_PTRACE — Required for CUDA IPC and IMEX channel operations across GPUs.
- IPC_LOCK — Required for pinning memory used by GPUDirect RDMA.
To set these with Helm:
helminstallmy-nimnim-llm/-fvalues.yaml\--setcontainerSecurityContext.capabilities.add[0]=SYS_PTRACE\--setcontainerSecurityContext.capabilities.add[1]=IPC_LOCK
Or add them to your values.yaml :
containerSecurityContext:capabilities:add:-SYS_PTRACE-IPC_LOCK

claim: The priorityClassName Helm value assigns a Kubernetes PriorityClass to NIM pods to prevent preemption by setting a higher priority, and this applies to both single-node and multi-node (LeaderWorkerSet) leader and worker pods, provided the PriorityClass resource exists in the cluster.
premises: Use the priorityClassName Helm value to assign a Kubernetes PriorityClass to NIM pods.
Without a priority class, pods are treated as lowest priority in the cluster and may be preempted by other workloads.
This is applied to single-node deployments and multi-node (LeaderWorkerSet) leader and worker pods.
Note: The PriorityClass resource must already exist in your cluster before referencing it.
To create a PriorityClass: [yaml block for PriorityClass]

claim: Verifying a NIM deployment involves checking pod and service readiness via kubectl, port-forwarding the service for local access, and confirming readiness via an HTTP 200 response from the /v1/health/ready endpoint.
premises: Check that the pods are running: kubectl get pods -l app.kubernetes.io/instance = my-nim
Check that the service is available: kubectl get svc -l app.kubernetes.io/instance = my-nim
Port-forward the service for local testing: kubectl port-forward svc/my-nim-nim-llm 8000 :8000
Call the readiness endpoint to confirm that the service is ready: curl -sS http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/health/ready
A healthy deployment returns an HTTP 200 response from the readiness endpoint.

claim: Model-free NIM enables serving any supported model using a generic container image without needing a model-specific container.
premises: By default, NIM containers ship with a built-in model manifest that defines which model to serve.
In model-free mode, you point a generic NIM container at any supported model, such as a Hugging Face repo, an S3 bucket, or a local directory.
NIM then generates a manifest at startup and serves that model.

claim: Model-free NIM supports various model sources, each identified by a specific URI prefix and requiring particular authentication credentials.
premises: The supported sources table lists prefixes: hf:// for Hugging Face Hub (auth: HF_TOKEN), ngc:// for NVIDIA NGC (auth: NGC_API_KEY), s3:// for AWS S3/S3-compatible (auth: AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY), modelscope:// for ModelScope Hub (auth: MODELSCOPE_API_TOKEN), gs:// for Google Cloud Storage (auth: GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS or ADC), and absolute path for local directory (auth: none).

claim: Deployment configuration for model-free NIM, including tensor parallelism, pipeline parallelism, and LoRA support, can be set via the NIM_MODEL_PROFILE environment variable or vLLM CLI arguments, with CLI arguments taking precedence when both are provided.
premises: Model-free NIM generates profiles for combinations of tensor parallelism (TP), pipeline parallelism (PP), and LoRA.
To select a deployment configuration, use either NIM_MODEL_PROFILE environment variable or vLLM CLI arguments.
If both are provided, vLLM CLI arguments take precedence.

Supported vLLM CLI arguments include --tensor-parallel-size (number of GPUs, default 1), --pipeline-parallel-size (number of nodes, default 1), and --enable-lora (enable LoRA adapter support, default disabled).

claim: The list-model-profiles command displays the profiles generated for a specific model, indicating which are compatible and runnable and which include LoRA support.
premises: Running the container with NIM_MODEL_PATH and HF_TOKEN and invoking list-model-profiles outputs available profiles.
Example output shows sections: 'Compatible with system and runnable:' and 'With LoRA support:' each listing profile IDs and descriptions.

claim: When using an S3 model source with model-free NIM, specific AWS environment variables must be set to provide authentication and configuration.
premises: The S3-specific environment variables table indicates: AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID (required), AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY (required), AWS_REGION or AWS_DEFAULT_REGION (required), AWS_ENDPOINT_URL (required only for S3-compatible endpoints), AWS_S3_USE_PATH_STYLE (required only for S3-compatible endpoints such as MinIO).

claim: In air-gap environments, model-free NIM's behavior depends on whether the model is specified via a local path or a remote URI, with local paths requiring no network or credentials and remote URIs leveraging a cached manifest after initial network-connected deployment.
premises: For a local path (e.g., /abs/path/to/model), NIM reads the model directory directly with no network access, no manifest regeneration, and no credentials needed.

For a remote URI (e.g., ngc://, hf://, s3://), NIM generates a runtime manifest from the URI on the first deployment and saves a copy in the container’s internal cache directory (NIM_CACHE_PATH); on subsequent restarts, including in a strict air-gap environment, NIM reuses the cached manifest without any outbound network or authentication calls.
This enables a workflow: first deploy with network and credentials to download and cache the manifest, then transfer the cache to the air-gap environment and redeploy without credentials or network.
To force manifest regeneration after an upstream model update, delete nim_runtime_manifest.yaml from the persistent cache directory.

claim: NIM LLM exposes an OpenAI-compatible inference API backed by vLLM along with NIM-specific management endpoints.
premises: NIM LLM exposes an OpenAI-compatible inference API backed by vLLM
NIM LLM exposes NIM-specific management endpoints

claim: The inference endpoints are provided by the vLLM inference backend and include OpenAI-compatible APIs for chat, completions, responses, and Anthropic-compatible messages.
premises: These endpoints are provided by the vLLM inference backend.
POST /v1/chat/completions: Multi-turn chat completions with message history. Supports streaming and tool calling.
POST /v1/completions: Single-turn text completions.
POST /v1/responses: Create a model response (OpenAI Responses API).
GET /v1/responses/{response_id}: Retrieve a previously created response.
POST /v1/responses/{response_id}/cancel: Cancel a streaming response.
POST /v1/messages: Anthropic-compatible messages endpoint.
POST /v1/messages/count_tokens: Count tokens for a messages request without running inference.
GET /v1/models: List models currently loaded and available for inference.
POST /tokenize: Tokenize input text into token IDs.
POST /detokenize: Convert token IDs back to text.

claim: Render endpoints return the formatted prompt without running inference for chat and completion requests.
premises: Render endpoints return the formatted prompt without running inference:
POST /v1/chat/completions/render: Render the chat template for a chat completion request.
POST /v1/completions/render: Render the prompt template for a completion request.

claim: The management endpoints are specific to the NIM container and are served by the NIM middleware layer or the nginx proxy.
premises: These endpoints are specific to the NIM container and are served by the NIM middleware layer or the nginx proxy.
GET /v1/health/live: Liveness probe. Returns 200 when the container is running (served by nginx; does not require model to be loaded).
GET /v1/health/ready: Readiness probe. Returns 200 when the model is loaded and inference is available.
GET /v1/metadata: Deployment metadata including active profile, model info, and license.
GET /v1/version: NIM release version and OpenAPI spec version.
GET /v1/license: License metadata and full license text.
GET /v1/manifest: Model manifest with available profiles and configurations.
GET /v1/metrics: Prometheus-compatible metrics (request latency, throughput, queue depth, GPU utilization).

claim: The /v1/messages endpoint implements the core Anthropic Messages API format and supports streaming via Server-Sent Events (SSE) with specific event types.
premises: NIM exposes vLLM’s Anthropic-compatible server at /v1/messages.
NIM routes these requests through the nginx proxy and does not rewrite the request or response body.
Streaming responses use Server-Sent Events (SSE) with Anthropic event types such as message_start, content_block_start, content_block_delta, content_block_stop, message_delta, and message_stop.
The Anthropic format uses a top-level system field instead of a system message.

claim: The Anthropic Python SDK can be used with NIM by pointing the client to the NIM endpoint and setting the API key to any non-empty string.
premises: To use the Anthropic Python SDK with NIM, point the client at the NIM endpoint and set the API key to any non-empty string.
import os import anthropic; client = anthropic.Anthropic(base_url="http://localhost:8000", api_key="not-used")
To count tokens without running inference: response = client.messages.count_tokens(model=os.environ["MODEL_NAME"], messages=[{"role":"user","content":"Hello, how are you?"}])

claim: Tokenization and detokenization are available via dedicated endpoints that require a model specification.
premises: To tokenize input text into token IDs, run the following command: curl -s http://localhost:8000/tokenize -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d "{\"model\": \"${MODEL_NAME}\",\"prompt\": \"Hello world\"}"
To convert token IDs back to text, run the following command: curl -s http://localhost:8000/detokenize -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d "{\"model\": \"${MODEL_NAME}\",\"tokens\": [9906, 1917]}"

claim: The list of available models can be retrieved via the /v1/models endpoint.
premises: To list the available models, run the following command: curl -s http://localhost:8000/v1/models
GET /v1/models: List models currently loaded and available for inference.

claim: Health checks for container liveness and model readiness are available via /v1/health/live and /v1/health/ready endpoints.
premises: To perform a liveness or readiness health check, run the following commands: # Liveness (container running) curl -s http://localhost:8000/v1/health/live # Readiness (model loaded, ready for inference) curl -s http://localhost:8000/v1/health/ready
GET /v1/health/live: Liveness probe. Returns 200 when the container is running (served by nginx; does not require model to be loaded).
GET /v1/health/ready: Readiness probe. Returns 200 when the model is loaded and inference is available.

claim: Deployment metadata, version, manifest, and license information are accessible via dedicated NIM management endpoints.
premises: To query the deployment metadata and version, run the following commands: curl -s http://localhost:8000/v1/metadata; curl -s http://localhost:8000/v1/version
GET /v1/version: Returns the NIM release version and OpenAPI specification version.
GET /v1/metadata: Returns deployment metadata including the active model profile ID and name.
