claim: Streaming is supported on the /v1/chat/completions endpoint by setting "stream": true in the request payload, returning Server-Sent Events (SSE) with reasoning tokens in delta.reasoning by default unless thinking mode is disabled.
premises: To receive responses incrementally as they are generated, you can enable streaming by adding "stream": true to your request payload. This is supported on the /v1/chat/completions endpoint.
When streaming is enabled, the API returns a sequence of Server-Sent Events (SSE).

Note: Reasoning is enabled by default, so reasoning tokens populate the delta.reasoning field (not delta.content ) until the model finishes thinking. If your client only reads the delta.content field, as in the standard OpenAI SDK for chunk in stream loop, set "chat_template_kwargs": { "thinking": false } as previously shown to stream the final answer directly in the delta.content field.

claim: NIM LLM is an enterprise orchestration layer for vLLM that packages vLLM into a production-ready container with curated model profiles, validated configurations, and enterprise features such as health management, observability, and security hardening.
premises: NIM LLM is an enterprise orchestration layer for vLLM . It packages vLLM into a production-ready container with curated model profiles , validated configurations, and enterprise features such as health management, observability , and security hardening.

claim: The NIM container runs two processes: a vLLM inference backend and a proxy.
premises: The container runs the following two processes: - vLLM inference backend : The model serving engine loads models, runs GPU inference, and exposes an OpenAI-compatible API. - Proxy : A thin proxy on the external port provides immediate liveness, model-aware readiness, request routing, TLS termination, and CORS handling.

claim: The architecture adheres to key design principles: OpenAI-compatible API, production-ready health probes, secure by default, and fail-fast supervision.
premises: OpenAI-compatible API : The proxy provides a drop-in replacement for OpenAI endpoints, including streaming. Existing client code works without changes.

Production-ready health probes : Separate liveness and readiness endpoints allow orchestrators to distinguish between a running container and one that is ready to serve inference. By default, these proxy health endpoints use NIM_SERVER_PORT . If you set NIM_HEALTH_PORT , they move to that dedicated listener instead.
Secure by default : Only explicitly configured endpoints are exposed. All other paths return 404 Not Found . TLS termination and CORS are configurable at the proxy layer.
Fail-fast supervision : Both processes are monitored. If either exits, the container shuts down cleanly so the orchestrator can reschedule.

claim: During container startup, NIM starts the proxy, selects a model profile, downloads the model, launches the vLLM backend, and reports readiness.
premises: Start the proxy : The proxy begins listening on NIM_SERVER_PORT (default 8000). By default, /v1/health/live and /v1/health/ready are also served on this port. If you set NIM_HEALTH_PORT , those health endpoints move to that dedicated listener.
Select a model profile : NIM detects the available GPU hardware and selects a model profile that matches. Override the selection with NIM_MODEL_PROFILE if needed.
Download the model : Model files are fetched to the local cache ( NIM_CACHE_PATH ). If the model is already cached, this step is skipped.

Launch vLLM : The inference backend starts on port 8001 (loopback only, not exposed outside the container). Configuration is merged from profile defaults, environment variables, and passthrough arguments.
Report readiness : After the model loads, nginx checks the backend /health endpoint, and /v1/health/ready begins returning 200 OK . The orchestrator then routes traffic to the container.

claim: NIM proxies vLLM’s OpenAI-compatible API, routing specific endpoints to inference, management, or health categories, and returns 404 for all other paths.
premises: /v1/chat/completions | Inference | Multi-turn chat completions with message history.
/v1/completions | Inference | Single-turn text completions.
/v1/embeddings | Inference | Vector embedding generation.
/v1/models | Management | List models available for inference.
/v1/health/live | Health | Liveness probe, served directly by the proxy on NIM_SERVER_PORT by default or NIM_HEALTH_PORT when configured.
/v1/health/ready | Health | Readiness probe, served by the proxy and backed by the backend /health check.
All other paths | – | Rejected with 404 Not Found .

claim: NIM uses a two-port architecture by default, with the proxy on the external port (default 8000) and the vLLM backend on port 8001 loopback, and health endpoints can be moved to a dedicated port via NIM_HEALTH_PORT.
premises: NIM uses a two-port architecture by default. The external port (default 8000) is where the proxy listens for inference and management traffic. The vLLM backend listens on port 8001 and serves the native /health endpoint. If you set NIM_HEALTH_PORT , nginx exposes /v1/health/live and /v1/health/ready on that additional port.
Override the external port with NIM_SERVER_PORT if port 8000 conflicts with another service.

claim: NIM provides three observability surfaces: health probes, Prometheus-compatible metrics, and logging/tracing with configurable levels and distributed tracing header forwarding.
premises: Health probes : /v1/health/live confirms that the container is running (no backend dependency). /v1/health/ready confirms that the model is loaded and serving inference.
Metrics : Prometheus-compatible metrics are exposed at /v1/metrics , covering request latency, throughput, and GPU utilization.
Logging and tracing : Configurable log levels, structured JSON Lines output, and distributed tracing header forwarding ( X-Request-Id and Traceparent ) are supported.

claim: NIM supports TLS termination (including mutual TLS) and configurable CORS policies at the proxy layer.
premises: NIM supports TLS termination (including mutual TLS) and configurable CORS policies at the proxy layer. Refer to Advanced Configuration for TLS and CORS behavior and examples, and to Environment Variables for the full set of SSL/TLS and CORS variables.

claim: Related pages provide detailed documentation on API reference, environment variables, model profiles, logging and observability, advanced configuration, quickstart, and troubleshooting.
premises: API Reference : Inference and management API endpoint details, request and response schemas, and usage examples
Environment Variables : Full list of all NIM environment variables including SSL/TLS, CORS, and proxy configuration
Model Profiles and Selection : How model profiles are discovered, selected, and configured
Logging and Observability : Log levels, structured logging, and metrics collection
Advanced Configuration : Passthrough arguments, configuration priority, and advanced tuning
Quickstart : Getting started with your first NIM deployment
Troubleshooting : Common issues and diagnostic steps

claim: NIM for LLMs is invoked as a container entrypoint where the first positional argument selects the action and remaining arguments are passed to the underlying backend vLLM.
premises: NIM for LLMs is invoked as a container entrypoint.
The first positional argument selects the action to perform; any remaining arguments are passed through to the underlying backend (vLLM).

claim: When no action is specified, nim-serve is used by default.
premises: When no action is specified, nim-serve is used by default.

claim: The nim-serve action starts the NIM inference server, forwards remaining arguments to vLLM, and supports the --dry-run flag to preview configuration without launching.
premises: Start the NIM inference server. This is the default action.
Remaining arguments are forwarded to vLLM.
Supports the --dry-run flag to preview the resolved configuration without launching.

claim: The nim-serve-ray action starts the NIM server with Ray for multi-node tensor-parallel inference and requires either --head or --head-address.
premises: Start the NIM server with Ray for multi-node tensor-parallel inference.
Requires --head (leader) or --head-address (worker).

claim: The list-model-profiles action lists all available model profiles for the current hardware.
premises: List all available model profiles for the current hardware.

claim: The download-to-cache action downloads the selected model profile to the local cache without starting the server, accepting --all to download all profiles or -p <profile> for a specific one.
premises: Download the selected model profile to the local cache without starting the server.
Accepts --all to download all profiles, or -p <profile> for a specific one.

claim: The create-model-store action materializes a cached model profile into a model store directory, requiring -p <profile> and -m <path>.
premises: Materialize a cached model profile into a model store directory.
Requires -p <profile> and -m <path>.

claim: The show-build-info action prints build metadata such as git SHAs and versions.
premises: Print build metadata (git SHAs, versions).

claim: The mirror action mirrors cached model profiles to an S3-compatible bucket or GCS bucket.
premises: Mirror cached model profiles to an S3-compatible bucket or GCS bucket.

claim: NIM LLM provides both an OpenAI-compatible inference API backed by vLLM and NIM-specific management endpoints.
premises: NIM LLM exposes an OpenAI-compatible inference API backed by vLLM , along with NIM-specific management endpoints.
These endpoints are provided by the vLLM inference backend.
These endpoints are specific to the NIM container and are served by the NIM middleware layer or the nginx proxy.

claim: The inference API includes endpoints for chat completions, completions, OpenAI Responses, Anthropic messages, tokenization, detokenization, model listing, and prompt rendering.
premises: The inference endpoints include POST /v1/chat/completions, POST /v1/completions, POST /v1/responses, GET /v1/responses/{response_id}, POST /v1/responses/{response_id}/cancel, POST /v1/messages, POST /v1/messages/count_tokens, GET /v1/models, POST /tokenize, POST /detokenize.
The render endpoints include POST /v1/chat/completions/render and POST /v1/completions/render.

claim: NIM provides management endpoints for health checks, metadata, version, license, manifest, and metrics.
premises: The management endpoints include GET /v1/health/live, GET /v1/health/ready, GET /v1/metadata, GET /v1/version, GET /v1/license, GET /v1/manifest, and GET /v1/metrics.

claim: To use the API, one can retrieve the model ID via the models endpoint and set it as the MODEL_NAME environment variable for subsequent requests.
premises: The examples below use ${MODEL_NAME} as a shell variable. To find the model ID for your deployment, query the models endpoint:
Then export it for use in subsequent commands:
The model ID matches the value of NIM_SERVED_MODEL_NAME when the variable is set explicitly. If the variable is not set, NIM derives the name automatically.

claim: The Chat Completions API supports both non-streaming and streaming requests with configurable max_tokens and optional tool calling.
premises: Multi-turn chat completions with message history. Supports streaming and tool calling.
Example non-streaming chat completion command includes model, messages, and max_tokens.
Example streaming chat completion command sets stream to true.

claim: The Completions API accepts a prompt and returns a text completion up to a specified max_tokens.
premises: Single-turn text completions.
Example completions command includes model, prompt, and max_tokens.

claim: The Responses API endpoint creates a model response from an input string and allows retrieval and cancellation.
premises: Create a model response (OpenAI Responses API).
Example responses command includes model and input.
Additional endpoints are GET /v1/responses/{response_id} to retrieve and POST /v1/responses/{response_id}/cancel to cancel a streaming response.

claim: The Anthropic-compatible Messages endpoint supports standard and streaming requests, a system field, token counting, and is compatible with the Anthropic SDK, with certain features depending on model and vLLM version.
premises: NIM exposes vLLM’s Anthropic-compatible server at /v1/messages . NIM routes these requests through the nginx proxy and does not rewrite the request or response body.
Example non-streaming message request includes model, messages, and max_tokens.
Example streaming message request sets stream to true.
Example with a top-level system field instead of a system message.
Example token counting command uses /v1/messages/count_tokens.
NIM does not validate the x-api-key header; when using Anthropic SDK clients set the API key to any non-empty string.

The /v1/messages endpoint implements the core Anthropic Messages API format. Some Anthropic-specific features depend on the model and vLLM version: tool use (tool_use and tool_result content blocks) requires a model with tool-calling support; extended thinking (thinking content blocks) depends on model and vLLM support; the anthropic-version header is accepted but not enforced; batch and admin endpoints are not supported.

claim: The Anthropic Python SDK can be used with NIM by setting the base_url to the NIM host and providing any non-empty string as the API key.
premises: To use the Anthropic Python SDK with NIM, point the client at the NIM endpoint and set the API key to any non-empty string.
Example code creates an Anthropic client with base_url set to http://localhost:8000 and api_key set to not-used.
Streaming example shows using client.messages.stream and iterating over text_stream.
Token counting example uses client.messages.count_tokens and prints input_tokens.

claim: The tokenize and detokenize endpoints convert between text and token IDs for a given model.
premises: Tokenize input text into token IDs.
Example tokenize command includes model and prompt.
Convert token IDs back to text.
Example detokenize command includes model and tokens array.

claim: The models endpoint returns the list of models currently loaded and available for inference.
premises: GET /v1/models List models currently loaded and available for inference.
Example command: curl -s http://localhost:8000/v1/models

claim: Liveness and readiness health checks indicate container running status and model readiness for inference.
premises: GET /v1/health/live: Liveness probe. Returns 200 when the container is running (served by nginx; does not require model to be loaded).
GET /v1/health/ready: Readiness probe. Returns 200 when the model is loaded and inference is available.
Example commands show how to invoke liveness and readiness checks.

claim: The metadata and version endpoints provide deployment details and release information.
premises: GET /v1/version Returns the NIM release version and OpenAPI spec version.
GET /v1/metadata Returns deployment metadata including active profile, model info, and license.
Example commands show how to query metadata and version.

claim: NIM exposes manifest, license, and Prometheus-compatible metrics endpoints for observability and licensing.
premises: GET /v1/manifest Returns the full model manifest describing available profiles and their configurations.
GET /v1/license Returns license information for the running NIM container.
GET /v1/metrics Prometheus-compatible metrics (request latency, throughput, queue depth, GPU utilization).

claim: The configuration system resolves values from multiple sources with a defined priority where higher-priority sources overwrite lower-priority sources.
premises: Priority list: 1 CLI Arguments, 2 Passthrough Arguments, 3 Environment Variables, 4 Runtime Config, 5 Profile Tags, 6 NIM Defaults (highest to lowest).
Higher-priority sources overwrite lower-priority sources. If the same parameter is set in multiple sources, the highest-priority value wins.

claim: NIM resolves configuration values from CLI arguments, passthrough arguments via NIM_PASSTHROUGH_ARGS, NIM-specific environment variables, runtime_config.json, model profile tags, and built-in defaults.
premises: CLI arguments are passed after nim-serve.
NIM_PASSTHROUGH_ARGS environment variable passes CLI-style arguments.
NIM_* environment variables map to vLLM arguments.
runtime_config.json in the model workspace is read automatically.
Profile tags (tp, pp) provide parallelism values.
NIM Defaults apply when no other source sets the field.

claim: Command line arguments passed after nim-serve use the vLLM CLI argument format, with boolean flags handled via argparse.BooleanOptionalAction, and duplicate or contradictory CLI arguments resolved by the last one winning.
premises: CLI arguments use the vLLM CLI argument format.
vLLM uses Python’s argparse.BooleanOptionalAction for boolean flags: --enable-prefix-caching sets True, --no-enable-prefix-caching sets False.
If both NIM_PASSTHROUGH_ARGS and direct CLI arguments set the same parameter, the direct CLI argument takes precedence.
Duplicate or contradictory CLI arguments (e.g., --enable-xyz followed by --no-enable-xyz) result in the last one winning.

claim: NIM_PASSTHROUGH_ARGS environment variable allows passing CLI-style arguments when direct CLI arguments are not available, supporting all vLLM CLI arguments, boolean flags, and shell-style quoting via shlex.split().
premises: For environments like Kubernetes where direct CLI arguments are not available, use NIM_PASSTHROUGH_ARGS to pass CLI-style arguments through an environment variable.
Passthrough arguments support all vLLM CLI arguments, boolean flags, and shell-style quoting using shlex.split().
JSON values can be passed through NIM_PASSTHROUGH_ARGS using appropriate quoting.

claim: NIM provides specific environment variables that map to vLLM arguments for commonly used parameters with defaults, and any vLLM argument lacking a dedicated NIM environment variable can be set via NIM_PASSTHROUGH_ARGS.
premises: NIM_TENSOR_PARALLEL_SIZE maps to --tensor-parallel-size (int, default 1).
NIM_PIPELINE_PARALLEL_SIZE maps to --pipeline-parallel-size (int, default 1).
NIM_MAX_MODEL_LEN maps to --max-model-len (int, default auto).
NIM_TRUST_CUSTOM_CODE maps to --trust-remote-code (bool, default false).
NIM_DISABLE_CUDA_GRAPH maps to --enforce-eager (bool, default false).
For any vLLM argument that does not have a dedicated NIM environment variable, use NIM_PASSTHROUGH_ARGS.

claim: A runtime_config.json file placed in the model workspace directory is automatically read by NIM, with unknown keys passed through to vLLM as-is.
premises: Example runtime_config.json: {"tensor_parallel_size":2,"enable_prefix_caching":true,"max_model_len":8192}.
Unknown keys are passed through to vLLM as-is.

claim: Model profile metadata tags tp and pp configure tensor_parallel_size and pipeline_parallel_size respectively when a profile is selected.
premises: Profile Tag tp maps to tensor_parallel_size.
Profile Tag pp maps to pipeline_parallel_size.
Example: a profile named vllm-fp8-tp2-pp1 sets tensor_parallel_size=2 and pipeline_parallel_size=1 at profile priority.

claim: NIM applies built-in default values for tensor_parallel_size and pipeline_parallel_size only when no other source sets the field.
premises: Default for tensor_parallel_size is 1.
Default for pipeline_parallel_size is 1.
These defaults are applied only if no other source sets the field.

claim: NIM logs warnings when a higher-priority source overrides a lower-priority source, and setting NIM_STRICT_ARG_PROCESSING=true treats such warnings as errors, causing the container to exit on overrides between non-default sources.
premises: Override detection logs a warning: e.g., "WARNING: Config override: 'tensor_parallel_size' changed from 2 (RUNTIME) to 8 (CLI)".
Setting NIM_STRICT_ARG_PROCESSING=true treats override warnings as errors.
In strict mode, the container exits with an error if any configuration override is detected between non-default sources.
This setting is useful in CI/CD pipelines and production deployments to catch configuration conflicts and ensure determinism.

claim: Using --dry-run with nim-serve prints the fully resolved configuration and resulting vLLM arguments with provenance, without starting the server.
premises: Example command: dockerrun ... nim-serve --dry-run.
This prints the resolved configuration with provenance for each parameter, showing which source provided each value.

claim: Certain vLLM CLI arguments are denied in NIM containers because they are managed by nginx or other system components; passing them results in a warning and the argument being ignored, with NIM providing alternative environment variables.
premises: Denied arguments include --host, --port, --ssl-keyfile, --ssl-certfile, --ssl-ca-certs, --ssl-cert-reqs, --root-path, --api-key, --uvicorn-log-level, --middleware, --allowed-origins, --allowed-methods, --allowed-headers.
Reasons: networking, port, SSL/TLS, API routing, authentication, logging, middleware, CORS are managed by nginx or NIM.

NIM alternatives exist, e.g., NIM_SERVER_PORT, NIM_SSL_MODE, NIM_SSL_KEY_PATH, NIM_SSL_CERTS_PATH, NIM_SSL_CA_CERTS_PATH, NIM_LOG_LEVEL, NIM_CORS_ALLOW_ORIGINS, NIM_CORS_ALLOW_METHODS, NIM_CORS_ALLOW_HEADERS.
If a denied argument is passed, NIM logs a warning and ignores it.

claim: NIM validates configuration at multiple stages (CLI parsing, env parsing, runtime config, config merge, vLLM startup) with specific error behaviors, handling invalid NIM parameters as warnings, unknown parameters as passed-through, and invalid vLLM parameters as fatal errors at startup.
premises: CLI Parsing: argument format, type conversion – warning logged, invalid arg skipped.
Env Parsing: type conversion – warning logged, invalid value skipped.
Runtime Config: JSON syntax, type conversion – warning logged, invalid key skipped.
Config Merge: override detection – warning (or error in strict mode).
vLLM Startup: argument validity, model compatibility – vLLM exits with error.
Invalid NIM parameters: logged as warnings; container continues with remaining valid values.
Unknown parameters: passed through to vLLM as-is; vLLM handles its own validation.
Invalid vLLM parameters: vLLM validates and reports errors at startup.

claim: NIM tracks the source of every configuration parameter, emitting a structured config_resolved JSON event at startup showing provenance, and when overridden includes previous value and source; this can be inspected via --dry-run.
premises: Example config_resolved JSON: {"tensor_parallel_size":{"value":4,"source":"CLI"},"pipeline_parallel_size":{"value":1,"source":"PROFILE"},"gpu_memory_utilization":{"value":0.9,"source":"ENV"},"enable_prefix_caching":{"value":true,"source":"RUNTIME"}}.
When overridden, previous value and source are recorded: e.g., {"tensor_parallel_size":{"value":4,"source":"CLI","previous_value":2,"previous_source":"ENV"}}.
Use nim-serve --dry-run to inspect the full provenance report without starting the server.

claim: NIM prevents OOM failures via automatic clamping of gpu_memory_utilization based on hardware conditions and a post-selection memory warning that estimates VRAM usage and advises reducing context length if needed.
premises: Automatic GPU Memory Clamping table: vGPU guest cap 0.75 (shared/partitioned GPU), UMA device cap 0.50 (CPU/GPU shared memory), busy GPU cap free_ratio - 0.05 (prevent contention), with minimum floor 0.10.
The clamped value is applied at low internal priority, so explicit settings from environment variables, CLI arguments, or --gpu-memory-utilization take precedence automatically.
Post-Selection Memory Warning: after profile selection, NIM estimates VRAM required and compares to available memory; if estimate exceeds, logs warning with suggestion to reduce --max-model-len.
Example warning: "WARNING: Estimated VRAM (45.2 GB) exceeds available GPU memory (39.6 GB). Consider reducing context length with --max-model-len=4096 (estimated 30.1 GB)."

claim: NIM terminates TLS at the nginx proxy, denying native vLLM SSL arguments and providing NIM SSL environment variables to configure TLS or MTLS modes.
premises: NIM_SSL_MODE (DISABLED, TLS, MTLS) defaults to DISABLED.
NIM_SSL_KEY_PATH: path to TLS private key.
NIM_SSL_CERTS_PATH: path to TLS certificate.
NIM_SSL_CA_CERTS_PATH: path to CA certificate (required for MTLS).
To enable TLS: set NIM_SSL_MODE=TLS requiring NIM_SSL_CERTS_PATH and NIM_SSL_KEY_PATH.
To enable MTLS: set NIM_SSL_MODE=MTLS requiring NIM_SSL_CERTS_PATH, NIM_SSL_KEY_PATH, and NIM_SSL_CA_CERTS_PATH.
Example: docker run with -eNIM_SSL_MODE=TLS -eNIM_SSL_KEY_PATH=/certs/server.key -eNIM_SSL_CERTS_PATH=/certs/server.crt -v/path/to/certs:/certs:ro.

claim: CORS is handled by the nginx proxy via NIM_CORS_* environment variables, while vLLM CORS arguments are denied.
premises: NIM_CORS_ALLOW_ORIGINS defaults to *.
NIM_CORS_ALLOW_METHODS defaults to GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, PATCH, OPTIONS.
NIM_CORS_ALLOW_HEADERS defaults to Content-Type, Authorization, X-Request-Id, X-Session-Id, X-Correlation-Id.
NIM_CORS_EXPOSE_HEADERS defaults to X-Request-Id.
NIM_CORS_MAX_AGE defaults to 3600 seconds.
Note: vLLM’s --allowed-origins, --allowed-methods, --allowed-headers are denied in NIM because CORS is managed at the nginx layer; use the NIM_CORS_* variables instead.

claim: A direct CLI argument overrides an environment variable for the same parameter, with NIM logging a warning about the override.
premises: Example: export NIM_TENSOR_PARALLEL_SIZE=2 then run nim-serve --tensor-parallel-size 4 resolves<tr> to 4.
NIM logs the warning: "WARNING: Config override: 'tensor_parallel_size' changed from 2 (ENV) to 4 (CLI)".

claim: When all sources set a value for a parameter, the resolved value follows the priority order: CLI > Passthrough > Env > Runtime Config > Profile Tags > Defaults.
premises: Example: runtime_config.json tensor_parallel_size=1, env NIM_TENSOR_PARALLEL_SIZE=2, NIM_PASSTHROUGH_ARGS --tensor-parallel-size 3, CLI nim-serve --tensor-parallel-size 4 --no-enable-prefix-caching.
Resolved tensor_parallel_size=4 (CLI overrides passthrough overrides env overrides runtime).
Resolved enable_prefix_caching=False (CLI --no- overrides runtime true).

claim: In Kubernetes, vLLM arguments can be passed via the NIM_PASSTHROUGH_ARGS environment variable in the container specification.
premises: Kubernetes manifest example: env - name: NIM_PASSTHROUGH_ARGS value: "--enable-prefix-caching--max-num-batched-tokens8192--enable-chunked-prefill".
Other env vars shown: NIM_MODEL_PATH, NIM_CACHE_PATH.

claim: TLS can be enabled for a NIM container by setting NIM_SSL_MODE=TLS and providing key and certificate paths via NIM_SSL_KEY_PATH and NIM_SSL_CERTS_PATH, with a volume mount for the certificates.
premises: Example docker run command: -eNIM_SSL_MODE=TLS -eNIM_SSL_KEY_PATH=/certs/server.key -eNIM_SSL_CERTS_PATH=/certs/server.crt -v/path/to/certs:/certs:ro.
After container start, TLS can be validated with curl using the CA certificate.

claim: NIM provides structured logging with configurable log level and JSON Lines output via environment variables.
premises: NIM outputs logs to stderr.
NIM_LOG_LEVEL controls log verbosity, accepting standard Python logging levels (DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR, CRITICAL) with default WARNING.
NIM_JSONL_LOGGING, when set to true, emits logs as JSON Lines for machine parsing; default false.
Default log output uses a human-readable format.
When NIM_JSONL_LOGGING=true, all log output from both NIM and the vLLM backend is formatted as one JSON object per line using a unified schema.
Both NIM and vLLM logs share the same JSON schema, allowing a single log parser configuration to handle all container output.
NIM_LOG_LEVEL controls both the NIM and the vLLM backend; to override backend level independently, set VLLM_LOGGING_LEVEL in addition.

claim: NIM exposes Prometheus-compatible metrics at the /v1/metrics endpoint that are identical to the native vLLM metrics, enabling existing dashboards and alerting rules to work without modification.
premises: NIM exposes metrics at /v1/metrics.
The metrics can be retrieved via curl to http://localhost:8000/v1/metrics.
NIM passes through the inference backend’s native Prometheus metrics without modification.
The metrics available at /v1/metrics are the same metrics produced by vLLM, covering request latency, throughput, queue depth, token counts, and GPU utilization.
NIM does not wrap, rename, or abstract these metrics.
Existing vLLM dashboards and alerting rules work without changes.
For a full list, refer to the vLLM production metrics documentation.
To scrape with Prometheus, add a scrape_configs job with metrics_path "/v1/metrics" and interval 15s.

claim: NIM forwards tracing headers (X-Request-Id and traceparent) from clients to the inference backend on inference endpoints, enabling request correlation and distributed tracing when the backend is configured for OpenTelemetry.
premises: NIM supports request correlation and distributed tracing through standard HTTP headers.
The proxy layer forwards tracing headers from clients to the inference backend on the endpoints: /v1/chat/completions, /v1/completions, /v1/embeddings, and /v1/responses.
Tracing headers are not forwarded on management or health endpoints.
The X-Request-Id header is forwarded and adopted by the backend as the internal request ID; if absent, the backend generates a random ID.
The traceparent header (W3C Trace Context) is forwarded to the backend to propagate trace context.

The backend creates OpenTelemetry spans from traceparent only when tracing is enabled via the OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TRACES_ENDPOINT environment variable; otherwise, it logs a warning and discards the trace context.
Example curl commands demonstrate adding X-Request-Id and traceparent headers to requests.
When OpenTelemetry tracing is enabled on the backend, inference spans appear in existing distributed traces alongside upstream and downstream services.

claim: NIM LLM supports environment variables for configuring logging, model selection, server ports, LoRA/PEFT adapters, model cache, authentication, inbound and outbound TLS, CORS, AWS SageMaker compatibility, and advanced runtime behavior.
premises: This page documents all environment variables supported by NIM LLM.
The following variables control log format and verbosity:
The following variables control model selection, model loading, and related runtime behavior:
The following variables control server and health-check ports:
The following variables control LoRA and PEFT adapter discovery and refresh behavior:
The following variable controls the model cache location inside the container:
This one controls the timeout in seconds for the model cache discovery:
The following variables provide credentials for authenticated model downloads:

NIM uses TLS in two distinct directions. Inbound TLS secures client connections to the NIM inference API (nginx layer). Outbound TLS secures connections the container makes from itself when downloading model artifacts from NGC, Hugging Face, or a corporate registry such as JFrog Artifactory.
The following variables control TLS termination at the nginx proxy layer:
When the NIM container downloads models from a registry that uses a certificate signed by a private or corporate CA, you must provide that CA certificate to the container.
These variables configure Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) policy at the nginx proxy layer.
The following variable controls SageMaker BYOC (Bring Your Own Container) compatibility mode.
The following variables control advanced argument handling and runtime behavior:

claim: For outbound TLS verification when downloading models from registries with private or corporate CAs, SSL_CERT_FILE must be set to a CA bundle that includes the corporate CA certificate.
premises: When the NIM container downloads models from a registry that uses a certificate signed by a private or corporate CA, you must provide that CA certificate to the container.

This applies to two common scenarios: Corporate registry with private CA — for example, a JFrog Artifactory instance whose TLS certificate is signed by your organization’s internal CA (no proxy involved). TLS-inspecting proxy — a corporate proxy that decrypts and re-encrypts HTTPS traffic using a corporate CA.
In both cases, set SSL_CERT_FILE to a CA bundle that includes the corporate CA so that outbound TLS verification succeeds.
A proxy (HTTPS_PROXY) is not required for SSL_CERT_FILE to take effect.

claim: NIM_SSL_* variables configure only inbound TLS for the nginx layer and do not affect outbound model downloads.
premises: NIM uses TLS in two distinct directions. Inbound TLS secures client connections to the NIM inference API (nginx layer). Outbound TLS secures connections the container makes from itself when downloading model artifacts from NGC, Hugging Face, or a corporate registry such as JFrog Artifactory.

Important: The NIM_SSL_* variables below configure inbound TLS only. They do not affect outbound model downloads. To trust a corporate Certificate Authority (CA) for outbound connections, see Outbound TLS (Model Downloads).

claim: When AWS SageMaker BYOC compatibility mode is enabled, NIM listens on port 8080 and implements the GET /ping health check and POST /invocations endpoints required for SageMaker real-time inference.
premises: The following variable controls SageMaker BYOC (Bring Your Own Container) compatibility mode.
When active, NIM listens on port 8080 and implements the GET /ping health check and POST /invocations inference endpoints required by SageMaker real-time inference.

claim: Archived versions of NIM LLM documentation are available for versions 1.0.0 through 1.6.0.
premises: Use the following links to access archived versions of NIM LLM documentation:

claim: NIM requires the NFD Operator and NVIDIA GPU Operator to make GPUs available as schedulable resources on OpenShift.
premises: NIM requires NVIDIA GPUs to be available as schedulable resources.
This requires the Node Feature Discovery (NFD) Operator and the NVIDIA GPU Operator.

claim: The NGC API key is required to pull NIM container images and download model artifacts from nvcr.io.
premises: An NGC API key for pulling NIM container images and downloading model artifacts
Create an image pull secret so OpenShift can pull NIM container images from nvcr.io
Create a secret that stores your NGC API key for use by the NIM container

claim: The nonroot-v2 SCC must be granted to the default service account in the nim-llm namespace to allow the NIM container to run with OpenShift-assigned UIDs while using GID 0.
premises: OpenShift enforces SecurityContextConstraints (SCCs) that restrict which user IDs a pod can run as.
The NIM container defaults to UID 1000 (non-root) but supports arbitrary UIDs — including the random UIDs that OpenShift assigns — as long as the container runs with GID 0 (root group).
Grant the nonroot-v2 SCC to allow this: oc adm policy add-scc-to-user nonroot-v2 -z default -n nim-llm
The Helm chart defaults ( runAsUser: 1000 , runAsGroup: 0 , fsGroup: 0 ) are compatible with the nonroot-v2 SCC.

claim: Storage class selection for the NIM model cache PVC depends on the OpenShift edition, with specific storage classes and access mode considerations for ROSA and OpenShift Dedicated on GCP.
premises: Adjust storageClassName based on your OpenShift edition:
| OpenShift Edition | StorageClass Name |
| Self-managed OCP with ODF | ocs-storagecluster-cephfs |
| Self-managed OCP with NFS | nfs-client |
| ROSA (AWS) | gp3-csi |
| ARO (Azure) | managed-premium |
| OpenShift Dedicated (GCP) | standard-csi (default) |

Note: gp3-csi (ROSA) and standard-csi (OpenShift Dedicated on GCP) only support ReadWriteOnce. Change the accessModes in the PVC manifest from ReadWriteMany to ReadWriteOnce when using these StorageClasses.

claim: The NIM LLM Helm chart is pre-configured for OpenShift with defaults for security context, GPU resources, image pull secrets, NGC API secret, and service configuration, requiring only deployment-specific overrides.
premises: The NIM LLM Helm chart is compatible with OpenShift.
The chart defaults handle security context, GPU resources ( nvidia.com/gpu: 1 ), image pull secrets ( ngc-secret ), the NGC API secret ( ngc-api ), and service configuration.
Override only the values that are specific to your deployment.

claim: GPU machine pools or machine sets must be deleted during cleanup for ROSA, ARO, and OpenShift Dedicated on GCP if they were created for GPU workloads.
premises: If you created a GPU machine pool for OpenShift Dedicated on GCP, delete it: ocm delete machinepool --cluster=${CLUSTER_NAME} gpu-pool
If you created a GPU machine pool for ROSA, delete it: rosa delete machinepool ${GPU_POOL_NAME} -c ${CLUSTER_NAME} --yes

If you created a GPU MachineSet for ARO, scale it down and delete it: oc scale machineset ${GPU_MACHINESET_NAME} -n openshift-machine-api --replicas=0; oc delete machineset ${GPU_MACHINESET_NAME} -n openshift-machine-api

claim: Latent diffusion models achieve state-of-the-art image synthesis with reduced computational requirements by operating in the latent space of pretrained autoencoders.
premises: Diffusion models achieve state-of-the-art synthesis results on image data but typically operate directly in pixel space, consuming hundreds of GPU days for training and expensive inference due to sequential evaluations.
To enable DM training on limited computational resources while retaining quality and flexibility, we apply them in the latent space of powerful pretrained autoencoders.
Training diffusion models on such a representation allows for the first time to reach a near-optimal point between complexity reduction and detail preservation, greatly boosting visual fidelity.

Our latent diffusion models (LDMs) achieve new state of the art scores for image inpainting and class-conditional image synthesis and highly competitive performance on various tasks, while significantly reducing computational requirements compared to pixel-based DMs.

claim: Cross-attention layers enable latent diffusion models to flexibly handle general conditioning inputs like text or bounding boxes for high-resolution synthesis in a convolutional manner.
premises: By introducing cross-attention layers into the model architecture, we turn diffusion models into powerful and flexible generators for general conditioning inputs such as text or bounding boxes
high-resolution synthesis becomes possible in a convolutional manner

claim: Out-of-memory errors occur when the model's memory requirements exceed the available GPU VRAM.
premises: Out-of-memory (OOM) errors are one of the most common startup failures when deploying LLM NIM containers.

These errors occur when the model’s memory requirements exceed the available GPU VRAM, typically because of a mismatch between the selected model profile and the hardware, or because of misconfigured system parameters.

claim: During startup, GPU memory is allocated in stages with model weights as the largest consumer, and the fraction of memory budgeted for model operations is controlled by the --gpu-memory-utilization parameter.
premises: During startup, NIM and the vLLM backend allocate GPU memory in stages. The largest single consumer is the model weights.
You can estimate weight memory from the model’s parameter count and the precision of the profile.

The --gpu-memory-utilization parameter (with a default value of 0.9) controls what fraction of total GPU memory is budgeted for model operations. The remainder is left unreserved for post-load operations such as CUDA graph compilation.

claim: OOM errors during weight loading indicate that the GPU lacks sufficient memory to hold the model weights at the selected precision and tensor parallelism degree.
premises: The OOM error appears early in startup, during model loading, before any messages about KV cache or graph compilation.

The GPU does not have enough memory to hold the model weights at the selected precision and tensor parallelism (TP) degree. For example, a 70-billion-parameter model in BF16 requires approximately 140 GB of weight memory, which does not fit on a single 80 GB GPU.

claim: OOM errors during KV cache allocation due to insufficient memory indicate that the model's default context length requires more KV cache memory than fits in the GPU budget after weights, activations, and overhead are subtracted.
premises: The error occurs after weights are loaded, during memory profiling or KV cache block allocation.
Look for log messages mentioning KV cache, determine_available_memory, or block allocation failures.

NIM may also print an advisory warning before the crash similar to: 'WARNING: Estimated VRAM (45.2 GB) exceeds available GPU memory (39.6 GB). Consider reducing context length with --max-model-len=4096 (estimated 30.1 GB).'
The model’s default context length (max_position_embeddings from config.json) requires more KV cache memory than fits in the GPU budget after weights, activations, and overhead are subtracted.

claim: OOM errors during KV cache allocation due to fragmentation occur when the PyTorch CUDA allocator cannot find contiguous memory blocks despite sufficient total free memory.
premises: The error occurs during KV cache allocation and reports that the free memory is less than the requested allocation size.
The error also mentions a large amount of memory 'reserved by PyTorch but unallocated' and suggests setting expandable_segments:True.

The PyTorch CUDA memory allocator requires contiguous memory blocks for each tensor allocation. During model loading and torch.compile, many temporary allocations fragment the GPU address space into small, non-contiguous pieces.
When KV cache allocation begins, the total free memory may be sufficient, but no single contiguous block is large enough for individual per-layer KV cache tensors (typically 1+ GiB each).
This is particularly common with hybrid architectures (such as NemotronH models that combine Mamba and attention layers) where torch.compile creates extensive temporary allocations.

claim: OOM errors during CUDA graph capture or sampler warmup occur because the unreserved memory (default 10% of GPU memory) is insufficient to accommodate CUDA graph allocation.
premises: The OOM error appears after weights and KV cache are successfully allocated, during CUDA graph capture or sampler warmup.
Typical log patterns include torch.OutOfMemoryError: CUDA out of memory, preceded by messages such as 'Graph capturing finished in ...' or 'compile_or_warm_up_model'.

The unreserved memory (by default, 10% of total GPU memory) is not large enough to accommodate CUDA graph capture, which can consume 1 to 5 GB depending on GPU architecture and model size. Smaller GPUs are disproportionately affected because 10% of a 24 GB GPU is only 2.4 GB, while CUDA graphs on some architectures require more than that amount of memory.

claim: Setting the NIM_LOG_LEVEL environment variable to INFO or DEBUG enables detailed GPU memory reporting and diagnostics to aid in troubleshooting OOM errors.
premises: NIM prints a GPU Memory Report at startup when NIM_LOG_LEVEL is set to INFO (the default) or DEBUG.

At the INFO or DEBUG log levels, NIM also prints GPU Diagnostics (GPU summary, NVLink status, NVLink capabilities, and GPU topology from nvidia-smi) before model loading begins, and the startup banner includes estimated memory per GPU and the CPU core count required by the model configuration.
To enable detailed logging, set the NIM_LOG_LEVEL environment variable.

claim: Latent Diffusion Models (LDMs) reduce computational costs while maintaining high-resolution image synthesis performance.
premises: Training the most powerful diffusion models in pixel space often takes hundreds of GPU days (e.g., 150-1000 V100 days) and inference is expensive due to repeated evaluations on high-dimensional RGB image space.
LDMs train diffusion models in a learned latent space that is perceptually equivalent to data space but computationally more suitable due to lower dimensionality and better scaling properties.
LDMs enable efficient image generation from latent space with a single network pass.

LDMs significantly lower computational costs for training and sampling compared to pixel-based diffusion approaches while achieving competitive performance on tasks like unconditional image synthesis, inpainting, and stochastic super-resolution.

claim: LDMs enable efficient, high-fidelity image generation for densely conditioned tasks such as super-resolution, inpainting, and semantic synthesis at megapixel resolutions.
premises: For densely conditioned tasks such as super-resolution, inpainting and semantic synthesis, LDMs can be applied in a convolutional fashion.
This allows rendering large, consistent images of ∼1024² px.
LDMs achieve competitive performance on multiple datasets while significantly lowering computational costs.
LDMs do not require delicate weighting of reconstruction and generative abilities, ensuring extremely faithful reconstructions with little regularization of the latent space.

claim: LDMs support multi-modal conditioning via a cross-attention mechanism, enabling class-conditional, text-to-image, and layout-to-image generation.
premises: We design a general-purpose conditioning mechanism based on cross-attention.
This enables multi-modal training.
We use it to train class-conditional, text-to-image and layout-to-image models.
For text-to-image tasks, we connect transformers to the DM’s UNet backbone to enable arbitrary token-based conditioning.

claim: Pretrained LDM and autoencoder models are publicly released for reuse across various tasks beyond diffusion model training.
premises: We release pretrained latent diffusion and autoencoding models at https://github.com/CompVis/latent-diffusion.
These models might be reusable for various tasks besides training of DMs.
The universal autoencoding stage need only be trained once and can be reused for multiple DM trainings or different tasks.

claim: The proposed method introduces an explicit separation of compressive and generative learning phases using an autoencoder to reduce computational demands in diffusion model training for high-resolution image synthesis.
premises: Diffusion models allow ignoring perceptually irrelevant details by undersampling loss terms but still require costly function evaluations in pixel space, causing high computational demands.
We propose to circumvent this drawback by introducing an explicit separation of the compressive from the generative learning phase (see Fig. 2).
To achieve this, we utilize an autoencoding model which learns a space that is perceptually equivalent to the image space, but offers significantly reduced computational complexity.

claim: The perceptual compression model uses an autoencoder with perceptual and adversarial losses to produce reconstructions confined to the image manifold, avoiding blur from pixel-space losses alone.
premises: Our perceptual compression model is based on previous work [23] and consists of an autoencoder trained by combination of a perceptual loss [102] and a patch-based [32] adversarial objective [20, 23, 99].

This ensures that the reconstructions are confined to the image manifold by enforcing local realism and avoids bluriness introduced by relying solely on pixel-space losses such as _L_<sub>2</sub> or _L_<sub>1</sub> objectives.

claim: The compression model preserves structural details of the input image better than prior approaches by avoiding 1D ordering of the latent space and instead leveraging its two-dimensional structure.
premises: Because our subsequent DM is designed to work with the two-dimensional structure of our learned latent space z=E(x), we can use relatively mild compression rates and achieve very good reconstructions.

This is in contrast to previous works [23, 64], which relied on an arbitrary 1D ordering of the learned space z to model its distribution autoregressively and thereby ignored much of the inherent structure of z.
Hence, our compression model preserves details of x better (see Tab. 8).

claim: Diffusion models learn a data distribution by denoising a normally distributed variable through a fixed Markov chain process, with training objective based on predicting noise in perturbed inputs.
premises: Diffusion Models are probabilistic models designed to learn a data distribution p(x) by gradually denoising a normally distributed variable, which corresponds to learning the reverse process of a fixed Markov Chain of length T.
For image synthesis, the most successful models rely on a reweighted variant of the variational lower bound on p(x), which mirrors denoising score-matching.

These models can be interpreted as an equally weighted sequence of denoising autoencoders ε_θ(x_t,t); t=1...T, which are trained to predict a denoised variant of their input x_t, where x_t is a noisy version of the input x.
The corresponding objective can be simplified to L_DM = E_{x,ε∼N(0,1),t}[||ε - ε_θ(x_t,t)||_2^2], with t uniformly sampled from {1,...,T}.

claim: Latent Diffusion Models (LDMs) improve generative modeling efficiency by operating in a compressed latent space derived from perceptual compression models, enabling focus on semantic content and reduced computational cost.
premises: With our trained perceptual compression models consisting of E and D, we now have access to an efficient, low-dimensional latent space in which high-frequency, imperceptible details are abstracted away.

Compared to the high-dimensional pixel space, this space is more suitable for likelihood-based generative models, as they can now (i) focus on the important, semantic bits of the data and (ii) train in a lower dimensional, computationally much more efficient space.

Unlike previous work that relied on autoregressive, attention-based transformer models in a highly compressed, discrete latent space, we can take advantage of image-specific inductive biases that our model offers.
This includes the ability to build the underlying UNet primarily from 2D convolutional layers, and further focusing the objective on the perceptually most relevant bits using the reweighted bound.

claim: The training objective for Latent Diffusion Models is adapted to the latent space by encoding input data through the perceptual compression model, maintaining the same noise prediction structure as standard diffusion models.
premises: The neural backbone ε_θ(∘,t) of our model is realized as a time-conditional UNet [69].
Since the forward process is fixed, z_t can be efficiently obtained from E during training, and samples from p(z) can be decoded to image space with a single pass through D.
The objective for LDMs is defined as L_LDM := E_{ℰ(x),ε∼N(0,1),t}[||ε - ε_θ(z_t,t)||_2^2], where ℰ(x) denotes the encoded latent representation.

claim: ControlNet is a neural network architecture that enhances large pretrained text-to-image diffusion models with spatially localized, task-specific image conditions.
premises: ControlNet injects additional conditions into the blocks of a neural network.
Suppose F(·; Θ) is a trained neural block with parameters Θ that transforms an input feature map x into another feature map y.
To add a ControlNet, the parameters Θ of the original block are locked (frozen) and the block is cloned to a trainable copy with parameters Θ_c.
The trainable copy takes an external conditioning vector c as input.

When applied to large models like Stable Diffusion, the locked parameters preserve the production-ready model trained with billions of images, while the trainable copy reuses the pretrained model as a strong backbone for handling diverse input conditions.

claim: Zero convolution layers in ControlNet initialize to zero, ensuring that at the start of training the ControlNet output equals the original block output, thereby protecting the pretrained model from harmful noise.

Two instances of zero convolutions with parameters Θ_zl and Θ_zl are used.
The complete ControlNet computes y_c = F(x;Θ) + Z(F(x+Z(c;Θ_zl);Θ_c);Θ_zl).
In the first training step, since both weight and bias parameters of a zero convolution layer are initialized to zero, both Z terms evaluate to zero, yielding y_c = y.
Moreover, Z(c;Θ_zl)=0 and the trainable copy receives the input image x, so the trainable copy is fully functional and retains the capabilities of the large pretrained model.
Zero convolutions protect this backbone by eliminating random noise as gradients in the initial training steps.
