claim: Existing LLM serving systems suffer from significant memory fragmentation and cannot exploit KV cache sharing opportunities due to contiguous memory allocation requirements.
premises: Existing systems store the KV cache of a request in contiguous memory space as required by most deep learning frameworks.
The KV cache dynamically grows and shrinks over time, and its lifetime and length are not known a priori.
Pre-allocating contiguous memory for maximum request length causes internal fragmentation when actual length is shorter.
Pre-allocation prevents shorter requests from using unused parts of reserved chunks, causing external fragmentation.
Profiling results show only 20.4% - 38.2% of KV cache memory is used to store actual token states in existing systems.
Memory sharing is not possible in existing systems because KV cache of sequences from advanced decoding algorithms (e.g., parallel sampling, beam search) is stored in separate contiguous spaces.

claim: PagedAttention is an attention algorithm that improves KV cache memory management by using non-contiguous paged memory blocks, inspired by OS virtual memory and paging.
premises: PagedAttention divides the request’s KV cache into blocks, each containing attention keys and values of a fixed number of tokens.
The blocks for the KV cache are not necessarily stored in contiguous space.
PagedAttention is inspired by the operating system’s solution to memory fragmentation and sharing: virtual memory with paging.
Blocks can be thought of as pages, tokens as bytes, and requests as processes.
This design alleviates internal fragmentation by using relatively small blocks and allocating them on demand.
It eliminates external fragmentation as all blocks have the same size.
It enables memory sharing at the granularity of a block across sequences of the same request or across different requests.

claim: vLLM is a high-throughput distributed LLM serving engine built on PagedAttention that achieves near-zero waste in KV cache memory and improves serving throughput by 2-4× over state-of-the-art systems without affecting model accuracy.
premises: We build vLLM, a high-throughput distributed LLM serving engine on top of PagedAttention.
vLLM achieves near-zero waste in KV cache memory.
vLLM uses block-level memory management and preemptive request scheduling co-designed with PagedAttention.
vLLM supports popular LLMs such as GPT, OPT, and LLaMA with varying sizes, including those exceeding single GPU memory capacity.
Evaluations on various models and workloads show vLLM improves LLM serving throughput by 2-4× compared to state-of-the-art systems [31, 60].
The improvements do not affect model accuracy at all.
Improvements are more pronounced with longer sequences, larger models, and more complex decoding algorithms.

claim: Language modeling factorizes the joint probability of a token sequence into the product of conditional probabilities (autoregressive decomposition).
premises: The task of language modeling is to model the probability of a list of tokens (x_1,...,x_n).

Since language has a natural sequential ordering, it is common to factorize the joint probability over the whole sequence as the product of conditional probabilities (a.k.a. autoregressive decomposition [3]): P(x)=P(x_1)·P(x_2|x_1)⋯P(x_n|x_1,…,x_{n-1}).

claim: Transformers are the de facto standard architecture for large-scale language modeling, with self-attention layers as their most important component.
premises: Transformers [53] have become the de facto standard architecture for modeling the probability above at a large scale.
The most important component of a Transformer-based language model is its self-attention layers.

claim: In a Transformer self-attention layer, queries, keys, and values are derived via linear transformations, attention scores are computed from query‑key dot products, and the output is a weighted sum of the value vectors.
premises: q_i=W_q x_i, k_i=W_k x_i, v_i=W_n x_i.
a_{ij}=exp(q_i^⊤ k_j/√d) / Σ_{t=1}^i exp(q_i^⊤ k_t/√d), o_i=Σ_{j=1}^i a_{ij} v_j.

claim: Besides self-attention, all other Transformer components (embedding, feed‑forward, layer normalization, residual connection, output logit, and QKV transformations) are applied independently per token position.
premises: Besides the computation in Eq. 4, all other components in the Transformer model, including the embedding layer, feed‑forward layer, layer normalization [2], residual connection [22], output logit computation, and the query, key, and value transformation in Eq. 2, are all applied independently position‑wise in a form of y_i = f(x_i).

claim: LLM serving consists of a parallelizable prompt phase and a sequential autoregressive generation phase that relies on KV caching, is memory‑bound, and underutilizes GPU resources.
premises: The prompt phase takes the whole user prompt as input, computes the probability of the first new token, generates key and value vectors for all prompt tokens, and can be parallelized using matrix‑matrix multiplication on GPUs.

The autoregressive generation phase generates tokens sequentially; at each iteration it uses cached key and value vectors from previous tokens, computes only the new key and value vectors, and performs matrix‑vector multiplication, which cannot be parallelized due to data dependency.
This phase becomes memory‑bound and accounts for most of the latency of a single request.

claim: PagedAttention is an attention algorithm that allows storing continuous keys and values in non-contiguous memory space by partitioning the KV cache into KV blocks.
premises: PagedAttention is introduced to address memory challenges in §3.
PagedAttention is inspired by the classic idea of paging in operating systems.
Unlike traditional attention algorithms, PagedAttention allows storing continuous keys and values in non-contiguous memory space.
PagedAttention partitions the KV cache of each sequence into KV blocks, where each block contains key and value vectors for a fixed number of tokens (block size B).

claim: Fine-grained batching mechanisms like cellular batching and iteration-level scheduling improve LLM serving throughput by reducing queueing delays and eliminating padding inefficiencies.
premises: Fine-grained batching mechanisms operate at the iteration level, unlike traditional request-level batching.
After each iteration, completed requests are removed from the batch and new ones are added.
A new request can be processed after waiting for a single iteration, not the entire batch to complete.
With special GPU kernels, these techniques eliminate the need to pad inputs and outputs.
Reducing queueing delay and padding inefficiencies significantly increases the throughput of LLM serving.

claim: LLM serving throughput is memory-bound primarily due to the large and growing memory requirements of the KV cache, which scales with sequence length and model size.
premises: The number of requests that can be batched together is constrained by GPU memory capacity, particularly the space allocated to store the KV cache.
For the 13B parameter OPT model, the KV cache of a single token demands 800 KB of space (2 × 5120 × 40 × 2 bytes).
OPT can generate sequences up to 2048 tokens, so one request’s KV cache can require up to 1.6 GB.
Concurrent GPUs have memory capacities in the tens of GBs, allowing only a few tens of requests even if all memory is allocated to KV cache.
Inefficient memory management further decreases achievable batch size.
GPU computation speed grows faster than memory capacity (e.g., A100 to H100: FLOPS increases >2x, memory stays at 80GB).

claim: Decoding algorithm choice significantly impacts KV cache memory usage through sharing opportunities, with beam search enabling up to 55% memory savings.
premises: LLM services offer decoding algorithms with varying implications for memory management complexity.
When users request multiple random samples from a single input prompt, the KV cache of the prompt part (12% of total KV cache memory) can be shared.
During autoregressive generation, KV cache should remain unshared due to differing sample results and context/position dependence.
In beam search, different request beams can share larger portions of their KV cache, enabling up to 55% memory saving.
The sharing pattern evolves as the decoding process advances.

claim: Variable input and output lengths in LLM service requests necessitate dynamic memory management, including KV cache swapping or deletion, to prevent memory exhaustion during decoding.
premises: Requests exhibit variability in input and output lengths.
As output length grows during decoding, the memory required for a request’s KV cache expands.
This expansion may exhaust available memory for incoming requests or ongoing generation.
The system must make scheduling decisions such as deleting or swapping out KV cache of some requests from GPU memory.

claim: Existing LLM serving systems waste memory due to static chunk pre-allocation and fragmentation.
premises: Since most operators in current deep learning frameworks [33, 39] require tensors to be stored in contiguous memory, previous LLM serving systems [31, 60] also store the KV cache of one request as a contiguous tensor across the different positions.

Due to the unpredictable output lengths from the LLM, they statically allocate a chunk of memory for a request based on the request’s maximum possible sequence length, irrespective of the actual input or eventual output length of the request.

The chunk pre-allocation scheme in existing systems has three primary sources of memory wastes: _reserved_ slots for future tokens, _internal fragmentation_ due to over-provisioning for potential maximum sequence lengths, and _external fragmentation_ from the memory allocator like the buddy allocator.

The external fragmentation will never be used for generated tokens, which is known before serving a request. Internal fragmentation also remains unused, but this is only realized after a request has finished sampling. They are both pure memory waste.

Although the reserved memory is eventually used, reserving this space for the entire request’s duration, especially when the reserved space is large, occupies the space that could otherwise be used to process other requests.
We visualize the average percentage of memory wastes in our experiments in Fig. 2, revealing that the actual effective memory in previous systems can be as low as 20.4%.

claim: vLLM introduces PagedAttention and a paged KV cache manager to overcome memory waste and enable efficient memory sharing.
premises: In this work, we develop a new attention algorithm, _PagedAttention_, and build an LLM serving engine, _vLLM_, to tackle the challenges outlined in §3.
The architecture of vLLM is shown in Fig. 4.
vLLM adopts a centralized scheduler to coordinate the execution of distributed GPU workers.
The _KV cache manager_ effectively manages the KV cache in a paged fashion, enabled by PagedAttention.
Specifically, the KV cache manager manages the physical KV cache memory on the GPU workers through the instructions sent by the centralized scheduler.

claim: The vLLM design supports variable-length input/output sequences and various decoding methods while enabling distributed operation.
premises: Next, We describe the PagedAttention algorithm in §4.1.
With that, we show the design of the KV cache manager in §4.2 and how it facilitates PagedAttention in §4.3, respectively.
Then, we show how this design facilitates effective memory management for various decoding methods (§4.4) and handles the variable length input and output sequences (§4.5).
Finally, we show how the system design of vLLM works in a distributed setting (§4.6).

claim: vLLM uses virtual memory-inspired techniques to manage KV cache by organizing it into fixed-size logical and physical blocks, enabling dynamic memory allocation without pre-reserving space for maximum sequence length.
premises: The key idea behind vLLM’s memory manager is analogous to the virtual memory in operating systems.
OS partitions memory into fixed-sized pages and maps user programs’ logical pages to physical pages.
Contiguous logical pages can correspond to non-contiguous physical memory pages, allowing user programs to access memory as though it were contiguous.
Physical memory space needs not to be fully reserved in advance, enabling the OS to dynamically allocate physical pages as needed.
vLLM uses the ideas behind virtual memory to manage the KV cache in an LLM service.
Enabled by PagedAttention, we organize the KV cache as fixed-size KV blocks, like pages in virtual memory.
A request’s KV cache is represented as a series of logical KV blocks, filled from left to right as new tokens and their KV cache are generated.
On GPU workers, a block engine allocates a contiguous chunk of GPU DRAM and divides it into physical KV blocks.
The KV block manager also maintains block tables—the mapping between logical and physical KV blocks of each request.

claim: During decoding, vLLM dynamically allocates physical KV blocks as needed, stores newly generated KV cache in available slots of logical blocks, and updates block table mappings to enable efficient memory reuse and batching across requests.
premises: In the prefill step, vLLM generates the KV cache of the prompts and the first output token with a conventional self-attention algorithm.
vLLM then stores the KV cache of the first 4 tokens in logical block 0 and the following 3 tokens in logical block 1.
The remaining slot is reserved for the subsequent autoregressive generation phase.
In the first autoregressive decoding step, vLLM generates the new token with the PagedAttention algorithm on physical blocks 7 and 1.
Since one slot remains available in the last logical block, the newly generated KV cache is stored there, and the block table’s #filled record is updated.

At the second decoding step, as the last logical block is full, vLLM stores the newly generated KV cache in a new logical block; vLLM allocates a new physical block (physical block 3) for it and stores this mapping in the block table.
Globally, for each decoding iteration, vLLM first selects a set of candidate sequences for batching and allocates the physical blocks for the newly required logical blocks.

During LLM’s computation, vLLM uses the PagedAttention kernel to access the previous KV cache stored in the form of logical KV blocks and saves the newly generated KV cache into the physical KV blocks.

Storing multiple tokens within a KV block (block size > 1) enables the PagedAttention kernel to process the KV cache across more positions in parallel, thus increasing hardware utilization and reducing latency.

As all the blocks are filled from left to right and a new physical block is only allocated when all previous blocks are full, vLLM limits all the memory wastes for a request within one block, so it can effectively utilize all the memory.
Once a request finishes its generation, its KV blocks can be freed to store the KV cache of other requests.

claim: vLLM enables efficient memory sharing for parallel sampling by sharing KV cache blocks for common prompts and using copy-on-write for divergent outputs.
premises: In parallel sampling, one request includes multiple samples sharing the same input prompt, allowing the KV cache of the prompt to be shared as well.
Via its PagedAttention and paged memory management, vLLM can realize this sharing easily and save memory.
At the generation phase, the two outputs sample different output tokens and need separate storage for KV cache.
vLLM implements a copy-on-write mechanism at the block granularity for the physical blocks that need modification by multiple sequences.

Specifically, in Fig. 8, when sample A1 needs to write to its last logical block, vLLM recognizes that the reference count of the corresponding physical block is greater than 1; it allocates a new physical block, instructs the block engine to copy the information, and decreases the reference count to 1.
Next, when sample A2 writes to physical block 1, the reference count is already reduced to 1; thus A2 directly writes its newly generated KV cache to physical block 1.

claim: vLLM reduces memory overhead in beam search by enabling dynamic sharing of KV cache blocks across candidates and applying copy-on-write only when necessary.
premises: Unlike parallel decoding, beam search facilities sharing not only the initial prompt blocks but also other blocks across different candidates, and the sharing patterns dynamically change as the decoding process advances.
Fig. 9 shows how vLLM manages the KV blocks for a beam search example with k=4.
As the original candidates 0 and 3 are no longer among the top candidates, their logical blocks are freed, and the reference counts of corresponding physical blocks are reduced.
vLLM frees all physical blocks whose reference counts reach 0 (blocks 2, 4, 5, 8). Then, vLLM allocates new physical blocks (blocks 9-12) to store the new KV cache from the new candidates.
Previous LLM serving systems require frequent memory copies of the KV cache across the beam candidates.

In vLLM, most blocks of different beam candidates can be shared. The copy-on-write mechanism is applied only when the newly generated tokens are within an old shared block, as in parallel decoding. This involves only copying one block of data.

claim: vLLM reduces redundant computation by caching KV cache of shared prefixes across user prompts, enabling efficient mapping to pre-allocated physical blocks.
premises: Commonly, the LLM user provides a (long) description of the task including instructions and example inputs and outputs, also known as system prompt.
The description is concatenated with the actual task input to form the prompt of the request.
For this type of application, many user prompts share a prefix, thus the LLM service provider can store the KV cache of the prefix in advance to reduce the redundant computation spent on the prefix.

In vLLM, this can be conveniently achieved by reserving a set of physical blocks for a set of predefined shared prefixes by the LLM service provider, as how OS handles shared library across processes.
A user input prompt with the shared prefix can simply map its logical blocks to the cached physical blocks (with the last block marked copy-on-write).
The prompt phase computation only needs to execute on the user’s task input.

claim: vLLM supports distributed execution of large language models using Megatron-LM style tensor model parallelism on Transformers.
premises: Many LLMs have parameter sizes exceeding the capacity of a single GPU.
Therefore, it is necessary to partition them across distributed GPUs and execute them in a model parallel fashion.
vLLM is effective in distributed settings by supporting the widely used Megatron-LM style tensor model parallelism strategy on Transformers.

claim: vLLM uses a centralized KV cache manager that is shared across GPU workers to enable coherent distributed execution.
premises: Each model shard processes the same set of input tokens, thus requiring the KV Cache for the same positions.
vLLM features a single KV cache manager within the centralized scheduler.
Different GPU workers share the manager, as well as the mapping from logical blocks to physical blocks.
This common mapping allows GPU workers to execute the model with the physical blocks provided by the scheduler for each input request.

claim: vLLM is evaluated under various workloads to assess its performance in serving large language models.
premises: In this section, we evaluate the performance of vLLM under a variety of workloads.
We use OPT models with 13B, 66B, and 175B parameters and LLaMA with 13B parameters for our evaluation.
We synthesize workloads based on ShareGPT and Alpaca datasets, which contain input and output texts of real LLM services.

claim: FasterTransformer is used as a baseline with a custom scheduler implementing dynamic batching due to the absence of its own scheduler.
premises: FasterTransformer is a distributed inference engine highly optimized for latency.
As FasterTransformer does not have its own scheduler, we implement a custom scheduler with a dynamic batching mechanism similar to existing serving systems such as Triton.
Specifically, we set a maximum batch size B as large as possible for each experiment, according to the GPU memory capacity.

claim: Three variants of Orca are implemented to evaluate performance under different KV cache memory reservation strategies.
premises: Orca is a state-of-the-art LLM serving system optimized for throughput.
Since Orca is not publicly available, we implement our own version.
We assume Orca uses the buddy allocation algorithm to determine the memory address to store KV cache.

We implement three versions of Orca based on how much it over-reserves space for request outputs: Oracle (knows true output length), Pow2 (over-reserves by at most 2×), and Max (reserves up to maximum sequence length of 2048 tokens).

claim: Normalized latency is used as a key metric to evaluate serving throughput, particularly under high request rates.
premises: We focus on serving throughput.
Specifically, using the workloads with different request rates, we measure normalized latency of the systems, the mean of every request’s end-to-end latency divided by its output length, as in Orca.
A high-throughput serving system should retain low normalized latency against high request rates.

claim: ControlNet can add conditional control to a large pretrained diffusion model, exemplified by Stable Diffusion.
premises: We use Stable Diffusion [71] as an example to show how ControlNet can add conditional control to a large pretrained diffusion model.

claim: Stable Diffusion's U-Net consists of an encoder, decoder, and middle block with specific block counts and internal layer composition.
premises: Stable Diffusion is essentially a U-Net [72] with an encoder, a middle block, and a skip-connected decoder.
Both the encoder and decoder contain 12 blocks, and the full model contains 25 blocks, including the middle block.
Of the 25 blocks, 8 blocks are down-sampling or up-sampling convolution layers, while the other 17 blocks are main blocks that each contain 4 resnet layers and 2 Vision Transformers (ViTs).
Each ViT contains several cross-attention and self-attention mechanisms.
For example, in Figure 3a, the “SD Encoder Block A” contains 4 resnet layers and 2 ViTs, while the “⨉3” indicates that this block is repeated three times.

claim: Text prompts are encoded by a CLIP text encoder and diffusion timesteps are encoded by a time encoder with positional encoding.
premises: Text prompts are encoded using the CLIP text encoder [65], and diffusion timesteps are encoded with a time encoder using positional encoding.

claim: ControlNet is constructed by adding trainable blue blocks and white zero convolution layers to the locked gray Stable Diffusion U-net structure (encoder blocks and middle block).
premises: Figure 3: Stable Diffusion’s U-net architecture connected with a ControlNet on the encoder blocks and middle block. The locked, gray blocks show the structure of Stable Diffusion V1.5 (or V2.1, as they use the same U-net architecture). The trainable blue blocks and the white zero convolution layers are added to build a ControlNet.

claim: ControlNet creates a trainable copy of Stable Diffusion's 12 encoding blocks and 1 middle block, applies it at each encoder level, adds its outputs to the 12 skip-connections and the middle block, and this design is likely transferable to other models due to the typical U-net structure.
premises: The ControlNet structure is applied to each encoder level of the U-net (Figure 3b).
In particular, we use ControlNet to create a trainable copy of the 12 encoding blocks and 1 middle block of Stable Diffusion.
The 12 encoding blocks are in 4 resolutions (64×64,32×32,16×16,8×8) with each one replicated 3 times.
The outputs are added to the 12 skip-connections and 1 middle block of the U-net.
Since Stable Diffusion is a typical U-net structure, this ControlNet architecture is likely to be applicable with other models.

claim: Connecting ControlNet via frozen locked copy eliminates gradient computation in the original encoder, making training faster and reducing GPU memory usage, with empirical overhead of ~23% more memory and 34% more time per iteration on an NVIDIA A100 PCIE 40GB.
premises: The way we connect the ControlNet is computationally efficient — since the locked copy parameters are frozen, no gradient computation is required in the originally locked encoder for the finetuning.
This approach speeds up training and saves GPU memory.

As tested on a single NVIDIA A100 PCIE 40GB, optimizing Stable Diffusion with ControlNet requires only about 23% more GPU memory and 34% more time in each training iteration, compared to optimizing Stable Diffusion without ControlNet.

claim: To condition ControlNet, input images (e.g., edge, pose, depth) are resized from 512×512 pixel space to 64×64 feature vectors using a tiny network of four convolution layers with specific kernel sizes, strides, and channel widths, activated by ReLU and initialized with Gaussian weights.
premises: To add ControlNet to Stable Diffusion, we first convert each input conditioning image (_e.g._, edge, pose, depth, _etc._) from an input size of 512 ⨉ 512 into a 64⨉64 feature space vector that matches the size of Stable Diffusion.

In particular, we use a tiny network \(\mathcal{E}(\cdot)\) of four convolution layers with 4⨉4 kernels and 2⨉2 strides (activated by ReLU, using 16, 32, 64, 128, channels respectively, initialized with Gaussian weights and trained jointly with the full model) to encode an image-space condition **_c_**<sub>i</sub> into a feature space conditioning vector **_c_**<sub>f</sub> as,

claim: vLLM achieves higher throughput than Orca when input prompts share a common prefix, with throughput improvement increasing as more prefix examples are shared.
premises: The model used is LLaMA-13B, which is multilingual.
The workload is the WMT16 English-to-German translation dataset with synthesized prefixes: one-shot (single example, 80 tokens) and few-shot (5 examples, 341 tokens).
As shown in Fig.16(a), vLLM achieves 1.67× higher throughput than Orca when the one-shot prefix is shared.
As shown in Fig.16(b), vLLM achieves 3.58× higher throughput than Orca when the five-shot prefix is shared.

claim: vLLM sustains higher request rates than Orca baselines for chatbot workloads because it handles long prompts efficiently via PagedAttention, avoiding fixed output space reservation.
premises: Chatbot implementation concatenates chatting history and last user query into a prompt, limited to 1024 tokens due to OPT-13B context length, with generation up to 1024 tokens.
The ShareGPT dataset used to synthesize chatting history yields many long conversations, resulting in input prompts of 1024 tokens for most requests.

Orca baselines use a buddy allocation algorithm that reserves space for 1024 tokens for request outputs regardless of predicted output lengths, causing similar behavior among the three Orca baselines.
vLLM does not store KV cache between conversation rounds and uses PagedAttention to resolve memory fragmentation and reservation issues.
Fig.17 shows that vLLM can sustain 2× higher request rates compared to the three Orca baselines.

claim: vLLM is an end-to-end serving system with a FastAPI frontend and a GPU-based inference engine.
premises: vLLM is an end-to-end serving system with a FastAPI [15] frontend and a GPU-based inference engine.
The frontend extends the OpenAI API [34] interface, allowing users to customize sampling parameters for each request, such as the maximum sequence length and the beam width k.
The vLLM engine is written in 8.5K lines of Python and 2K lines of C++/CUDA code.
We develop control-related components including the scheduler and the block manager in Python while developing custom CUDA kernels for key operations such as PagedAttention.
For the model executor, we implement popular LLMs such as GPT [5], OPT [62], and LLaMA [52] using PyTorch [39] and Transformers [58].
We use NCCL [32] for tensor communication across the distributed GPU workers.

claim: vLLM develops several GPU kernels to optimize PagedAttention by fusing operations and ensuring coalesced memory access.
premises: Since PagedAttention introduces memory access patterns that are not efficiently supported by existing systems, we develop several GPU kernels for optimizing it.

(1) Fused reshape and block write. In every Transformer layer, the new KV cache are split into blocks, reshaped to a memory layout optimized for block read, then saved at positions specified by the block table. To minimize kernel launch overheads, we fuse them into a single kernel.

(2) Fusing block read and attention. We adapt the attention kernel in FasterTransformer [31] to read KV cache according to the block table and perform attention operations on the fly. To ensure coalesced memory access, we assign a GPU warp to read each block. Moreover, we add support for variable sequence lengths within a request batch.

(3) Fused block copy. Block copy operations, issued by the copy-on-write mechanism, may operate on discontinuous blocks. This can lead to numerous invocations of small data movements if we use the cudaMemcpyAsync API. To mitigate the overhead, we implement a kernel that batches the copy operations for different blocks into a single kernel launch.

claim: vLLM implements various decoding algorithms using the fork, append, and free methods to manage sequences.
premises: vLLM implements various decoding algorithms using three key methods: fork, append, and free.
The fork method creates a new sequence from an existing one.
The append method appends a new token to the sequence.
Finally, the free method deletes the sequence.

For instance, in parallel sampling, vLLM creates multiple output sequences from the single input sequence using the fork method. It then adds new tokens to these sequences in every iteration with append, and deletes sequences that meet a stopping condition using free.
The same strategy is also applied in beam search and prefix sharing by vLLM.
We believe future decoding algorithms can also be supported by combining these methods.

claim: vLLM sustains higher request rates than Orca and FasterTransformer on ShareGPT and Alpaca datasets due to efficient memory management via PagedAttention enabling better batching.
premises: vLLM can sustain 1.7×-2.7× higher request rates compared to Orca (Oracle) and 2.7×-8× compared to Orca (Max) on ShareGPT dataset while maintaining similar latencies
vLLM’s PagedAttention efficiently manages memory usage and enables batching more requests than Orca
for OPT-13B, vLLM processes 2.2× more requests at the same time than Orca (Oracle) and 4.3× more than Orca (Max) as shown in Fig. 13a
compared to FasterTransformer, vLLM can sustain up to 22× higher request rates because FasterTransformer does not utilize fine-grained scheduling and inefficiently manages memory like Orca (Max)

on Alpaca dataset, results follow similar trend to ShareGPT except in Fig. 12(f) where vLLM’s advantage is less pronounced due to large GPU memory availability for OPT-175B and short sequences in Alpaca making systems compute-bound

claim: In parallel sampling and beam search, vLLM achieves greater performance benefits over Orca due to memory sharing in PagedAttention, with beam search showing higher memory savings than parallel sampling.
premises: in parallel sampling, all parallel sequences in a request can share the KV cache for the prompt
with larger number of sequences to sample, vLLM brings more improvement over Orca baselines as shown in first row of Fig. 14
second row of Fig. 14 shows beam search results with different beam widths, and since beam search allows for more sharing, vLLM demonstrates even greater performance benefits
improvement of vLLM over Orca (Oracle) on OPT-13B and Alpaca dataset goes from 1.3× in basic sampling to 2.3× in beam search with width of 6
Fig. 15 shows 6.1%-9.8% memory saving on parallel sampling and 37.6%-55.2% on beam search in general experiments
in same experiments with ShareGPT dataset, 16.2%-30.5% memory saving on parallel sampling and 44.3%-66.3% on beam search

claim: PagedAttention introduces 20-26% higher attention kernel latency but still yields significant end-to-end performance improvement over FasterTransformer.
premises: Dynamic block mapping in PagedAttention adds overheads of accessing the block table, executing extra branches, and handling variable sequence lengths.
As shown in Fig. 18a, this leads to 20-26% higher attention kernel latency compared to the highly-optimized FasterTransformer implementation.
Despite the overhead, PagedAttention makes vLLM significantly outperform FasterTransformer in end-to-end performance (§6).

claim: The overhead introduced by PagedAttention is limited to the attention operator and does not affect other model operators such as Linear.
premises: We believe the overhead is small as it only affects the attention operator but not the other operators in the model, such as Linear.

claim: If the block size is too small, vLLM may not fully utilize the GPU’s parallelism for reading and processing the KV cache.
premises: If the block size is too small, vLLM may not fully utilize the GPU’s parallelism for reading and processing KV cache.

claim: If the block size is too large, internal fragmentation increases and the probability of sharing decreases.
premises: If the block size is too large, internal fragmentation increases and the probability of sharing decreases.

claim: A block size of 16 provides a good trade‑off between GPU utilization and fragmentation, leading vLLM to adopt it as the default block size.
premises: In the ShareGPT trace, block sizes from 16 to 128 lead to the best performance.
In the Alpaca trace, while the block size 16 and 32 work well, larger block sizes significantly degrade the performance since the sequences become shorter than the block sizes.
In practice, we find that the block size 16 is large enough to efficiently utilize the GPU and small enough to avoid significant internal fragmentation in most workloads.
Accordingly, vLLM sets its default block size as 16.

claim: The overhead of recomputation and swapping, as well as the serving performance, vary with block size.
premises: Figure 19.(a) Overhead of recomputation and swapping for different block sizes.
Figure 19.(b) Performance when serving OPT-13B with the ShareGPT traces at the same request rate.

claim: vLLM can process requests with different decoding preferences simultaneously, which existing systems cannot efficiently do.
premises: Decoding methods exhibit diverse memory sharing and accessing patterns.
vLLM conceals complex memory sharing between different sequences via a common mapping layer that translates logical blocks to physical blocks.
The LLM and its execution kernel only see a list of physical block IDs for each sequence and do not need to handle sharing patterns across sequences.

claim: vLLM uses a first-come-first-serve (FCFS) scheduling policy to ensure fairness and prevent starvation, preempting the latest arrived requests first.
premises: When request traffic surpasses system capacity, vLLM must prioritize a subset of requests.
vLLM adopts FCFS scheduling for all requests to ensure fairness and prevent starvation.
When preemption is needed, earliest arrived requests are served first and latest requests are preempted first.

claim: vLLM implements an all-or-nothing eviction policy for sequence groups to manage GPU physical block exhaustion.
premises: As requests and outputs grow, vLLM can run out of GPU physical blocks to store newly generated KV cache.
All blocks of a sequence are accessed together.
Multiple sequences within one request (e.g., beam candidates) are gang-scheduled as a sequence group.
Sequences within one sequence group are always preempted or rescheduled together due to potential memory sharing.

claim: vLLM uses swapping to CPU memory as a technique to recover evicted blocks when needed again.
premises: To recover evicted blocks, vLLM considers swapping as a technique.
Swapping copies evicted blocks to CPU memory via a CPU block allocator.
When GPU blocks are exhausted, vLLM evicts sequences and transfers their KV cache to CPU RAM.
Once a request completes, its blocks are freed and preempted sequence blocks are brought back to continue processing.

claim: vLLM uses recomputation as an alternative technique to recover evicted blocks by regenerating the KV cache from the original prompt and generated tokens.
premises: To recover evicted blocks, vLLM considers recomputation as a technique.
Recomputation regenerates the KV cache when preempted sequences are rescheduled.
The tokens generated at decoding can be concatenated with the original user prompt as a new prompt.
Their KV cache at all positions can be generated in one prompt phase iteration.
Recomputation latency can be significantly lower than original latency.

claim: PagedAttention is a new attention algorithm that allows attention keys and values to be stored in non-contiguous paged memory.
premises: This paper proposes PagedAttention, a new attention algorithm that allows attention keys and values to be stored in non-contiguous paged memory

claim: vLLM is a high-throughput LLM serving system with efficient memory management enabled by PagedAttention.
premises: This paper proposes PagedAttention, a new attention algorithm that allows attention keys and values to be stored in non-contiguous paged memory, and presents vLLM, a high-throughput LLM serving system with efficient memory management enabled by PagedAttention.

claim: vLLM achieves 2-4⨉ throughput improvements over the state-of-the-art systems.
premises: Our experiments show that vLLM achieves 2-4⨉ throughput improvements over the state-of-the-art systems.

claim: The research was partly supported by gifts from multiple companies and institutions including Andreessen Horowitz, Anyscale, Astronomer, Google, IBM, Intel, Lacework, Microsoft, Mohamed Bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence, Samsung SDS, Uber, and VMware.
premises: This research is partly supported by gifts from Andreessen Horowitz, Anyscale, Astronomer, Google, IBM, Intel, Lacework, Microsoft, Mohamed Bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence, Samsung SDS, Uber, and VMware.

claim: Swapping incurs excessive overhead with small block sizes, whereas recomputation overhead is constant and never exceeds 20% of swapping latency, making recomputation more efficient for small block sizes and swapping more efficient for large block sizes, with comparable performance for medium block sizes (16-64).
premises: vLLM supports both recomputation and swapping as its recovery mechanisms.
To understand the tradeoffs between the two methods, we evaluate their end-to-end performance and microbenchmark their overheads, as presented in Fig. 19.

Our results reveal that swapping incurs excessive overhead with small block sizes because small block sizes often result in numerous small data transfers between CPU and GPU, which limits the effective PCIe bandwidth.
In contrast, the overhead of recomputation remains constant across different block sizes, as recomputation does not utilize the KV blocks.
Thus, recomputation is more efficient when the block size is small, while swapping is more efficient when the block size is large.
Recomputation overhead is never higher than 20% of swapping’s latency.
For medium block sizes from 16 to 64, the two methods exhibit comparable end-to-end performance.

claim: The idea of virtual memory and paging is effective for managing the KV cache in LLM serving due to dynamic memory allocation and GPU memory capacity bound, but does not generally hold for every GPU workload.
premises: The idea of virtual memory and paging is effective for managing the KV cache in LLM serving because the workload requires dynamic memory allocation (since the output length is not known a priori) and its performance is bound by the GPU memory capacity.
However, this does not generally hold for every GPU workload.
For example, in DNN training, the tensor shapes are typically static, and thus memory allocation can be optimized ahead of time.
For another example, in serving DNNs that are not LLMs, an increase in memory efficiency may not result in any performance improvement since the performance is primarily compute-bound.
In such scenarios, introducing the vLLM’s techniques may rather degrade the performance due to the extra overhead of memory indirection and non-contiguous block memory.
However, we would be excited to see vLLM’s techniques being applied to other workloads with similar properties to LLM serving.

claim: vLLM re-interprets and augments virtual memory and paging by leveraging application-specific semantics, including an all-or-nothing swap-out policy and recomputation method, and mitigates memory indirection overhead by fusing GPU kernels for memory access with other operations such as attention.
premises: vLLM re-interprets and augments the idea of virtual memory and paging by leveraging the application-specific semantics.
One example is vLLM’s all-or-nothing swap-out policy, which exploits the fact that processing a request requires all of its corresponding token states to be stored in GPU memory.
Another example is the recomputation method to recover the evicted blocks, which is not feasible in OS.
Besides, vLLM mitigates the overhead of memory indirection in paging by fusing the GPU kernels for memory access operations with those for other operations such as attention.

claim: Topic-following behaviour for LLMs is a specific case of instruction tuning that ensures engagement with on-topic requests and serves as a safety filter.
premises: Topic-following behaviour for LLMs is a specific case of instruction tuning.
Ideally, given a complex instruction describing the topic of the task to be solved by the assistant, the LLM should be able to respect these topical instructions when generating its responses.
Topic-following ensures engagement with on-topic requests, serving as a safety filter.

claim: Instruction-tuning datasets for LLMs use diverse sources like OpenAssistant and FLAN 2022, incorporating crowd-sourced and synthetic data, and are aligned with human preferences including safety alignment to avoid harmful topics.
premises: Instruction-tuning for LLMs uses diverse datasets like OpenAssistant (Köpf et al., 2024) and FLAN 2022 (Longpre et al., 2023), featuring prompt-response pairs from crowd-sourced and synthetic data (Honovich et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2022).

These datasets, complemented by human feedback (Ouyang et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2023b), align LLMs with human preferences, including safety alignment to avoid harmful topics (Bai et al., 2022; Inan et al., 2023).

claim: Dialogue inpainting is used to synthesize conversations from brief text documents and has been adapted for niche dialogues such as child-centric conversations and teacher-student interactions.
premises: To create the CANTALKABOUTTHIS dataset, we use dialogue inpainting (Dai et al., 2022), a technique for synthesizing conversations from brief text documents.

Initially used in conversational question answering (Hwang et al., 2023), it has been adapted for niche dialogues, such as child-centric conversations (Lee et al., 2023) and teacher-student interactions (Wang et al., 2024).

claim: Topic-following is evaluated using benchmarks like MMLU and domain-specific ones, with recent works introducing RuLES, Castricato et al.'s entity-focused discussions, and CONSCENDI for task-oriented chatbots in reservation tasks.
premises: Instruction-tuned LLMs are evaluated on benchmarks for complex tasks like MMLU (Hendrycks et al., 2020) and domain-specific ones like math or coding.
Recent studies examine LLMs’ ability to follow rules within prompts, aligning with topic-following.
Mu et al. (2023) introduce the RuLES benchmark with rules to be followed for 14 simple scenarios related to gaming and computer security.
Castricato et al. (2024) explore discussions focused on specific entities.
CONSCENDI (Sun et al., 2023) creates synthetic datasets for task-oriented chatbots in reservation tasks.

claim: OpenAI's Custom GPTs enhance task-oriented chatbots with topic-following capabilities, but details on performance metrics and training methodologies are undisclosed, and practical deployment remains challenging with reported failures in simple scenarios.
premises: Recently, OpenAI introduced Custom GPTs (OpenAI, 2023), enhancing task-oriented chatbots with topic-following capabilities.
Despite their potential, details on performance metrics and training methodologies are undisclosed.
Practical deployment remains challenging, with reports of failures even in simple scenarios.

claim: Hierarchical rule-following establishes instruction hierarchy to make LLMs robust against prompt injections and jailbreaks by training them to ignore lower priority prompts that contradict higher priority ones.
premises: LLMs are vulnerable to prompt injections, jailbreaks, and similar attacks, where adversaries manipulate the model’s original instructions using malicious prompts.

Wallace et al. (2024) introduce the concept of instruction hierarchy - a framework of explicit rules that define the precedence when faced with conflicting instructions (e.g. system prompt surpasses any user instruction).

Using an automated synthetic data generation pipeline, this approach trains LLMs to internalize this hierarchy, making them more robust against various attacks with minimal impact on model helpfulness.

Lu et al. (2024) generate synthetic conversations where only instructions with a high priority can change the rules of the interaction. Any lower priority request (e.g. from a user) that contradicts a higher priority prompt should be ignored.

The main objective of these approaches is to establish a hierarchy based on priorities between different types of prompts and requests that might appear in a complex user-LLM interaction, and to learn to refuse lower priority prompts if they contradict any higher priority one.

claim: Topic-following improves general alignment, rule-following behavior, and safety moderation performance even without explicit safety-related data, while hierarchical/priority-based alignment is more geared towards security vulnerabilities.
premises: Both topic-following and the priority-based alignment focus on making the instruction-following behavior in LLMs more reliable.
Our approach aims at improving the faithfulness of models on task-oriented dialogue scenarios while the hierarchical/priority-based alignment is more geared towards security vulnerabilities.
We also find that topic-following (TF) improves general alignment, rule-following behavior, and safety moderation performance, even without explicit safety-related data.

claim: Topic-following is a different and more fine-grained task than out-of-domain utterance detection, providing a generic alignment method for instructing LLMs how to behave in task-oriented conversation.
premises: While TF might seem similar to OOD utterance detection (Lane et al., 2006; Zheng et al., 2020), it is important to note that TF is actually a different and more fine-grained task.

While OOD utterance detection is a specific type of outlier identification, TF is more generic, providing a fine-grained alignment method for instructing LLMs how to behave in task-oriented conversation.

claim: The CANTALKABOUTTHIS dataset enables language models to stay on topic during task-oriented interactions.
premises: The dataset consists of synthetic dialogues on a wide range of conversation topics from different domains, interspersed with distractor turns that intentionally divert the chatbot from the predefined topic.

Fine-tuning language models on this dataset helps make them resilient to deviating from the assigned role and improves their ability to maintain topical coherence compared to general-purpose instruction-tuned LLMs like GPT-4-TURBO and MIXTRAL-INSTRUCT.

claim: Training on the CANTALKABOUTTHIS dataset improves language models' performance on fine-grained instruction following tasks, including safety alignment.
premises: Preliminary observations suggest that training models on this dataset also enhance their performance on fine-grained instruction following tasks, including safety alignment.

claim: Topic-following combines instruction-tuning and moderation to define when a chatbot should respond or steer away during dialogues.
premises: Topic-following is a combination of instruction-tuning and moderation.

This concept revolves around defining complex instructions that dictate how an intelligent assistant should interact with users, including examples of user interactions the assistant should engage in and scenarios where the user deviates from the given instructions (denoted as distractors), in which cases the chatbot should either decline to respond or tactfully guide the conversation back to the relevant topic.

claim: The CANTALKABOUTTHIS dataset is created via a three-step prompting-based approach: generating topic-following prompts, creating dialogues via dialogue inpainting, and integrating distractors.
premises: The dataset creation process involves a three-step prompting-based approach that focuses on both diversity and quality: 1) generate topic-following prompts across a variety of scenarios; 2) create dialogues adhering to these topical instructions, employing a technique akin to dialogue inpainting; 3) integrate distractors into these dialogues to test topic following.

claim: Fine-tuning on CANTALKABOUTTHIS yields side benefits of improved overall instruction-following and zero-shot safety alignment comparable to LLAMAGUARD.
premises: Our approach to teaching LLMs topic-following has two key side benefits: firstly, it aids in improving overall instruction-following abilities; secondly, models trained for topic-following exhibit comparable efficacy to LLAMAGUARD in safety alignment, even in a zero-shot setting.

claim: There is a notable gap in instruction-tuning datasets for aligning language models to maintain topic relevance in conversations, which the CANTALKABOUTTHIS dataset addresses.
premises: Recent advancements in instruction-tuning datasets have predominantly focused on specific tasks like mathematical or logical reasoning.
There has been a notable gap in data designed for aligning language models to maintain topic relevance in conversations - a critical aspect for deploying chatbots to production.
We introduce the CANTALKABOUTTHIS dataset to help language models remain focused on the subject at hand during task-oriented interactions.

claim: The CANTALKABOUTTHIS dataset is designed to improve the ability of LLMs and chatbots to maintain topical focus during interactions.
premises: The data pipeline involves identifying specific scenarios, formulating system instructions describing the topic of the conversation, generating dialogues that respect the topical system instructions, and producing distractors that would make the chatbot go off-topic.
Its main aim is to improve the ability of LLMs and chatbots powered by LLMs to maintain topical focus during interactions.

claim: The data pipeline for CANTALKABOUTTHIS includes identifying scenarios, formulating system instructions, generating dialogues respecting instructions, and producing distractors.
premises: The data pipeline involves sev eral stages: identifying specific scenarios, formulating system instructions describing the topic of the conversation, generating dialogues that respect the topical system instructions, and producing distractors that would make the chatbot go off-topic.

claim: The CANTALKABOUTTHIS dataset covers nine specific domains: health, banking, insurance, travel, taxes, legal, education, computer troubleshooting, and real estate.
premises: We focus on generating specific scenarios within nine different domains: health, banking, insurance, travel, taxes, legal, education, computer troubleshooting, and real estate.

claim: Scenario creation for CANTALKABOUTTHIS uses few-shot LLM prompting to generate 10 scenarios simultaneously, incorporating previously generated scenarios to enhance diversity.
premises: Given a domain, we prompt an LLM using a few-shot setting to generate 10 relevant scenarios simultaneously.
To enhance diversity and prevent repetition, we include the previously generated scenarios in subsequent prompts to the LLM.

claim: Filtering of scenario pairs for CANTALKABOUTTHIS ensures diversity by applying lexical similarity (ROUGE-L F-measure <0.7) and semantic similarity (MiniLM cosine <0.9) thresholds, with manual evaluation and empirically chosen cutoffs.
premises: To ensure diversity among the generated scenarios, we form a cartesian product of scenario pairs and employ two similarity-based filtering criteria: 1) lexical similarity - the scenario pairs should have a ROUGE-L (Lin, 2004) F-measure lower than 0.7, and 2) semantic similarity using MiniLM (Reimers and Gurevych, 2019) cosine score lower than 0.9.
Pairs flagged using these criteria are manually evaluated, and the scenarios considered too similar are discarded.
The thresholds were chosen empirically, by analyzing the set of scenario pairs identified as highly similar.

claim: The CANTALKABOUTTHIS dataset was created using two LLM backbones: OpenAI gpt-4-turbo-1106 and Mixtral-Instruct 8x7B to enable bias comparison, demonstrate high-quality data generation with smaller open models, and ensure commercial usability.
premises: To develop the CANTALKABOUTTHIS dataset, we conduct experiments using two LLM backbones: OpenAI gpt-4-turbo-1106 and the Mixtral-Instruct 8x7B model (Jiang et al., 2024).

Using two different LLMs has several advantages. First, we can compare whether the models, including baselines, are biased towards distractors generated by a specific LLM. Second, we show that we can obtain high-quality topic-following data with smaller open models. Third, the dataset generated with the Mixtral model should be commercially usable.

claim: gpt-4-turbo-1106 is more effective than Mixtral-Instruct at generating appropriate distractors, as Mixtral-Instruct tends to produce false positives by incorrectly labeling on-topic turns as distractors.
premises: A manual review of the generated distractors indicates that gpt-4-turbo is more adept at generating appropriate distractors compared to Mixtral-Instruct.
We observe that the latter often include false positives, where the model incorrectly outputs on-topic turns as distractors.

claim: Distractors are generated by prompting an LLM with the topical instruction and the on‑topic conversation to produce an off‑topic user utterance and to specify the bot turn after which it should be inserted.
premises: Distractors are user utterances designed to divert the conversation from its intended course or the bot’s operational scope (off‑topic turns).
To obtain a dataset for training a chatbot to avoid off‑topic engagement, we require the generation of such distractors.
To obtain such distractors, we prompt an LLM with the topical instruction and the generated on‑topic conversation as input.
The LLM is tasked to generate a user utterance that is off‑topic, which the chatbot should recognize and not engage with.
Additionally, it is asked to pick a particular bot turn after which the distractor should be inserted into the conversation.
For each conversation in our dataset, we create five such distractors.

claim: The alignment dataset is formed by inserting each distractor user utterance immediately after its corresponding agent turn in a base conversation and assigning a templated refusal response, enabling fine‑tuning of LLMs to stay on‑topic.
premises: A standard conversation in our dataset is an alternating sequence of user and agent exchanges, denoted as [_u_<sub>1</sub>_,a_<sub>1</sub>_,...,u<sub>n</sub>,a<sub>n</sub>_].
We integrate each distractor user utterance into the conversation sequence, positioning it immediately following the corresponding agent turn _a<sub>i</sub>_.
The chatbot’s response to these distractors is initially set to a standard template, i.e. "I am sorry! I can only answer questions related to the scenario.".

This dataset can be used to fine‑tune LLMs to ensure they remain focused on their assigned roles, thereby improving their capability to handle real‑world scenarios while staying within the scope of their designated tasks.
We also explore generating and using mitigations instead of template refusals (Appendix §C.1) as an ablation.

claim: Organizing train and test splits by domain ensures that domains in the training set are not present in validation or test sets to prevent overfitting.
premises: We organize the train and test splits by domain.
This setup guarantees that domains included in the training set are not present in the validation or test sets to prevent overfitting.

claim: A small human-annotated test set was created by selecting 20 random dialogues from the banking domain and having two experts generate five distractors per conversation.
premises: We select 20 random dialogues from the banking domain
Manually ask two experts in dialogue systems to create five distractors per conversation

claim: Due to data imbalance where only 11% of turns are distractors, evaluation focuses on precision, recall, and F1 score for both distractor and on-topic turns.
premises: Given the data imbalance, as only 11% of turns are distractors
We focus on evaluating the precision, recall, and F1 score for both distractor and on-topic turns

claim: Model effectiveness in avoiding engagement with distractors is assessed using heuristics that check for key phrases from the template response.
premises: We apply specific heuristics to determine the model’s effectiveness in avoiding engagement with distractors

These include checking for the inclusion of key phrases from the template response, such as 'related to the scenario,' as well as other indicative phrases like 'I am sorry' or 'unrelated to the scenario.'

claim: Applying LoRA to the 43B base model with batch size 128, adapter dimension 32, learning rate 1e-4 for five epochs with early stopping on the CANTALKABOUTTHIS dataset produces the STAY-ON-TOPIC-43B models.
premises: We use LORA (Hu et al., 2021) for training 43B-ALIGNED with CANTALKABOUTTHIS with a batch size of 128, adapter dimension of 32, and a learning rate of 1e-4.
We train the model for 5 epochs with early stopping giving us STAY-ON-TOPIC-43B.

claim: Training LLAMA3-8B with LoRA using batch size 4, adapter dimension 32, learning rate 1e-4 for five epochs yields the STAY-ON-TOPIC-8B model, which will be open-sourced to support topic-following research.
premises: To further advance research in this area, we employ LORA to train LLAMA3-8B using a batch size of 4, an adapter dimension of 32, and a learning rate of 1e-4 for 5 epochs.
This training process results in the STAY-ON-TOPIC-8B model.
We will open-source this model to facilitate community engagement and enable easy adoption for topic-following applications.

claim: Distractors in synthetic test sets predominantly violate the allowed topics rule, making them easier to detect due to clear deviations from the main topic.
premises: Using gpt4-o, we prompt the model with the distractor, the system instruction divided into four categories (flow, allowed topics, disallowed topics, and tone) and ask the model to determine which category is being violated.
In the synthetic dataset, Topic/Subject Allowed has 0.667 distribution, the highest among all rule types.

We find that most distractors in the synthetic test set violate the main topic of the system instructions, making these distractors relatively easy to identify as they predominantly deviate from the main topic of the system instruction.

claim: Human-generated distractors are more challenging for models to detect because they are evenly distributed across rule categories and often involve subtle topic shifts.
premises: In the human test set, the distractors are more even distributed across different categories.
Conversely, in the human test set, the distractors are more even distributed across different categories, presenting a more challenging setting for task-oriented bots as shown in Table 4.
It can be seen that human distractors have a higher similarity compared to those generated by GPT-4, correlating with the observation that models find human distractors more challenging.

claim: Longer conversations increase susceptibility to distractors across nearly all models.
premises: Additionally, we examine the impact of the number of turns in a conversation on susceptibility to distractors, finding that nearly all models exhibit increased susceptibility as conversations become longer (more details in Appendix §I).

claim: Subtle topic shifts, such as asking about beaches during a flight booking conversation, are harder to detect as distractors because they appear contextually relevant but deviate from the assigned task.
premises: The main challenge in detecting distractors largely depends on the nature of the topic shift. While abrupt topic changes are relatively easy for models to identify, subtle shifts involving a bridge<tbc> entity often pose a greater challenge in conversational task-oriented dialogue settings.

Looking at the following example, the distractor inquiring about the best beaches stays contextually relevant by inquiring about tourist attractions, which could seem like a natural extension for a flight booking conversation. However, this subtly steers the dialogue away from the assigned task of helping with flight reservations only.
On the other hand, the distractor asking for a book recommendation is abrupt and can easily be identified as unrelated to the flight reservation theme.

claim: STAY-ON-TOPIC-43B significantly improves rule-following performance on the RuLES benchmark relative to the baseline 43B-ALIGNED model.
premises: The RuLES benchmark measures rule-following ability of language models on 14 scenarios related to games and security.
STAY-ON-TOPIC-43B significantly improves over the baseline 43B-ALIGNED model, increasing the score from 0.50 to 0.69.
This improvement positions STAY-ON-TOPIC-43B at rank 13 on the RuLES benchmark.

claim: Topic-following improves model adherence to topical instructions and enables safety alignment, content moderation, and helpfulness improvements.
premises: Topic-following is a task that helps language models understand complex topical system instructions while allowing them to steer away from off-topic user requests.

The CANTALKABOUTTHIS dataset, a small synthetic dataset of on-topic conversations and distractors, can be used to fine-tune models with remarkable performance compared to strong LLMs on a small human-annotated distractor dataset.
Topic-following can be used for safety alignment, content moderation, and improving the general helpfulness of instruction-tuned models.
The dataset has been used as part of the instruction-tuning alignment blend by powerful models from the Nemotron family (Adler et al., 2024).

claim: The taxonomy of topical instructions in system prompts consists of four categories: topic/subject allowed, conversation tone/style, conversion flow, and topic/subject disallowed.
premises: We analyze the different types of instructions contained in system prompts for each scenario.
Using manual annotation of the topical instructions for a small sample, we propose the following taxonomy to categorize the instructions in system prompts:
• Topic/subject allowed: Specifies the permissible subjects for discussion, ensuring relevance and appropriateness (_"Help schedule an eye exam. You can discuss vision care."_).
• Conversation tone/style: Dictates how the conversation should be conducted and how responses should be provided (_"Use a supportive and informative tone."_).
• Conversion flow: Guides the logical progression and structure of the dialogue (_"Inform about items to bring."_).
• Topic/subject disallowed: Outlines the subjects to be avoided to maintain the appropriateness of the conversation (_"Avoid personal medical opinions."_).

premises: We find that on average, each system prompt includes 5-6 instructions on conversation flow, 2-3 instructions on conversation tone/style, and 2-3 instructions on topics/subjects allowed, with 1 restriction on topics/subjects disallowed.

claim: In the health domain scenario of scheduling an eye exam, the system instruction requires the model to act as a supportive assistant, guide users through scheduling steps, handle forgotten identification or insurance details, provide general eye health advice, and prioritize user privacy and safety without diagnosing medical conditions.
premises: Domain: health Scenario: scheduling an eye exam and discussing vision care

You will act as an intelligent assistant to help a user schedule an eye exam and discuss vision care. Throughout the interaction, maintain a supportive and informative tone, providing detailed guidance on the steps the user should take to schedule an eye exam, including identifying local clinics or providers, explaining the types of eye exams available, and understanding insurance coverage if mentioned. If the user expresses uncertainty about what type of eye exam they need, ask clarifying questions to determine their visual needs and any symptoms they may be experiencing.

Additionally, be prepared to inform the user of the typical items they should bring to an eye exam, such as current eyeglasses, contact lenses, a list of medications, and any relevant medical history. If the user forgets or is unaware of the identification or insurance information they need to provide, remind them politely of the standard requirements, such as a government-issued ID, insurance card, and possibly a referral from a primary care doctor, if applicable.

In case the user has questions about vision care, provide general advice on eye health, like the importance of regular eye exams, protective eyewear, and potential warning signs of vision problems. Should the user express concerns about eye symptoms or issues, encourage them to seek professional medical advice promptly, as you are not able to diagnose or offer medical opinions.
Be responsive to the user’s inquiries and provide information in a clear and concise manner, but refrain from making any assumptions about the user’s health status or personal information.

If the user provides personal health information, handle it sensitively and maintain privacy. Always prioritize the user’s safety and privacy, and if the conversation reaches a point where professional medical intervention is necessary, advise the user to contact a healthcare provider directly.

claim: Mitigations are bot responses that redirect conversation back to the relevant topic, improving user engagement and experience by acknowledging user queries while steering dialogue to the intended focus.
premises: Rather than relying on templated responses to refuse engagement with off-topic turns, we propose a more nuanced strategy involving the creation of _mitigations_. A mitigation is a bot response that redirects the conversation back to the relevant topic, thereby improving user engagement and experience.

The process of creating the mitigation turns involves presenting the LLM with the original on-topic conversation and the inserted distractor, prompting it to generate a response that guides the dialogue back to its intended focus.

To show how mitigations are different from distractors, we consider the following example. In this case, the mitigation acknowledges the user’s query about security questions but also steers the conversation back to the main task of resetting the banking password to facilitate the international transfer.

claim: Reframing the distractor detection problem as a classification task using chain-of-thought prompting improves model performance compared to conversational settings.
premises: The problem is re-framed into a classification task by prompting the model with conversation history and current user turn to determine if the turn causes the conversation to go off-topic.
The prompt includes: <detailed system instruction><conversation><distractor user turn>Is the last turn in the conversation respecting the scenario?Think step by step.
Using such a prompt significantly improves performance, indicating that employing the LLM as a classifier is more effective than using it in a conversational setting.

claim: General-purpose LLMs become increasingly vulnerable to distractors as the conversation progresses, with higher distractor engagement in later turns.
premises: An ablation study was conducted by inserting distractors at turn numbers 1, 3, 5, 7, and 9 in 20 randomly chosen on-topic conversations from the test set.
The model's response was observed to determine whether it engaged or deflected the distractor turn.
Findings reveal that as the conversation progresses, general-purpose LLMs become increasingly vulnerable to distractors.
This implies models are more likely to engage with distractors during later stages of a conversation.

claim: Proper STL configuration is required for optimal model performance with the DoMINO-Automotive-Aero NIM.
premises: The vehicle STL must be a single part; separate STLs for body, wheels, spoilers, etc., need to be combined into one before use with the NIM.
STL should be watertight.
STL units are in meters.
STL must be oriented such that axial flow direction is from -x to +x, vertical flow direction from -z to +z, and side flow direction from -y to +y.
The front wheel center of the car is kept at x=0, wheels should touch the ground plane at z=-0.318469 m, and the vehicle’s geometric center must lie on the xz plane.
The vehicle STL dimensions must be under 6.3 meters in length, 2.2 meters in height, and 2.5 meters in width for best model performance.
Model accuracy depends on STL resolution, with higher resolution corresponding to higher accuracy; a recommended resolution is >300k points.
PhysicsNeMo utilities can be used to combine STLs.

claim: Velocity inlet settings must align with the flow direction and magnitude range to achieve maximum accuracy.
premises: Velocity inlet is specified in the flow direction (along the x-axis).
Cross flow is not supported.
Velocity inlet magnitude should range from 20 m/s to 50 m/s for maximum accuracy.

claim: Stencil size influences prediction accuracy and computational cost.
premises: Stencil size is a parameter to control accuracy of the predictions by modifying the number of neighborhood points sampled around the point where the solution fields are evaluated.
Large stencil sizes correspond to improved accuracy, but higher computational costs.

claim: Surface and volume field evaluation accuracy depends on STL resolution and sampling point density.
premises: Volume fields are evaluated on the sampling points, which are uniformly sampled in the computational domain, and fidelity of the results increases as the number of points increases.
Surface fields are directly evaluated on the STL; higher resolution STL corresponds to higher accuracy of surface fields and corresponding drag and lift force.

Two receivers are defined: - The OTLP receiver is capable of receiving both metrics and trace data from the NIM. - A Prometheus receiver is used for scraping Triton’s own metrics.

Three exporters are defined: - An OTLP exporter to export to a downstream collector or backend. For example, Datadog . - A debug exporter which prints received data to the console. This is useful for testing and development purposes.

Traces are configured to be received exclusively by the OTLP receiver, and exported by the debug exporters. Metrics are configured to be received by both the OTLP and Prometheus receivers, and exported by the OTLP and debug exporters.

claim: LoRA enables serving a base model with fine-tuned adapters without retraining or rebuilding the full model.
premises: LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) lets you serve a base model plus one or more fine-tuned adapters without retraining or rebuilding the full model.

claim: NIM VLM supports two LoRA serving modes: static and dynamic.
premises: NIM VLM supports two LoRA serving modes: Static LoRA : Adapters are discovered from a directory at startup. Dynamic LoRA : Adapters can be loaded and unloaded while the server is running.

claim: Shared LoRA setup requires mounting an adapter directory, setting NIM_PEFT_SOURCE, and optionally passing vLLM LoRA flags to ensure adapter discovery and LoRA-capable deployment.
premises: Before you configure static LoRA or dynamic LoRA, complete the shared setup in this section. These settings tell NIM VLM where to find adapters and ensure that the deployment uses a LoRA-capable profile.

Complete the following setup for both static LoRA and dynamic LoRA: - Mount a directory (containing LoRA adapters) to the container. - Set NIM_PEFT_SOURCE to that directory. - Optionally, pass native vLLM LoRA flags.
NIM passes the following LoRA-related flags to vLLM: --enable-lora, --max-loras, --max-cpu-loras, --max-lora-rank

claim: Selecting a -feat_lora profile ensures the deployment uses LoRA-compatible runtime settings.
premises: When available for your model, select a -feat_lora profile so the deployment uses LoRA-compatible runtime settings.
Example: exportNIM_MODEL_PROFILE=vllm-fp16-tp1-pp1-feat_lora
If you are not sure which profiles are available in your deployment, query the model and profile metadata from your environment. Then choose the LoRA-capable profile.

claim: In static LoRA mode, adapters are loaded at startup and require a container restart to reflect changes after modification.
premises: After you complete the required LoRA setup, NIM VLM uses static LoRA when NIM_PEFT_REFRESH_INTERVAL is not set.
In static LoRA mode, the NIM container discovers adapters in NIM_PEFT_SOURCE during startup and loads valid adapters.
If you add, remove, or update adapters after startup, restart the NIM container to apply those changes.

claim: Dynamic LoRA enables adapter updates without restarting the deployment via directory monitoring or runtime API calls.
premises: Use dynamic LoRA when you need to add or remove adapters without restarting the deployment.
You can manage adapters through directory monitoring, runtime API calls, or both.
After you complete the shared LoRA setup, set NIM_PEFT_REFRESH_INTERVAL (polling interval in seconds) to enable dynamic LoRA through directory monitoring.
When NIM_PEFT_SOURCE and NIM_PEFT_REFRESH_INTERVAL are set, NIM starts the LoRA watcher and enables runtime LoRA updates for vLLM.
You can also use vLLM runtime endpoints for manual control: POST /v1/load_lora_adapter, POST /v1/unload_lora_adapter

claim: Multiple LoRA adapters can be served simultaneously, subject to GPU memory limits, and discovered via /v1/models.
premises: You can serve multiple adapters at the same time, subject to GPU memory limits.
Use /v1/models to discover available adapter IDs, then send the adapter ID in the request model field.

premises: The following example shows a minimal local workflow for serving a fine-tuned Llama model with LoRA. It includes shared setup, static and dynamic startup commands, model discovery, and an inference request that targets a loaded adapter.

premises: If NIM detects a previously loaded profile in the cache, it serves that profile from the cache.

premises: Before deploying in an air gap environment, you need to download the model profiles on a system with internet access.

premises: Set up environment variables on the connected system: CONTAINER_NAME, IMG_NAME, LOCAL_NIM_CACHE.
Launch the NIM container with docker run, mounting LOCAL_NIM_CACHE, setting NGC_API_KEY.
Inside the container, list available model profiles with list-model-profiles.
Download a profile matching the air-gapped profile with download-to-cache --profile <profile ID>.
Exit the container after the download completes.

premises: Copy the entire cache directory from the connected system to the air-gapped system.
Set environment variables on the air-gapped system: CONTAINER_NAME, IMG_NAME, AIR_GAP_NIM_CACHE.
Ensure the cache directory exists and copy the transferred cache into it.
Launch NIM with docker run, setting NIM_MODEL_PROFILE, mounting AIR_GAP_NIM_CACHE, and exposing port 8000.
